FOREWORD

Al Anthony wrote this for the First Edition in 1996. It still holds
true, although we’ve added a few of those missing pieces in the
years since. We still look to Al for guidance.

THE TASK OF WRITING this foreword is my penance for doubting Al Hayes
and John Blom. When they asked me to write it, I thought I was safe in
agreeing, because I knew a book like this could never happen.
     I was the one who questioned Al’s buying methods, and I was the one
who told him not to waste money on insignificant pieces. The last thing I
thought was that those insignificant pieces could add up to what you see in
these pages.
   But this book is hardly an insignificant effort. It organizes and explains
the techniques and development of Southwestern pottery from its
prehistoric beginnings, telling who those early people were, where they
migrated, what happened to them, who their descendants were, and what
they made. It also presents a thorough introduction to the history of the
Southwest during its settlement by the Spanish, and later, Mexicans and
Americans.
   That this book does what it does so well creates a dilemma for me. As a
dealer in fine Southwestern pottery, I have to wince at their buying rules
and at the implication that anyone can go out and buy what they bought at
the prices they paid. If you try it, I’d bet you won’t succeed (although I’d
have bet against Al and John, too). They made it for two reasons.
   The first reason is Carol Hayes. She has an antiques business in
California, and is an accomplished restorer who has worked for several
high-end California antiques dealers. Her skill allowed Al and John the
latitude to choose nearly hopeless pieces that, in restored condition, are
worth much more than what they paid for them.
   The second reason is that they avoided the truly rare and valuable. The
reader should be alert to the fact that pottery from the historic period was
far different from the pieces in this book, both physically and

philosophically. It was made primarily for the maker’s use, while virtually
every pot in these pages, including much of the prehistoric ware, was made
for trade. Perhaps the greatest shortcoming of John and Al’s collection is
that it doesn’t contain any of those extremely rare pieces made between
1600 and 1880.
   Having made this disclaimer, I’d like to voice my support for the main
points of the book. This art form is every bit as important and almost as
accessible as John and Al think it is. Those of us in the business—dealers,
collectors, curators—for the most part are involved because we love the art,
and we see truth in their belief that Southwestern pottery is America’s first
important art form. We don’t use the words “art form” lightly. It may have
been utilitarian ware, but it evolved into art quite early, and it remained art.
   This book mostly shows non-utilitarian pieces from the post-1880 era—
small, non-functional, sometimes European-influenced shapes and
modernized designs. It names several hundred potters and shows their
work. I wish the book could have included several hundred more, but this
art form is too vast for any one book to cover. Thousands upon thousands of
beautiful pieces of pottery by other potters are out there for the finding, in
an infinite variety of shapes, sizes and decorations.
   What caused these changes in shape, size, decoration and quality during
the last few hundred years? Alien influence and market pressures.
   Change first occurred among the tribes as a result of contact with other
Indian groups. The Plains Indians influenced the Pueblos and Navajos
through trade, as did the Indians of today’s Mexico. Any time two people of
differing experiences meet, each imparts something to the other, and the
Southwestern Indians were no exception.
   The Spanish conquerors also had a major impact on their ways of life.
Some Indians were enslaved, most were Christianized, and many were
killed—all in the name of Church and Crown. Subjugation took its toll on
their daily lives, on their food supplies, and on what we refer to today as
arts and crafts—although these were then their daily utility kitchen wares
and clothing.
   Spanish floral, foliage and lacy motifs crept into the designs on Pueblo
pottery. Vessel shapes slowly changed to accommodate the needs of the
new arrivals from across the ocean.
   The rate of change was magnified hundreds of times three centuries
later when the railroad arrived. After 1880, the Easterners came, drawn by

the pristine landscape and the indigenous peoples romanticized by the
railway’s poster artists. No visit, of course, was complete without an
authentic native souvenir.
   The Smithsonian and other institutions mounted expeditions in the late
1800s to document the lives of these peoples and to collect all their material
culture before these “poor Indians” vanished forever (an imminent prospect,
according to standard 1900 thinking). They gathered items by the thousands
—pottery, weapons, clothing, adornments and other cultural artifacts—and
shipped them back East to be stored in museums.
   At the same time that government officials and educators were stripping
away the daily necessities of Indian life, visitors were looking for curios to
scatter about their already overdecorated Victorian homes.
    In response, potters produced pots specifically for tourists. At first, they
made beautifully decorated replicas of the ones made for their own use.
Quickly, they learned they could speed up the process and sell more if they
took less time on each piece. The period of magnificent historic pottery
came to an abrupt end and the period of tourist wares began.
   For the next hundred-plus years, market fluctuations shaped
Southwestern pottery’s development. The modern section of this book tells
that story, and it shows what is available on the market today—except, of
course, for those fabulous pieces that exceed Al and John’s budget ceiling
by ten or even a hundred times.
   Al and John’s claim that the 1990s represent a Golden Age has a basis
in fact. Today’s pottery is more carefully made and designed than ever
before because pottery manufacture has always followed the market and
market standards right now are at an all-time high. The market rewards
potters who make pieces for discerning collectors and penalizes those who
make lesser pieces for casual tourists.
   What can we expect in the future? I anticipate continued improvement.
As collectors like Al and John become even more discriminating, the
standards will keep going up, because now people like John and Al have
become the people for whom the potters are creating their work. Even this
book should contribute to the improvement simply because it will add to the
collector’s knowledge base.
     If you decide to try collecting yourself, you can learn from Al and
John’s experiences, but let it be a learning experience that launches you into
building the collection of your dreams, not of mine or theirs. If my vision of

future improvement proves correct, it should turn out to be quite a
collection.

                                    ALEXANDER E. ANTHONY, JR.
                                                  Adobe Gallery, Santa Fe, New Mexico

PREFACE TO THE SECOND EDITION


WHEN THIS BOOK FIRST CAME OUT, it showed a combined collection that
pretty well explained the nearly two thousand year history of the art.
   That was almost twenty years ago. Since then, we’ve been distracted by
the dot-com boom, the foreclosure crisis, smart phones, social media and
perpetual war in the Middle East. More than a few Indians became casino
rich, and a noted Native American artist, Ben Nighthorse Campbell, served
twelve years in the U.S. Senate. New artists became pottery royalty with
prices to match while once-prominent ones became yesterday’s news.
   The turn-of-the-century Golden Age we anticipated in 1996 happened,
but not quite the way we expected. Major players like Acoma and Hopi
evolved much as expected without a lot of surprises, but tradition-breaking
Pueblos like Cochiti and Santa Clara stretched the envelope beyond what
we’d imagined. Pueblos that were under the radar like Pojoaque and San
Felipe produced pottery that grabbed everyone’s attention. Other pottery
centers like Maricopa and Ohkay Owinge slowed down.
  We learned that collecting Southwestern Indian pottery was a pretty
good idea. Pottery weathered fashion swings and economic slumps quite
well. Indian art in general held most of its value in the recession years
around 2010.
   Over those years, the Hayeses and the Bloms kept collecting, which
explains why we could do a revised, expanded and updated book. We kept
adding artists and finding pieces that filled holes in our pursuit of a one-of-
each array.
   Three more books about pottery followed, and we fattened our
collections for them. Predictably, both couples found excuses to dig deep
for choice items we never could have afforded under the skinflint buying
rules we adhered to throughout the first edition.
   Our collecting followed different paths.
   John and Brenda Blom slowed down their buying as they filled up their
available space and made room by giving pieces to their kids and to
museums. By 2012, their collection was so impressive that the Nevada
Museum of Art put on an exhibit of more than a hundred of their pieces

titled, not surprisingly, Southwest Pottery from Anasazi to Zuni, Selections
from the Brenda and John Blom Collection.
   Al and Carol Hayes, with a smaller home than the Bloms, chose a
different path. Since Carol already had an antiques business, they became
dealers, although they never embraced a proper dealer mentality. Al
explains that they’re dealers only in self-defense, to gain house room and to
finance more collecting. Despite selling a few hundred pieces, their house
remains filled. An English publisher asked Al and Carol to do a little book
on the history of the art, and Pottery of the Southwest came out in 2012. The
500 pots in its pages came almost entirely from their own collection,
augmented by a few borrowed pieces that included a handful from the John
Wing of the John & Al Museum.
   So, after all those years, the joint 1,500-pot collection that filled up the
first edition grew to more than 4,000, all photographed, measured and
cataloged. It seemed time to put many of those new pieces into this revised
effort. Here and there, you’ll find treasures like the Zia olla on the previous
page. That particular jar was way outside our original buying rules and is on
the later edge of qualifying as one of those “those extremely rare pieces
made between 1600 and 1880” that Al Anthony lamented weren’t included
in the original edition.
     If the occasional pricey piece dilutes the integrity of the book, we
apologize. In our defense, we can say that more than 90% of the pots in this
book, including some of the most spectacular ones, fell within those old
buying rules and that the others make the story more complete.
   Here’s Southwestern Pottery again, retold with twenty years of
hindsight.

1. GETTING STARTED





                          Jemez, Aaron Cajero, 5³/₈" diameter, 2013

THERE’S NOTHING ELSE IN THE WORLD quite like Southwestern American
Indian pottery,
   The same people have made it in the same place in the same way for
going on two thousand years. The pot you bought last week carries the
imprint of long-vanished ancestors—the Anasazi, Mogollon, Hohokam,
Salado and Sinagua—whose ruins add magic to the Arizona and New
Mexico landscape. Yet Southwestern pottery bears all this tradition with a
youthful, even frisky energy. This is its Golden Age, a dazzling half-century
burst of productivity and innovation. Now it’s almost a given: next year’s
work will be better than this year’s, and the year after, better still.
   Despite all the creativity, painstaking craft and historic value, this
pottery remains implausibly accessible, more so than any other important
art form. As in the first edition, the Bloms and the Hayeses actually bought

every pot pictured in this book. When we started, we felt that owning them
and holding them was the only way we’d understand them well enough to
write about them. We were two pairs of beginners with full-time other lives
who didn’t know any other collectors or dealers, who wouldn’t part with
big dollars for anything, and who lived a thousand miles away from Santa
Fe and the center of pottery activity.
   Now, more than twenty years and four books later, we’re no longer
beginners. Our collections have more than doubled and hold dozens of
pieces we never dreamed we could afford when we started. However, we
still believe that owning and holding a pot is the best way to understand it.
The pots in this book are proof of how accessible the art remains. Anyone
who cares enough can do what we did.
   Al started in 1989 with an eight-dollar souvenir, and Carol’s first piece
came the next year from the Santa Fe Flea Market. John didn’t succumb
until August 1992. Within days after John plunged in, Brenda and Carol
were talking about “the John & Al Museum.”
   Like any museum it had, and still has, its share of mistaken acquisitions
and might have a mislabeled specimen or two, but its amateur accumulation
represents all major tribal groups in the Southwest and tells a beginning-to-
the-moment history of a major art form.
     If, after you look through these new, updated pages, you’re intrigued
enough to consider owning a pot of your own, we have a few suggestions.
It’s no great feat to build a good collection of anything if you’re willing to
pour in endless hours and endless dollars, but most of us are short of both.
   The management of the John & Al Museum has always qualified as
short on both counts. If you can relate to that, you might also relate to some
of our alternate philosophies and techniques.

Before you spend a nickel. It’s smart, of course, never to buy anything
before you learn a little about what you’re buying. So look through this
book and take it with you, preferably to the nearest museum that has a
pottery collection. (We’ve listed a few good collections in the back of this
book.) Even better, if they’re not too far away, go to Santa Fe or Phoenix or
Tucson or Flagstaff or Albuquerque or Los Angeles and look at the
museums there. Not that you ever have to go there at all, but once the bug
bites, you’ll probably want to.

If this book nudges you into making a special trip, you’ll get more out
of it after you’ve looked at a few pots long enough to have them speak to
you, and probably after you’ve taken a few home.
  We learned early on that there’s no learning experience quite like living
with a pot, holding it and letting it teach you. Native American potters tell
how moved they are by the process, a combination of bonding with the land
and with the past. They see each pot as a living entity rather than as an
object. We won’t guarantee that you’ll become mystical over the first pot
you buy, but if you have any poet in your soul, you’ll find out they do start
to talk. Seeing a pot at a store usually isn’t enough. You touch it and you
look at it, but you don’t truly understand it until it comes home.
   Seeing a pot in a museum is even more remote. It’s behind glass, and if
it speaks, it doesn’t say, “Take me home.” It says, sometimes untruthfully,
“I’m in a museum and you can’t have anything like me.” The little card
next to it tells you dates, types and points of origin, but that’s not what you
really need to know. Those facts can’t substitute for holding a pot and
staring at it as long as you want.

Don’t be afraid to buy. Just watch what you spend. The first pots you buy
are more than souvenirs or ornaments, they’re tuition expenses. Don’t
worry if you don’t get a keeper in the first few. As long as you follow the
John & Al Museum Spending Guidelines, you won’t hurt yourself.
   Here are our revised, updated beginner’s rules.

     If it’s over $50, think hard about it.
     If it’s over $200, think real hard about it.
     If it’s over $500, don’t think about it at all.

We’ve had twenty years of mild inflation since the book came out. We
modified the original numbers, which were $40, $100 and $400, but we
kept the principle. Over and over, we’ve bought within those numbers and
brought home treasures worth ten times what we paid for them.
   This cheapskate attitude flies in the face of sound conventional wisdom.
Before we go any further, you should know what right-thinking people have
to say on the subject.

GENERALLY AGREED-UPON GOOD ADVICE

1) Never buy a cracked, broken or flawed pot. You’ll throw your money
   away.

    2) Buy the biggest, best and finest example you can afford. You’ll never
    regret it.





                       The dreadful pot: tuition expense illustrated.
                           Acoma, 4¾" diameter, circa 1955

JOHN & AL’S ALTERNATE WISDOM

    1) If you buy a beat-up or cracked pot, you’ll get it far cheaper than it’ll
    cost you to buy a good example. It’s a great way to have, hold and learn
   from those types you’d never be able to afford otherwise.

    2) Buy the smallest example you can find. It’s cheaper. Buy the big one
    later, after you learn more.

One good learning method is to buy a pot one place, then show it around to
people who really know what they’re talking about. But be careful about
what you show. Al made the mistake of showing a disreputable, truly
crummy old pot to a highly respected expert. That particular expert is the
nicest man in the world, but he couldn’t help himself. He looked at the pot

like it was something dead he’d found on the doorstep and pummeled Al
just for owning it. The flogging went like this: “Why do you waste your
money buying cracked, defective pots? You’ll never get your money back if
you try to get rid of them, and if you saved the money you spent on ten of
these, you’d be able to buy one really good pot that meant something.”
   He was right, of course, but the lecture didn’t turn Al into a right-
thinking collector. The little pot became a mascot for the collection,
prominently displayed alongside far nobler examples. A few years later,
after gaining a bit of celebity through the book, it sold for a lot more than it
cost.
   Another respected dealer said the same thing in another way. Al had
been admiring pots in the stratospheric price range, and before he’d let on
that he had no intention whatever of buying, the dealer volunteered this
information: “There’s a natural progression with collectors. They start
buying inexpensive things and then gradually upgrade. So whether their
year’s collecting budget is ten thousand dollars or thirty thousand dollars,
they learn to buy two or three things of real value rather than buying ten
things of minor worth.”
    Well, that’s the true dealer’s viewpoint, and there’s great wisdom in it, at
least from a dealer’s standpoint. We march to a different drum. Al never did
get his head around the idea of buying ten pots of minor worth for three
thousand dollars each.
   Yet that collector’s escalation we were warned about came about exactly
as threatened. In the years since we wrote the book, both the Bloms and the
Hayeses set better judgment aside, bought some of those pots of minor
worth and paid the $3,000. Sorry to report, but the escalation happens.

Don’t specialize early. Go for variety. Our museum happened because we
tried to buy one of each. The quest is impossible, but it’s hugely
educational. When you’ve owned and handled, say, a couple of hundred
different types, you start to know a little something about pottery. By then,
you might even know enough to think about specializing. This too is
contrarian advice.
   One could just as easily argue that the field is so vast, so intimidating,
that the beginner should narrow early. If you limit your collecting and
specialize, the reasoning goes, you’ll learn to recognize the fine examples

more quickly and know how to negotiate for them. That way, you waste less
on pots like the clunker that caused the expert to box Al about the ears.





                              Collector’s scalation: bigger, better, older
                         San Ildefonso, 10" diameter, circa 1910

   But you’ll have less fun. You’ll spend far more time searching, and
you’ll find an interesting pot far less often. Each of the more than a
thousand Southwestern pottery types has something to say, and until you’ve
seen, held and lived with a lot of them, you won’t really begin to appreciate
the place each holds in the flow of history.
   You can turn up examples of almost all of those types. Almost all.
Some, especially those made between 1500 and 1850, are super-rare. The
most eloquent argument in favor of our tolerance of small, flawed pots is, if
you limit yourself to fine large investor’s examples from the mid-eighteenth
century, you’ll have to shell out between five and fifty thousand dollars. Or
more. Each.

If you go the John & Al Museum acquisition route, you won’t find
many of the pricey types. But even if you never get an Ako Polychrome olla
(we didn’t) or a figured Mimbres bowl (we did, but years later), there are a
thousand other types to pursue. And even some of the difficult ones have
turned up in our museum, acquired within our original buying rules. Like
that Mimbres bowl.

When all else fails, trade. But not until... Yes, you can trade with other
collectors and with dealers who want to freshen their inventory. If you run
out of money, trading might solve the problem.
   But if you’re following our alternative wisdom, you won’t trade a single
pot until you’ve learned everything it has to teach you. If you’re serious
about all this, you’ll also photograph the pot and write down everything you
want to remember about it. However, be forewarned. That’s what we did,
and we got in so deep we ended up writing a book. We bought cheap, but
we couldn’t keep the dollars from adding up.
   Don’t be too quick to trade. Once a pot is gone, it’s almost certain you’ll
never get it back. Also, many of these guys are traders, Indians and non-
Indians alike. They’re not used to getting the short end of the stick. In fact,
Native Americans have a long and illustrious trading record. Four hundred
years ago, Aztec traders were known as people “who take more than they
give.”
   You should know that “trader” and “dealer” aren’t synonymous. Dealers
sell merchandise they buy from potters, traders, collectors and other dealers.
Traditional Indian traders set up posts on or near the reservations and learn
the languages. Some Indian artists still see the trader as their main contact
with the world of Anglo commerce.

Pick brains. And don’t be afraid to ask. Four years before we wrote the
first edition, we didn’t know anybody in the field. It didn’t take long before
we felt we knew everybody, just from wandering into Indian stores and
from going to the many Indian shows that come up in our area (and
undoubtedly in yours as well). Our success in making contacts has nothing
to do with our resourcefulness or our wonderfully attractive personalities. It
has everything to do with those traders and dealers.
    Sure, they prefer coming out ahead in a deal, and they’d rather make a
sale than talk. But they’re in the business because they too are infected with

whatever it is that infected us. If you’re willing to learn, they’ll teach you
and help you.
  We found almost immediately that some of the biggest names in the
field would patiently take time to correct our mistakes. When we’d visit the
priciest galleries on Santa Fe’s Canyon Road (New Mexico’s Rodeo Drive),
we’d find owners who’d answer our dumb questions, even when we made it
pretty clear we were nowhere near buying anything that day.
   Without them, there wouldn’t be a John & Al Museum. Don’t be
intimidated by their prestige or their prices. Find them, talk to them and ask.

Now that you’ve got this book, buy a few more. We wrote this to be the one
book we wished we had when we were starting, but if you’re anything like
us, one book won’t do. John & Al Museum policy dictates that if we see a
book on Southwestern pottery, the Bloms and/or the Hayeses buy it.
   Use the bibliography in the back as a possible shopping list. Books go
in and out of print (two of ours have already), and new ones come out all
the time, so that list may not help much at your neighborhood bookstore, if
you still have one. But look through book booths at Indian or Western
shows and check out shops in museums with pottery collections. And, of
course, try Amazon.
   Even if you find a lot of the books we’ve listed, good overviews are
scarce. Most books appear more thorough than they are because they’re
either specialized or were done as catalogs, limited by whatever was in a
particular exhibit or collection. This book has the same failing, but with one
difference. We tried to come as close as we could to getting at least one
example of everything that’s reasonably available in today’s market. Fault
us for completeness, but give us points for relevance.

Surf wisely. The Internet brings the art right into your home. It’s tempting
to use the Net as a prime learning resource, but be careful. If, say, you’d
like to see a broad range of Zuni pottery, the easiest way is Googling Zuni
pottery images. You’ll see hundreds of beautiful pots, but not all of them
will be from Zuni. Google’s selectivity keeps improving, but the last time
we did that, we also saw pieces from Hopi, Zia, Kewa, Acoma, Ohkay, San
Ildefonso, Santa Ana and Isleta, factory-made Navajo pieces and non-
Indian commercial pottery. Unless you click on the images and their visit

page buttons to see what those pots really are, you can get totally wrong
information.
   The Internet puts thousands of pots in the marketplace every day. Many
dealers have excellent retail sites, and general shopping sites like eBay
compound the opportunities. Even though we have one of those sites
ourselves, we mention this with our fingers crossed. Buying off the Web is
risky. If you buy a pot online, don’t be surprised if you find that it’s not
quite as advertised. Even the best sites, the ones that offer no-questions-
asked returns and reimbursement for shipping costs, can’t compensate you
for the annoyance of packing up and returning a disappointing piece. If the
site gives you the option of a comfortable phone and email discussion
before you buy, it helps a lot.

Get on mail lists. Much of the John & Al Museum came from vacations in
the Southwest, a week or two or three out of the year. As many more came
from sources in our own backyard.
   The Hayeses live in Northern California and the Bloms now live across
the border in Nevada—probably easier places to find this sort of thing than
New Hampshire or South Carolina, but not exactly a hotbed of pottery
activity. In Santa Fe, you can buy a pot on every corner. Where we live,
only a handful of stores within a hundred miles sell Southwestern pottery.
   However, there are a surprisingly large number of traders and dealers
who don’t have stores. They sell at Indian, Western and antique shows, and
there’s something going on most weekends. Google Indian Art Shows and
you’ll find enough to keep you occupied for hours surfing and for days at
events. When you go to a show, give them your snail mail and email
addresses. The more you do this, the more the show notices will pile up.
   Some of the shows are exceptionally good, drawing dealers from across
the nation. You’ll see and learn more walking through the booths at a good
show than you ever will visiting a store.
     If you go to the shows, you’ll find out about upcoming auctions. Some
are traveling events, some are always held in the same place, some are
online only, some accept mail and phone bids. Once you contact one, you’ll
get announcements.
     If auctions scare you a bit, just go to one and watch until your
confidence builds. Granted, it’s easy to get carried away and make a foolish
purchase, but there are bargains to be had. Sometimes everybody is asleep

when a treasure comes up. Keep your eyes open and your mouth shut, be
careful, and you’ll do just fine. We have, although we’ve paid some tuition
along the way.
   You have a tremendous array of opportunities to build a collection
without a lot of driving.

Try reading this book. It’s organized for quick reference. That’s because if
you’re anything like us, you bought this book to flip through the pages, look
at the pictures, and every so often, try to find out something about the pot
you just bought.
   So fine. But if you read it (bite-sized chunks, a culture or a Pueblo at a
time will do), perhaps you’ll understand a bit more about the scope and
wonder of it all. And why the John & Al Museum happened in the first
place, and why you might even consider building a museum of your own.

2. POTTERY COUNTRY





                      Mancos Corrugated, 7⅛" high, circa 1100

THE FUN BEGINS the minute you pick up a map. So does the mystery. For all
is not as it seems with Southwestern pottery.
     If you want to pin down where it comes from, the obvious answer is
“Arizona and New Mexico.” And if you’re curious about who made it, the
equally glib answer is “the Indians.” But, depending on what you define as

Southwestern pottery and the exact historic period, the boundaries creep
into northern Mexico and Nevada, Utah, Colorado, California and Texas,
and “the Indians” include peoples from the American plains, Mexico and
even Canada.
   Today, most pottery comes from a reclining L-shaped blob that starts
northeast of Flagstaff on the Hopi Reservation and runs eastward roughly
along I-40 through the Navajo reservation and the Pueblos—Zuni, Acoma,
Laguna, Zia and Jemez—then over to Isleta, then turns north along the Rio
Grande all the way up to Taos. A smaller amount comes from around
Phoenix and Tucson and west past the Colorado River, and some of the best
comes from Chihuahua in northern Mexico.
   This doesn’t mean that American pottery doesn’t, or hasn’t, come from
other areas. It came from all over Mexico, Central America and Peru. In the
United States, pottery has been excavated along the Mississippi from Ohio
to Louisiana, in Tennessee, in New England and almost everywhere else. In
this book, it came from the American Southwest, an area once described as
extending from Las Vegas, Nevada to Las Vegas, New Mexico and from
Durango, Colorado to Durango, Mexico. Here at the John & Al Museum,
we cut it off farther north, well above the city of Chihuahua, and extend it
west to the California coast.
   What makes the pottery we’ve focused on worth special attention isn’t
its quantity or even its quality so much as its continuity. The pottery from
other areas appeared and died out as the makers moved on. In Arizona and
New Mexico, it’s been made continuously for almost two thousand years,
and current archeology is finding traces of it that go back for another two
thousand years. Tracking the evolution of styles over the years is a
fascinating detective game.
     It’s not just a simple excursion into art history. It’s perhaps the most
important key to the total history of the people of the Southwest. In the
early 1900s, scholars drawn to the cliff dwellings and stone ruins realized
that well-preserved pottery and potsherds were excellent clues for
reconstructing history. The examples are plentiful, and they’ve received
intense academic attention and spawned intense academic argument ever
since.
  A lot of otherwise sane people have been seduced into devoting a
lifetime to the investigation. At a glance, everything seems quite clear, but
the more one learns, the more confusing it becomes—confusing enough to

throw the scientific community into a state of near-paralysis whenever it
tries to explain what actually happened to the peoples who made all that
pottery five hundred and a thousand years ago. One archeologist lamented,
“It would all make so much sense if we didn’t know so many facts.”
    Archeologists began digging up the Southwest in the last quarter of the
nineteenth century, and by 1890, poking around Arizona and New Mexico
was becoming a national craze. Those early scientists/adventurers wrote
important books about what they found, and each book influenced the
thinking of those who followed. Unfortunately, the pioneers didn’t use the
tools of modern archeology. Stratigraphic dating—estimating the age of
objects according to how deep they’re buried—didn’t become standard in
the Southwest until after 1915, even though Thomas Jefferson used it in the
eighteenth century when he excavated Indian mounds in Virginia.
Dendrochronology—dating by tree rings—wasn’t in place until 1929.
Carbon-14 dating came along after World War II, and after that, a dizzying
array of still more methods. Now we have thermoluminescence dating,
archeomagnetic dating, rehydroxylation dating and more.
   During all those years and right up to the present, books have
hypothesized about the comings, goings and doings of the prehistoric
peoples of the Southwest. Traces of human occupancy of the Southwest
date back to the Ice Age, but written history begins quite late in Arizona
and New Mexico. There, “prehistoric” means anything that happened
before Coronado arrived in 1540.
   Theorizing about prehistory revolves around architecture, burial
customs and artifacts. Because pottery is the most easily identifiable and
best preserved artifact, much of the theory, current and discredited, starts
with conclusions drawn from examining it. Those who play the detective
game have spent nearly a century pigeonholing all that pottery with ever-
increasing accuracy.
   By now, we have perhaps fifteen hundred types of Southwestern pottery,
and if you’re an interested beginner who hopes to make an accurate type
identification of a pot made much before the beginning of the twentieth
century, good luck. No book we’ve ever found manages to discuss more
than a few hundred of those types. And no book we’ve ever found includes
all the pots we stumbled on in the first few months of buying.
   But even the current plethora of types won’t cover everything. In the
introduction to Stewart Peckham’s From this Earth, J.J. Brody divides the

experts into “lumpers” and “splitters.” The lumpers group types together
while the splitters keep discovering more types. They’ve been arguing ever
since the early explorers started digging.

Classification. In the 1930s, the experts stopped arguing long enough to
give us a classification system. It uses a Period/Culture
Center/District/Ware/Type hierarchy much like the biologist’s
Phylum/Class/Order/Genus/Species. If you’re schooled in its elements, and
if you have access to a lot of obscure publications, you can do a reasonably
accurate identification of most prehistoric sherds.
   The classification system helps explain how Southwestern pottery
developed and begins to give context for understanding the Southwest as a
whole. We’ll try to walk you through it without bogging down in academic
details.
   The system doesn’t go out of its way to help the beginner. The names of
the major cultures who made the pots—the Anasazi, Mogollon and so forth
—either barely appear or don’t show up at all. To cloud the issue further,
people only use the type name when they refer to a pot, the way biologists
don’t bother with Phylum/Class/Order. We’re not Chordata Vertebrata
Mammalia Homo Sapiens, we’re just plain old Homo Sapiens.
   The type names—Reserve, Snaketown, McElmo, Sikyatki and the rest—
are places where explorers first recorded the pottery as a separate type.
Many of those names were used years before anyone worried about a
classification system, and, since pottery was widely traded, some may not
indicate the true source of the type.
   Under the current but ever-revising typology, this beat-up old pitcher (it
shows up again on page 41) is properly identified like this:

PERIOD: Pueblo II/III
CULTURE CENTER: Little Colorado
DISTRICT: White Mountain
WARE: Black-on-red
TYPE: Wingate Black-on-red

   This accumulation of information tells you it’s probably around nine
hundred years old, is red with black decoration, and the best expert guess
says it was made somewhere near where I-40 crosses the Arizona/New
Mexico border. (Fort Wingate was a military outpost near Gallup.) If you
know enough to read between the lines, you can figure out that it’s red-
slipped grayware and, according to current theory, was made by the
Mogollon. But when you see the pot, you’re not expected to acknowledge

all that. You’re expected to nod knowingly and say, “Hmm, yes, Wingate,
and not all that great an example, either.” Sounding smart takes homework.
The first step in sounding smart is learning a litde about the pigeonholes of
the classification system.

Periods. They identify the date the pot was probably made, which should be
clear enough. But even here, nothing is simple. The period names in the
classification system set up in the 1930s have nothing to do with pottery.
Instead, they refer to cultural changes based on migrations and
developments in architecture and agriculture, and only for one area of the
Southwest. By now, that period sequence shows its age, but books still cling
to it, and so do the little cards in the museums. This chronology was
supposed to explain everything, but it doesn’t.

    Basketmaker II       50 B.C. – A.D. 450
    Basketmaker III        A.D. 450 – 700
   Pueblo I            700 – 900
   Pueblo II           900 – 1100
   Pueblo III           1100 – 1300
   Pueblo IV           1300 – 1600
    Historic            1600 – 1880
   Modem             1880 – 1950
   Contemporary       1950 – present

Problem is, it was developed by people who focused on Anasazi/Cibola
prehistoric ware and modern Pueblo pottery from Hopi and New Mexico
and ignored the rest.
   The Basketmaker-to-Pueblo chronology assumed that all Southwest
cultures before Basketmaker II were hunter-gatherer nomads with no
agriculture and no ceramics. Now we know that there were cultures in
southern Arizona and Chihuahua that made pottery and irrigated fields as
early as 2000 B.C. There’s no tidy chronology for all of them—Anasazi,
Mogollon, Hohokam, Sinagua, Salado, Chihuahuans and more. Now those
others have separate chronologies, and we’ll try to put each in context as we
go through the book.

It’s true that pottery didn’t become widespread in our Southwest until
somewhere around 400 A.D. It’s not that they were unaware of it. Pottery
technology had been mature in South America and Mexico for centuries,
and there’s evidence of trade with neighbors to the south in prehistory.
Excavations have turned up Mexican metalwork, exotic bird feathers and
the like, but they didn’t trade for pottery until they needed it. As long as
they were wanderers, they needed more easily portable ware, and their
definition of portability was narrow. They had no horses, burros, cattle or
other beasts of burden and no wheeled vehicles. If a smallish dog could
drag it or carry it, okay, but otherwise it was carry it yourself or forget it.
Not surprisingly, well-made weavings and baskets preceded pottery by
hundreds of years.





                                Ancestry, Western Mexico, A.D. 100
                         Nayarit, Chinesco Orange-on-white, 7" diameter

    Pottery only became practical across the Southwest when the Indians
started irrigating and shifted their emphasis to agriculture. Once they were

tied to specific land parcels, portability dropped below permanence on the
priority list. After pottery began to appear widely around 200 A.D., its
popularity grew and its quality and variety improved steadily until around
1400. About then, several factors reduced the population and invading
tribes began contributing the occasional massacre.
   Not too many years later, European civilization arrived, catapulting the
natives out of stone age technology and adding horses, smallpox, STDs and
enforced religion to the mix. Before 1600, pottery was widely traded by
people free to move about at will. After 1600, the Spanish put the Pueblo
Indians to work building missions, shutting down their mobility and trade.
Pottery became unimportant to the native economy and was made in small
quantities for people who used it until it broke.
    Pottery made between 1600 and 1880—the historic period—is the rarest
of all. The Spanish discouraged it as unsuitably pagan and Anglos
dismissed it as aboriginal trivia. By the end of the period, manufactured tin,
glass and crockery took care of the utilitarian needs, and what little pottery
was left stayed within the Pueblo with the Indians.
   As Europeans laid claim to the land, the Indians lost their freedom to
relocate and rebuild. Now they were prisoners of the European concept of
real estate ownership, and they clustered together into fewer and fewer
settlements. Most of the twenty Arizona and New Mexico Pueblos of today
have been where they were for three centuries or more. Archeologists don’t
excavate them, any more than they dig up the towns where the authors live.
Put all these influences together, and they explain why there’s a dramatic
scarcity of historic pottery compared to the amount of prehistoric pottery
that’s floating around today.
    After 1880, the pattern reversed. Railroads came through, bringing
tourists along with a new crop of merchants/traders who told the Indians
what to make for the tourists. Big storage ollas wouldn’t fit in a traveler’s
suitcase, so potters turned to making smaller pieces. Soon pottery
resurfaced as a factor in the native economy. Also, curious Anglos began
gathering specimens for museums—something the Hispanics apparently
never did. It’s a sad fact that there isn’t a single known collection of
Southwestern pottery that was gathered before 1870, either here or
overseas.
   Today’s pottery is made by a people who stubbornly adhere to tradition,
but whose definition of tradition has been deeply affected by the flow of

history and by outside pressure, whether it came from Spaniards, Catholic
and Mormon missionaries, Santa Fe gallery owners, museum directors or
the nomadic Athapascans from Canada whom we now know as the Navajo
and Apache.

Culture centers and districts. The culture centers and districts in the pottery
classifications don’t much match our perceptions of the people who made
the pots. This is because they’re based on river drainages and topography
rather than the cultures themselves. Pick up any recent book about the
Southwest and by page three, you’ll see reference to Ancestral Puebloans,
the mysterious Anasazi who populated the Four Corners area, where the
borders of Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado meet. The Ancestral
Anasazi disappeared in the limbo of history, and instead of resurrecting
them, archeological types give us culture centers like “San Juan” and “Little
Colorado” and districts like “Chaco” and “Mesa Verde.” They’re mostly
Ancestral, but you wouldn’t know it without studying local history and
geography.
   Unless the books are specifically about prehistoric pottery types, they’ll
talk instead about the principal peoples: the Anasazi from the north; the
Mogollon who spread east, west and north along the southern Arizona-New
Mexico border and south into northern Chihuahua; the Hohokam from
around Phoenix and Tucson; the Chihuahuans and Sonorans from just
across the Mexican border; the Salado from central Arizona; and the
Sinagua, who left ruins up and down the Arizona map and whose history
and geography seem tangled with the Salado, Hohokam and Hopi.
   The research staff of the John & Al Museum is far more interested in
people than in river drainages, so this book won’t devote much space to
culture centers and districts.

Wares. The ware names don’t help as much as they might. They often don’t
tell you what pots are made of, which is a good clue to where they came
from. Redware simply means that the surface of the pot is red and has
nothing to do with the color of the clay under the surface.
   Then there are variations of materials and manufacture. As you read the
books, you’ll run into all kinds of confusing distinctions, none of which is
readily apparent when you look at a pot with anything less than a

magnifying glass and a well-tutored eye: coiled vs. paddle-and-anvil
construction, mineral vs. vegetal paint, sherd vs. coarse sand temper.
   Enough already.
    All this goes to explain why the research staff here at the John & Al has
chosen to lump shamelessly and excessively. When we show a picture of a
pot, we’ll try to identify it as correctly as we can. But when we talk about
wares and sources in a historical context, we’ll portray the trends and types
with a broad brush. Or more accurately, with an eighteen-inch-wide roller.
   As an answer to “where it comes from,” we’ll start with an ultra-
simplified definition of “it.” Forget the classification system. As far as
we’re concerned, there are only five kinds of Southwestern pottery.

   Brown
   White (including gray)
    Buff
   Red
   Yellow

We’ll put each of those colors where it belongs geographically, but you may
have a few questions. Like what about orange—is it yellow or red? When
does buff become yellow? Are we talking about the clay in the core or the
slip on the surface? What about blackware? And what about temper? And
paint?
   For the moment, our museum staff simply ignores such questions.

Types. These are the identifications you’re supposed to throw around as if
you knew what you were talking about.
   From our lumpers’ point of view, there are far more types than we’ll
ever need. The fine lines between types can become almost
indistinguishable. Some types are scarce, some are downright unobtainable,
and other, better-known types attract their share of misidentification.
   As a final indignity, there are little twists and turns in the classification
system to confound the unwary. Since we were speaking of “Wingate” a
few pages back, we might mention a similar type called St. Johns
Polychrome. St. Johns is a bit south and west of Gallup, just across the
Arizona state line, not far from Fort Wingate. It looks almost exactly like

Wingate Black-on-red, except that it has white decoration on the outside of
the vessel (there are a couple on page 41). Clear enough? Sure, except
there’s a St. Johns Black-on-red with no white and a Wingate Polychrome
with white on the outside. The splitters are ever-active, even while we
sleep.
    Sigh. These maps give an answer to the initial question of this chapter
—“Where does it come from?”—according to the John & Al Museum’s
Simplified System.
     If we connect those clay colors with the names of prehistoric cultures, it
works out something like this.

   Brown  =   Mogollon
    White   =   Anasazi
    Buff    =   Hohokam/Casas Grandes
   Red    =   Salado/Sinagua
    Yellow  =   Hopi

Sure, there’s some overlap, but it’s a place to start. It produces a map that
looks like this.

Pottery country, circa 1000

The trading areas of each of these peoples exploded way beyond their areas
of settlement, which explains why people dig up brown pots north of
Flagstaff and gray pots from California to Oklahoma.
   Since then, we’ve had a thousand years of migration, famine, disease
and real estate crunch. Tribal populations have grown, but the settlement
areas have shrunk. They still make a little pottery in Hohokam country and
even less across the Colorado in California, but most of the made-in-U.S.A.
Southwestern Indian pottery we value today comes from the area where the
Mogollon and the Anasazi overlapped, from the Hopi reservation in
Arizona, across to Albuquerque and up to Taos in New Mexico.
   Meanwhile down south, the Chihuahuans started making beautiful
traditional pottery in the remote town of Mata Ortiz, near the Pueblo ruins
of the ancient Casas Grandes culture.
   Those clay colors square up with modern pottery like this:

   Brown  =   Navajo and a bit along the Rio Grande

white   =   Acoma/Zuni
    Buff   =   Northern and middle Rio Grande, southern Arizona and
               Mata Ortiz
   Red    =   Middle Rio Grande
    Yellow  =   Hopi





                                      Pottery country, now

Less area, but more pottery than ever. Nobody makes much pottery in
Mogollon and Salado country these days, but nobody did much along the
Rio Grande back then, and that’s where much of it comes from now.
Redware has moved, brownware left for a while but is on its way back, and
buff remains in southern Arizona and Chihuahua, where it always was.
    That’s pottery country according to our lumped view.
