3. WHAT TO LOOK FOR IN A POT





                        Hopi, Lena Charlie, 11½" diameter, circa 1940

FIRST, YOU MIGHT WANT an answer to the question, what’s a good pot? The
answers vary, depending on who’s doing the answering.
   Here at the John & Al Museum, Al is a sucker for good painting and
that elusive ingredient called “character.” Others care more about the
potter’s craft. John looks for what he sees as “degree of success,” upgrading
or downgrading his calls based on what he thinks the state of the art was
when and where the pot was made.
   Al will happily bring home another rain god—junk from the day it was
made, junk forever into the future—just because it’s a nearly vanished piece

of pottery history. John will buy yet another owl figurine from a potter he
likes, even though he already has several.
   We’ll miss a lot of the fun if we ever become elitist, or even particularly
disciplined. Sure, we’re capable of turning up our noses at mass-produced
refrigerator magnets and wind chimes, but we’re delighted to find their
now-scarce counterparts from earlier times—uncleanable Hopi ashtrays
from the 1930s or Isleta cream pitchers from the 1920s. Someday we may
regret not having picked up a wind chime while we could still get one.
(Parenthetical aside: twenty years after we wrote that, we’re still waiting for
that moment.)
   Everybody agrees that a perfectly made, ambitious pot is nice. But
given an attractive, less-than perfect pot, would you prefer a well-painted
one that’s a touch lopsided or a beautifully made one with slightly sloppy
decoration? And what if it actually was perfect except for a few scratches?
Just because John leans one way and Al leans the other doesn’t mean either
of us is right. When you start your own museum, you can set your own
priorities.
   Meanwhile, here’s some information that helped us set ours.

Shapes. Some books show a lot of little drawings of shapes to teach you
who does what. Frankly, they confuse us. We learned all that much better by
looking at pots.
   However, it might help to learn a little vocabulary. If somebody offers
you an olla (they’ll say “oya”—it’s Spanish for big jar), it’s nice to know
what one is. Here’s a list of shapes. Some are so obvious they’re not even
listed.

Baskets
           BACK: Santa Clara, Lorencita Tafoya, circa 1965; Zuni, circa 1970.
              FRONT: Mojave, Annie Fields, circa 1960; Isleta, circa 1910.
                           The Zuni basket is 6⅝" in diameter.

“Ladle” means a ladle, “dish” means a dish. But other shapes can be tricky.
➤ BASKET: Confusing only because “Indian basket” means a woven basket,
not a piece of pottery. Baskets are bowls with handles across the top. Some
books avoid the word by talking about bowls with strap handles, a
definition that seems inadequate for some of these examples, especially
when the handles get twisted around as with two of the examples in the
picture.
➤ BEAN POT: A deep bowl, somewhere between the size of a grapefruit and
a volleyball, almost always Picuris, Taos or Jicarilla Apache, made from
micaceous clay, often with a lid, fired at a high temperature and oven-safe.
Purists insist that beans cooked any other way simply don’t taste right.
➤ BOWL: A low vessel with a big opening. The lines between dish, bowl,
jar and vase are blurry.

➤ CEREMONIAL JAR, BOWL OR VESSEL: Squared or stepped bowls from the
nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, or pieces with figures or symbols
that don’t normally appear on tourist or utility pottery from a particular
Pueblo. “Ceremonial” can also mean something strange that the dealer
thinks should have some added mystery. “If we don’t know what it is, it’s
ceremonial” is an archeologist’s cliché. Genuine ceremonial artifacts
shouldn’t be sold. Odds are that any “ceremonial” piece that’s for sale was
never used in a ceremony.





                                      Fetish bowl—genuine
                               Zuni, Edna Leki, 3¼" diameter, 1994

➤ CHILE BOWL: A small bowl used for individual servings. See “Dough
bowl.” Note the proper Southwestern spelling. “Chili” is something you
buy in a can or get at a fast-food restaurant. Chiles are the peppers that
energize Southwestern food. Chile bowls and dough bowls from the same
period and Pueblo are often identical except for size.
➤ CURIO: Or souvenir, or tourist pot. Ashtrays, cowboy hats, hornos and the
like.
➤ DOUGH BOWL: A large diameter shallow bowl, 14" or bigger, big enough
to allow you to knead dough with both hands. They were more common in

historic times, but they’re still being made.
➤ EFFIGY: Any vessel in the shape of a human, animal or even a plant,
either literal or implied. Some prehistoric pieces that anthropologists
identify as effigy pots require a long leap of the imagination. “Effigy” can
also refer to applied decoration. See “Figurine.”
➤ FETISH BOWL OR FETISH JAR: Generally, any pot with appliquéd animal
figures. Specifically, a Zuni pot made to hold carved stone fetishes, usually
covered with crushed turquoise. It can have a hole in the sidewall for
feeding cornmeal to the fetishes, and it contains a bit more magic than the
average Zuni feels comfortable selling to outsiders. The one you bought at
the gift shop was probably made by a Navajo, but one Zuni fetish carver,
Edna Leki, made them for sale in recent years.
➤ FIGURINE: Another point on the pots-shaped-like-living-things
continuum. We shake it out like this: a figurine is a little clay statue. An
effigy is a jar or a vase in the shape of a creature, human or otherwise. A
fetish pot is a bowl, jar or vase with the creatures attached.





                                    Horno
                        Santa Clara, Minnie Vigil, 3½" long, circa 1960

➤ HORNO: The traditional Pueblo earthen bread oven, miniaturized into an
ashtray or an incense burner. Pueblos made a lot of them for tourists in the
incense-happy, Age-of-Aquarius sixties.
➤ JAR: A bowl with a constricted neck or opening, tall or squatty.
➤ KIVA JAR OR BOWL: A pot with a stepped shape to the opening, like the
Zuni basket on the previous page. Kivas are the underground ceremonial
chambers that have been used at Pueblos since prehistory. These are “kiva
pots” because the steps on the rim suggest the steps down into the kiva.
➤ MATCH HOLDER: A little ashtray companion designed to hold wooden
matches. A highly practical accessory in a different age.
➤ MELON JAR: A jar with an impressed design of vertical fluting that
reminds you of a casaba melon or an acorn squash. Potters like Helen
Shupla and Angela Baca built their reputations with them. The modern
melon jar started at Santa Clara, probably suggested by imported Mexican
or Peruvian pieces, although they existed in the prehistoric Southwest as
well. They also make them at Jemez, Ohkay Owinge and Mata Ortiz.
➤ MINIATURE: Broadly, any piece too small to be used for anything,
including bowls, jars, figurines and curios under three inches in their largest
dimensions. True miniatures are scaled down versions of larger pieces.
➤ MONO: A nineteenth-century term, Spanish for “monkey,” originally
intended as a put-down for fanciful Cochiti and Tesuque figurines. Now,
those monos are back big-time, especially at Cochiti.
➤ MUTTON BOWL: A serving bowl with a flared rim, peculiar to Hopi
pottery. There’s one on page 73.
➤ PLAQUE: See “Tile.”

Rain God, Tesuque
                             6½" high, circa 1920

➤ RAIN GOD: An endearingly ugly figurine from Tesuque, mass-produced
from the 1890s into the 1930s. In the early days, a candy company gave
them away as a premium.
➤ SEED JAR: A jar with a small opening or mouth meant for shaking out
seeds. The shape occurs in prehistoric and modern pottery. Some recent
ones have holes so tiny you’d have a hard time putting the seeds in one at a
time.
➤ SERVICE VESSEL: In prehistoric pottery, a blanket designation describing
anything that isn’t a utility vessel. If it’s painted, decorated or in any way
fancy, so goes the logic, it must have been made to serve something to
somebody. See “Ceremonial” and “Utility” vessel.

➤ SINGING MOTHER: See “Storyteller.” Helen Cordero intended her original
storyteller dolls to represent her grandfather, so all storytellers are supposed
to be male. A female storyteller is a singing mother, even though you’ll
seldom hear a collector or a dealer use the term. Singing mother monos date
back to the late 1800s at Cochiti.
➤ STEW BOWL: Halfway between a dough bowl and a chile bowl.
➤ STORAGE JAR: A big olla, up to 24" high and sometimes even bigger, that
usually held grains, sometimes water. Modern ollas are usually only 10" to
12". The big old ones were made for use rather than show and they’re now
rare. Today, beautiful historic storage jars go for astronomical prices at
high-end auctions.
➤ STORYTELLER: A surprisingly long-running fad that really only slowed
down around 2000. In the 1960s, Helen Cordero of Cochiti Pueblo started
making figurines of a seated figure with tiny people sitting all over it,
ostensibly listening to a story. These caught on so spectacularly that thirty
years later, most of the pottery output from Cochiti and a good portion from
Jemez was devoted to making storytellers, singing mothers and
anthropomorphic versions with turtles, bears and the like. A few older
potters still make them.

Storyteller, Cochiti
                           Marie Suina, 5⅜" high, circa 1985

➤ TILE: A round, square or rectangular flat trivet encouraged around 1900
at Hopi by trader Thomas Keam.

Tulip vase, Hopi
                                    11" high, circa 1935

➤ TULIP OR CYLINDER VASE: A Hopi pottery shape, borrowed from
mainstream art pottery. It occasionally pops up at other Pueblos.
➤ UTILITY VESSEL: Undecorated bowls, jars and ollas whose owners may
have used them to put something in, cook something in or eat something
from. See “Service vessel.”
➤ VASE: A bowl or jar that’s taller than it is wide, or a long-necked jar, like
a bud vase. The shape is uncommon in prehistory.
➤ WEDDING VASE: A two-necked canteen that allows bride and groom to
share a ceremonial drink. Santa Clara claims it, most Pueblos make it, and
tourists buy it. They show up in weddings now, but the ceremony behind
them was probably fabricated in Santa Fe about 1900 by trader John
Candelario.

A Candelario-era Wedding Vase
                              Santa Clara, 12" high, circa 1900

The potter’s craft. Southwestern Indian pottery resists change. Traditional
potters dig their own clay, grind and mix it by hand, shape their pieces
without a wheel, polish them with a stone or gourd, dry them outdoors and
color them with pigments boiled down from plants or dug from the earth,
paint them with brushes made from the chewed ends of yucca fibers, and
fire them in pits they build themselves, just as their distant ancestors did
more than a thousand years ago.
   This doesn’t mean that progress never intrudes. Today, some potters fire
in an electric kiln. Many use store-bought paintbrushes. A few use store-
bought paints and some, store-bought clay. At the souvenir level, potters
decorate pre-cast pots called greenware.
   But today’s Golden Age has little to do with modern production
methods. The really good potters concentrate on doing it the old way, only
better. Each year, pots get thinner, carving gets more precise, painting gets
more accurate.
   One of the best-known contemporary potters, Nathan Youngblood of
Santa Clara, said this in Fourteen Families in Pueblo Pottery:

I get a lot of feedback from people who say, “Why do you fire that way? Why don’t you fire in a
  kiln? Why do you prepare your clay? Why don’t you go to the store and buy it?” I guess the
  reason I don’t want to go down that road is because when I lived with my grandparents, the one
  thing they constantly tried to instill in me was that the way we do our pottery, the traditional
  way, was the way that was handed to us by the spirits that came before us. In order to show the
  proper respect for the clay and to the clay, we need to keep doing it the old way.

The old way is laborious, but Pueblo women have defended it well. At
different times in different locations, the craft has been entirely the property
of women, traditionally passed down from mother to daughter. In some
Southwestern indigenous cultures, families are matrilineal (when you’re
born, you automatically belong to your mother’s clan, not your father’s),
which may have something to do with the custom, or may not.
   But times are changing. Early observers wrote of male potters who
disguised their gender, dressed as women, and performed women’s duties.
The “man-woman” potter suffered no social stigma and was seen as an
important figure in Pueblo society.
    In the early twentieth century, celebrated potters including Nampeyo of
Hopi and Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso, two of the most celebrated,
began leaving painting to their husbands. The ratio of men to women in the
craft is increasing. Pueblo Indians are as open to Equal-
Opportunity=male/female thinking as any of us.
   Here’s what you go through to make a Southwestern pot.

➤ THE CLAY: First, you mine your clay yourself and lug it home, just as it’s
been done for the last thousand years. Sure, you can buy some from the
Clay Man on his swing through the Pueblo, but it’s not the same.
   Mining clay is no small task. Today, you might throw a sack in the back
of the pickup, but until recently, you’d walk home with it, most likely for
several miles, carrying enough to make the trip worthwhile. And you’d be
hauling a sack of dense, sometimes damp dirt.
   With few exceptions, potters don’t go far afield looking for the clay they
like best. They learn to make pots out of the clay that’s nearby, and they
treasure it. They’ve been known to keep the location of the family clay
mine a secret for generations.
    That’s why clay is Southwestern pottery’s first clue to identification.
Acoma potters use white clay. Ohkay Owinge potters use red clay. Taos
potters use golden-buff clay with shiny mica flecks. Zia clay has an
unfortunate time-bomb characteristic caused by tiny chunks of limestone

that can pop out months after the pot is fired, creating little dings that
blemish both the pot and the potter’s reputation.
  On our first trip to Santa Fe, we watched an educational video at the
Wheelwright Museum and came away convinced that potters were fanatic,
even irrational about clay. One broke down and cried as she recounted how
a soulless neighbor had actually THROWN SOME OUT. Now we understand the
fanaticism. Good clay is rare, hard won and greatly valued.
➤ TEMPER: Most clays won’t fire up to produce a sturdy pot unless you mix
in a tempering substance. Instead, they’ll shrink and crack. It’s like the
difference between cement and concrete. Like clay, cement doesn’t have
much strength, but temper it with sand and rocks, and you have concrete.
   Southwestern potters figured this out more than fifteen hundred years
ago. Almost immediately, they learned the first principle of brickmaking
and mixed straw with the mud. Other tempers came along quickly, and
today, they vary from Pueblo to Pueblo. At Ohkay and Santa Clara, they use
a coarse sand of ground-up tufa, the volcanic stone the Navajo use to make
casts for their silver work. At Acoma, they grind up potsherds, even
prehistoric ones salvaged from the dumps below the mesa. Hopi potters are
luckier with their clay, and many get by with no temper at all. Because of
their exploding clay, Zia potters use ground-up basalt, sometimes almost as
much temper as clay.
   The combination of clay and temper tells scientists and archeologists
most of what they need to know about the source of any given pot. If a pot
is chip-free, well slipped and polished, you can’t tell much about temper. If
you care more about science than you do about art, you won’t much like
nice, well-polished pots. A freshly broken fragment is a treasure trove of
information. An intact, unblemished pot is a crime against science.
➤ PREPARATION: The preparation is like mixing concrete, only far more
delicate. The potter grinds and sifts the lumps out of the clay and grinds the
temper down to the smallest possible particles. Some older pottery shows
big, obvious chunks of temper, but nobody gets away with that now. The
marketplace ignores potters who aren’t skilled enough to deliver a perfect
surface.
    After the grinding, you have to arrive at the right mix of clay, water and
temper and knead it into a smooth, workable mass. It takes hours and hours,
and if you mess up the proportions, you’ve blown it. Too little temper, and

your pot breaks in the firing or cracks in the drying. Too much, your pot
breaks in the handling. Too much water and you can’t work the clay. Too
little and you can’t get an even mix.





                                 Coiled pottery, undisguised
    Center of the base of a Tularosa Banded Corrugated bowl circa 1050, shown about half size
➤ COILED POTTERY: Most of us remember making a snake out of clay as one
of our first artistic expressions. For two thousand years, Pueblo potters have
done just that. They roll out snakes and coil them slowly and laboriously
from the base up until they form the shape of the finished pot. Potters
usually start their bases in a mold called a “puki,” which is often the bottom
of a broken jar. In prehistory, some potters started with skinny coils and
wound them all the way up the pot, never smoothing them out. A pot like
the one on page 6 makes you understand coiled construction.
   The only mystery is how potters manage perfect symmetry without a
wheel. It would be foolish to maintain that no Southwestern Indian pottery
has ever been made on a wheel, but you’ll be hard-pressed to find an
example. Pueblo potters have become incredibly adept at building those
long clay snakes into round vessels. Doubters have measured their work
and found jars as big as a basketball to be within hundredths of an inch of
true round.

These days, potters usually coil snakes into hoops that are somewhat
greater in diameter than the final thickness of the pot and pile them up on
the puki base, shaping and smoothing them with the tool of their preference:
an old potsherd, a shell, a fragment of gourd, a rock or a piece of wood.
    There’s no magic to the perfect roundness of a good pot. It’s just the
product of hands and eyes conditioned by countless hours of practice and
enough patience to meet exceptional standards.
   These days the standards truly are exceptional, raised higher and higher
by a natural competitiveness among potters and the ever-increasing stakes
in the market. The better the pot, the better the potter’s reputation, and the
better the reputation, the higher the price and the quicker the sale. Quality
pays.





                        Mata Ortiz: state-of-the-art pinch pot
                          Guadelupe Gallegos, 5¼" high, 1997

➤ PINCH POTS: As a general rule, if the base of the pot is smaller than the
palm of your hand, the potter started with a ball of clay and hand-sculpted
the pot. If the pot is larger, it was probably made by coil-and-build, yet
potters have made pinch pots ten inches or more high.
    Purists might dismiss jars and bowls that depart from the traditional
multiple-coil technique as lesser creatures. But before you turn up your
nose, look at one of the better Mata Ortiz pinch pots. They roll out the base,
then make one big doughnut for the side walls and shape it by hand.
Acoma’s finest potters never made pottery any thinner or more beautifully
finished.
➤ PADDLE-AND-ANVIL: Prehistoric Hohokam and Mogollon potters used a
different method, and it persists in O’odham, Maricopa and Southern
California pottery. Instead of a coil, the potter rolls out a flat pie crust of
clay and shapes it upward, pinching and smoothing it together.
   The potter holds an anvil—a suitably curved piece of wood, rock or
gourd—inside the jar or bowl and worries the outside with the paddle—a
flat rock or piece of wood—until the pot assumes the proper shape. If the
potter hasn’t spent much time smoothing the inside of a jar, you can
recognize the method by the anvil dents on the interior. There’s a wonderful
video called Native Clays by California potter Tony Soares that shows him
making a giant Cahuilla water jar with paddle and anvil. We can write about
it forever, but until you see the video, you’ll probably have questions.
➤ SMOOTHING, SLIPPING AND POLISHING: Once pots are shaped and dried,
potters smooth them with a carved gourd rind, sandpaper or whatever other
tool they prefer. This is no quick process. Smoothing and polishing to
achieve a properly deep, rich sheen can take hours. The quality of the polish
influences the value of the pot, and with some pots, it provides most of the
value.
    After smoothing, the potter gives the pot its final background color by
putting on the slip, a highly diluted coat of clay. The clays used in slips are
usually rarer and choicer than the clay the pot was made from, and they’ve
gathered them from all over, selected for their fineness and color. A pot
can’t simply be painted an attractive color because paint can’t be polished
like clay. Slip, on the other hand is clay, and the final coat gets the final
polish.

The potter applies the thin coats of slip with a brush, a cloth or a piece
of leather. The traditional glossy surface of Santa Clara pottery comes from
polishing with a river stone. The stone has to be a good one with an
unblemished surface and correct shape. A really good one gets passed down
from generation to generation.
➤ IMPRESSION, INCISING, CARVING AND SGRAFFITO: Long before any Mogollon
or Anasazi painted the surface of a pot, they poked sticks and reeds into
them, creating impressed patterns that occasionally approached fine art and
which some of today’s potters still emulate.
   Impression is soft-edged tool sculpture. Classic latter-day example: the
Santa Clara Pueblo hallmark, a bear-paw imprint that’s little more than a
three-eyed happy face.





                                 Sgraffito and carving on the same pot
                     Santa Clara, Madeline Naranjo II, 3¾" diameter, 1993

    Incising takes impression one step further. Before firing the pot, the
potter cuts through the surface to create a change of color or texture. San
Ildefonso, Santa Clara, Ohkay Owinge, Acoma, Jemez and the Navajo all
do fine incised work. In the 1990s, the Utes cranked out multi-colored

tourist pottery with incision in parallel rows, and Navajo and Acoma potters
joined in with a flood of imitations. There’s a factory-made Navajo version
at right-center on page 123.





                                   The Bear Paw
                       Santa Clara, Angela Baca, 4¾" high, circa 1990

   Carving comes closer to true sculpture. The highest form of the art these
days takes place at San Ildefonso and Jemez and especially at Santa Clara,
with a few potters at other Pueblos doing magnificent work. Potters seem to
be competing on two levels, trying to see how deep they can carve the bas-
relief while at the same time trying for the thinnest possible pot. The better
you are, the higher the price of your pots.
    Sgraffito, unlike carving and incising, takes place after firing. It's fine
ornamentation etched through the slip to reveal the color of the base clay.
The Santa Clara pot at left shows the difference between carving before
firing and carving after. The carved part fired black like the surface, while
the sgraffito reveals the clay.
➤ SCULPTURE AND APPLIQUE: Sculpted pottery has been around from the
beginning. Most of it, like the pre-Columbian sculpture from Mexico and
South America you see in books, is hand-molded, helped along here and

there with a tool. This little beaver, a traditional Santa Clara animalito, is
just a blob of clay, deftly pinched into a simple shape—the pottery
counterpart of a dashed-off sketch by a skilled painter, a pinch pot at its
simplest level.





                        A pinch here, a pinch there
                              Santa Clara, 5⅜" long, circa 1940

   True sculpture most commonly occurs in figurines like storytellers from
Cochiti, Jemez and Acoma and in appliquéd pieces, most likely from Hopi,
Zuni and Acoma, but no Pueblo has a patent on any sculptural style.
➤ PAINTING: If you’ve ever tried to do any decorative painting yourself,
you’ll be impressed watching a good Pueblo potter paint a design.
Traditionally, potters used a brush made from yucca leaves, chewed until
they separate into strands, usually between one and twelve. These days,
most use commercial paintbrushes. One potter told us he tried to chew
yucca, but one taste and the experiment was over. Another told us she
bypassed the problem by using her baby’s hair.

Poster paint as low-end curio, acrylic as art
                         LEFT: Jemez,6½" high, circa 1970
                      RIGHT: Zia, Ralph Aragon, 6" high, 1992

    Potters might draw the design in pencil, but if they’re really good,
they’ll probably just start painting somewhere and keep going around the
pot until, miraculously, it all comes out right. If you want to appreciate the
extent of the miracle, look at this lightning pattern from an Acoma jar on
page 61 and try to draw it from memory. Then think about making it come
out even and level, row after row, all around the pot, each circuit scaled to
match the pot’s circumference. Some artists with great painting skills team
with a talented potter, and some of the finest examples in this book came
from one of those collaborations, including that lightning-bolt pot.

Kids, don’t try this at home
                        Acoma, J. Estevan and M. Patricio, 1992

    Paints come from many sources. The usual black comes from boiled-
down Rocky Mountain bee plant (“wild spinach”) but some say that almost
any plant, reduced enough, will work. Reds and yellows are usually
mineral, from ground-up ocher or other clay. But colors can also come from
the art supply store.
    In the 1930s, Tesuque and Jemez potters made garish pieces with poster
paints. In the 1960s, Zia and Jemez potters started using acrylics. Like
poster paint, acrylics are applied after firing, but are more durable. Each
Pueblo has its traditional decorations, and you can pretty well tell where a
pot came from by its painting. The Jemez potter who made the piece at the
right called it a “teaching pot.” It shows coil construction, appliqué and
matte and polished painting with elements that show up at Hopi, Santa
Clara, Zia, San Ildefonso, Acoma and Zuni.

The Teaching Pot
                          Jemez, J. Fitzgerald Toya, 10¾" high, 1994

➤ HORSEHAIR: In the 1990s, someone, either Navajo or from Acoma, found
you could decorate a pot by putting horsehair in the clay and firing it. It
makes distinctive patterns, and the trick caught on quickly in the tourist
shops. Purists dismiss horsehair pottery as irrelevant, and much of it is
greenware, but as potters played around with the medium, they created
some pieces with impressive artistry, like the one from Acoma on page 63.
A Navajo potter put on his best deadpan expression and told us the hard
part was getting the horse to stand still during the firing.





                                        Horsehair

Acoma, Gary Louis, 5" diameter, 1998

➤ FIRING: The technique varies from Pueblo to Pueblo. Traditionally, the
potter digs a shallow pit and covers the bottom with fuel. Potters from the
Anasazi to the present have used everything from coal to corncobs. Today,
it’s usually wood or sheep dung, but there are proponents of the cow and
horse variety as well.
   When the fuel is smoldering, the potter sets a well-dried vessel on a
rack above the coals, surrounds it with potsherds or scraps of sheet metal
and covers it. If the potter isn’t careful, the coals scorch the slip, creating
dark fire clouds on the surface. If the potter hasn’t mixed the clay and
temper right, or if the heat is uneven, the pot can crack or the paint can
burn. And if it starts to rain or the wind comes up, the potter packs it in or
risks ruining the pots.
    All this explains the appeal of the electric kiln. Very few Acoma,
Laguna or Zuni potters or Hopi whiteware potters have fired in the
traditional way since the 1960s, and even the holdouts understand the lure
of the controlled, weatherproof kiln. But the old ways refuse to die out, and
there’s evidence the trend is reversing. A pot on page 101 by one of
Laguna’s leading potters has the shaded coloring that we think of as
something we only find on traditionally fired Hopi pieces.





                               Fire clouds: why Acoma uses the kiln
                           Acoma, 11½" diameter, circa 1960

The last to convert to kiln firing will be the Pueblos who produce
blackware. It requires a “reducing” fire, one with a smothering enclosure
over the pit. Redware from Santa Clara, San Ildefonso and Ohkay Owinge
starts with the same clay and slip as the blackware, but it’s fired in an open,
oxidizing fire. The smothered fire reacts with the hematite in the clay to
create a black surface which can be refired back to red.





                         Same clay and slip, different firing
                 LEFT: Santa Clara, Carol Velarde, 2¾" diameter, 1993
                  RIGHT: Santa Clara, Marie Suino, 3" diameter, 1992

   The firing techniques of blackware potters are worth long chapters in
specialized books. If you’d like to know more, Stephen Trimble’s Talking
with the Clay reports long conversations with great potters, and it’s
excellent reading.

Tourist Kitsch
                               Navajo, Warren, 6½" high, 1996

Quality. As with any art form, you can find Southwestern pottery at all
levels of quality. At the bottom, it’s cheap and mass-produced, painted in
strange colors by people who may be authentic Native Americans but
clearly aren’t authentic potters. Spend an hour looking at the real thing in a
good gallery and you can spot the lowest level instantly.
   “Greenware” can be up a notch, and harder to spot. Greenware is
unfired pottery, almost always cast in a mold, sold to be decorated and fired
by someone other than the maker. It’s commercially cast, but the best is
decorated by a serious potter and fired at the Pueblo.
   At the top end, you have exquisitely crafted hand-formed pottery fired
outdoors in an open pit, made exactly the same way the potter’s ancestors
worked a thousand years ago.
   But “traditional” is a continuum, not an either/or matter. Some potters
fire outdoors during the summer and indoors during winter. Others are
simply better painters than they are potters and augment their traditional

output with an occasional piece of greenware. Not that there isn’t quite a bit
of tradition even with this. Archeologists have turned up molds for
sculptural pottery elements in Mexican ruins. Cast pottery goes back to B.C.
days, and some of today’s best-known traditional potters started out with
greenware.

Some things to look for when judging a pot:
➤ MOLD MARKS: Cast pottery is made in two-part molds, so unless the
potter has taken extra time sanding them away, you can find seams. If you
feel suspicious bumps or divots on opposite sides of a jar, the jar is
presumed guilty. Seed jars are a favorite greenware type because they don’t
give themselves away as readily. If you can’t get your finger in a hole, you
can’t find a seam.
➤ PROTRUDING FLECKS OF TEMPER: Greenware never shows a lump of
foreign substance protruding through the slip. If you see a little chunk of
sand or rock sticking out somewhere, you can be pretty sure the pot is
traditional. Look for little flaws, and if they don’t disfigure the pot, be glad
you found them.
➤ LOPSIDEDNESS: A good pot should be round, the hole in a seed jar
shouldn’t be slightly off to one side and so forth. The people who make cast
pottery don’t make off-balance pots. If your pot is off-center, it’s probably
traditional. However, the potter loses points for skill. It’s a no-win situation.
➤ GOOD FIRING: Traditional firing often means imperfect firing. Underfiring
is subtle, and you can hear it more easily than you can see it. Santa Clara
and San Ildefonso blackware and redware are fired at low temperatures, and
they don’t ping. But if a thin-walled Acoma or Zuni pot doesn’t ring like a
bell when you tap it, it hasn’t been fired hot enough or it has a crack.
Overfiring is rare on modern pottery, but it shows up on prehistoric pieces
as burned-off or discolored paint. Fire clouds can disfigure pristine white
Acoma and Zuni pottery. On the other hand, fire clouds can give yellow-to-
orange Hopi pottery a pleasing burnished amber variation. You decide
whether a fire cloud ruins the pot or enhances it. Or whether you can just
turn that dark spot to the wall and forget it.

Green left, traditional right. Not easy, is it?
           Acoma, Marcella Augustine, 6½" diameter, 1992 and 4½" diameter, 1990

➤ GREENWARE CLUES: When you see colors not found in nature—pinks,
turquoises, lavenders and such—the greenware buzzer should go off in your
head. Likewise, if you see slick painting on a large, new-looking white olla
and if the price is too good to be true, think greenware. Tap a pot with your
knuckle and listen to its ring. Commercially cast pottery is fired at a high
temperature and usually has a higher-pitched ring than traditional pottery.
Also, greenware tends to have a bottom that looks flat but is slightly
concave. Slightly is the key word. Traditional ollas usually had, and have,
really concave bottoms that sit snugly when you balance them on your
head.

➤ GRACE AND BALANCE: An esthetic call. Some shapes seem awkward,
some seem graceful. The more practiced your eye, the more you’ll see that
some pots are more equal than others.
➤ AN UNFLAWED FINISH: If you see pits, blisters or scratches, the pot is
damaged. If you see sgraffito in the wrong place, the potter probably tried

to hide a glitch. Some people feel the slightest flaw is disqualifying. We’re
not that hard-nosed.
➤ EVEN THICKNESS OF THE WALLS: We recently saw a nice-looking Mata
Ortiz blackware pot, flawlessly formed on the outside. When we reached
into the opening, the inside felt like craters of the moon and the pot
downgraded from “impressive” to “forget it.” Generally, the thinner and
more uniform the walls, the more admirable the pot.
➤ GOOD PAINTING AND CARVING: These qualities are high on the list with the
curators of this museum. A shaky line in a design that calls for accuracy, a
graceless curve instead of a smooth one, a badly drawn animal instead of a
stylish one, tasteless colors or ham-handed design—these bother us.
➤ ORIGINALITY WITHIN THE RULES: If we see a pot that clearly falls within
the tradition of a specific Pueblo, and we can still say, “Hey, we’ve never
seen anything like that,” we dig deep and buy it.
➤ AGE AND WEAR: This is a personal call. Anew pot should look new. With
an older one, you can forgive increasing amounts of wear. The definitions
of “honest patina” and “dilapidated” are up to you.
   The pots below tell different stories. The big one started life about 1890
as a splendid Zuni olla, the kind rich collectors now pay five figures for. Its
original owners took it to the river, filling it with water every day and
abrading its rim a little more each time. Today, it’s a pure example of
historic wear created by Pueblo use. Many collectors wouldn’t touch it
because of its condition, but we spent a lot for it.

Too much history?
               Zuni, 13½" diameter, circa 1890 and Kewa, 8½" diameter, circa 1925

   Back then, when a pot lost its usefulness, the owners fixed it. The
equally admirable 1880 Zuni olla to the right has a large crack from the rim
that an owner sealed up with pitch more than a hundred years ago.

Historic repair: pine tar
                                 Zuni, 11½" diameter, circa 1880

   The bowl below has a huge chunk missing from its side. We showed it
to an expert who’s normally a stickler for condition, and he was quite taken
with it. We asked whether we should restore it, and he surprised us when he
said, “No, that’s the history of the pot.” Well, that “history” prompted a
previous, probably far less affluent owner to throw it away. It now sits on a
high shelf, missing chunk to the wall, its fatal flaw unseen and forgotten.
   The first wear that shows on a pot is a softening of the colors from age
and handling. You see age when you see a color difference between the
body of the pot and the base, which sits protected from sun and air pollution
through the years.
   The paint on much recent decorated pottery is fragile. Santa Clara and
Hopi painted pieces seem especially susceptible to wear. If you have a nice
traditional Hopi pot from one of the great pottery families, be aware that if
it rubs up against hard surfaces, it might start looking like the one on the
right. Never handle a pot, especially a matte-finished one, while you’re
eating a bag of french fries. Oil and grease from your fingers can make an
unpleasant stain.

Sticky tape: bad idea

   Other villains will attack the surface of an innocent pot. The taped-on
price tag is a fearsome enemy. (Antiques dealer Carol Hayes says never put
a sticky label on anything other than glass or commercially fired glazed
crockery.) When the dealer yanks off the tag, wham!—a little tape-shaped
patch of picked-off slip and paint. If your pot has something stuck to it, take
it off with a little dab of solvent and a Q-tip (nail polish remover works).
Even the most careful fingernail exploration can bite you before you know
it. However, if you see an original trader’s label on an old pot, leave it there.
It adds to the value and confirms the pot’s history.
    All the things that age a pot—exposure, handling, abrasion, water
damage—accumulate over the years, and in each case, you have to decide.
Is a chip honest wear or a fatal flaw? How old does a pot have to be before
a crack is okay? How rare does a pot have to be before you accept a
reassembled one? You make the call one pot at a time, and your call might
not agree with ours.

Water and Southwestern pottery. When pottery isn’t glazed, “vase” only
means a shape, not a use That Southwestern vase isn’t waterproof.
Depending on the temperature at which it was fired, water can either
discolor it or eat it alive.
   You can cook in a Taos pot without much happening to it. A well-fired
Acoma pot may have held water for generations and only suffered a little
discoloration, while the slip on a similar Zuni olla might crack and start to
peel away. A Hopi vase won’t leak but will discolor badly. And all those
Eastern tourists who bought Maria Martinez masterpieces from San

Ildefonso and put flower arrangements in them learned the worst. Modern
blackware doesn’t just discolor, it can disintegrate. This has nothing to do
with the quality of the pottery. The prized black color and polish require a
low firing temperature and the pot remains porous and sadly, water soluble.

Restoration and reconstruction. In prehistoric pottery, a reconstructed pot
—a broken one that’s been pasted back together—is almost as elite as an
intact pot, providing it’s complete.





                              Water plus blackware: bad idea
                             Okkay Owinge, circa 1963

    “Intact” dosen’t mean “flawless.” Many intact pots have stress cracks,
not surprising in a breakable object that may have been buried for centuries.
Intact pots might be “stabilized.” That means some good soul has put glue
in the cracks to keep it from falling apart. Those cracks aren’t the sole
property of ancient pieces. They show up in modern pieces as well,
sometimes as a result of a firing accident.

Reconstructed, but at its age, that’s okay
                   Cibola, Cedar Creek Black-on-red, 7¾" diameter, circa 1400

   Restored pottery is lower on the prestige list. A restored pot has missing
pieces filled in and replaced. Many experts and many museums like the
patching to be obvious so you can tell new from old at a glance.
   One archeologist we know mildly disagrees. She thinks of restoration as
a simple act of respect for a worthy object. We take no official position, but
we do think complete pots look nicer than the ones that look like Swiss
cheese.

Scratchy handling: bad idea
                               Hopi, 8½" diameter, circa 1940

    Restoration is a big issue once money and misrepresentation enter the
picture. Flawless pots are worth more than beat-up pots, and it’s dirty pool
to fix up an old pot and pretend it’s in mint condition. At the lower end,
concealed restoration makes little difference. As the stakes go up, it can be
classified as fraud. At our level of acquisition, it’s simple. Is the pot worth
the asking price regardless of its history? If we like it at the price, fine. If it
was restored, so what. If it wasn’t so much the better. And if we never find
out, we didn’t expect to anyway.
   Most repairs show up under black light, but it’s an inexact lie detector.
We use it from time to time, but we’re not compulsive about it. There’s one
sure-fire test that you won’t like. Experts drill sample holes and do a
laboratory analysis. Then you know, but your unrestored pot now has holes
in it that need restoration.

Kill hole

KILL HOLES AND RIM KILLS: The prehistoric Mogollon buried bowls with
their owners, and down in Mimbres country, they ceremonially punched a
hole in the center. Later, they stopped punching the center hole and simply
broke out a piece from the rim. The custom has fascinated archeologists,
curators and traders for a century or more. If a Mogollon pot has a nicked
edge and a shaky provenance, it’s almost inevitable that someone will
identify that nick as a kill. It’s more romantic than calling it a rim chip. Or,
as one archeologist suggested, “gnawed by rodents.”

The signature. The potter’s signature is almost universal today, but it’s a
recent phenomenon. Before 1940, despite the diligent efforts of government
Indian schools, many potters didn’t speak English and even fewer wrote it.
A potter’s name on the bottom of an old pot is apt to have been written by
the buyer or the trader who sold it.

By the way, signatures can wear off the base of a pot just from being
moved around. You should rest all your pots on soft fabric, and one of these
days, we’ll get around to doing it.
   This 1940s-vintage bowl has “Nampeyo” written on the bottom in
pencil, almost certainly by a hopeful seller trying to inflate its value by
adding the name of a world-famous potter, some of whose pots looked
something like this one. It may have been made by a member of her large
and productive family, but the odds are astronomical against its having been
made by the original Nampeyo, a potter whose work, done a century ago, is
the single strongest influence on contemporary Hopi pottery. By the time
this was made, Nampeyo, who died in 1942, probably wasn’t even alive.
  On pots made from the 1930s to the 1970s, a crude signature is often
what dealers call “graffito,” added the way you’d write your name on the
flyleaf of a book. When you bring a bowl of chile to the potluck at the
Pueblo, you want to be sure you get your bowl back. We have pots with
names on them written in everything from Sharpies to silver nail polish.
   Signing work is an Anglo market-driven concept. Until the last thirty
years or so, most Navajo and Zuni silversmiths didn’t sign their work, and
Zuni carvers didn’t sign fetishes until more recently. Acoma potters once
thought signing their work was an inappropriate expression of ego.
    In the 1920s, some Hopi potters began signing with symbols, but the
custom of name-on-the-bottom of the pot really began with Maria Martinez
of San Ildefonso. Putting her name on her pots wasn’t her idea. In the
1920s, she was already a celebrity and much closer to the Santa Fe world of
art-as-commerce. At the suggestion of market-focused Anglos, she began
signing, but started out by signing her pots “Marie” instead of “Maria.” Her
advisors had been careful to explain that tourists wouldn’t buy pots made by
foreigners.

Not Nampeyo, despite the signature
                               Hopi, 5¼" diameter, circa 1945

   Other potters followed. Margaret Tafoya and Lela Gutierrez, the leading
Santa Clara potters, were signing by 1930, and in 1928, when Nampeyo
was nearly blind and unable to paint, her daughters began putting
Nampeyo’s name on pots they’d painted for her. Also in the 1920s,
“Acoma, N.M.” and “Laguna N.M.” started appearing on the bottom of
tourist pots. Fortunately, they resisted writing “souvenir of” and putting it
out where you could see it. By the 1960s, potters at every Pueblo were
signing, but not all of them and not always.
   These days, the market is heavily influenced by what a trader friend of
ours calls “bottom collectors”—people who buy a pot for the signature
rather than for the pot itself. Bottom collectors have pushed the price of
work by some potters up tenfold over what potters of nearly the same
ability can get. This holds for the work of historic figures like Maria
Martinez and Margaret Tafoya or of contemporary masters like Tammy
Borts Garcia, Diego Romero and Russell Sanchez.

We try to avoid acting like those bottom feeders, but we have to admit
that a good signature does elevate a pot’s attraction, and from time to time
we’ve bought pieces we wouldn’t otherwise have bought because of the
name on the bottom. If you find a fine pot from a fine potter, you’ve struck
gold, and you’ll find several of those in this book, quite a few found within
our buying rules.
   However, if you’ve paid attention to everything we’ve said, you may
never find a pot worthy of purchase. This combination of beauty,
originality, flawless execution, immaculate condition and artist’s prestige
almost never falls within a mere mortal’s price range.

4. PREHISTORIC POTTERY





                Hohokam, Santa Cruz Red-on-buff, 5½" diameter, circa 900

IN OUR SOUTHWEST, pottery fragments first appeared in the desert four
thousand years ago, but this book is about the mud-lined baskets that
evolved into modern bowls and jars that first showed up around 100 A.D.
Until recorded history began in the sixteenth century, a dozen or more
native and invading peoples had passed through, and pottery tells much of
their story. Science can date a pot from the tree rings in the timbers of the

room where they find it and figure out trade patterns based on where it
traveled.
    Happily, prehistoric pottery is plentiful and reasonably priced.
Unhappily, you’ll hear a great many political, ethical and moral reasons
why you shouldn’t even think about owning a single piece—reasons like
these.

Why nobody should ever buy a prehistoric pot. In the old days, scientists,
hobbyists and in-it-for-the-money pothunters dug up thousands of pots,
filling mantels, trading posts and museums. There are as many as two
archeological sites per square mile over vast areas of Arizona and New
Mexico—over a hundred thousand locations, many excavated, many more
still unexplored, each with its share of pots, a handful from one, a hundred
from another.
    In the 1890s, pothunting picnics made fashionable outings. Traders sold
“pottery from the Ancient Ruins” by mail order. At Walnut Canyon near
Flagstaff, enterprising excavators sped up the process with a little dynamite.
   Quite early, observers recognized that pothunters were damaging sites.
Congress passed laws in 1906 to curtail excavation on federal land, but
enforcement didn’t begin until the 1970s. Scientists complained about
treasure hunters bulldozing sites, and Native Americans spoke up about
grave desecration and loss of sacred objects. Congress responded to the
political pressure with the Archeological Resources Protection Act of 1979
(ARPA). It had prohibitions against disturbing burial sites and set scary
penalties like a year in jail and $100,000 in fines for a first offense.
   The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990
(NAGPRA) added still more teeth. In 2009, government agencies took to
heavy-handed enforcement. Blanding, Utah, is a small town in a rural area
surrounded by prehistoric sites. FBI agents watched the town for weeks
with the aid of a local paid informant, then raided. They held targeted
residents at gunpoint, interrogated, intimidated and arrested them.
Simultaneous raids harassed homes in Arizona and New Mexico. All the
raids achieved was a brief jail term for one person in Blanding and
probation for ten other Blanding residents. The Blanding town doctor and
another resident committed suicide, as did the alcoholic paid informant, and
scores of others across three states had their lives shaken up. The FBI may
have thought the raids were a good idea, but they had tragic consequences.

Today, collecting prehistorics has become so politically incorrect that
any defense sounds self-serving and greedy. In this highly polarized and
dangerous world, most dealers don’t sell prehistorics, and their attitudes
range from a bland “I prefer not to deal in them” to “I wouldn’t touch them
with a stick.”
     If you’re tempted to buy one, bear in mind that it could have been a
sacred object looted from a sacred site, that the seller might be a criminal,
and that you might go directly to jail.

Why we bought them anyway. We’ve talked this through with Native
Americans, archeologists, traders, and interested lawyers, including one
who prosecuted related cases, and listened to FBI people who raided
Blanding. Here’s how we sort it out:
➤ ITEM: There are thousands of prehistoric pots now legally owned by
dealers, museums and private collectors, all buried for many years and
bought in good faith under existing laws. They can never be returned to
their sites undisturbed. Except for a tiny percentage of sacred vessels, we
haven’t observed tribes or Pueblos asking to get them back.
➤ ITEM: The alternatives to open buying and trading of legally acquired
prehistoric pottery seem worse. Take away the legitimate market, and
prehistorics become even more politically incorrect. In response to
increasingly negative attitudes, we believe that museums will become more
reluctant to display their collections, and the black market will take over.
Prohibition attracts profit.
➤ ITEM: Excavation on private land away from burial sites is legal in
Arizona and New Mexico. Unless you believe that all archeology is looting,
and many do, it makes no sense to condemn those who excavate prehistoric
pottery legally and with respect for its archeological context.
➤ ITEM: Conventional wisdom says that most prehistoric pottery comes
from burial sites. In fact, it was a commodity, widely traded and often left
behind when a group moved on. Almost all prehistoric pottery comes from
excavated living quarters at abandoned sites. Yes, there are still a few grave
robbers out there, but government action is curbing their activities. Similar
wisdom says all prehistoric pottery was originally dug by looters. Actually,
much surfaced accidentally. Traders have described more than one piece
we’ve seen as “1-40” pottery, referring to pots turned up by construction
crews from Flagstaff to Albuquerque. Convenient explanation or not, it’s

true that Arizona’s Salt River Project has a museum full of pottery salvaged
during its earth-moving projects.
   So why do we collect them? We consider them beautiful, important
pieces of history to be admired, respected and given care, and we’d rather
they didn’t all languish forever in museum basements. Buying properly
documented specimens is perfectly legal, and we feel it’s perfectly moral as
well.

Forgeries. Could any of the pots in this book be forgeries? Probably not.
Serious art forgery involves organized crime, six- and seven-figure sums,
and the occasional murder, but those don’t apply here. The John & Al
Museum buying rules make fraud a long shot. Nobody counterfeits dollar
bills.
     If you’re worried about forgeries, buy from a trustworthy dealer. The
odds are heavily on your side, but really good forgeries can fool the experts,
as curators the world over can attest.

A word about dates. Take the dates in this book with a grain of salt. Most of
our prehistoric pots were dug up years ago, their provenances lost. Under
these conditions, proper scientists never commit themselves. We saw one
obscure type helpfully dated as circa 1150 to modern (?).
   Since we’re not proper scientists, we put dates on everything. We check
out the type, take the middle of the range of dates the books give us, and
add a circa. If we say circa 1050, the type may have been made from 1025
to 1075 or from 900 to 1200. If we miss a date by a couple of hundred
years, our defense is that we’ve never seen a definition of “circa” narrow
enough to make us feel guilty.

How to buy a prehistoric pot legally. Buy it on the open market, not off the
back of a truck from a guy you met in a bar. Insist on documentation, then
pay with a check or credit card and get a receipt. We have a provenance for
every prehistoric pot we own. Most reputable sellers provide paperwork
like this lawyer-approved form recommended by the Antique Tribal Arts
Dealers Association (ATADA). We gave this one to a museum with a minor
piece.

Now, does this form protect us completely? Of course not. A true crook
will sign one whether the pot has been stolen, forged or dug illegally. We
only have the same protection we have when we buy any antique: open
purchase from a reputable dealer in good faith plus good paperwork. That
matches both the letter and the spirit of the law.

MOGOLLON - THE BROWN POTTERY

Beginnings. The Mogollon (say MAWG-uh-yon, not muh-GOLL-on as we did
until someone corrected us) might well have been the earliest Southwestern
potters, except for a mysterious and vanished culture called the Tucson
Farmers who occupied the Tucson basin on and off for a couple of thousand
years in B.C. days. Archeologists pick up the Mogollon around 300 B.C. in

eastern Arizona, where they lived for over a thousand years, branching out
north, east and south.





   By 1150, the Mogollon had spread through the Mimbres Valley to West
Texas and into Mexico. About then, they started the process of folding into
other cultures of the north and south, and by 1300, the last pockets of
Mogollon culture remained clustered around the Mogollon Rim area of
Arizona where they had first appeared. By 1450, they were gone, absorbed
into other cultures.
   The Mogollon began lining or patching baskets with clay somewhere
around 100 A.D., and by 200 or so, were making a lumpy pit-fired
brownware that could be called true pottery. Century by century, their
sophistication increased, and they made beautiful coil-and-build brownware

for the remainder of their history. In the years around 1000, they made some
of the finest plainware ever, ancient or modern.
   From the beginning, they put texture on their pottery. Some of the
earliest examples have an undulating surface created when potters drew
their fingers through the wet clay. Soon after, they added simple textures by
poking their vessels with sticks and reeds. By 1000, these textures had
developed into full corrugation, perhaps borrowed from the Anasazi to the
north. Whether or not the Mogollon invented corrugation, they
experimented with every variation on the theme.
   Mogollon and neighboring Hohokam potters turned their bowls upside-
down during firing, which made the insides turn black. On the oldest
pottery, these smudged interiors were light gray and probably unintended,
but on later pottery, they had a deep enough color and high enough polish to
rival modern blackware.
   The best Mogollon brownware came from the Mimbres Valley in
southwestern New Mexico. By 700, the Mimbres, which many books define
as a separate culture, were in touch with their Hohokam neighbors to the
west. The Three Circle and Boldface pieces in the picture at right have a
Hohokam feel, but by 950 the Mimbres had moved on to their own unique
whiteware.
    Trendsetters to the end, the Mimbres were among the first Southwestern
people to vanish, which happened by 1200. Vanishing became an
unfortunate habit. Science has lost all of the prehistoric peoples in the
Southwest. The Mogollon/Mimbres, the Anasazi, the Hohokam, Salado,
Sinagua and Casas Grandes cultures all disappeared within a few years of
1400.





                Where this book starts Alma Plain, 2¾" diameter, circa 400

To anyone who hasn’t studied the subject, it seems obvious that those
ancient cultures are the direct ancestors of today’s Pueblo and southern
Arizona Indians. It’s equally obvious to the Indians, whose spoken history
identifies its ancestors, and each seems to refer to one of these early
cultures.
     It’s not so simple for archeologists, who aren’t satisfied that all those
spoken histories match the physical evidence. Scientists can date pueblo
construction and abandonment to the exact year and can identify a culture
by burial customs, but they still won’t state flatly that any current peoples
have Mogollon ancestry. Yet unless they were carried off by the same space
aliens who carried off the Mimbres, they went somewhere.
   We’ll talk more about this on later pages.

Artist and pottery student Charles Parker called the pot on the opposite
page “the mother of all pottery.” The Mogollon made the style for a
thousand years, so this may not be as old as we think, but whenever it was
made, it’s right at the beginning philosophically. Before it, almost nothing.
After it, everything in the book.
   By 600, the Mogollon were playing with the surface. Their polish was
centuries ahead of its time, and the red and brown polished jars at left go
back to the early days. If they didn’t polish the surface, they tooled it.
Decorations became increasingly more ornate. The fancy corrugation on
the bowl in the center is actually a rather tame example.
   Over the next three hundred years, Mogollon pottery got better and
better. The large Mimbres Plain jar in the top row is probably the single
finest prehistoric vessel in this museum—uniformly round, a perfect one-
eighth of an inch thick overall, feathering to a sixteenth of an inch at the
rim. Even in today’s Golden Age, nobody does much better.
   Early Mogollon painted pottery gave little hint of the visual delights to
come. When the Mogollon started painting around 700, they took their first
cue from red-on-buff Hohokam ware. In evolutionary steps, the little

Mogollon Red-on-brown jar led up to the Mimbres Boldface helmet bowl,
which got closer to the Mimbres Classic to follow, but still looks Hohokam.
The Three Circle Red-on-white bowls, made fifty years before the helmet
bowl, are brown with a white slip on the inside like Mimbres Classics on
pages 30 and 31.
   The painted corrugateds came at the end of Mogollon days, fifty years
after the Mimbres evaporated.

ANASAZI – THE GRAY POTTERY

Diverging development up north. Books assign the Anasazi to the high
plateaus surrounding the Four Corners area, and recent ones won’t call them
Anasazi. Early archeologists thought the word meant “Old Ones,” but
“Anasazi” is actually Navajo for “Ancient Enemies.” The name rankles
their descendants and is being replaced by the more accurate “Ancestral
Puebloans.”
   They first lived in caves and pithouses like the Mogollon, but by 800,
they’d developed the high-rise architecture that caught the attention of
nineteenth-century anthropologists. Ever after, the Anasazi got the publicity
while the Mogollon got no respect.
   Like the Mogollon, the Ancestrals were planters and irrigators, but more
cosmopolitan. Chaco Canyon was a thriving trade center by 900, with a
population of perhaps ten thousand (a figure that latter-day archeologists
keep revising up and down). Its ruins reveal trade with Mexico: macaw
feathers, turquoise ornaments, even copper bells. None of the peoples in
this book’s Southwest used metal until the Spanish came. By 1200, the
Anasazi had another great complex at Mesa Verde with remarkable towers,
cliffside apartments and a half-million gallon reservoir. But no Ancestral
settlement held its population for much more than a century. They farmed
out the soil, cut down the firewood and moved on.

At Mesa Verde, they invented the coffee mug Mesa Verde Black-on-white, 4¾" high, circa 1100

    Ancestral Puebloans began making plain gray pottery around 500 and
quickly found clays and pigments to make a thin, high-fired ware decorated
in black. Decoration appeared as early as 600, and by 850, the designs on
their pottery had become sophisticated. Also by 850, they were making
corrugated pottery for cookware. Although the Mogollon took the idea
further, the Anasazi can claim simultaneous, if not prior, development.
   Although the Mogollon had a head start, the Ancestral Puebloans
probably developed pottery for trade earlier. Many books talk about the
significance and symbolism of the designs on prehistoric pottery, but the
rapid transformation of Anasazi pottery from a plain utilitarian craft into a

fanciful art may have had more to do with commercial pressure than with
ceremonial needs.
   By the time the Ancestrals were settled in at Chaco, they’d found clays
to make pure white slips that covered the gray, and they’d learned to make
ever-blacker vegetal and mineral paints. Black-on-white remained the
predominant Anasazi ware into the 1200s, when the fashion pendulum
swung to redware.
   As they spread from the four corners to the south, east and west, they
encountered other cultures—Mogollon and Sinagua, and, less pleasantly,
fifteenth-century immigrants: nomadic Navajo from the north and Apache
from the plains. By the 1300s, the Ancestrals had left Mesa Verde and,
according to tourist literature, became lost in the fog of history. They
weren’t lost in Pueblo oral tradition. At San Ildefonso, Santa Clara and
Zuni, they point to nearby ruins, and at Hopi, they identify prehistoric
artifacts with Hopi clans.
   The pottery we’ve collected tells its own story, and we’re trying our best
to understand it.

The first Anasazi grayware, like the gourd-shaped ladle, was as unassuming
as the first Mogollon brownware. In fact, the earliest Ancestral pieces were
probably brown. But gray-and-white became the Anasazi signature for
seven hundred years. Almost immediately after they turned to grayware,
they began decorating with black paint, sometimes made from boiled-down
plants and sometimes with a blacker paint made from minerals, as on the
jar at left.
   Corrugated cookware first appeared around 850. The Ancestrals
quickly became masters of the genre, as the surprisingly thin and even more
surprisingly white-slipped example at top right indicates. The Chaco cup at
left middle demonstrates an Anasazi specialty, the “clapboard” style.
   By 900, black-on-white was hitting stride. Designs became more
interesting, and pottery walls became thinner and finer. The Black Mesa
bowl to the right of the ladle is so fine it’s almost translucent, and the Kana-
a in the top row is paper thin.
   Designs continued mainly geometric, and the Tusayan jar at the right
end of the middle row with its “sheet music” motif represents the defining
model for Anasazi pottery in general. Figurative portrayals were scarce. If

you see one on apiece made before 1200, it’s most likely Mimbres. But every
so often, you see something like the little fellow with the six-fingered hands
in the Mancos bowl at lower left.
   The Ancestral Puebloans made imaginative shapes quite early, and until
the Casas Grandes people started making effigies around 1300, their
pitchers, dippers and coffee mugs showed a variety that few other
prehistoric Southwestern peoples ever matched.

CIBOLA & MIMBRES – MOGOLLON GOES BLACK-ON-WHITE

Cultural exchange. By 1000, the Mogollon and the Anasazi were meeting
all along the Mogollon Rim, the shelf that divides Arizona’s high-altitude,
pine-covered north from its desert south. And if the Ancestrals had copied
Mogollon brownware five hundred years earlier, the Mogollon returned the
compliment many times over. From present-day Pinedale in central Arizona
to Socorro in central New Mexico, the Mogollon began producing thin,
elegant and finely painted black-on-white.
    Into the early 1980s, anthropologists said black-on-white wares from
the territorial overlap areas were Anasazi. As it became evident that many
later wares were Mogollon-created, they adopted a designation that spared
them from having to pin down who made what: Cibola ware, a convenient
blanket term that covers all Ancestral and Mogollon pottery made between
I-40 and the Rim.
   Mogollon black-on-white quickly matched Anasazi ware for its
sophistication. By 1050, it had redefined the standards. The finest of all
came from the Mimbres Valley in southeastern New Mexico. Mimbres
pottery has been both the most prized and the most shunned of all the
prehistoric wares. Where most prehistoric pottery was traded widely,
Mimbres Classic black-on-white was closely held.

Classic Mimbres: figures, geometry and a kill Mimbres Classic bowl, 8¼" diameter, circa 1050

    Pictorial representations are uncommon on prehistoric pottery. Most
designs are so abstract that only an anthropologist can explain what they
represent. With the Mimbres, there’s no question. Google Mimbres pottery
or pick up some Mimbres-design dinnerware, and you’ll think that all they
ever did was stylized pictures of bunnies, bugs, birdies and mom doing
household tasks. The creatures on the piece below are typical. On the other
hand, less-publicized Mimbres depictions explore a lurid tapestry of sex and
violence: rapes, decapitations, bestiality, you name it.
   The Mogollon buried their dead, unlike their Hohokam neighbors who
cremated, but went a step further. They placed a bowl over the face of the
dead and punched a ceremonial “kill hole” through the bottom. A good
portion of Mimbres Classic pottery has kill holes and comes from burials.
   Almost none of it comes from other areas. A couple of theories suggest
why, unlike other competent prehistoric potters, the Mimbres didn’t trade
their pottery. The usual theory is that it was so sacred that they refused to let

others have it. Another suggests that they were a pariahcult. The bizarre
nature of many of their images makes us lean to the cult theory. In a time
when all decoration was conventional and trade-oriented, Mimbres pottery
probably seemed disturbingly weird.
   The aura surrounding killed Mimbres pottery has fueled a myth that all
prehistoric pottery is burial-related. Actually, Mimbres burial pottery
comprises only a tiny percentage of prehistoric Southwestern pottery, and
perhaps not as much came from burials as we think. There are few Mimbres
bowls with holes punched from the wrong side. If you caringly place a bowl
over the face of a loved one and make a hole so the departed’s spirit can
escape to the next world, you punch the hole through the back. This
provides a clean break on the outside and a jagged break on the inside, like
the pieces on these pages. On the other hand, if you’re a pothunter who
wants to add a little romance to a Mimbres bowl, you set it down, look at
the image, and punch from the front, being careful to avoid the best part of
the design, which leaves the clean break on the inside.
   This doesn’t mean that a wrong-side punch is any proof of funny
business by a trader or pothunter. It’s just one more thing to wonder about,
one more piece of lore added to the Southwest’s most lore-burdened
pottery.

The Mogollon learned fast—witness the Puerco mug in the bottom row.
Mugs and pitchers were an Anasazi specialty. Even early Mogollon Black-
on-white had a finish and style that probably made the Anasazi sit up and
take notice, like the Chupadero bowl in the bottom row. Cibola decoration
has influenced potters ever since.
   Down at Mimbres, the Mogollon were developing Mimbres Classic, and
the examples on these pages show the precision and design sensitivity that
made Mimbres Classic the most sought-after prehistoric pottery. Figurative
pieces are the most highly prized. On the fragment at bottom right, a
coatimundi stands on his tail and glowers at the world. Both the beauty of
the figure’s design and its unfriendly attitude are quintessentially Mimbres.
There’s great beauty but little warmth in Mimbres imagery.
    In the days after the Mimbres evaporated, Tularosa Black-on-white from
the mountains just to the north set new design standards. Tularosa swirls
and lightning bolts have reappeared ever since in the neighboring areas.
For later interpretations of the swirls on the pitcher in the front row,
seepages 45, 53, 55 and 101. For the lightning bolts on the jar on the right,
go to pages 57 and 58.

The Chupadero and Tularosa pieces are almost up to Mimbres
standards of precision, and they came from areas near present-day Acoma.
Snowflake ware has an unintentionally apt name—slips tend toward a
dazzling white, and the large Socorro bowl at top left is so extravagant that
we’re tempted to call it Mimbres Classic.
    Art has fashions, however, and black-on-white was about to go out of
style.

HOHOKAM – THE BUFF POTTERY

The canal builders. One book may tell you the Mogollon were the first
serious potters in the Southwest, but another will credit the Hohokam, the
quiet people who lived in Arizona and spread their influence into Sonora
and Chihuahua.
   Current thinking has the Hohokam as short-distance immigrants from
northern Mexico who came to southern Arizona around 300 B.C., displaced
the earlier Tucson Farmers, and hung around until about 1450.
   The Hohokam were the first to build large settlements in our Southwest.
Instead of densely populated pueblos, they built widely spaced one-family
rancherias, a land-use custom that persisted into the twentieth century in
Hohokam country.
   Snaketown, south of Phoenix on I-10, covered four hundred acres and
had a population of five hundred to a thousand at its peak—hardly high-
density, more like a modern suburb with two-acre-minimum lots, but the
closest thing to a city in the United States around 600. It had one of the
most intricate complexes of irrigation canals of any prehistoric North
American community. The Hohokam used the seasonal downpours and
burning heat to maximum agricultural advantage, growing enough corn and
beans to live a peaceful and abundant life in the same location for a
thousand years.
   Between 500 and 1000, their empire expanded east, south and north of
Phoenix, where Hohokam sites exist alongside and sometimes under or on
top of Salado and Mogollon sites. This spawned theory upon theory. One
suggests the Salado never existed at all but were merely the Hohokam in a
different guise. Scholars believed that for years although, like the
Mogollon, the Salado buried their dead while the Hohokam cremated.

Pottery offers little clarification. After 1000, there’s great crossover
between Hohokam, Salado and Sinagua plainware.





               Hohokam beginnings Vahki Plain, 10¼" diameter, circa 400

    Pottery at Snaketown probably doesn’t go back before the second
century A.D., if that far. However, it would be naive to think that pottery-
making was fresh news to Snaketown’s early settlers. The Tucson Farmers
had made little pots for a couple of thousand years, and if the Hohokam
came from Mesoamerica, they’d made pottery for centuries.
   Snaketown’s oldest pottery supports the connection. Normally, you’d
think of primitive pottery as crude, bumpy stuff, but Snaketown’s oldest
pottery is well-fired, smooth, carefully shaped, thin and surprisingly
sophisticated.
   Hohokam architecture wasn’t sophisticated, however. They lived in
pithouses long after other cultures abandoned them, possibly because the
snow-free Southern Arizona climate made housing needs less demanding.
Archeologists think the Hohokam used their buildings only for shelter in
bad weather.

They were a strangely ephemeral people. Their name comes from an
Akimel O’odham word meaning “those who have vanished.” Despite
contempt for their possible forebears—Akimel oral history tells of ancestors
vanquishing the weak, arrogant Hohokam—current thinking names the
O’odham as their likely descendants.
   However, today’s mainstream O’odham pottery doesn’t look like
Hohokam pottery. It looks more like Salado redware. The Salado lived in
the mountains northeast of Snaketown, and if there’s truth in the ancient
legends, the Salado sound a lot like those people who swooped down from
the east.
   More about that on the next pages.

This picture shows how little Hohokam pottery evolved between 600 and
1050. The bowl on the opposite page, made 200 years earlier, shows where
it began.
   The Hohokam continued making plainware during those years, but once
they started decorating their pottery in red, they kept the style for centuries.
They hit their paddle-and-anvil construction and their design stride early.
The Snaketown bowl in the front row dates from 600, and Hohokam ware
kept this look for the next 800 years.
   Between 750 and 950, Hohokam culure spread from the Phoenix basin
into outlying provinces. Textbooks call those expansionist years the
Colonial Period. During those years, they built Mesoamerican-style ball
courts over much of southern Arizona, one of the key archeological links
between the Hohokam and the cultures to the south. Pottery, development,
however, stayed close to home. The early types get their names from
landmarks right around Snaketown. Gila Butte is a couple of miles to the
west, the Gila and Santa Cruz rivers flowed through Snaketown, and
Sacaton is the next town over in modern Arizona.

The Colonial Period types, Gila Butte and Santa Cruz, represent a high
point in Hohokam pottery art. Colonial pottery was well-fired and durable,
with a texture more like an orange peel than like the dinner-plate surface
the Mogollon achieved.
   The Hohokam left colonial expansion behind and morphed into a
comfortable Sedentary Period around 950. In those years, they went
nowhere and did little, and their pottery got heavier and less refined. Those
were prosperous times, and art from that period seems more mass-
produced.

HOHOKAM – BUFF MEETS RED

Culture clash. By 1050, all was well in Hohokam. Snaketown’s population
grew, the satellite cultures flourished, and there was enough paddle-and-
anvil red-on-buff pottery for everyone.
     It had taken more than 700 years to reach that level of comfort. Science
currently sees Hohokam evolution as including a Pioneer Period from 300
to 750, moving into the Colonial Period from 750 to 950, then to the
Sedentary Period from 950 to 1150 and ending in the Classic Period from
1150 to 1450.
   Through Colonial days, Hohokam culture spread, and books will tell
you about a lot of other cultures the Hohokam influenced and who made a
lot of pottery that looks Hohokam. You’ll see names like the Trincheras
culture, the Dragoon culture, the San Simon culture and the Babocomari
culture, all clustered in southern Arizona and northern Sonora. Now,
fastidious scholars get uncomfortable when you call the Tucson Basin
culture Hohokam, and Tucson has a different timeline and different period
names. The ethnic partitioning has the Hohokam shrunk back to the
Phoenix Basin and Snaketown and little else. This ware is easier to
understand if you lump what early archeologists called the “red on buff”
cultures together and call them Hohokam.
   Between these cultures, there’s so much overlap in pottery styles, burial
customs and architecture that it’s certain that they all knew each other and
traded with each other. It makes sense that a culture advanced enough to
build Snaketown and the Phoenix canal system influenced the people
around it. It follows that there would be differences in art, craft and customs

between sophisticated, “urban” Snaketown and less cultured “rural”
outlying provinces.





   Sedentary times in Tucson Rincon Red-on-brown, 8½" diameter, circa 1050 and Rillito Red-on-
                              brown, 5½" diameter, circa 1000

   Sedentary Hohokam in the Phoenix basin had close to a thousand miles
of canals irrigating tens of thousands of acres and the comforts of a
prosperous life: traded-in upscale artifacts from Mexico and ball courts
surrounded by berms that could accommodate a few hundred spectators. It
was a society affluent enough to afford spectacle and games for its field
workers.
   The Hohokam couldn’t stay Sedentary forever.
     It was the beginning of the Classic Period, the time of the Hohokam’s
greatest works. Around 1250, they built the Casa Grande canal. It ran for 20
miles along the Gila River, and, according to one study, required two years
of full-time work by a crew of a hundred people who moved almost
200,000 cubic yards of earth.

The ironically named Classic Period was also a time when the Hohokam
culture disintegrated, a time when those restless people from the mountains,
the Salado, moved down the hill to Hohokam country.
   The culture contact is obvious in the pottery. The Salado had been
making coiled red pottery since about 900, and suddenly the Hohokam were
making redware that looked Salado. At the same time, the Salado who
stayed up in the mountains returned the favor by making red on brown pots
that looked like Hohokam ware.
   To appreciate the crossover between the cultures during the Classic
Period, visit Casa Grande National Monument. It’s the last Hohokam great
work, so tall it served as a landmark for pioneers, so grandiose it makes you
think much more of government ego than of practical use. Then look at the
pots in the Visitor Center. You’ll see Casa Grande Red-on-buff like the ones
in the picture, but those won’t be what you’ll remember. You’ll see Salado
polychromes and big red fire-clouded jars that bring to mind Akimel oral
history.
     It was the Hohokam’s final gasp. They’d used up their natural resources
and suffered drought years, an arrogant government, a water-management
bureaucracy, a polluted water supply, undesirable immigrants, and years of
ever-more difficult hardscrabble farming. By 1450, the Hohokam had
abandoned the area. We think a lot of them left the dust bowl and went to
California.
