During the Classic Period. The Hohokam still made red-on-buff, but it
didn’t look the same. Classic Period Casa Grande Red-on-buff was heavy
and covered with a thick creamy slip and the red had become a purplish
brown. Towards Safford to the east, jars like the one in the middle picked up
on Anasazi designs.
   But the real difference in the pots is that there weren’t all that many of
them. During the Sedentary days, Sacaton Red-on-buff was abundant, and
today, it’s one of the most common prehistoric types. However, in twenty
years of collecting, we’ve only found three Casa Grande pieces, the one at
top left and the two at bottom left, and only one transitional piece, the one
at right center.
     It’s a lot easier to find Hohakam redware. The bowl at the lower right
has a Hohokam feature from the Sedentary period, a sharp break between
the sidewall and underbody called the Gila Shoulder. The bowl at upper
right looks Salado, but we know it’s Hohokam because it came from near
Casa Grande. The bowl with the white designs picks up an idea from the
Sinagua, another neighboring culture. The effigy jar at right is a Salado

shape that some call a bird effigy and others call a submarine. The red
melon jar has a Mesoamerican shape, but we’ve also seen it on a gray,
really early (650 A.D.) Anasazi Obelisk Plain piece. The Wingfield catfish is
neither Hohokam nor Salado. Stragglers after the abandonment became the
Sobaipuri in Southeastern Arizona, and they made Salado-looking pottery.

SALADO – THE RED POTTERY

The people up the hill. Just who were these people who lived up present-
day Highway 80 from the Hohokam? Akimel oral history says they
descended on the Hohokam and sent them running, but until recently,
textbooks told a different story.
   This much, we know. Drive east from Phoenix to Globe Arizona, visit
Roosevelt Lake, then head north on endless dirt roads, and you’re in Salado
country—a little saguaro and sage and a lot of pine forest and mountain
meadow. We know Salado pottery, Salado architecture and Salado burial
customs, but scholars still argue about the rest.
    In 1925, Erich Schmidt excavated Togetzoge and Armer Ruin, revealed
when Roosevelt Lake’s level dropped during a drought. The New York
Times ran a fanciful article describing Armer as a five-thousand-year-old
ruin with apartment houses larger than Park Avenue’s. It wasn’t all that big,
and five hundred years old was more like it, but the article pointed to the
Salado as a separate culture.
    In the 1930s, Harold Gladwin named them after the Rio Salado, or Salt
River, which runs through the Little Grand Canyon on the San Carlos
Apache reservation and continues into Phoenix. In 1945, Emil Haury called
the Salado a blending of Mogollon and Anasazi who the Akimel say
invaded and displaced the Hohokam. Albert Schroeder said they were a
blend of Hohokam and Sinagua. Charles Di Peso said they were outpost
traders from Paquimé in Chihuahua. Others said they didn’t exist at all. In
Schmidt’s day, archeologists felt that “pottery equals people,” but later
scholars dismissed the idea as simplistic. Current thinking has more time
for the concept, acknowledges that Gladwin and Haury had a point, and lets
pottery tell more of the story.

The Salado started out like this Salado Red, 6⅜" diameter, circa 1050

   Salado redware shows up from Arizona to New Mexico and from above
the Mogollon Rim to below the Mexican border. They weren’t the only
ones to make it. The Hohokam and Sinagua made similar pieces as did
others in Sonora and Chihuahua, but if you find a red piece that looks like
the ones in the picture, odds are that it’s Salado.
   The picture shows how, at one point, the Salado set their redware aside
and copied the Hohokam. San Carlos Red-on-brown looks Hohokam, but it
has two big differences. Most pieces have Salado-style deep black smudged
interiors which the Hohokam only used after they started copying the
Salado. More telling, the Salado pieces have a suede-smooth surface
nothing like the orange-peel texture of Hohokam red-on-buff. Some time
around 1200, the Salado noticed what the Cibola potters were doing up
around today’s St. Johns and Pinedale and started making black, white and
red pottery for trade using designs derived from (or swiped from) their
White Mountain neighbors. If we think of prehistoric pottery as market-
driven, the next 200 years of Salado pottery is the most market-driven of
all.
    Pinto Polychrome dates from 1200 and persists to 1350. It flows
smoothly into Gila Polychrome, one of the most widely traded prehistoric
styles. Gila shows up around 1300 and lasts into the fifteenth century.

Tonto Polychrome, the most consistently flamboyant of all the made-in-
U.S.A. Southwestern pottery styles, first appears around 1350. It bothers
some purists. Florence Hawley’s Field Guide to Prehistoric Pottery uses
words like “gaudy use of red, black and white,” “bizarre effect” and
“decadent in design.”
   Decadent, as in The Last Days of the Salado Empire. By 1450, the
Salado were history.

Typical early Salado redware is “obliterated corrugated,” with the
corrugations visible but mostly smoothed out, like the little red jar in the
center. Its quality isn’t typical, however. It’s as good as they come—thin,
perfectly round and precisely and evenly smoothed.
   Uncorrugated Salado redware sometimes came in effigy form, like the
bird in the front.
   When the Salado switched to black and white on red, the earliest
examples had thin slips, sometimes watery black vegetal paint and designs
borrowed from their Cibola neighbors. If the bowl at middle right didn’t
have a red exterior, it could pass for one of several Anasazi types.
   The bowl standing on its side at upper left is Gila Polychrome. One
distinguishing feature of a Gila bowl is the “lifeline,” a heavy black band
on the inside just below the rim. It shows up at Hopi and on White
Mountains pottery as well. The lifeline is usually broken, and if you read a
dozen books, you’ll find a dozen different explanations of the custom. The
little gap is called a spirit or ceremonial break, or simply a line break, and
some Pueblos still use it.

The cup at lower left is Tonto Polychrome at its most garish, and the
other examples in the picture describe the style. The jar at lower right is a
less common later type made down the hill a bit, south and west of the
Salado heartland.
   By the fourteenth century, the Salado had a lot of contact with the
Hohokam, and they tried an alternate style. The big red-on-brown jar at the
top and the two smaller ones in the front row show what the Salado did
when they decided to copy the Hohokam.

SINAGUA – THE OTHER RED POTTERY

The waterless people. Sinagua history intertwines with the Hohokam, the
Salado and the Anasazi, and the connections have kept anthropologists
arguing for years.
   The Sinagua came from waterless country, and the name sin agua
means “without water.” Spanish explorers called the San Francisco Peaks
near Flagstaff the Sierra Sin Agua. They became master irrigators and made
do quite well with what little water they found.
   The Sinagua had two homelands: one around and to the north of
Flagstaff and one in the Verde Valley below Sedona. Archeologists date
northern branch settlements from 500 and southern branch settlements
appeared from about 700. Back then, they lived in pithouses like the
Hohokam, with whom they traded freely. They happily traded with Anasazi,
Mogollon and Salado as well.
   The northern branch had its ups and downs. Sunset Crater, by Wupatki
ruin north of Flagstaff, was created when a volcano blew up in 1064 and
erupted for years after. The resulting layer of ash combined with years of
heavy rainfall created an agricultural area attractive enough to encourage
immigration. Pithouses turned into citified complexes with Hohokam-style
ball courts and, a bit later, improbable cliff dwellings. By 1350, however,
things took a turn for the worse and the northern Sinagua were gone,
perhaps to join their southern neighbors.
   The southern branch developed equally impressive architecture.
Montezuma’s Castle and Montezuma’s Well appear on almost as many
postcards as Chaco Canyon and Pueblo Bonito. Both ruins were at the south
end of the Palatkwapi Trail, a trade route from the Verde Valley to the Hopi
Mesas. But by 1425, the Southern Sinagua were gone too—probably up the

trail to meet the people who settled the other end almost four hundred years
earlier and were now established as the Hopi.
   Between 1200 and 1400, the cultural lines were blurring between the
desert, the adjacent hills and the mountains to the north. Sinagua
architecture, burial customs and settlement patterns make it easy to connect
them with the cliff-dwelling Anasazi and their Cibola descendants. Their
pottery, however, bore almost no resemblance to Anasazi pottery. The
Anasazi made black on white pots, and later, after 1200 or so, redware
decorated with fussy black and polychrome designs, while the Sinagua
made redware much closer to Salado ware, but with some Hohokam
elements.





   Sinagua pottery doesn’t attract much immediate attention. At first
glance, it seems like undecorated utilitarian ware, but the contributions and
innovations are there. Three elements stand out, and whether or not the
Sinagua invented them, they impressed others.
   The first thing you notice when you examine Sinagua ware is the high
polish. The Mogollon had made shiny pots in southern New Mexico for

seven hundred years or so, but the Sinagua brought the idea to Arizona and
into the Hohokam and Salado world and did it better than anybody else.
  On a small percentage of pieces, the Sinagua had picked up the idea of
adding white linear decoration. Whether they did it first or the Salado did it
first, it was just about the only painted decoration the Sinagua ever put on
their pottery, and the idea showed up on late-period Hohokam redware as
well. There’s a Hohokam piece on page 35 and a Salado piece on the next
page.
   The Hohokam also borrowed the third Sinagua pottery characteristic:
intentional fire-clouding. Placing carefully selected substances against a
pot’s surface during firing creates chemical reactions that produce striking
multi-colored designs, as on the big bowl opposite. The Hohokam used the
technique on large late-period storage jars, sometimes controlling it so well
that they created carefully designed symmetrical patterns. Until the Sinagua
put their noses in the cultural mix, fire-clouds almost never appeared on
Hohokam or Salado pottery, but you can see them on the red Hohokam
pieces on page 35.
   Sinagua pottery confirms that by 1300, everybody in Arizona was
talking to everybody else.

You can find yellow, green, bronze and a touch of purple in the halos
around the black scorches. The pitcher and the olla give you a milder
version of the phenomenon.
   The big olla is from Perry Mesa, an area a bit south and east of
Tuzigoot, where the others came from. It doesn’t play the colors game, but
its polish and shape are fabulous, so much so that when we first saw it, we
were convinced it was made hundreds of years later by the great potters of
the Tewa Pueblos north of Santa Fe.
   The painted pieces underscore the confusion. The jar at the right with
the white decoration could be Hohokam, but it has a peculiar indented
bottom treatment that we’ve seen on Sinagua pieces and nowhere else. The

taller pitcher, is pure Salado—smudged interior, obliterated corrugated
surface, purple-red color—but with Sinagua white line decoration. And the
two white-decorated pieces at the left have typical Sinagua white tracery
but come from different Sinagua branches: the big one at upper left from the
south and the small one at far left from the north.
   To us, these pieces show how three different cultures were on the same
wavelength.

WHITE MOUNTAIN – CIBOLA GOES RED

A 300-year fashion swing. Earlier in the book, we made sweeping,
simplistic assignments of specific pottery colors to specific people. “Red”
went to the Salado and the Sinagua. We ignored the fact that the Hohokam
made a bit of it, as did the Anasazi, and ultimately, it was the Mogollon-
turned-Cibola who made redware into the predominant form.
  Up until 1100 or so, black on white was king, and if you wanted to trade
your bowls and jars for food or other treasures, you worked to make your
black on white better than the black on white from the next settlement. But
around 1100, near the Arizona-New Mexico border in the White Mountains
south of where 1-40 runs today, change was afoot.
    Instead of painting black on white, the northern Mogollon hill people
started painting black on red. The first White Mountain black on red looked
a lot like the Cibola black on white of the same period. In fact, the designs
on the Wingate, Puerco and St. Johns pieces at right would have looked at
home on Gallup, Puerco or Tularosa Black-on-white pieces.
    But, because they were black on red, these pieces foreshadowed a
fashion trend that persisted to the end of the prehistoric Southwest, a
changeover that demonstrates how pervasive trade was from Flagstaff to El
Paso.

Early Katsina image. Later, they’re everywhere. Cedar Creek Polychrome bowl, 6¾" diameter, circa
                                       1325

   The second stage hit somewhere between 1250 and 1300. A hundred
years earlier, White Mountain potters had added white to the outside of
black on red bowls and created St. Johns Polychrome. This turned out to be
profoundly influential. Before St. Johns, polychrome pottery barely existed,
but the new style took hold so completely that for more than two hundred
years, polychromes made up almost all of the trade-for-food pottery in
Arizona, New Mexico and Chihuahua and Sonora.
   Four Mile and its allied polychrome types, Pinedale, Cedar Creek, Show
Low and Kinishba, define the polychrome style. They evolved from St.
Johns and spread all over the pottery-trading area. The polychromes on the
Salado, Hopi and Zuni pages in this chapter show how quickly the other
cultures picked up on the idea and ran with it.
    Collectively, these Four Mile types, almost entirely bowls, represent the
last major Anasazi/Mogollon pottery style. They segued into later types
such as Kiet Siel from Hopi and Heshotauthla from Zuni and persisted up to

the sixteenth century when pottery trade between the Pueblos almost
disappeared.
   Some of the type names of prehisoric pottery piqued our curiosity. We
wondered about “Show Low” until we actually visited the town and found
that the main artery is named Deuce of Clubs Street. The name “Fourmile”
proved less colorful. We wondered “four miles from what?” Answer: the
name comes from Four Mile Wash, just outside the town of Taylor, a bit
south of St. Johns and not far from Show Low. It’s in the mountains of
eastern Arizona where the Anasazi, Salado, Mogollon and Sinagua cultures
overlapped.
    Archeologists never stop arguing about who overlapped whom. Books
written before the mid-1980s call Four Mile and White Mountain Redware
Anasazi. However, in a display of aggressiveness they never exhibited
during their existence, the Mogollon have grabbed an alarming amount of
territory since then. Without shooting a single arrow, they’ve snatched away
Snowflake, Reserve, Wingate, St. Johns, Tularosa, Puerco and a dozen other
pottery types from the Anasazi.
  A lot of their leap forward in academic circles stems from rock art
evidence that the Katsina (or Kachina) Cult, a belief system which swept
through the Pueblos in the fourteenth century, came up from Mogollon
country in southeast New Mexico. From 1300 on, we see katsina images on
pottery from everywhere, which makes it look like the Mogollon were
running things back then.

The pitcher at top left is early black on red, cruder than most. The design
looks Anasazi, but the piece, like all the others on this page, is Mogollon.
The ladle has a more elegant treatment. The black-on-red bowl to the right
of the pitcher comes from the Rio Puerco—Pig River, named for
thejavelinas that populate the White Mountains. Puerco pottery uses bold,
black pennant shapes with linear mazes that are often more intricate than
they first appear.
   Early in the black-on-red period, potters put white decorations on the
outsides of black-on-red bowls and created Wingate and St. Johns
Polychrome. This three-color look caught on so well it became the
dominant pottery decoration style throughout the last years of the
prehistoric Southwest. We think of Hopi pottery as being yellow and Zuni
pottery as being white, but when we get to Hopi and Zuni on the next four
pages, you’ll see red polychromes.
   The Four Mile bowls in the picture all have a high-probability Four
Mile characteristic, the lifeline on the interior rim with a ceremonial break
like the Salado used on Gila Polychrome. Choice Four Mile examples have
a heavily decorated interior, but many, like the two bowls in the center, left

the insides blank except for the lifeline. Cedar Creek and Pinedale
Polychromes are allied types from the late days of White Mountain redware.
The Pinedale bowl is a modest, off-center example, but the Cedar Creek
bowl surprises us with parrots. A Pinedale four pages ahead shows how far
White Mountain redware evolved.
   The little red Show Low seed jar at left center came at the end of the
black-on-red period, by the time black on red had said all it had to say. Up
at Show Low, they were far more interested in polychromes, and the Show
Low jar at the right shows what they really liked to do up in that corner of
the White Mountains.

HOPI – THE YELLOW POTTERY

The ones who didn’t vanish. The latter-day universal popularity of red
pottery forced us to equivocate about giving that color entirely to the Salado
and the Sinagua, but there’s no ambiguity about yellow and the Hopi.





   The Hopi have had a separate identity longer than any other Southwest
group for three reasons: isolation, language and pottery. Their three mesas
in northern Arizona northeast of Flagstaff have kept them relatively
undisturbed for the last thousand years. Old Oraibi, on Second Mesa, goes
back to the twelfth century and might be the oldest continually inhabited
city in the United States. If you walk across the parking lot, you’ll step on

thousands of tiny Anasazi sherds, broken and rebroken through the
centuries.
   Hopi’s Uto-Aztecan language may have been what the Anasazi spoke,
but no other Puebloans speak it. As for pottery, the yellow clay set Hopi
apart. Other than briefly in the sixteenth century, when the Zuni
experimented with yellow polychrome, all the people in our Southwest
made and still make pots on gray, buff, red or brown clay.
    Until 1150 or so, yellow-to-orange pottery meant the Anasazi who
settled in northern Arizona and southern Utah and whom archeologists,
ethnologists and the Hopi themselves agree were the Hopi’s direct
ancestors.
   The Hopis don’t like it when you use the name Anasazi. You force them
to listen to the Navajo word that describes their forebears as ancient
enemies. Both historically and in modern politics, Hopi and Navajo have
lived side-by-side in an uneasy relationship. The Hopis much prefer the
name Hisatsinom, a Hopi word for “long-ago people,” but if you can’t
pronounce it, you’re okay with Ancestral Puebloans. We use the word
Anasazi in this book only for clarity, with no slight intended.
   The Ancestrals first made orange-to-yellow pottery about 600. When
the Sinagua lived by the Hopi, they made yellowish plainware, really more
red than yellow. Today we see the Sinagua as a separate culture, but Hopi
elders identify Sinagua artifacts as belonging to modern Hopi clans.
   About 1150, northern Anaszi redware became orange. Jeddito Black-on-
orange appeared by 1250, and Jeddito Black-on-yellow after 1300. During
those years, the Anasazi built pueblos on the Hopi mesas, and now it’s clear
that by then, they weren’t Anasazi any more, they were Hopi.
   Ever since, yellow-to-orange pottery has meant the Hopi, who have
lived on and near their mesas for a thousand years. Jeddito lasted almost
until 1600, then segued to yellow and then red polychrome styles, and
finally into the yellow Sikyatki, San Bernardo and Payupki polychromes
that define modern Hopi pottery.

They made this 500years before they were Hopi Abajo Black on orange, 10⅛" diameter, circa 650

   The big red olla on the opposite page is something else. For a few years
around 1350, adventurous Hopi went south and made pottery that looks
almost like their homegrown Kiet Siel Polychrome. But Maverick
Mountain Polychrome used to be called Tucson Polychrome, which tells
how far south the Hopi wandered.
   This continuity of style makes Hopi pottery unique among the
Southwestern wares. Most modern pottery appeared rather suddenly, taking
shapes and using clays and slips that differentiate it from prehistoric wares
nearby. You can’t take a fifteenth-century pot from the Puyé Ruin and
compare it to a modern piece made across the road at Santa Clara Pueblo
and see the connection. But Hopi pottery has a clear, unbroken link to those
supposedly vanished ancestors.
   When you look at Hopi pottery, it’s hard to believe in disappearances.

Experts choose to call the little Kayenta Anasazi piece on the right red
rather than orange, but it foreshadowed the future.
   The Jeddito pieces show a wide range of design. Much Jeddito was
complex and mannered in design, picking up on the Anasazi styles of the
day and replicating them in black on yellow and orange, as on the pitcher
and jar on the right of the middle row. The bowl below them is down the
middle of the style of the day. The design would look at home on a dozen
different Anasazi, Mogollon and Salado types. The bowl at left in the bottom
row gives an idea of the range of design inventiveness in later prehistoric
pottery. It was fired unevenly, to the point where it almost makes you think
it’s a black and red polychrome. The bowl with the three fish came as a total
surprise, completely off the design chart.
   The Hopi succumbed gradually to the fashion of the day, first by adding
a white outline around the black design to create Bidahochi Polychrome.
Next, they added red and simplified the geometry to make Tusyan

Polychrome. Then they went all the way to redware as on the Homohvi bowl
and the off-campus Maverick Mountain olla.
   The Bidahochi at the left of the middle row and the one below it to its
right also tell us a bit about Hopi lifestyle and what they admired back then.
They both show parrots, exotic creatures imported from the south, with
feathers prized for ornament. In the Hopi landscape, bright greens and
bright reds were a rare sight.
   From there, the Hopi went back to yellowware. Next came Sikyatki
Polychrome like the ladle in the frontispiece, and then on to modern times,
when nineteenth-century potters brought back the styles from earlier days.

ZUNI – THE MELTING POT

The crossroads. If there was a Great Melting Pot in our Southwest, it was
along the northern Arizona–New Mexico border. Between 1400 and 1600,
Zuni Pueblo sat at the confluence of four cultures.
  Up in the northwest, the western Anasazi and the Sinagua had become
the Hopi. The eastern branch of the Anasazi still occupied the northeast, but
sparsely. The Mogollon lived in the southeast, and the Salado lived in the
southwest.
   Most books connect the Zuni with the Anasazi and remind us that there
was a prehistoric road between Zuni and the great Anasazi settlement at
Chaco Canyon. But the fit isn’t quite that tidy. The Zuni language falls so
far outside all the Southwestern language groups that Nancy Yaw Davis, a
Ph.D. anthropologist, wrote a book called The Zuni Enigma. She suggested
that both the Zuni language and glaze paint, a Zuni contribution to
Southwest pottery, came about because a group of monks sailed from Japan
in the thirteenth century and found their way from California to Zuni.
   Hard-nosed academics dismiss books that strain to connect prehistoric
America with Europe and Asia as diffusionist pseudoarcheology, but The
Zuni Enigma made us smile at little things we’ve wondered about. In
Gallup, I-40 crosses the Miyamura Drive exit, named after a World War II
hero.
   You don’t have to look across the Pacific to find cross-culturation in
Zuni art. Just look at the next page. Zuni pottery took influences from
Anasazi, Salado, Hopi and Mogollon alike, and influenced them right back,
starting with glaze paint.

The earliest style anyone calls Zuni Springerville Polychrome, 8½" diameter, circa 1300

   Southwestern pottery isn’t glazed like commercial ceramics. Its shine
comes from polishing. A bit before 1400, the Zuni started using a thick
copper-based black paint that fired into a shiny glaze. Copper or lead glaze
paint shows up on pots from around Zuni, along the Rio Grande around
Albuquerque, and in Casas Grandes on a late type called Carretas
Polychrome.

Glazes were almost gone by 1650, which must have improved the
health of the potters, who no longer worked with lead- or mercury-
contaminated paintbrushes. Before and since, paints have been nontoxic,
boiled-down plants and earth colors.
   Zuni glaze pottery underscores the cultural mingling. Some of it looks
like an extension of the prevailing Four Mile styles of the day, some looks a
lot like Salado polychromes, while other pieces almost look like Anasazi
black on white, and on one of our pieces, even picks up the Mogollon
Tularosa swirls.
    (Parenthetical aside: Al was embarrassed at a museum presentation
when someone asked him to explain the difference between glaze paint and
other mineral paints, and while he was waffling, a museum employee bailed
him out by explaining that silicon-based glazes create a glass-like surface.
This gave A1 his “well, duh” revelation: glaze = glazier = glass, which
he’ll remember for the rest of his life.)
    There’s a Zuni-Mimbres connection as well. The Mimbres had scattered
by 1250, but the kill holes stuck around on Carretas ware at Casas Grandes

and also on Zuni’s sixteenth-century Matsaki bowls. Matsaki can have kill
holes, but it imitates Hopi yellowware, and kill holes have nothing to do
with any Hopi custom.
   We’re left with enigmatic questions. Like why an outlying Zuni Pueblo
is named Matsaki.

allied that we put a White Mountain Pinedale bowl at the left to show how
close the wavelength was.
   Then, at upper center, we have one of the most surprising pieces in the
John & Al Museum: Tularosa Swirls, just like they did them 200years
earlier in the mountains to the east, but in glaze paint. You can’t see it in the
picture, but just to let you know it’s not one of those old-fashioned black-on-
whites, it has a discreet red stripe around the base. Sitting to its right,
there’s glaze paint at its drippiest on a jar whose shape and design
philosophy seems to have been lifted directly from Salado polychromes.
   The small ladle front right has a black-on-white Anasazi feel, but no
Anasazi pot ever had a black paint that turned red on one side of the pot
and green on the other, as it did on the little ladle. The white polychrome
glaze bowls came a century or so later.
   The yellow bowls at the top and in the middle are Zuni’s sixteenth-
century shift in direction—no glaze paint, a Hopi look and a strange
tendency to have Mimbres-style kill holes.
   The low bowl at upper left is the last Zuni glaze type. After they played
around with Hopi yellow, the Zuni went back to glazes and got even more
cosmopolitan. The latest thinking suggests that Hawikuh Glaze Polychrome
is a combined Zuni and Acoma type, and that the piece in the picture is just
as apt to be from Acoma as it is from Zuni.
   Many questions, almost no answers.

CASAS GRANDES – LAST ONES OUT

Down Mexico way, serious players. In 700, according to Charles Di Peso,
whose research described this culture, the Casas Grandes area of Chihuahua
had a primitive agrarian population.

He explaiued the magificent ruins of Paquimé as the remnants of a
northern distribution center built by traders who represented the business
interests of advanced central Mexican cultures. Between 1250 and 1450
Paquimé became the Southwest’s biggest city—the casas grandes reported
by Spanish explorers.
    In Di Peso’s view, perhaps a thousand villages across Chihuahua and
Sonora were Paquimé outliers, suppliers of goods that went to the Anasazi,
Hohokam, Sinagua, Hopi and Zuni: copper bells, macaw feathers and the
macaws themselves. A vast irrigation system with thousands of check
dams, terraces and trenches brought water to the empire, and these
trincheras still exist today.
   Nothing else in the Southwest rivaled Paquimé for opulence, not even
Chaco Canyon, 400 miles north and 200 years older. Writers suggest a
Paquimé/Chaco archeological connection, but the pottery disagrees.

Chaco’s quiet black-on-white has little to with the exuberant colors and
designs of Casas.
    Apparently, Paquimé missed the Spanish conquistadores by about
fifteen minutes. There are pots on the opposite page that might have been
made as late as 1500. Cortez landed in 1519. In 1565, Baltasar de Obregon
wrote that Paquimé looked like a great city built by the ancient Romans. It
was no ancient ruin, it was a fairly recent ghost town.
   What happened? There’s evidence of a large-scale massacre and
burning. Circumstantial evidence suggests the recently arrived Apache.
Behavioral evidence points to the Aztecs, whom the Spanish recorded as
sacrificing unfortunates by the tens of thousands. It might have been
internal strife. The gruesome little effigy on the opposite page suggests
religious undertones of the sort that, in our day, cause people to blow each
other up.
     If the survivors of Paquimé ran, where to? Look at the pots. Escondida
Polychrome looks like Salado Polychrome, which looks like polychromes
from Zuni with shiny glaze paint like on Carretas Polychrome. We’ve seen
a Carretas bowl with a Mimbres-style kill hole. Madera Black-on-red looks
like El Paso Polychrome, made by the Rio Grande Jornada people between
El Paso and Santa Fe.





           Casas in the Viejo days Anchondo Red-on-brown, 6½" diameter, circa 750

But, as we keep reminding ourselves, we’re too sophisticated to believe
that pottery equals people. So officially, the people of Casas Grandes
vaporized, just like everyone else.
   And unofficially? Try this: Anasazi west to Hopi and east to the Rio
Grande Pueblos. Mogollon splitting, northern group merging with the
Anasazi to populate Zuni, Acoma and beyond, southern group including the
Mimbres to Casas Grandes and on to Tarahumara. Hohokam splitting, some
to California, some to Paquimé. And what was left of Paquimé, scattering in
all directions. Some of this may have been prompted by Navajo and Apache
raids, although their time periods barely overlapped, and some perhaps by
an occasional outbreak of hantavirus, the “Navajo flu” that frightened the
country in the 1990s.
   Okay, none of the above may be true, but at least it’s tidy.

At first, Casas Grandes pottery didn’t give much hint of where it was
headed. The piece on the opposite page looks like present-day Tarahumara
pottery, and the red incised Playas piece looks like Mississippian pottery
from Texas.
     It didn’t take long for the pottery to hit stride, first with painting on the
incised pieces and later with more elaborate painting and what seems to be
a Casas invention, the hooded effigy, a jar with an attached head. It came in
many human and animal forms. Here, mixed in with the owl and the people,
there’s one that substitutes a gourd for the head. The bird in the front row
has lost his strap handle, but he demonstrates the design extravagance that
makes the best examples of Casas ware the showiest of all Southwestern
prehistorics.
   The Escondida pieces look Salado, which gave ammunition to the early
scholars who looked for connections between Hohokam and Casas,
especially those who thought the Salado were Hohokam. Current thinking
sees Escondida as a later copy of traded-in Salado ware.

Pure black is rare in prehistory. Now we identify polished blackware
with the Rio Grande Pueblos, but Casas potters really understood black.
Ramos Black is light, thin, deep in color and high-fired, almost like
porcelain.
    Finally, the bowl in the middle is the mysterious Carretas Polychrome.
Its glaze paint and kill holes tantalize us with who-went-where clues that, so
far, aren’t all accepted as evidence in the great Archeological Courtroom.

RIO & GRANDE – PREHISTORY LINGERS

An era ends, but not abruptly. During most of the Southwest’s prehistory,
the fertile lands along the Rio Grande were lightly populated. In the 1300s,
migration increased and the area started to fill. By the fifteenth century,
what was left of the northern Anasazi met others from Cibola and the south
and found their way to the Rio Grande. The Pueblos of today began to take
shape.
   Archeology gives the broad picture, and pottery fills in some of the
blanks. We know there were significant settlements at Bandelier in the
mountains west of San Ildefonso Pueblo, on the hill at Puyé next to Santa
Clara Pueblo and in the hills above Jemez, and that they made their share of
Anasazi-looking black-on-white.
   Glaze paints weren’t part of the Anasazi culture north of Santa Fe.
Those fifteenth- and sixteenth-century black-on-whites had a matte finish
and vegetal paint, and Eurocentric observers named them biscuitware after
nineteenth-century French bisque porcelain. New Mexico’s biscuitware
shows up in the two odd ashtray-looking examples on the opposite page,
one from Jemez and one from Bandelier. The other white pieces in the
picture use black glaze paint.
   The glazes came in from the south, most likely by way of Zuni. By
1500, the Zuni had set aside glaze paint in favor of their side-trip to Hopi
and yellow pottery, but the technology caught on in the Pueblos from
Acoma east to the Rio Grande and north and south from Albuqerque.
Where Zuni glaze paint was copper-based and turned green, the glaze on
Rio Grande ware was usually lead-based and fired to a thick, messy, super-
shiny black. One observer told us while he was examining an array of late
Rio Grande glazeware, “They were great potters, but they were lousy
painters.”
Prehistory’s last gasp. Gobernador Glaze Black-on-gray, 9½" diameter, circa 1700

Glaze paint gradually disappeared as populations diminished in the
glazeware Pueblos. We can’t be sure that lead glazes contributed to
population shrinkage at deserted Pueblos like Pecos and San Lazaro, but it’s
a safe bet that they didn’t help. Glazes persisted here and there through the
1500s and on into the 1600s.
   Once the Spanish settled into New Mexico after the 1580s, we were
officially out of the prehistoric era and into the times of recorded history.
Not all the Indians got caught up in that historic flow, however, and Spanish
chronicles leave a lot out. That’s why scholars came up with the word
“protohistoric” to describe pieces like the ones on the next page that fall
into a messy gap between archeology’s theoretical reconstruction and
proper written history.
   You can argue that in one isolated corner of northwest New Mexico,
prehistory and prehistoric glazeware pottery lasted for more than a hundred
years after the Spanish came. The glazeware tradition’s final quiver of life
came in the hard times after the 1692 Reconquest that followed the 1680

Pueblo Revolt. As Spanish control tightened, several hundred fugitives
from Jemez and other Pueblos made their way west to Gobernador Canyon,
an isolated area in Navajo country.
   They settled there for a few decades, free of Spanish control, and lived
with the Navajo in a prehistoric lifestyle. Together, Puebloans and Navajos
made crude pottery that sometimes had black glaze paint like the bowl at
the left.
   When the last stragglers turned out the lights at Gobernador in the
eighteenth century, prehistory was finally done.

This gives you a look at the last moments of the Southwest’s prehistory. The
oldest piece in the picture is the fifteenth-century Bandelier biscuitware

bowl at the far right. People who interpret such things tell us that the
ashtray-like indentations allow the owner to sprinkle pollen to the Four
Directions. Whether or not that’s accurate, it’s true that the indentation
were according to custom. The Jemez bowl, made more than a century later,
has a similar feature.
   The two little pollen jars came from the same place. The Spanish filled
in the kiva at Pecos Pueblo and in 1910, a Native American salvaged these
at the then-abandoned Pueblo. Eventually, his grandson sold them. Like the
two four-directions bowls, these have a parallel feature. They both had lug
handles, and on both, prehistoric owners broke off one lug and sprinkled
pollen through a hole drilled where the lug used to be. The jar on the right
has messy abstract designs, but the one on the left, with thicker glaze paint,
gives us dragonflies and a stick-figure human.
   Although we know nothing for sure, it’s tempting to start speculating
about ancient religious meanings for the two little pollen jars and the two
gray four-directions bowls.
   The four large bowls straddle a century of Rio Grande glazeware and
they give a quick overview of its evolution. The early Cienguilla and
Espinoso bowls have fairly well controlled black painting and the Espinoso
manages a showy effect. The Medio bowl, fifty years later, has thicker,
messier paint and two of those Mesoamerican parrots. The Puaray bowl,
from a century after that, has paint piled on in the thickest, gooiest glaze
fashion, another example of the “they were great potters but lousy
painters” critique.

5. MODERN POTTERY





                                  Zuni, 6⅛" diameter, circa 1870

RECORDED HISTORY BEGINS with Hernan Cortez, who came in 1519, and by
1521 had conquered Mexico City and the Aztecs. He managed the feat with
only five hundred men, but his sixteen muskets undoubtedly helped.
   His success brought thousands of Europeans looking for gold, including
the improbably named Alvar Nuñez Cabeza de Vaca. Cabeza de Vaca
means “cow-head,” and his cow-headed fabrications did immense damage
to the natives of the Southwest. After a disastrous 1528 expedition that
began in Florida and included a shipwreck on the Texas coast, he spent six

years mostly as a captive of whatever Indians he encountered as he moved
west.
    In 1534, he and a Moorish slave named Estebán, or Estevancio, finally
made their way across the Rio Grande and down to the center of New Spain
in Mexico City. He told fantastic tales of the Seven Cities of Cibola, where
the houses were of gold and the doors were inlaid with turquoise, all in the
upper Rio Grande. It’s been suggested that the Aztecs in Mexico City had
seen traded-in Jeddito and Sikyatki yellowware from Hopi and were quite
willing to reinforce Cabeza de Vaca’s stories by telling the new Spanish
government of Indians to the north who drank from vessels of gold.
   His stories prompted a 1539 excursion led by Fray Marcos de Niza and
Estebán, who found their way to the Zuni Pueblo of Hawikuh. Estebán went
on ahead and the Zunis, perhaps terrified by the unexpected appearance of
this large black man, promptly did him in. In a display of cowheadedness
worthy of his original informant, the good Friar concluded that the Zunis
must have dispatched Estebán because they did in fact have a golden city to
defend. Besides, those rocks looked pretty yellow in the late afternoon light.
He went no farther. Instead, he turned the expedition around, returned to
New Spain, and gave the Viceroy his message: “We’ve found the treasure,
send an army.”
   The army was Francisco Vasquez de Coronado’s and the year was 1540
—year one of the modern, European-governed Southwest. Coronado went
to Zuni, found no gold, shot some angry Indians and moved on. He
harassed the Hopi without finding any gold there either, found the Grand
Canyon, found Acoma was too inconvenient to plunder, and moved to the
Rio Grande and the Tiguex Pueblos near modern-day Albuquerque.
   The Tiguex residents objected to the raping and pillaging, and Coronado
responded by burning the villages. Ironically, you can now visit a restored
Tiguex kiva north of Albuquerque at a national monument named in honor
of Coronado.
   By the time he returned to New Spain in 1542, Coronado had ventured
as far as Kansas, but he never found any gold.

Government, Spanish-style. The best fallout from the Coronado expedition,
as far as the Ancestral Puebloans were concerned, was that the Spanish
didn’t bother them for another forty years. But the trickle of immigrants and
adventurers began again in 1581, and by 1598, Nuevo Mexico had a

government headed by the impressively titled Governor Captain General
Juan de Oñate and a capital at Ohkay Owinge Pueblo, which he renamed
San Juan de Caballeros. Oñate established his government quickly, helped
by the fact that the Spanish had guns and horses and the Indians didn’t.
   Oñate was a loyal Catholic and a highly successful proselytizer for the
faith, at least by decree. He ordered that all Indians be immediately
converted, outlawed traditional Indian religions and banned the use of the
kiva. That was particularly significant, as the kiva served as the ceremonial
chamber and political center of the Pueblo.
   Modern accounts that portray Oñate as a villain have considerable
justification, but the outlawing of religion was less a villainous act than an
implementation of Spanish policy. A country smaller than Texas couldn’t
have enough soldiers and support staff to manage most of the land in the
Western Hemisphere. The only way the system could work was to enlist the
Indians as allies. The most convenient method of conscription and the one
that worked best was conversion to the Faith.
   By the time the Pilgrims hit Plymouth Rock, the building boom was on
in New Mexico. Most Pueblos had resident padres who cared more about
the spiritual welfare of the Indians than for their physical well-being. The
first order of business was usually the construction of an imposing mission,
built with backbreaking effort by forced labor.
    In dry years, the Spanish taxed the Indians to the brink of starvation,
and young padres soon learned that unbending authority backed by the local
militia was the only way they could control their reluctant parishioners. The
padres bullied and flogged their way through most of the seventeenth
century. Eventually, the Puebloans could stand no more. In 1675, the
authorities arrested forty-seven tribal leaders on witchcraft charges and
hanged or publically whipped them. Had they foreseen the future, they
would have hanged one more.

The Pueblo Revolt. An Ohkay Owinge leader named Popé escaped the
noose but didn’t forget the injustice. He spent five years figuring out how to
get rid of the Spanish, and on August 10, 1680, heavily armed warriors
from nearly every Pueblo attacked the Spanish in outlying villages and the
countryside. They killed more than four hundred men, women and children,
including twenty priests, and burned most of the great missions to the
ground.

A week later, they attacked Santa Fe, by then the capital of Nuevo
Mexico, and the governor and fifteen hundred refugee Spanish fled to El
Paso. Once again, the Pueblos were free of foreign control. The paradise
didn’t last. After an abortive effort in 1681, the Spanish hit hard in 1688,
sacking and burning Zia and killing six hundred residents.
    In 1692, it was over. Don Diego de Vargas rode north from El Paso with
two hundred soldiers and entered Santa Fe without firing a shot. The war-
weary Indians capitulated and accepted Catholicsm and the Spanish. To this
day, Santa Fe celebrates the heroism of de Vargas and the bloodless
restoration in the annual Fiesta de Santa Fe.
   Of course, it wasn’t quite bloodless. De Vargas had to recapture Santa
Fe by force a year later, and in the process, slaughtered quite a few Indians
before he gained a semblance of control.

Two more governments. During the eighteenth century, the misery evolved.
There were fewer atrocities, but there was hunger, hardship, Navajo and
Apache raids, a smallpox epidemic, and despite a better accommodation
with the Church, efforts to submerge native religion continued. Life
remained grim for the Pueblo people, and once-great Pueblos dwindled and
vanished.
    In 1821, Spain ceded the Southwest to Mexico, which brought new
bureaucrats and new regulations, but the culture shock was mild compared
to what was to come.
    In 1846, America took over. The good news: T,he Indians were now
free of enforced Catholicism. The bad news: They suffered new regulations,
new officials who spoke an unfamiliar language, and missionaries every bit
as enthusiastic as the padres who had hectored them for centuries. Now
Methodists and Mormons were in charge, but the message was the same:
Join our church or else.
     It’s not difficult to understand why today’s Pueblo Indians remain
secretive about the details of their religion. If you’d spent four hundred
years being told by people with guns that your religion was not only false
but against the law, you’d be a bit hesitant to talk about it, too.
   When the Americans poured in during the second half of the nineteenth
century, some good things happened as well. A new class of citizens
emerged: the Indian traders. Their motives may have been commercial, but

they were smart enough to realize that their own welfare was directly
connected to the welfare of the Indians.
   Government efforts for the first hundred years of American
administration were focused on making the Indians good tax-paying,
English-speaking citizens. Church efforts focused on making the Indians
good Christians. Neither group was particularly interested in how the
Indians felt or what the Indians wanted.
   The traders, however, needed the Indian artists and craftworkers. They
learned the Indian languages and looked after the Indians’ needs. Those
traders, as much as anyone, are responsible for what’s in the rest of this
book.


ACOMA


The People of the White Rock. Acoma (the natives pronouce it ACK-oma)
is in New Mexico, south of I-40 between Grants and Albuquerque. It’s a
sprawl of villages—Acomita, McCartys, Anzac, San Fidel and Seama—
with three thousand people spread over four hundred square miles of
farmland. But it’s hard to think of it that way.
   Every visitor to Acoma who gets past the casino on the highway is
drawn to Sky City, the old Pueblo of Acoma, America’s most implausible
seven acres of real estate. It claims to be the oldest continuously occupied
settlement in the United States. Although the Hopi village of Old Oraibi
probably has a stronger case for the distinction, Sky City is undoubtedly
ancient.
     It’s also spectacular: a sheer-sided 350-foot high mesa covered with
connected adobe homes, great pools in the natural rock and a seventeenth-
century church that defies belief. Today there’s a bulldozed road, and you
can ride the tour bus up to the mesa. In 1629, though, when Fray Juan
Ramirez began building the church, every sack of sand for the adobe walls
had to be carried up the narrow accesses, one step at a time, and every
timber for the roof beams had to be carried from Mount Taylor, thirty miles
away.

They dipped for water in a sandstone well
                                  11" diameter, circa 1880

   And yet, there’s the church: 60-foot high walls, 10 feet thick at the base,
a 150-foot-long hall under a roof supported by 40-foot long, 14-inch square
timbers resting on massive sculptured corbels, all carved with stone tools. It
stands as mute testimony to the amount of labor the priests could extract
from the natives.
   As proof of Sky City’s inaccessibility, even the greedy Coronado
wouldn’t attempt it. One of his lieutenants said it flatly: “No army could
possibly be strong enough to capture the village.”
   Once the bus gets you to the mesa, you can take the old stairs back
down. While you’re navigating them, you can think about how, over the
centuries, those stairs must have been made into a more visitor-friendly
passage than the mission-builders climbed in 1629.
   Coronado’s lieutenant underestimated future armies. In 1599, Vincente
de Zaldivar and his troops gained the mesa top, dragging a cannon up with
them. Under Governor Oñate’s orders, they pacified the uncooperative

Indians by killing six hundred and taking six hundred others prisoner. To
ensure the peace, Oñate sentenced the surviving women to slavery and cut
one foot off every surviving male. Even so, it took another hundred years
for a defeated Acoma to submit to Spanish rule. And today, more than four
hundred years later, New Mexicans still wince at the memory.
    In Acoma legend, the sacred twins led their ancestors to Ako, their
forever home, a magical white rock with the whitest, finest clay in all the
Southwest. Since the eighteenth century, Acoma potters have made thin-
walled, large ollas, slipped in pure white and decorated in red and black, a
description that hardly begins to suggest the intricate and dramatic designs
that characterize Acoma pottery.





    In 1880, the railroad came to neighboring Laguna, bringing traders and
tourists. Acoma pottery adapted almost immediately. Since tourists couldn’t
fit fourteen- and sixteen-inch storage jars in their suitcases, potters and
traders devised a whole new class of eccentric little pieces.
   From 1750 to the present, however, Acoma’s standard for fine pottery
has been defined by the large, thin-walled white olla. Tempered with the
ground-up sherds of broken pottery, the surface of a smooth, softly polished
Acoma jar has a matte velvet feel that ware from other Pueblos seldom
approaches.

This is the pottery that brought immediate attention to Acoma more than a
century ago. These were all made between 1880 and 1930, and all except
the canteen and three small pieces in the front row have the traditional
indented bottom, the better to provide stability when carried on one’s head.
Or, for more mundane practicality, the better to help it sit flat on a table.
   The black-on-white 1895 olla at lower right center has a design that
echoes pieces from the mid-nineteenth century. The earlier one on the
opposite page lived a full, hard life, collecting water from the sandstone
pools on the Mesa top, abrading the rim with every refilling. That olla
wasn’t made for tourists, it was made to be used, and the wear on it puts it
in a special category, distinguished from “railroad pots” from the same
period: the ones bought at the railroad station and taken east on the train.
   Acoma design often displays strikingly dramatic graphics. They could
be surprisingly asymmetrical, as on the pitcher at bottom right. Sometimes

Acoma potters would borrrow designs, like the Zuni birds and volutes on
the olla at bottom left or the Tularosa swirls on the olla at top center
(attributed to Mary Histia, Acoma’s most celebrated potter of the first half
of the twentieth century). Every so often, they’d put a new spin on an old
design, like the orange Tularosa swirl on the vase at front center.
   Two pieces, the jar with the abraded and smoothed rim at top left and
the bowl down front have a touch of the dark red paint that disappeared for
almost a century in the early 1900s. Old Acoma “four colors” that include
some of that dark red along with the orange are prized today.
   Acoma could be painstakingly traditional, but every so often, potters
would set the rules aside. The olla in the center has a Hopi yellow slip,
almost never seen at Acoma.


ACOMA – FOR THE TOURIST

Anything goes, as long as it’s cute and “Indian.” The olla may represent
the highest achievement of the Acoma potter’s art, but through the 1960s,
even the most respected Acoma potters would ignore the purist collector
and earn a living making unashamed tourist pieces. When they worked in
the tourist mode, none of them seemed to care whether the designs came
from an Acoma tradition, from a picture in a magazine, or from a drawing
handed to them by a trader who knew exactly what the tourists were
looking for.

1910: pocket-sized

    Large-scale tourist production didn’t happen overnight. It began quietly
in the 1880s when the railroad came to the Pueblo next door, and Santa Fe
traders were building a curio market in their shops. At first, they just bought
whatever the Pueblo potters were making, but they quickly caught on to
tourist tastes and suggested shapes, designs and suitcase-friendly sizes for
the potters. After 1900, pieces got smaller and smaller. The little jar in the
picture above is only three-and-a-half inches high.
   The railroad stopped a few miles east of Acoma at Laguna, almost
within walking distance and an easy cart ride. It didn’t take potters long to
learn that if they brought pieces to the station, tourists would get off the
train and buy them. By 1900, making pottery for tourists was an important
part of the Acoma economy, and hundreds of pieces left on the trains for the
east and west coasts.
   By 1920, tourist pottery was Acoma’s leading industry. The pieces on
the next page give an idea of the unlimited assortment of shapes and of the
range of pottery skills involved. The turtle is by Mary Histia (1881–1973),
the “Acoma Mary” supposedly pictured on a famous postcard and the best-
known Acoma potter before Lucy Lewis and Marie Chino came into
prominence. The olla with the Tularosa swirls on the previous page
suggests why she reached her level of fame.
   Most of these tourist pieces are unsigned or signed “Acoma, N.M.” on
the bottom. At least almost always. The pitcher at far right on the next page
has it written on the footed base. The Acoma N.M. pieces were made
between 1920 and 1965, a time when Acoma potters felt that it was an
inappropriate display of ego to put one’s name on a pot. Potters’ signatures
first appeared on Acoma pottery in the 1950s and weren’t universal at the
Pueblo until the 1970s.
   The latter days of that period were also a time of embarrassment for
Acoma’s potters. Inexplicably, Acoma’s beautiful clay developed
impurities, and those impurities led to spalling: little pits that pop out during
and after firing and occasionally months after. Spalling became so prevalent
that Acoma’s potters just about gave up. In other times, as now, the rare pot
that spalled was ground up for temper. Back then, such a high percentage
spalled that even the best potters sold them anyway. You can look at a
spalled Acoma pot and say “1960” and be pretty close.

1960s: spalled

  No one was exempt. The next four pages include spalled pots by two of
Acoma’s most revered potters, Lucy Lewis and Marie Chino—pieces that
under other conditions, neither would have admitted to, much less signed
proudly.
   From the 1970s into the 1990s, Acoma’s tourist pottery production
comprised largely of greenware, some painted, some with incised designs,
all made for sale at gift shops and cut-rate Indian stores often owned by
people from some other continent. By the 2000s, those pieces and those
stores were disappearing. Today’s Acoma tourist pottery has more integrity,
like Dorothy Patricio’s basket in the front row. Although now they're mostly
fired in an electric kiln, current tourist pieces look and feel a lot more like
the good ones from the old days.

The pristine ashtray in the bottom row says a lot. The very fact that it’s an
ashtray tells how little Southwestern potters cared (and care) about utility
when it came to making curios for the tourist. Unglazed Southwestern
pottery makes terrible ashtrays, all fated to be stained forever after their
first encounter with a cigarette. The design is the “Thunderbird,” an
omnipresent motif on ashtrays and other tourist pottery after 1910. The
design evokes the Russian double eagle, and writers have suggested it
actually was created by an early-twentieth-century Albuquerque trader.
   Cute figurines sold well, and there was a slightly longer tradition
behind them. As early as the late nineteenth century, interest in pre-
Columbian figurines from Mexico prompted Santa Fe traders to offer
grotesques from the potters of Cochiti, Tesuque, Zuni, Acoma and Laguna
as ancient pottery. Mary Histia’s turtle, Connie Cerno's owl at lower left,
the owl on the right and the turkey are all much less grotesque than their
predecessors.

From 1930 on, inspiration came from everywhere. Pitchers and
canteens were commonplace, almost none of them meant to hold water, as
were little vases not really meant to hold flowers. Rattles were never
common. The few that were made, too fragile to survive handling by babies,
were probably made for dances. And then as now, wedding vases with
cowheads were scarce.
   Not all tourist pieces were suitcase-friendly smalls. The big one in the
back row with the Tularosa swirl is a serious piece of pottery, but it gives
away its for-the-tourist origin. The wedding vase shape and the rope handle
were tourist crowd-pleasers.


ACOMA – LUCY LEWIS

The Seven Families #1: Lewis. In 1974, the Maxwell Museum at the
University of New Mexico had a showing by members of seven families of
Pueblo potters, each descended from a celebrated matriarch—Lucy Lewis
and Marie Chino of Acoma, Maria Martinez and Rose Gonzales of San
Ildefonso, Sara Fina Tafoya and Lela Gutierrez of Santa Clara and
Nampeyo of Hano (the Nampeyo) from Hopi.
   The exhibit had a profound effect on the development of modern
pottery, and the thin little catalog remained in print until the 1990s. The
show gave the anointed families a great leap ahead in the marketplace,
much to the frustration, we suppose, of deserving families that weren’t
included. At Acoma alone, one could make a compelling argument that
Jessie Garcia and Juana Leno were as deserving to be considered as
matriarchs, and, in terms of today’s family importance, the almost-forgotten
Dolores Sanchez was probably the most powerful matriarch of all.
   The Seven Families lead has shrunk over the years. Rick Dillingham,
the exhibit’s original curator, wrote Fourteen Families in Pueblo Pottery,
which came out in 1994. The original seven’s jump-start, however, was
strong enough to attach premium prices to their work into the twenty-first
century, and the seven matriarchs’ names continued to get attention when
other, equally deserving artists became yesterday’s news.
    In her time, Lucy Martin Lewis (1900?–1992) became the most famous
Acoma potter, second only to Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso, the best-
known of all Southwestern potters. Lucy began her career in the 1920s and

had a following by the 1940s. She and Marie Chino started signing their
pots around 1950, and by the late 1950s, the two of them had brought
sufficient attention to their use of prehistoric design motifs to create a new
fashion in Acoma pottery.
   Many writers credit this design influence to Kenneth Chapman of the
Museum of New Mexico. As Jesse Fewkes had introduced Nampeyo to
Sikyatki pottery at Hopi years earlier, Chapman encouraged Lucy to study
the museum’s extensive collection of Anasazi and Mimbres pottery.
   However, all this could hardly have been a revelation to Lucy. She’d
been exposed to Anasazi and Mogollon Black-on-white sherds all through
her life, and, like other Acoma potters, was already doing Tularosa-inspired
hatched designs when she met Chapman. Back then, Acoma potters didn’t
particularly care which ground-up sherds they used as temper, and
prehistoric ones are so plentiful in the trash dumps around the mesa that
we’ve seen potters sell nice big ones for fifty cents each.
   The two jars at left were made thirty years apart by two of Lucy’s
daughters. For the inspiration for the lightning bolts on these and on the
orange one by a third daughter on the next page, check out the Tularosa jar
on the right of the picture on page 31.

Lucy lived to see six children become highly regarded Acoma potters,
and to see her son Ivan become equally well known for his work at Cochiti.
The family tradition has eroded under the pressure of modern life, however.
None of her adult grandchildren became well-known potters.
   However, Lucy's daughters still had energy after 2000. Dolores and
Emma remained active while the youngest, Carmel, born in 1947, continued
to produce surprises like the cylinder jar at right on the next page.
   The picture shows more than fifty years of Acoma work by Lucy and
her children. The Mimbres figures on Lucy’s jars, made in the 1960s, and
Emma’s and Carmel’s jars, made in the 2000s, remind us how important
prehistoric elements remain in Lewis family pottery.

can see an old one on page 31.

gave us a Mimbres coatimundi and a strange man, and Emma produced the

Carmel's cylinder at the far right did something new with the geometry.
Eventually, even institutions like the Lewises move on.


ACOMA – MARIE CHINO

The Seven Families #2: Chino. Although Marie Chino and Lucy Lewis got
the same amount of attention in the Seven Families exhibit, Marie never
quite achieved Lucy’s degree of stardom. In 1984, Lucy became the subject
of a coffee-table biography, a distinction she currently shares only with
Maria Martinez and Sara Fina Tafoya’s daughter Margaret.
   This may not have been quite fair. Both Marie and Lucy had lengthy
careers, both had famous potter children, and both influenced the pottery of
their Pueblo for years.
   Marie Zieu Chino (1907–1982) was a celebrated potter from the
beginning. She was a prizewinner at the first Southwestern Indian Fair in
1922, the event that ultimately evolved into Indian Market, the World Series
of Southwestern Indian art. She and Lucy Lewis were friends as well as
competitors and occasionally did each other’s designs. Actually, according
to Betty Toulouse in her 1977 book, Pueblo Pottery of the New Mexico
Indians, Marie did black-on-white pots with fineline hatching based on
intricate prehistoric designs several years before Lucy started doing them.
Perhaps Lucy owed more to Marie Chino than the books concede.

1967 award winner
                  10¾" diameter, third prize at the Gallup Ceremonial

   Marie took her inspiration from the prehistoric sherds she found around
the Pueblo and adapted the designs to modern shapes. She may have had
other sources. Erich Erdoes, a Santa Fe dealer, told us a story that comes to
mind every time we look at a Lewis/Chino prehistoric-inspired piece, and
especially every time we see a piece like Mary Histia’s Tularosa swirls on
page 53. Erich’s family had a close friendship with an Acoma potter active
in the 1930s, and she told of a cave filled with prehistoric pottery whose
location her family had kept secret for generations. They visited it only to
learn designs for their own work. Since the northern edge of the Tularosa
mountains is within a day’s walk from Acoma, it’s no surprise that the
borrowed designs have a heavy Tularosa emphasis.
   By the 1940s, Marie and Lucy were in full stride, and the rest of Acoma
struggled to keep pace. There were potters of almost equal skills working
back then, but their reputations took longer to catch up. When Acoma
opened its beautiful new Ha’aku Museum at the foot of the mesa in 2006, it
greeted visitors with a pottery exhibit titled The Matriarchs. Of course,

Marie and Lucy were there as expected, but now two others were elevated.
Juana Leno and Jessie Garcia got equal billing.
   Marie had five potter daughters, and three achieved prestige almost
comparable to their mother’s—a body of work whose importance rivals the
total output of all seven of Lucy Lewis’s potter children. Grace, Carrie and
Rose did their mother’s designs, and each carved out a niche. Carrie Chino
Charlie (1925–2012) became the master of black-on-white fineline
hatchure. Grace Chino (1929–1995) became known for her severely precise
geometric polychromes. Rose Chino Garcia (1928–2010) produced the
most imaginative designs. In another parallel to Lucy’s life, none of Marie’s
grandchildren managed to achieve celebrity as potters.
   Today, there’s still considerable vitality in a few of the anointed Seven
Families. The Tafoya family dominates Santa Clara pottery, and the
Nampeyo family gets most of the attention at Hopi. At Acoma, however,
the Lewis/Chino influence is coming to an end. The stars of the twenty-first
century come from different bloodlines.

Like Lucy Lewis, Marie Chino also worked in the traditional Acoma mode,
and her work also suffered spalling, as the parrot jar in the center
demonstrates. And like Lucy and Jessie Garcia, she experimented with
corrugated pieces, perhaps under Kenneth Chapman's urging. But the rest
of the pieces display the style that attracted attention to Marie and her
family.
   The two tall vases and the small black-on-white jars scattered through
the picture qualify as unmistakable Chino (or Chino/Lewis) designs, and
Acoma potters still produce variations of them today. The seed jar next to
the little turkey is by a young Carrie and the larger, more typical one above
and to its right barely hint at the incredible accuracy she displayed when
she made large jars with fine hatchure. Likewise, the wedding vase was
done by a young Rose. It doesn’t suggest her mature style, and the fineline
jar at left center is more like what we'd expect from Carrie.
   The round polychrome seed jar at front left and the olla at top right
describe Grace, while the polychrome jar at right center gives a better idea
of Rose. Although her mother originally developed the design, Grace made
the jar on the left many times over, and it became something of a signature

piece, one that shows up often in books on Southwestern pottery. Rose’s jar
is more free-spirited, and the difference in approach between the two pieces
gives a neat little summary of the differences in work between the two
sisters.


ACOMA – STARS AND SUPERSTARS

Rising above it all. During the 1970s and 1980s, new phenomena
threatened to bury the old pottery traditions at Acoma. Kiln firing became
prevalent, and the economics of greenware drew more and more potters.
   The kiln’s attraction is hard to dispute. If the appeal of your work
depends on its pristine whiteness and a fire cloud destroys it, it’s relatively
easy to embrace the kiln and leave fire clouds behind forever. The only
argument against it is, “That’s not the traditional way,” and if your financial
well-being is directly related to the number of successful pots you can
produce, tradition can plummet on your priority list.
   Greenware—unfired, undecorated pottery—has an even greater
attraction. It takes hours to make a pot, and unless you’re a superb potter,
it’s apt to be less than perfect once you’ve made it. On the other hand, if
you buy a slip-cast blank, you have a well-made pot with no effort at all.
With a little care in finishing and some nice painting, the pot will bring in
enough money to make the work involved in producing a traditionally made
and fired piece seem like wasted effort. Under these pressures, the amount
of traditionally made pottery dwindled steadily through the 1980s at Acoma
while the amount of kiln-fired greenware increased.

   Most post-1990 Acoma potters resisted greenware. Although most
turned to the kiln, they stayed with traditional coiling and finishing.
     If you were a low-end potter, you could sell your greenware for almost
as much as you could sell a handmade pot. But once you built a reputation,
handmade work put you in a higher price category, and it was no longer
made sense to waste time painting slip-cast wares. Family pressures came
into play as well. If you were from a respected pottery family, senior
members made sure you kept up family standards.
   Many of the best post-1990 Acoma potters were from established
Acoma pottery families, and many of them were descendants of the
matriarchs that Acoma increasingly appreciates.
   When we saw Jessie Garcia and Juana Leno placed alongside Lucy
Lewis and Marie Chino at the Ha'aku Museum, we felt the exhibit was one
matriarch short, so we're adding Dolores Sanchez to the group. She was
nowhere near as celebrated in her lifetime as the others, but her children
and grandchildren rank as Acoma’s twenty-first century royal family. On
the next pages, you’ll see ten of them represented.
   The pots in the picture at right were made by those matriachs and by
members of the elite. Florence Aragon made homages to the old pieces.
Barbara and Joe Cerno made great traditional parrot ollas. Dorothy Torivio

created an iconic design that put her on the highest level of twentieth-
century Acoma pottery, a level she shared with Dolores Sanchez’s
granddaughters, Rebecca Lucario, Rachel Concho, Corrine Garcia and
Charmae Natseway, and with Jessie Garcia’s daughter, Stella Shutiva. All
contributed mightily to raising Acoma’s standards.

ACOMA – THE NEXT WAVE

New incentives, old pressures. If you’re a young potter at Acoma today,
you’re no longer bound by tradition. You can use commercial clay (one
euphemism for it is “storyteller clay”) and store-bought paints and run the
risk of never amounting to much, or you can do it the hard way and pay
your dues learning the craft.
   The incentives that pushed potters down the kiln-and-greenware path in
the 1970s and 1980s are disappearing. These days most potters use kilns,

but greenware is increasingly confined to junky tourist stores. New pieces
are scarcer, but older ones clutter the aftermarket. Major retailers in the
Southwest who sold large quantities of greenware in 1985 carried very little
in 1995 and almost none in 2005. They’ve phased it out because their
customers are able to recognize it and therefore to avoid it. And because
customers avoid it, more potters turn away from it in favor of more easily
saleable traditional pieces.
   The trend feeds on itself. As the market rejected greenware, the price
gap between slip-cast and hand-coiled pottery increased, making the effort
involved in doing it the old way seem more attractive. Fashion and publicity
add more pressure, and the pressure is really felt at Acoma. As once-
superhot potters like Dorothy Torivio (1946–2011) pass from the scene,
rising potters from other Pueblos move into the spotlight. In the years after
2000, few next-generation potters from Acoma have commanded the
attention and the accompanying five-figure prices that the leading Santa
Clara, San Ildefonso, Cochiti and Hopi potters have brought.

A traditional potter takes a side trip
                  Glazed ceramic jar, C. Maurus Chino, 11½" diameter, 2006

     If the direction continues, Acoma pottery has some catching up to do. It
ended the twentieth century on a high note, but it hovered around that note
ever since while other Pueblos have moved forward. The precision and
intricacy of Mata Ortiz pottery threatened and perhaps overtook Acoma’s
ownership of the precise-and-intricate genre.
   To compete with Mata Ortiz, the best potters of the new generation need
either to switch direction a bit or to approach their craft with a
competitiveness that pushes the standards even higher. If it’s thin, make it
thinner. If the lines should be fine, make them finer. If they should be
straight, make them straighter. And if the design should be fresh, make it
even fresher. The work on the next page is brilliant, but most of it is no
longer fresh news in Acoma’s corner of the Southwest. Compared to the
past, however, it’s light years ahead. If you could step in a time machine

with Frederica Antonio’s black-on-white fineline jar, Diane Lewis’s little
pitcher or almost any of the pots on the next page and take them back to
1960, Lucy Lewis and Marie Chino would have trouble believing what you
brought. Those great pioneers will remain famous for decades to come, but
neither could have made many of these pieces. However, if things progress
at the rate they’re moving right now, a time machine trip to 2050 won’t
show you the same kind of dramatic improvement.
   For today’s Golden Age to remain golden, Acoma’s potters need to
reach beyond what we see here. We suspect that potter and painter C.
Maurus Chino, who made the totally traditional Tularosa canteen on the
previous page, felt some of that restlessness when he started working with
ceramic glazes and began making spectacular jars in pigeon’s-blood red like
the piece below. Although it seems to have left Southwestern pottery
traditions behind, it honors its Acoma heritage. You can see the same
Mimbres lizards on two jars on the opposite page.
    Pieces like this suggest a future. If we had to place a bet, it would be
that Acoma’s potters will continue to expand the boundaries.

COCHITI

In the shadow of the dam. Like most of the Pueblos of the Southwest,
Cochiti (it’s pronounced CO-chitee) predates the Spanish.
   Archeology suggests that the Cochiti once occupied the Anasazi village
of Tyuonyi in the Jemez mountains to the west and moved down to their
present location by the Rio Grande long before the Spanish came.
   Coronado missed Cochiti, but the first padre arrived in 1581. Fray
Rodriguez had a brief ministry. Warriors from a nearby Pueblo dispatched
him within weeks, but the respite ended soon. The Spanish kept returning,
and by 1600, European civilization had settled in permanently. Cochiti’s
mission of San Buenaventura went up around 1630 and lasted until rebels
burned it in the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.
    After the revolt, Cochiti and Kewa Indians established a stronghold at
Cienguilla in the mountains, which came in handy after de Vargas
reappeared in 1692. A year later, as part of his bloodless return, de Vargas
stormed Cienguilla, killed twenty warriors and captured three hundred
women and children. He rounded up most of the rest, returned them to
Cochiti, and set them to work building a grand new mission. It still stands
on the main plaza. The ones who got away fled west, eventually
establishing Laguna Pueblo in 1699.
   Today, Cochiti is a 175-square-mile reserve below the gigantic Cochiti
Dam, a looming earth-fill presence that created another world above:
Cochiti Lake, with its waterskiing, golf, charterboat fishing and vacation
timeshares. Down below, Cochiti itself might be considered up-to-date,
since many of its five hundred residents commute to jobs in Santa Fe and

Albuquerque. Nonetheless, it still gives the impression of being frozen in
earlier times.
    Cochiti pottery from the late eighteenth century on has been a gray-to-
cream-to-white-slipped polychrome with black and red decoration. It
entered the tourist market early, and mono (“monkey” in Spanish) figurines
were the reason. Jonathan Batkin’s Pottery of the Pueblos of New Mexico,
1700–1940 has a photograph of pottery from the shop of L. Fisher in Santa
Fe, taken about 1880. It shows fourteen Cochiti monos including
caricatures of Anglo missionaries and Catholic priests with a sign that reads
RARE SPECIMENS—ANCIENT MONTEZUMA POTTERY TAKEN FROM RECENT
EXCAVATIONS IN NEW MEXICO—ALSO OTHER INDIAN RELICS AND FIGURINES!
Early dealers had a simple principle: If it looks old, say it’s old, and so
much the better if it also looks strange.

Early mono: an operatic diva
                                    7" tall, circa 1885

    Cochiti entered the tourist market early for two reasons. Except for
Tesuque, it’s the closest Pueblo to Santa Fe, where traders were building the
tourist market. Just as important, Cochiti is right next to Peña Blanca. In the
1870s, Peña Blanca was a wide-open Hispanic town that offered every
worldly pleasure. As a result, Cochiti’s citizens had seen city ways and
were more sophisticated about the cultures that surrounded them than their
counterparts from other Pueblos. Potters at Cochiti were well prepared to
make money by caricaturing the non-Indians around them. The diva at left
might have beeen inspired by an 1880 Peña Blanca saloon singer.





   Production of mono figurines declined between 1900 and 1960 in favor
of more conventional shapes. In the 1960s, when the tribal government
deeded part of its land for the dam and the lake, Cochiti lost its supply of
gray clay, but pottery-making continued with a pink clay base, and largely
thanks to a potter named Helen Cordero, the late 1960s and 1970s were
boom years.
   Through it all, Cochiti potters retained their sense of playfulness,
mixing humor with more than a little pointed social commentary. Now as
then, Cochiti pottery remains the funniest, the most human and the most
whimsical.
