The picture gives a further taste of Cochiti monos, mostly from the 1880 to
1930 period. Although the large figure at left center is actually from around
1940, its size, attitude and peculiar expression go straight back to the
seated and standing figures from half a century earlier. Back then, museums
brought them back East as examples of what they considered savage art
from the wild west.
   The storage jar, the canteens and the bowls show what utilitarian
Cochiti wares looked like in the early tourist/railroad days. The larger bowl
is early Cochiti ware at its most refined, and the effigy pitchers from the
same years show how far afield Cochiti potters could stretch the definition
of “utilitarian.” The howling dog at top left and the big bird on the right
are extravagant examples. (We looked at the bird’s bovine head and decided

it was a cowbird.) The operatic snail in front of it pushes the ridiculousness
quotient up another notch.
   Dating these pieces is an inexact science. We’ve chosen dates ranging
from 1880 to as late as 1950 for pieces like the large canteen at front center,
and our authority for all those dates is simply our best guess. The only thing
we can say in our defense is that styles evolved slowly at Cochiti, and all
the authoritative reference books have the same problem.
   Many of these pieces are shy about revealing their ages, but the big
lizard in the front commits perjury. We would have labeled it as a hundred
years old without a moment’s hesitation if we hadn’t known it was by
Damacia Cordero, and that she made it around 1980. Cordero was born in
1905, started potting in the 1920s, and worked into the 1980s. To see how
Damacia went from almost-centrist to off-the-charts, check out her two
storytellers on the next spread.
   The little jar at front right identified itself. If it weren’t Cochiti, why else
would it have a big C on the side?


COCHITI – STORYTELLERS

Singing mothers and Helen’s grandfather. Cochiti pottery production went
into a gradual decline as the twentieth century progressed until 1964, when
a minor, unsuccessful potter paid attention to some advice.
   Helen Cordero asked her husband’s cousin, Juanita Arquero, to teach
her how to make pottery, but none of her pieces ever came out right.
Finally, Juanita gave up on Helen’s ability to make a proper bowl or jar and
suggested she try making figurines.
   As they say, the rest is history. She began with nativity scenes and
singing mothers, open-mouthed madonna-and-child figurines that had been
a staple design at Cochiti for eighty years. A folk-art collector bought one
of her singing mothers and asked her to make a larger one with multiple
children.
   As she told it, she kept seeing visions of her grandfather, a master
storyteller who was always surrounded by children. Her first storyteller had
five children hanging off her grandfather’s figure, and the idea caught on
immediately. The one in the picture at right is a curious, really early

unsigned one. It’s much like her earlier singing mothers, but it’s a male
figure.
   The storyteller’s origin has been told so often that it leaves the
impression of Helen’s grandfather as a sterotypical sweet old grandpa.
Nothing could be further from the truth. Santiago Quintana was far more
than that. He was a historic figure, Cochiti’s first celebrity, mentioned and
quoted in half a dozen books written between 1890 and 1930. He guided
Adolph Bandelier to the Anasazi ruins near Santa Fe that became a national
monument bearing Bandelier’s name.
   Helen responded to the collector’s challenge by adding more and more
children, and other potters topped her number, piling increasing numbers of
tiny children on a giant figure, like an infestation of crawling ants.
   By 1995, hundreds of potters had made storytellers. The craze spread to
other Pueblos, and in some, like Jemez, storyteller production dominated
the Pueblo’s output during the 1970s and 1980s. In a 1986 book, The
Pueblo Storyteller,Barbara Babcock listed 237 potters by name, and
probably as many more entered the game in the following years.
   Helen Cordero’s success plunged Cochiti back into the figurine business
almost overnight. By 1975, most Cochiti potters had stopped doing
whetever they were doing and started turning out their versions of the
storyteller. A few, like Ada and Marie Suina, Louis and Virginia Naranjo,
Felecita Eustace, Dorothy Herrera and Marie Laweka developed instantly
recognizable styles. Others, like Martha Arquero, Snowflake Flower and
the capricious Damacia Cordero (Helen’s sister-in-law) stretched the
bubble. Damacia’s giant singing mother on the next page, unexpectedly
fired to black, might predate Helen’s storytellers, but we’ll never know. We
credited it to Damacia on a “who else” basis and guessed at the date.

Corderos

   None of the potters who followed Helen made storytellers that looked
more like hers than Bufiy Cordero Suina, her granddaughter. The two at the

Helen Cordero’s storytellers had motion and expression, much like the
pieces on the opposite page or Louise Suina’s 1980 effort. Others developed
recognizable styles as well.
   Somehow, storytellers by Ada Suina and her daughter Marie Suina look
like linebackers, while Louis and Virginia Naranjo’s tableta-wearing family
groups look faintly Russian. Felecita Eustace’s unmistakeable storytellers
all have a sweet expression that no one else manages. Other members of the

Suina family have their own styles, and Denia’s twenty-eight-passenger
model is this museum’s highest-population storyteller. (The number isn’t all
that impressive. We've seen a Jemez storyteller with more than two
hundred.)
     It didn’t take long for potters to start exploring the genre, and Cochiti
potters have made storytellers out of almost every animal imaginable.
Snowflake Flower made coyotes, Rose Brown made a turtle and others did
owls, frogs and bears. Bears show up a lot. Dorothy Herrera made teddy
bears and the Naranjos made theirs almost as cuddly.
   And then there was Damacia Cordero, who made anything she felt like
making. Put the two storytellers on this page next to the somethingosaurus
on page 65, and you have an array of work by an artist who defies any kind
of categorization.
   Damacia had three potter daughters, all featured here and on the next
pages: Marie Laweka, whose work was almost as off-center as her
mother’s, Josephine Arquero, who made elegant figures, and Martha
Arquero who appears on the next pages and has a major role in post-2000
Cochiti pottery development.


COCHITI – BEYOND THE STORYTELLERS

Forward into the past. Nothing lasts forever. As the thirty-year dominance
of the storyteller wound down, Cochiti potters looked back to where they’d
been a century before and built on it, to the point where Cochiti artists are
now in the forefront of Southwestern art.
   This reversion to the past was probably overdue. The art establishment
had saddled figurative Southwestern pottery with a century-long
discouragement. It took until the 1990s for curators and dealers to look at
Cochiti figurines as anything other than low-end tourist kitsch.
   Back in the days of L. Fisher’s fleece-the-gullible marketing techniques,
hundreds of Cochiti mono figurines found their way to museums back East.
Once in the museums, experts decided they were debased, savage art,
contaminated by unacceptable commercial influences, and put them in the
basement, never again to disturb a museum visitor’s delicate sensibilities.

Not quite a storyteller
                          Ada Suina, 8¾" high, circa 1980

   From 1890 until not so long ago, critics wrote scholarly pieces about the
purity of ancient utilitarian pottery forms and decorative symbols. Dealers,
curators and exhibition judges turned their backs on any Southwestern
pottery that in their opinion was made neither for art’s sake nor for
tradition’s sake, but, perish the thought, only because someone might
actually want to buy it.
    Cochiti artists never managed to recognize those hard lines. They kept
making singing mothers and monos, and the storytellers were only a short
philosophical step from the old debased, savage art. Then, around 1995,

everybody woke up and realized what was happening at Cochiti. Young
artists weren’t making storytellers, they went back to the old traditions—
ollas, jars and bowls, figurative work and work that poked fun at the foibles
of the society around them.
   Diego Romero caught early attention. He makes beautiful thin bowls
decorated with images that combine barbed social commentary with a style
that blends Mimbres and classic Greek iconography with the comic-book
art he grew up with. Almost overnight, Diego’s “Chongo Brothers” bowls
were big news.
   By 2005, Diego’s fame was international, stretching across the ocean to
Europe. His Chongo Brothers pottery was featured in the book Free Spirit,
devoted to the work of five mold-breaking potters, published by the
Stedelijk Museum in the Netherlands in 2006. The Chongo Brothers
themselves are actually Diego and his equally famous brother, the painter
Mateo Romero. Together, they made a mischievous old-style silent-movie
video spoofing early archeology called Search for the Anasazi. A 2010
museum exhibit of Cochiti and Kewa pottery in Santa Fe devoted a room to
the video, the pottery Diego made for it and the paintings Mateo made to
accompany it. All you need to know to understand it is that the sacred idol
around which the video and the exhibit were based looked exactly like
Homer Simpson.
    Older, established potters picked up on the idea as well. For years,
Martha Arquero had made minor whimsical figurines—storytellers, frog
figurines, mermaids and the like. Sometime after 2000, she joined the new
wave and began making larger figurines like the Wagnerian diva choking on
her aria in the picture at right.
   However, it wasn’t Diego Romero who gave Martha the impetus to
make larger pieces. The real push came from another of those five potters
featured in that book from the Netherlands, and we’ve devoted the next two
pages to him and his family. Before Virgil Ortiz, Cochiti was a minor player
in the pottery world. Now it’s a high-powered artistic force. On the next
pages, an introduction to the remarkable Ortiz family.

At Cochiti, even the bowk and jars are fun. The falling-down Chongo
Brother on Diego Romero’s bowl (a metaphor for falling off the wagon, a
common Pueblo malady) and the lizards on Diego’s grandmother Teresita’s
olla have a cartoony friendliness that other Pueblos seldom achieve.
   Diego’s Chongo Brothers pieces blend Mimbres art with comic-book
art, and his success with the series has made him internationally
famous.The chongo is a traditional hair roll, as worn by the unfortunate
falling off the ladder. His son Santiago did the little mask in front of Diego’s
bowl.
   Some Cochiti potters kept making the standard shapes. Virginia and
Louis Naranjo and Snowflake Flower gave us pocket vases to hang on the
wall. Julius Eustace gave us everything: a smiling face like his

grandmother Felecita’s storytellers, a wooden Cochiti drum and a silver
concho belt. Others sent all the rules flying. In 2012, Jonathan Loretto gave
us a bobblehead doll and in 2014, Pablo Quintana gave us a River Man, a
scary Cochiti bogeyman.
    Cochiti potters kept kidding the Anglos. Dorothy Trujillo shows what
tourists look like from the other side of the lens. Married-in Ivan Lewis,
Acoma matriarch Lucy Lewis’s son, made a nineteenth-century cowboy with
a removable hat and a standing figure that John thinks of as a hotel
concierge.
   Damacia Cordero’s daughters all contributed. Marie Laweka made
strange, lumpy figures like the mermaid and the storyteller on page 67,
Josephine made beautifully crafted nativity sets, and younger sister Martha
became an important player after2000. Her opera star and Spider Man
carry on in Cochiti’s irreverent tradition.


COCHITI – ORTIZ

Virgil starts a tidal wave. It’s impossible to exaggerate Virgil Ortiz’s
influence on Cochiti and on how far beyond Cochiti his art has traveled.
   Each year when we visit Santa Fe in August, we look forward to seeing
another dazzling Virgil Ortiz display, but one at Shiprock Gallery in 2009
stands out for us. We went knowing we’d see his pottery, probably a lot of
fashion designs as a result of his ongoing collaboration with Donna Karan
and DKNY, and maybe some photography. What we didn’t expect was a
total Virgil Ortiz design experience: an entire room done with his carpet, his
wallpaper, his furniture and his fixtures.
   Despite all this intense activity and despite the fact that he’s now an
international celebrity, Virgil remains a completely traditional Cochiti artist,
involved in Pueblo activities, performing in Pueblo dances and mentoring
Pueblo youth.
   He’s also an inseparable part of a family of artists powerful enough to
merit a 2012 exhibit devoted to works by the entire family in Santa Fe’s
major Indian art museum, the Museum of Indian Art and Culture. The
display was by the entry desk, and it introduced you to the Ortiz family
before you even got into the museum. The exhibit deliberately re-created
the effect of nineteenth-century fake-backdrop photographs like L. Fisher’s

array. It consisted of a large group of figurines by all the family members
posed in front of a contrasty, antique-looking black-and-white photo Virgil
shot in Prague.
   By 1994, the Ortiz family was important enough to rate its own section
in Fourteen Families in Pueblo Pottery, but the family was nowhere near as
important in 1994 as it is today. The dynasty goes back to the years before
World War II, when Laurencita Herrera followed in her potter mother Reyes
Romero’s footsteps. She taught her daughter Seferina (1931–2007), who
married Guadalupe Ortiz. Seferina taught her kids: Virgil, Inez, Janice and
Joyce, and Inez taught her daughter Lisa Holt.
    All became superstar artists. Seferina made bowls and figurines, and her
bears appealed to one Santa Fe dealer so much that, according to him, he
bought enough of them to put Virgil through college. Her husband
Guadelupe made traditional Cochiti drums, but made some pottery as well.
   By 1995, Virgil was emerging as Cochiti’s hottest potter and his sisters
were becoming recognized. Inez had started with modest little bear
figurines, but by 2000, she was a highly regarded potter with a career that
only ended with her premature death in 2010. Meanwhile, sisters Joyce and
Janice, inspired by Virgil’s and Inez’s work, began making figurines that
broadened the family tradition. By the early 2000s, major Santa Fe galleries
tried to feature full-family exhibits, but those efforts ended quickly as
Virgil’s work became so desirable that it was almost unobtainable.

Grandma and Great-Grandma
       Laurencita Herrera, 6¼" wide, circa 1967 and Reyes Romero, 5¼ diameter, circa 1960

    After 2000, another family member, Inez’s daughter Lisa Holt, rocketed
to stardom. By 2010, her pieces were almost as pricey as Virgil’s. She
works with her husband Harlan Reano, a Kewa, who paints the designs.
When Santa Fe’s Museum of Indian Art and Culture had a giant 2010
exhibit titled A River Apart that featured Cochiti and Kewa pottery, they
didn’t put one of Virgil’s pieces on the brochure cover. They used one by
Lisa and Harlan.
   By 2013, another generation had joined the array. Joyce’s son Dominick
made an excellent traditional owl, and Virgil’s nephew Kyle created a
magnificent lumbering dinosaur after just a single year as a potter. Lisa and
Harlan’s daughter Dominique could be next. In 2013, she seemed about to
burst on the scene.
   What all this means is that, thanks to the Ortizes, the monos are back in
modern dress, and Cochiti’s art remains as happily uncivilized as ever. All
those curators and experts now agree that what caused them to dismiss
Cochiti art is actually the reason why it’s important.

The family evolved through generations. They began with predictable
grayware like great-grandma’s and grandma’s pieces on the opposite page
and mom’s lizard bowl on this page. Then, over a twenty-year span, they
became famous for pieces that bend the imagination.
    Virgil led the way in the early 1990s, but mother Seferina came in early
with pieces like the bearded figure at upper right from 1996. Early, Virgil
made pieces that suggested what was to come, like the canteen in the
middle and the Cochiti “rain god” at lower left (an inside joke—Tesuque
rain gods catch the rain in a bucket between their legs, but at dry Cochiti,
buckets don’t help). The big fantastic figures followed quickly.

Our conservative friends have trouble accepting that Virgil’s earnest s/m
dominatrix at top left is traditional Cochiti pottery. Someone gave Virgil a
copy of Madonna’s Sex book, a whole catalog of non-Indian foibles worthy
of ridicule. The trade calls these “Madonna figurines.”
   Daughters Inez, Janice and Joyce followed quickly, and granddaughter
Lisa Holt was right behind. Inez gave us traditional Four Directions
figures. Janice gave us Uncle Sam and Zozobra, the “Old Man Gloom”
who gets burned every year at the Fiesta de Santa Fe. Joyce gave us a
hippie. Lisa and Harlan gave us a looming frog, and newcomers Dominick
and Kyle contributed a traditional owl and a plodding triceratops. To
complete the family, we even have a bear by dad, Guadelupe.


HOPI

Multicultural, yes. Diversified, no. The three Hopi mesas have nine
villages, but First Mesa and the village of Hano have dominated Hopi
pottery since the 1890s. First Mesa potters use Hopi’s unique clay to make
great quantities of some of the finest of all Pueblo pottery.
   But Hopi pottery history goes back more than a thousand years, not a
hundred. At Acoma, you’ll be told that the Sky City Pueblo is the oldest
continually inhabited city in the United States. At Hopi, you’ll hear the
same about the Third Mesa city of Old Oraibi.
    Oraibi goes back to the twelfth century, and a look down its unpaved
streets confirms its age. With every step, you’ll see tiny Anasazi sherds,
broken and rebroken through the centuries.
   The Hopi reservation lies about eighty miles northeast of Flagstaff as
the crow flies. Thanks to bureaucrat-created geography and Navajo growth,
fifteen thousand Hopi now live in a three-thousand-square mile island
within the giant Navajo reservation. Land disputes between the tribes have
led to years of prickly relations, with each other and especially with the
government that drew the boundaries.

Hopi as Zuni
                       Polacca Polychrome, 5½" diameter, circa 1865

   The Hopi’s Sinagua and Anasazi ancestors probably spoke different
languages, a condition that seems to persist throughout Hopi history. The
Hopi now speak a Uto-Aztecan tongue, like many other Southwestern
tribes, but the histories and religions of Zuni and Hopi are intertwined, and
the Zuni speak still another language. A Zuni and a Hopi understand each
other’s belief systems, but these days, they only communicate in English.
After the Pueblo Revolt, Tewa-speaking fugitives from the Rio Grande fled
Spanish retribution and hid out at Hopi. They established the village of
Hano on the First Mesa and have been a wrong-language minority ever
since.
   The Hopi’s ancestors traded yellowware from the 600s on, but under
pressure from Spanish, Apache and Navajo, the wandering and trading
diminished, and pottery production had almost disappeared by 1800.
   Outside influence brought Hopi pottery back to life. In the early
nineteenth century, drought and epidemic caused a large number of Hopis to
take temporary refuge at less-afflicted Zuni. Those transplants learned how
the Zunis made pottery, and the lessons stuck.
   When the railroad came through Arizona in the 1880s, so did the
traders, who wanted to fill the demands of an exponentially enlarged tourist

market. The Hopi style of the day was Polacca ware, named for a town at
the base of the First Mesa. It was characterized by a less-than-perfect white
or yellowish slip that tended to craze into fine black hairlines over the entire
surface. It was the Hopi’s nineteenth-century long attempt to make pottery
the way the Zunis taught them. Polacca ware became the first Hopi trade
pottery since the sixteenth century.





    In the 1880s, Thomas Keam, the local trader, had potters reproduce
historic and archaic forms from abandoned pueblos, and Hopi pottery hasn’t
been the same since.
   By 1900, Hopi had the Southwest’s first celebrity potter, and she
dominates the next pages. What Nampeyo of Hano and her family achieved
defined twentieth-century Hopi pottery. The style was called “Sikyatki
Revival,” but the term has long been obsolete. Now it’s “Hopi pottery,” or
more precisely, “Hopi-Tewa” pottery, because most Hopi pottery still comes
from the Tewa potters in Nampeyo’s wrong-language village.

because of the design. We think that it could have been made by an old
potter who had her granddaughter paint those stylish new Zuni designs.
The tall canteen with the kachina face is early, pre-railroad Hopi.

with the Grecian-looking corn garlands and the canteen at far right are
pre-Sikyatki-revival Polacca. The jar at middle left and the dish at top right
are later Polacca, when designs came from prehistoric Hopi rather than
from eclectic Zuni. The one at upper center looks like pieces that often get

understood what Nampeyo was doing. Here, the design is Sikyatki and the

   Once Hopi potters left the Polacca slip behind, most work continued in
a lineal direction: Sikyatki ornament on polished yellow. The duck from
1910, the vase from 1925 and Sadie Adams’s tile from 1975 show a
Nampeyo-imposed continuity, a core part of Hopi pottery for more than a
century.
    After 1900, a few Hopi potters made red- and white-slipped ware, and
the people who name things called redware like the canteen Sichomovi
Polychrome and whiteware like the shoe Walpi Polychrome. Since Walpi,
Hano and Sichomovi are just a few steps from each other on the First Mesa,
the distinction seems a touch arbitrary.


HOPI – TOURISTS

Make whatever they want, but make it Hopi. Like the potters from most
other Pueblos in the first half of the twentieth century, Hopi potters fell
under the traders’ spell.
   The pottery-for-tourists industry really took off in the Pueblos that sat
near the rail lines. In the early 1880s, when Acoma entered the tourist
business at the Laguna station, you could buy Southwestern Indian tourist
pottery at other railroad stations as well. There were pieces shaped like
Wedgwood china made by the Mojave at the station in Needles and bizarre
little trinkets from the Zuni at the station in Gallup.
   During those years, the railroad was still miles from Hopi, but the
ethnologists from the East were swarming through, buying up as many
artifacts as they could from people they thought were a vanishing race. The
Hopis caught on quickly. Since the Easterners ignored their current work
and looked for ancient artifacts, they came to a sensible conclusion: If all
they want is the old ones, let’s make more of them.
   That answer could well have been helped along by Thomas Keam, who,
as the local trader, was the Easterners’ principal contact with the Hopi. He
had a lot to do with the Hopi’s transition from making Zuni-inspired
whiteware to making yellowware with prehistoric designs. The little pipe at
the left of the picture strikes us as exactly the sort of thing Keam would
have sold to travelers at his trading post.

Later, Tom Pavatea ran a trading post at Polacca and had a price list for
Hopi works, starting at fifteen cents for small pieces and ranging up to an
astronomical seventy-five cents for a twelve-inch bowl by Nampeyo.
   Since Nampeyo’s pieces commanded a premium, and since the
photographs identified as “Nampeyo” don’t all seem to show the same
person, modern-day cynics have accused Pavatea of trotting out any
competent resident potter to serve as the Nampeyo-of-the-day. If true, it
would have been a practical answer to the marketing needs of the times.
   Through the 1950s and beyond, Hopi potters made (and still make)
tourist souvenirs, from unassuming little cowboy hats to ambitious table
lamps. But, because they were Hopi potters, they made them with the
stubborn integrity that all Hopi pottery seems to exhibit. When Acoma
potters resorted to decorating pre-cast ceramics fired in kilns, Hopi potters
steadfastly kept to traditional ways. Yes, the kiln has made an appearance at
Hopi in recent years, but in the face of commercial pressure, and despite the
pedestrian, “un-Indian” nature of the teacups, ashtrays and salt-and-pepper
shakers that the Hopis turned out by the hundreds, the manufacture and
decoration of their tourist pottery remained pure Hopi.

The little pipe at the far left is the sort of curio Thomas Keam sold at his
trading post at the end of the nineteenth century.
   The lamp is by Sadie Adams, one of Hopi’s more important artists,
active from the 1920s into the 1980s. The lamp represents the high end of
tourist ware, and it probably sold for a high price when it was new.
   The turkey effigy and the two tall vases at left rear weren’t cheap to
begin with either, and the wall sconce/bookend was recent enough to
command the premium that good Hopi pottery now commands. Probably
none of the others sold for more than ten dollars when it was new, and the
smaller older ones, for a dollar or less. The tall vases were made after
1920. Before that, Hopi potters didn’t make that European art pottery
shape. If they didn’t have strong red paint, they were made before 1930.
That’s when Mary-Russell Colton who, with the authority of the Museum of
Northern Arizona, laid down the law: “Clean up your red paint, or we
won’t include your work in our shows.” Almost immediately, Hopi reds
changed to the richer color decorating Hattie Carl’s jar and Nellie
Douma’s salt shaker.

There’s no tedious utilitarianism here. Ashtrays, cups and vases stained
instantly, napkin rings break quickly, and that little mudhead scoop won’t
ever work as a shoehorn.


HOPI – NAMPEYO

The Seven Families #3: Nampeyo. In 1890, the Smithsonian sent
ethnologist J. Walter Fewkes to excavate the Sikyatki ruin on First Mesa.
He later wrote that he showed the pottery he’d unearthed to a Hano Tewa
potter named Nampeyo (1860–1942), the wife of one of his workmen.
   Some books date the beginnings of modern Hopi pottery design to that
meeting. By legend, the sight of these fabulous relics so impressed
Nampeyo that she created the Sikyatki Revival all by herself, and there’s
some truth to that. Trader Thomas Keam had potters including Nampeyo
making old designs in the 1880s, and in those years, Nampeyo became his
main resource. Fewkes contributed to the legend by wringing his hands
over the terrible wave of prehistoric imitations that he was sure that he,
himself, had unintentionally created.
   The first revival pieces put Sikyatki designs on Polacca slip, but by
1905, Nampeyo had dropped the slip and converted to an unslipped style
more like the old ware. Fewkes complained that her work might appear to
be forgery, but Keam, and later on Tom Pavatea had no such qualms. They
launched Nampeyo on a career that brought her celebrity until her death at
eighty-two.

Minor rarity: a signed Nampeyo

    In the 1900s, the Fred Harvey Company brought her to the Grand
Canyon, where she demonstrated Hopi pottery-making for the hotel guests.
She must have put on a good show, because they later took her to Chicago
for the United States Land and Irrigation Exposition in 1910, where she
introduced Southwestern pottery to the world.
   Nampeyo began losing her eyesight some time in the 1910s, and her
daughters, Annie, then Nellie, then Fannie, and finally Annie’s daughter
Rachel Namingha took over painting designs for her. They all became
accomplished potters working in their mother’s style, and, under Tom
Pavatea’s urging, started signing her pieces in 1928. Briefly, they just
signed “Nampeyo,” as on the piece below, but quickly began a convention
of signing reversed signatures if mother made the piece. If you find a piece
signed “Nampeyo Annie,” it means that Nampeyo made it and Annie
painted it. If it says “Annie Nampeyo,” Annie made it. All these signatures,
normal or reversed, appeared after 1928.
   Annie, Nellie and Fannie gave birth to generations of potters. In the
picture, there’s work by Annie’s daughter Rachel Namingha. She gave birth
to Dextra Quotskuyva, whose work is so varied that it’s said she never

makes the same pot twice, and Priscilla Namingha, who in turn gave us
Rachel Sahmie and Jean Sahme, who spells her last name without the “i.”
There’s a piece by Annie’s daughter Daisy Hooee, who studied at L’école
des Beaux Arts in Paris and knew Charles Lindbergh.
   By the time the family tree had reached Cheryl Naha and Jake Koopee,
it had spread over six generations. Fourteen Families in Pueblo Pottery had
genealogies for each family showing a dot for each member: black dot for
non-potters and red dot for potters. The Nampeyo chart had sixty red dots,
several times more potters than we could include in the picture. Now, more
than twenty years have gone by since Rick Dillingham put that chart
together.
    In answer to the question, “Who’s the number one Hopi potter,” the
answer has always been “______ Nampeyo.” You could fill in the blank
with half a dozen different names or you could leave the blank empty, and
from the 1890s on, you’d have been right. If instead of being artists
unstained by commerce, the Nampeyo family were a manufacturing
corporation, it’d be worth a Business Week cover story about how it
managed to stay on top of an entire market for more than a century without
changing product design.

Nampeyo’s designs appear over and over in family pottery. Variations on
the eagle pattern, as on the Nampeyo/Nellie jar at right center, show up
four times in this picture. The jar behind the white seed jar in the bottom
row and the little one a couple of steps above it are seventy years apart, one
attributed to Nampeyo by super-authority Francis Harlow, the other made
by granddaughter Priscilla Namingha.
   Harlow also attributed the little eagle jar next to Nampeyo’s as also by
Nampeyo, but others disagreed, pointing out that there’s a line break in the
rim, a device they believe Nampeyo never used. Some authorities maintain
that at Hopi at the turn of the twentieth century, the line break was only
used by potters hopeful of bearing children. Nampeyo’s eldest daughter
Annie was painting for her mother during this period, and her first
daughter Rachel was born in 1903. Whether or not Annie painted the little
jar, other experts give her full or partial credit for the white piece at front
center and the jar at lower right. Middle daughter Nellie painted the one at
right center and signed it with a reverse signature, indicating mother made
the pot, and Fannie, the third daughter, made and signed the bowl at the left
of the middle row and the little one in the front.

Fannie and her granddaughters did the pieces that demonstrate another
ubiquitous family design, the “migration” pattern. Fannie’s little jar in
front typifies the pattern. Almost every book on Hopi pottery written
between 1970 and 1990 had a migration bowl on the cover. Nampeyo’s
large 1905 jar at top right and Fannie’s 1940 jar show a third family
pattern, the batwing.
   The magnificent pieces in the top row by Jake Koopee and Priscilla
Namingha’s daughters, Rachel Sahmie and Jean Sahme, demonstrate how
strong the Nampeyo tradition remains.


HOPI – NAHA

Frogs and feathers. Perhaps the worst injustice of the Seven Families
exhibit was omitting the Nahas.
   Each of the Pueblos in the exhibit had work by a dominant family:
Martinez from San Ildefonso, Tafoya from Santa Clara, Lewis from Acoma
and Nampeyo from Hopi. But the other three Pueblos each had a second
family: Gonzales, Gutierrez and Chino. Where was the other Hopi family?
   Unquestionably, the Nahas would have been it. Paqua Naha (1890–
1955) was active and respected by the 1920s. Paqua means “frog” in
Spanish, and late in her career, she signed some of her pots with a frog
symbol. Somewhere along the line, she became known as Frog Woman, but
after her death, the name and the frog signature passed to her daughter Joy
(1919–2012) and stayed with her and her descendants ever since. There’s a
subtle distinction between Paqua’s frog signature and Joy’s. Look at the
feet. You’ll see that Joy’s frog has webbed feet, while Paqua’s has long
fingers.
   Since the 1960s, dazzling whiteware has been the family trademark.
According to Joy, Paqua made yellow pieces and the occasional red one for
most of her career, but began experimenting with white slips late in her life.
(There’s a yellow one and a red one by Paqua on the next page.) We’ve seen
very few if any dead-white pieces by Paqua. Instead, we think her white
was mostly the soft beige on the bowl on the opposite page.

FROGS

FEATHERS





   Once Joy settled on pure white, the direction was sealed, and the look
became a permanent Naha/Navasie institution.
   Paqua’s son Archie married Helen (1922–1993), and she too
concentrated on whiteware. She occasionally would use designs that looked
like Joy’s Sikyatki shapes, but she worked out a different ornamentation
style borrowed from earlier Awatovi prehistoric pieces rather than from the
Sikyatki Revival. She also devised her own signature. Since Joy had
appropriated the frogs, she signed her pieces with a feather.
   From then on, Frog Woman and Feather Woman and their children and
grandchildren dominated Hopi whiteware and made it into the other
important Hopi pottery.
   As in the Nampeyo family, younger potters stayed within the family
design convention. No matter when they were made, frog pots looked like
frog pots and once Helen hit her stride, feather pots have looked like feather
pots.
   During the 1990s, Maynard and Veronica and Marianne Navasie kept
Joy’s style moving forward and other family members contributed, but the
frog side of the family lost some momentum in the years after 2000.
    Increasingly, collectors paid more attention to Helen’s daughter Sylvia
(who didn’t inherit the Feather Woman name—she became Feather Lady).
Her designs evolved from Helen’s Awatovi style, and she remained a major
potter until her premature death in 1999.
    Sylvia’s brother Burel and sister Rainy (Rainelle, but nobody calls her
that) and her daughter Tyra continue in the feather style, and Rainy remains
a master. Burel has the mastery too, but adds a fascination with arachnids to

his work. His pieces often feature fancy insects like the bug on the seed jar
on the opposite page.

The rest of the photo shows the generations that followed: frogs and

and any one of the frog pieces in the picture looks as though it could have
been made by Joy herself.
    Helen’s children and grandchildren have stayed almost as close to
home. Helen’s jar pretty well describes the design style she adapted from
the abandoned Awatovi ruins at Hopi, and her children elaborated on it.
Sylvia became “Feather Lady” and the ranking potter among Helen’s
children until her early death in 1999. Many of her pots, like the seed jar at
the right, feature lizards. Her brother Burel favors spiders, and he headed
in yet another name direction. People began calling him “Spider Man.”
   These explorations beyond Helen Naha’s precise geometries aren’t
really design defections. Rainy’s narrow-necked vase at bottom left, Sylvia’s
seed jar next to it and Sylvia’s jar at right center remind us of just how
strong Feather Woman’s influence remained.
   With Sylvia gone, Rainy and Tyra remain the torchbearers of the
Feather Woman style, still producing major work in the twenty-first century.


HOPI – OTHER DIRECTIONS

Do anything you want, but don’t break the rules. As the twentieth century
wound to a close, Hopi potters found new freedom as long as they kept the
quality tradition. At Acoma, potters wrestled with the temptations of
greenware and commercial clay and surrendered to the lure of the kiln.
Despite Hopi’s size, many times the population of Acoma, and many
struggling potters, none that we know took the easy road. A few use the
kiln, but there’s no commercial clay or greenware at Hopi.
   The social pressures that kept Hopi potters pure in the tourist-ware days
of the first half of the last century seem to have been equally strong in the
pottery-as-art days that followed. If any piece in the picture at right wasn’t
traditionally fired, at least part of the way, we’ve been fooled.
  An aside on “traditional firing” and “part of the way”: Black-and-sienna
pieces, like the turtle at the bottom right by Robert Homer, require a double

firing. On any given pot, the potter may have fired the piece to black with
scrupulously traditional outdoor firing techniques, then, in the second
firing, created the sienna highlight. We can’t say for sure how any of them
were actually done, and the original masters of the art kept the technique a
closely guarded secret.

   Weight of tradition, family pressure and market pressure keep Hopi
potters from taking shortcuts. To avoid fire clouds, whiteware potters use a

kiln, but buyers expect and prefer Hopi yellow with shaded coloring from
traditional firing.
   Despite all these heavy influences, there were new directions. Dextra
Quotskuyva, Fannie Nampeyo’s daughter, has a personal principle of “no
two pots alike,” and to underscore the point, gave us the seed jar at middle
right: the only completely matte Hopi pot we’ve ever seen.
   Nampeyo family members like the Sahmie sisters, Les Namingha and
Dextra’s brother Tom Polacca gave traditional Hopi a new spin. (Footnote:
Tom Polacca shares the same name as his great uncle, Nampeyo’s brother
and one of the first Hopis to welcome Anglo contact. A town grew around
his home at the base of First Mesa, and in the 1890s, Anglos named it after
him. Unaware of the irony, Anglos then named nineteenth-century Hopi
pottery that had little to do with Nampeyo after the town.)
     Iris Youvella, another Nampeyo family member, made sensitive
sculptured plainware that followed a tradition begun by Elizabeth White
and Al Qoyawayma thirty years before. Mark and Dianna Tahbo came from
another illustrious line. Grace Chapella’s great-grandchildren, they
challenged the leading Nampeyo family potters for prestige.
    Preston Duweynie’s jar at lower left shows yet another direction.
Micaceous pieces with fine-tooled silver inlays brought him attention and
celebrity.
    Lastly we’d like to apologize to Garnet Pavatea (1915–1981) for what
another direction did to her memory. A side experiment of hers became so
popular that the world forgot who she was. In the 1970s, she started playing
with an old-style beer-can opener and made some redware jars and bowls
like the one at right in the picture below. Those few turned into hundreds,
and, unfair or not, they became what everybody remembers about her.
   The two pieces next to it show the real Garnet.

Experimentation at Hopi moved from just off center to the far edge.
Lawrence Namoki’s seed jar with the cornstalk figure is almost totally
traditional, although it doesn’t look it.
    Antoinette Silas, like Rondina Huma (not pictured, since we never found
one of hers in our price range) makes pieces that qualify as innovative only
because their patterns are so intricate. Much the same applies to Mark and
Dianna Tahbo and Gloria Kahe: traditional pots, exceptional painting—
raised standards rather than changed rules.
   Family members keep broadening the Nampeyo design vocabulary. Tom
Polacca’s jar (top center) is a sculptured style he created himself, one his
daughter Carla and Lawrence Namoki adopted. It only took two
generations for the Nampeyo family to range far afield.
   Here, from the Nampeyos, we have Jean Sahme’s cartoony Hopi maiden
ladle, Dextra’s matte seed jar and Rachel’s Navajo rug jar, kachina figures

by Loren and Darlene, Les Namingha’s miniature olla and Iris Youvella’s
carved jar.
   Other pieces in the picture stretch further. Robert Homer’s turtle is an
original. Gwen Setalla and the late Tracy Kavena gave us impossibly light,
delicate pieces, and Preston Duweynie’s silver-inlays leave the boundaries.
    Finally, the Kim Obrzut mudhead sculpture shows how far the definition
of a Hopi pot can expand. Granted, Kim doesn’t live on the reservation, and
granted, she’s part of the big wide art world (she’s mainly known for her
bronze sculpture), but this is real Hopi pottery, beautifully made, and the
mudheads emerging from a cloud are part of the Hopi creation story. The
tradition ever widens.


HOPI – THE 21ST CENTURY

After 2000, little change. The new millennium may have brought sweeping
changes across the entire planet, but there was no corollary cosmic shift in
Hopi pottery. Granted, the pieces on the next page suggest continuing
evolution, but there’s nothing there that’s more than a short step from pieces
done half a century earlier.
   Those short steps, however, produced some genuinely interesting
pieces, and new talent kept joining the parade, some of them with
longstanding family connections to the art. The plate in the inset photo was
done by Joshua Namingha, who was born in 1993, is descended from Grace
Chapella, and learned pottery-making from Jake Koopee and Mark Tahbo.
    Several pieces on the next page caught our attention.
     Iris Youvella’s son Nolan made the carved jar at top left on the opposite
page that features a cliffside Pueblo city carved on its upper body.
Compared to what’s in the rest of this book, it might seem like a dramatic
departure, but it’s really just a continuation of what Polyingaysa (Elizabeth
White) and Al Qoyawayma had been doing in the 1970s and before. We
regret that we’ve never been able to afford a piece by either of them, but if
you Google their work, you’ll see that Nolan’s piece is not all that different.

New talent

   Nolan’s mother Iris Youvella made the highly polished seed jar at lower
right, and it’s probably the most innovative piece on the entire page, the
only one whose innovation goes beyond a few new wrinkles in the painted
design.
   However, some of those design wrinkles are impressive.
   Rachel Sahmie’s large jar at front center has a shape that her great-
grandmother Nampeyo made before 1900, but she gave it a fresh look. Like
her aunt Dextra, Rachel and her sisters Jean and Nyla try not to repeat
themselves, but they keep their experimentation well within the walls of the
Hopi Sikyatki revival tradition. Nyla made a lidded box that could have
been made a hundred years ago.
   Val Kahe combined Hopi elements we’ve seen through the years, the
Pahlik Mana kachina and a prehistoric Awatovi border, and made a dish
with an updated look. Val’s mother, Gloria Kahe, who made the tall jar on
the right side is Navajo, but she’s so steeped in Hopi tradition that she and
her family have been accepted as Hopi potters for years.Yanalla Lucas

discarded all the old design conventions and came up with a striking
interpretation of what we suppose is a butterfly on the shallow bowl in the
center.
   Dorothy Ami made the seed jar at lower left in the standard Nampeyo
shape, but she put a bat on it unlike any bat we’ve seen so far.
   Darlene James Nampeyo stretched even further afield with the small tile
in the front row, giving us a freer, more relaxed design than we expect to
see on a Hopi piece.
   Beyond those half-dozen pieces, the only innovation comes from doing
the same thing only better. Gwen Setalla, who often signs her pieces Ras-
Ku-Mana, is a master of the potter’s craft. She makes some of the thinnest,
finest pieces any Hopi potter ever made, and in the years after 2000 has
become recognized as one of the leading Hopi potters. Nona Naha built a
career by painting her designs more meticulously than anyone else, and her
lizard seed jar in the bottom row attests to her skill. Carla Nampeyo’s giant
carved jar at top center is excellent, but a direct continuation of the style her
father pioneered in the 1980s.
   Karen Collateta’s tall wedding vase and Valerie Namoki’s kachina
figure are fine examples of Hopi pottery, but the only thing that separates
them from the Hopi mainstream is the fact that they were made in the 2000s
rather than in the 1980s.
   We’ll have to watch Hopi in the coming years. What we’ve seen so far
in this century only seems to hint at what’s coming next.

Late twentienth-century experimentation at Hopi may have bumped up
against the far edge, but we haven’t seen anything that extends that edge
much further in this one.
   The array above is as well made as any Hopi array in this book:
thinner, lighter, meticulously carved and painted. The only thing that’s
missing is surprises. The closest thing to a surprise is Iris Youvella’s high-
polish seed jar with a shaded polychrome sun face, and she made it back in
2000.
   So for innovation, we have to look to artists like Gwen Setalla, whose
cylinder vase may have what seems to be another typical Hopi design, but
whose delicacy and lightness, both in the painting and in the pot itself, set
the piece apart and suggest what could become a new bar-raising standard
for Hopi pottery.
   The other possible harbinger in the picture is Darlene James’s tile at
front center. If you compare her design and painting with the rest of Hopi
art, you see a freedom and light-hearted looseness that sets it apart.
  On the other extreme, Nona Naha’s lizards to its right suggest perhaps
another new standard: a precision that the Naha family whiteware artists

like Sylvia, Rainy and Burel have achieved in recent years.
     It’s hard to see a trend in Yanalla Lucas’s and Val Kahe’s shallow
pieces. They both have unusual designs, and Yvonne’s is especially
dramatic, but they don’t seem to project into new styles for the future.
   Maybe the best way to appreciate current Hopi pottery is to admire a
piece like Rachel Sahmie’s seed jar in the middle and forget about looking
for change. Enjoy it for what it is: a beautiful Hopi pot, made the Hopi way.


ISLETA

Just down the road from Albuquerque. The guidebook we used to check
the populations and areas of the various Pueblos didn’t hesitate to name
Isleta’s most admirable craft achievement: baking bread. It even called out
an eminent baker by name. Once Al got a different answer. He asked an
Isleta native to tell him what the people of Isleta were known for, and she
answered unhesitatingly, “Working in Albuquerque.”
   More than most of the larger Pueblos, Isleta (it’s pronounced Iz-LET-a)
has had its identity diluted by the affairs of the outside world. This is true
today, and it was true more than three hundred years ago. Isleta was first
settled around 1200 as part of the Anasazi westward movement. In 1581, it
had fifteen hundred residents, and today the Pueblo’s population is only
three thousand, even though the reservation covers thirteen hundred square
miles, some of it lush farmland but much of it with only marginal use.
    Isleta has always suffered from its proximity to Albuquerque and the
army. The padres built their first mission at Isleta in 1613. In 1680, Isleta
didn’t—or couldn’t—take part in the uprising, and the Spanish governor hid
out there on his ^ way to safety in El Paso after he escaped Santa Fe. The
next year, he returned with a troop detachment and found the mission
burned and the main structure used as a livestock pen. A quick about-face
brought him back to El Paso, but not without taking 385 Isleta natives with
him. They settled below El Paso in Isleta South. (Down there, it’s Ysleta del
Sur, with a “Y.”)
   The 1692 Reconquest found Isleta burned and empty. Governor de
Vargas ordered it resettled, and started it off with three hundred residents,
some returned from Ysleta del Sur and some relocated from Taos and
Picuris.

A note on language: The Zunis speak their own language, but the other
seventeen New Mexico Pueblos belong to one of two major language
groups, Keresan and Tanoan. Acoma, Laguna, Kewa, Cochiti, Santa Ana
and Zia speak Keresan. The rest speak one of three confusingly named
Tanoan dialects: Tewa, Tiwa and Towa. Today, Isleta and Sandia speak
Tiwa (pronounced TEE-wah), the language of Taos and Picuris in the north.
Jemez is the only remaining Towa-speaking Pueblo, and the other six
Pueblos north of Santa Fe speak Tewa (TAY-wah).
   By 1700, Isleta had a new, grander mission and a culture tied to the
ever-growing Hispanic populations of Albuquerque to the north and Belen
just to the south. Today, Isleta continues quietly on its way, largely ignored
by tourists who look for things other than good bread and old churches.
    Isleta pottery has an unassuming history. In the nineteenth century,
Tiwa-speaking natives produced a plain orange ware, similar to Ohkay
Owinge’s but paler, mostly the large bowls you’d expect in a community
devoted to baking. The one in the inset is typical, and, having seen it, you
wouldn’t be surprised if you saw a hundred others.

What they used to make
                       Dough bowl, 13½" diameter, circa 1910

    In the late nineteenth century, a group of disaffected Lagunas moved to
Isleta and from 1890 to 1930 made tourist pottery using white slip imported
from Laguna. The old Tiwa residents never bothered to learn how to make
it. Nothing was large, nothing was ambitious, everything was made solely
to be eyecatching. In the beginning, it was mostly bowls, but by 1900,
pitchers, ashtrays, pipes and especially baskets with twisted handles became
more and more common.
   The demand for these evidently died out by the Depression, but not until
they’d submerged any pottery tradition Isleta had. When the tourist ware
disappeared, it left almost no trace.
    In today’s Golden Age, Isleta can claim important potters, but they work
in styles evolved from other Pueblos and the world of art at large.

upper left seems to be a rare lineal descendant. Isleta pottery from this
period is almost nonexistent. The Jojola family remains, however, and we
found the little moccasins at lower right by Dora in 1992.
   The whimsical jar at the top right-center doesn’t fit anywhere in a nice,
orderly historical flow chart, but it too seems to have Laguna antecedents.
It’s unsigned and came from the end of the pre-greenware period of Isleta
pottery.
    In the 1970s, an Isleta hairdresser named Stella Teller started buying
greenware and decorating it, not always as perfectly as she might have. The
bowl in the upper middle is painted nicely enough, but it has a plan-ahead

mistake—the design didn’t come out right when she got back to the
beginning, so she faked it.
   But Stella learned and grew. In a Pueblo with a vanished pottery
tradition, Stella and her children began, if not a tradition, a style that for a
while in the 1980s and 1990s came to represent Isleta pottery as a whole.
The Teller story continues on the next pages.


ISLETA – TELLER TO CARPIO

Still looking for a tradition. As the 1970s became the 1980s, Stella Teller
the hairdresser became Stella Teller the full-time potter, and she got better
and better at her craft. By 1982, she’d honed her skills to the point where
the seed jar in the front row of the picture on the next page won a third prize
at the New Mexico State Fair. She was now well past decorating somebody
else’s pre-cast pots.
   Also by the 1980s, Helen Cordero’s storytellers were at the height of
their popularity. An obvious route to sales success was to start making
storytellers, and if they could be made with a little personal twist, so much
the better. Stella put all this together with just the right timing. By the late
1980s, she was considered one of the leading Southwestern potters, not just
from Isleta but from anywhere. Her own twist came in her choice of colors
—instead of the usual red and black, she painted hers in soft blue-grays.
   Also by the 1980s, Stella’s children had grown to become full-time
potters in their own right. Very quickly, Isleta had a genuine high-
production market-driven family pottery dynasty. The Tellers—Stella,
Chris, Mona, Lynette, Robin and Leslie—dominated Isleta pottery to the
point that you had to look hard before you found anyone else.

The other Isleta: brownware
                    Ron Martinez Looking Elk, 6½" diameter, 2008

   There were still Jojolas. Dora was still working, and there’s a pair of
moccasins by her at the bottom right of the previous page. And there was
Deborah, who made the amazing glazed ceramic water jar on the opposite
page. When we wrote this book the first time around, she’d already reached
recognition as a glass artist, and since then, she’s broadened into the full
field of visual arts. She still does imaginative pottery and sculpture, but
when she got her MFA from the University of New Mexico in 2008, it was
in printmaking.
   Meanwhile, Diane Wade and Isleta/Taos artist Ron Martinez Looking
Elk started making brownware. They made enough of it to create a style
subset for Isleta, but not enough to make you automatically associate the
style with the Pueblo. Later, after 2000, Kimo DeCora introduced finely

finished small black-on-white pieces that found their way to Andrea
Fisher’s prestigious Santa Fe gallery. These three artists produced an
impressive body of work, but it took a new dominant force to bring real
attention back to Isleta pottery.
   The 1996 Indian Market introduced us to Caroline Carpio, and it was
obvious she was a special talent. John brought the big white pot in the top
row home, and we started watching Caroline’s progress.
   Ten years later, there was no need to pay her special attention. We
couldn’t avoid and could barely afford her. Her distinctive polychromes and
sculptured pieces were all over the most prestigious galleries, and she was
selling as many bronze versions of her pottery as she sold of the pottery
itself.
   She’d reached such a superstar level that by 2010, a bronze version of
one of her polychrome turquoise-inlaid jars appeared on the cover of the
official Indian Market literature, a formal acknowledgement of her
prominence as an artist.
   Then, in 2012, the authoritative Indian Arts and Crafts Association
named Caroline Carpio Artist of the Year.
   As far as Isleta pottery in general is concerned, the future is still cloudy.
Caroline’s work is so personal that if others try to work in her style, they’ll
likely seem more like imitators than as participants in a new Pueblo
tradition.
    In retrospect, Isleta in 1990 was 90% Teller, 5% Jojola and 5%
everyone else. By 2010, as far as the broad attention Isleta pottery received,
it was 90% Carpio and 10% everyone else.

The army of little Teller singing mothers that fills the left side of the picture
tells most of the story of Isleta pottery during the 1980s and the 1990s. After
Stella began winning prizes for pieces like the seed jar at front center, she
turned to storytellers. The blue-and-gray theme persists in her daughters’
work as well.
   Her daughters weren’t linked totally and inflexibly within the genre.
Leslie’s “story bowl,” Chris’s diapered mudhead and Mona’s singing
mother/flower girl show some imagination, and Chris gave her singing
mother a Hopi maiden hairdo. When you look at an array of Teller pottery
from several family members, however, you’re more conscious of the
similarities than you are of the differences.
   During the Teller years, there were others. Deborah Jojola made the
amazing thirteen-inch tall water serpent (a glazed ceramic piece carafe
with a removeable head), but we’ve seen almost no pottery from her since.
Diane Wade, who made the large wedding vase and the bear in the picture
made polished, incised brownware since the 1990s, as did Ron Martinez
Looking Elk. She also surprised us with the owl on the right, not like
anything else from Isleta.

Starting in the late 1990s, the Isleta pottery attention shifted almost
entirely to Caroline Carpio, who caught everyone’s attention with
spectacular pieces like the inlaid jar at left center, the main reason she’s
moved to Southwestern pottery’s forefront by 2010. Kimo DeCora attracted
some notice with his geometric black-on-whites, but the current reality is
Caroline-in-charge.
   Meanwhile, Stella’s daughters remain active, and Mona’s cello-playing
bear from 2014 shows some evolution.


JEMEZ

What do you do when you lose a tradition? You build a new one, but not
right away. Between 1300 and 1750, potters in the Jemez Mountains (the
detached rectangle in the upper left-hand corner of the map) made some
sharp-looking black-on-white Anasazi pottery. After that, according to the
books, they didn’t make anything beyond a little plainware.
   By the time the Towa-speaking Jemez settled in their current space, they
were farmers who used their crops to buy pottery from Zia. In 1598,
Governor Oñate converted them all to Catholicism with a flourish of his
pen, and by 1622, the padres reported six thousand faithful attending the
three missions at Jemez.
    In 1680, however, their devotion wavered. When General de Vargas
returned in 1692 to restore the rule of Spain, he had to search out the people
of Jemez (pronounce it HAY-mis, the Spanish way). He found them hidden
in mountain strongholds and shot a lot of them in order to renew their faith.
Those he didn’t shoot, he rounded up and took south along the Jemez River
to build a new village where Jemez Pueblo now stands. Today, Jemez real
estate covers 550 square miles between the Jemez and the Salado Rivers,
sparsely populated by two thousand people.

The lowest point: acrylic paint
                             5½" high, circa 1970

   The history of pottery at Jemez is one of absence and rebirth. You can
look long and hard in books and in museums without ever seeing a Jemez
piece from Spanish times. After twenty years of collecting, the late
nineteenth-century olla on the next page is still the only old Jemez
polychrome we’ve ever seen. If we put that jar alongside the Jemez pieces
we showed on pages 48 and 49—the prehistoric black-on-white ashtray-
shaped dish and the questionably Jemez-connected Gobernador Canyon
bowl—those three pieces would display pretty much all we know about
early Jemez pottery.
     If a Pueblo loses its pottery tradition, and Jemez is by no means the only
one that has, pottery as a craft rarely reappears unless a potter from another

Pueblo marries in. If the Pueblo has a strong pottery tradition, the married-
in potter will almost always make pieces in the style of the Pueblo where
she now lives. There’s a wonderful example of this on page 193: a pure
Zuni pot by Daisy Nampeyo, who at the time she married Sidney Hooee,
was one of the most celebrated Hopi potters. She learned how to make Zuni
pottery and for years taught Zunis how to make it.
   Sometimes, marrying-in goes less smoothly. In the 1920s, a Santa Clara
potter named Monica Silva married into Kewa (back then, it still had its
Spanish-imposed name of Santo Domingo), and her mixture of styles
managed to annoy the elders of both Pueblos. She was an important potter,
but her skills didn’t keep her out of trouble. There’s more about her, her
skills and her troubles on pages 94–97.
  On the other hand, if the tradition is gone, potters don’t face the
problems Monica Silva faced. They’re free to make anything they want,
either work that resembles what they made at their native Pueblo or
whatever else the market wants.
  A handful of potters made an effort to revive traditional pottery at
Jemez in the 1920s, but nothing came of it. However, during the
Depression, potters found they could make a little money copying the
unfired, poster-paint decorated pieces they were turning out over at
Tesuque.





    After World War II, Jemez potters discovered acrylic paints, and one of
the lowest forms of lowest-common-denominator tourist pottery emerged.

Pottery purists have our permission to look as long as they wish at the
1890 olla to the right, then to avert their eyes quickly and turn the page. At
Jemez, the pottery tradition hit absolute bottom, and only those as perverse
as the people at the John & Al Museum enjoy exploring its depths.

The big old olla speaks for itself Since there’s little else to compare it with,
it has to stand as our total statement about what they did in and around the
nineteenth century at Jemez. We know that it’s Jemez and we know its date
only because Al Anthony, who sold it to us, told us that he’d seen a similar
documented one at the Denver Art Museum.

The little gray vase with the black decoration might echo revival efforts
from the 1920s, and the poster paint jar at upper right has really admirable
decoration that later pieces never approached, but the rest of the picture
describes the twentieth-century decline and fall of Jemez pottery.
   The other poster paint pieces are garish and banged out in a hurry, but
manage to have a jaunty charm. It’s hard to hate them, and at their best,
like the canoe and the eagle salt & pepper shakers, they bring a smile.
    After 1960, pottery at Jemez plummeted downhill rapidly. With acrylic
paints that chipped off substituted for poster paint that merely smeared, they
hit bottom. The vase on the opposite page and the little bowl at front right
are sad examples, but the cup & saucer set is even worse, so carelessly
made that the cup can barely stand upright on the saucer without tipping
over.
   We try not to be judgmental, but to us, that cup & saucer represent the
bottom of the pottery barrel.


JEMEZ – GROWING PAINS

Figuring out what to do. Given the dreadful state of Jemez pottery in the
1970s, any change would have been an improvement.
    Fortunately, during the hippie-dippy days of the late 1960s, general
interest in anything Indian picked up dramatically, and the pottery market
benefitted from the upswing. The citizens of Jemez may have been out of
the pottery loop, but they weren’t off the planet. They could see that higher-
quality pottery was bringing much higher prices, and they set about learning
how to make it.
   The easiest improvement was to switch to greenware, and some of
today’s fine potters started their career with it. Others took a longer look,
and artists like Mary Small and Mary E. Toya became champions of
traditionally coiled, well-made pottery.
   Today, with 20/20 hindsight, we can say that the two of them changed
everything. Mary Small continued making her white-slipped, gray-and-
orange decorated pieces into the next century, and she’s generally
considered to be the most influential potter of the twentieth-century Jemez
revival.

We might cast a minority vote for Mary E. Toya. Her early pieces, like
the large jar in the picture, demonstrate a mastery of the craft that few
artists ever achieve.





                         Pecos Glazeware re-created in the 1970s
                             Evelyn Vigil, 7" diameter, circa 1975

   The 1970s were a time of exploration, and not all explorations were
successful. Lorraine Chinana and her relatives experimented with new slip
colors, blues, greens and grays, and, although we personally gave them high
marks, they never caught on in the market. Vangie Tafoya started out with
greenware and grew as the Pueblo’s art grew. You can see her progression
from 1980 to 1993 on the next page (third from right in the bottom row and
at the left of the middle row). Then turn the page and see where she was in
2014.
   Meanwhile, Helen Cordero was taking off at Cochiti, and Jemez potters
discovered storytellers. Mary E. Toya switched early, and in our opinion,
never made pieces afterwards with the integrity of her earlier work. Maxine
Toya and Maxine’s mother Marie Romero followed right along. By the
1980s, Barbara Babcock’s The Pueblo Storyteller listed thirty-four Jemez
potters making them, mostly with the overly cute faces that make purists
look the other way.

Jemez quickly found a matte-paint storyteller convention as on Rosalie
Toya’s corn maiden on the opposite page, and a few potters still work that
way. The remarkable little guy on the kiva ladder down in the front row of
the picture was made in 2011, and it has the same surface and feel of
storytellers made thirty years earlier.
   One Jemez potter took a different road in the 1970s, and a few others
followed her. She searched far across the rivers to find a tradition at Pecos,
a Towa-speaking Pueblo thirty-nine miles southeast of Santa Fe. During
prehistoric and historic times, Pecos produced well-made Rio Grande
glazeware with piled-on, drippy glaze paint, sometimes to so high a relief
that you hesitate to touch it for fear you’ll chip some off.
   Evelyn Vigil traced her ancestry back to the last thirty-eight survivors
who fled a ravaged Pecos for Jemez in 1838, victims of Spanish, Apache
and Comanche depredations. Evelyn and a few colleagues spent much of
the 1970s and 1980s attempting to re-create Pecos glazeware. They did a
good job of it, as the example at left demonstrates.
   As the twentieth century ended, others found a new path, and it led to
the fine work Jemez is known for today. Pauline Romero, Geraldine Sandia
and Laura Gachupin were at the forefront.
   One family led the way. As far back as the 1980s, Glendora Fragua,
who made the incised jar in the bottom row, and her sister, B.J. Fragua,
guessed the future. On pages 92 and 93, the prophecy is fulfilled.

Between the 1970s and the 1990s, Jemez pottery made a giant step forward.
The date on Mary E. Toya’s traditional-looking jar on top center came from
someone who knew her, Flo Yepa. She told us that Mary made it at her
kitchen table and that she did the impressions around the neck with a butter
knife.
   Vangie Tafoya and Carol Pecos experimented with greenware (bottom
row left and third from right). Later, Carol and especially Vangie made
excellent traditional pottery. Mary Rose Toya wasn’t quite as successful as
Blue Corn over at San Ildefonso when she made pieces with odd colors on
them, but the blue paint design on her jar seemed like a good idea at the
time. Rosalie Toya’s corn mother storyteller used matte paint on matte
pottery, as did the anonymous potter who made the odd child in a shoe.
Matte on matte was the convention for Jemez storytellers for years, and
Peggy Chinana used it on her 2011 miniature in the front row. Laura
Gachupin’s owl is 90% matte, and no one else ever made anything like it.
   For years, Lorraine Chinana did pieces with a polished blue slip like
the jar second from right in the middle row, and her sister Gloria Vigil did
pieces with an equally unexpected muted green slip. They never caught on

with collectors, and for the moment seem to be something of a dead end. Ho
and Sal Yepa, to the right of Lorraine, experimented with mixed clays and
firing techniques.
   Back in the early 1980s, Glendora Fragua Daubs and her sister B.J.
Fragua were looking to the future. Incised, polished redware like
Glendora’s jar second from left in the bottom became the standard look for
upper-end Jemez pottery from the 1990s on. In the twenty-first century,
Jemez potters in general expanded the repertory, and Jemez is now a major
producer of fine pottery.


JEMEZ – THE MATURE VOICE

Skill, style and substance. A total turnaround. Hopi’s pottery tradition
built up over a thousand years, Acoma’s took several hundred and Santa
Clara’s styles needed about a century. But the instantly recognizable look of
fine Jemez pottery happened in barely more than twenty, and with each
passing year over the next twenty, it became more varied and more
impressive.
   Through the 1990s and into the 2000s, a lot of Jemez ware has been red,
and the best potters polish their pink clay to a brownish red that doesn’t
quite look like anyone else’s, or they leave it matte. Jemez pots often have
largely or totally matte surfaces, and at Jemez, “matte” doesn’t mean “soft
eggshell luster” like it does at Acoma. It means dead flat matte, like Verda
Toledo’s ghost bowl in the picture.
   Jemez potters use the forms that everyone else uses—jars, seed jars,
wedding vases, figurines and so forth. Many current pieces tend to the
smaller sizes, but that has nothing to do with the potters’ skills. These days,
the market increasingly looks for the small and elegant, and Jemez elegance
keeps constantly upgrading.
   They use the sculpture techniques: appliqué, carving and incising. They
use red, tan and cream slips and occasionally surprising greens and yellows.
But regardless of how they combine it, it all comes out looking like Jemez.

Jemez Black-on-white re-created in 2013
                               Joshua Madalena, 6½" high

   Al Anthony gives a lot of credit for this new tradition to Mary Small,
who insisted that Jemez potters should learn to make pottery right and
taught them how to do it back during the poster-paint and acrylic days.
     If Mary Small started it, families like the Fraguas confirmed it. It’s no
coincidence that the Pueblos strong in pottery can usually point to one or
two families with transcendent skills and acceptance in the marketplace.
Twenty years later, it might seem like Virgil Ortiz vaulted Cochiti into
prominence all by himself, but he couldn’t have done it if he hadn’t built on
what he learned from his family and if his relatives hadn’t supported him.
  On the previous page a 1982 piece by Glendora Fragua Daubs
anticipated the best Jemez work of the twenty-first century. “Anticipate” is
a weak word when you look at what you see on the next page. You can ask

whether the Fragua family really anticipated, or if it was a chicken-and-egg
situation. Did they anticipate, or did the rest of Jemez figure out what the
number one pottery family was doing? The answers are yes and yes. Thirty
years later, the Fraguas are still going strong. We see Glen again and sisters
B.J. and Felicia on the next page.
     It would be a mistake, however to look at Jemez and conclude it’s the
Fraguas and little else. Sculptor Kathleen Wall makes large, almost life-
sized matte Koshare clown figures and figures modeled after her own
children while Fannie Loretto makes matte Koshare masks, and both
Kathleen and Fannie have gained worldwide attention and attract prices like
those the Ortizes are getting at Cochiti.
    After 2010, Aaron Cajero emerged as a major potter, and we like his
work so much we started the book with one of his pieces. It’s on page 2. His
daughter Teri works in the same style. In 2013, we found the remarkable
bear-and-fish by Kathleen Wall’s brother Marcus, who already has a 2011
Best-of-Category award from Indian Market. In 2014, Loren Wallowing
Bull’s eagle storytellers brought new life to a tired genre. The imitative,
searching-for-a-style days of the 1970s and 1980s are over.
  Emma Yepa’s carved, polished piece has a distinctive, only-from-Jemez
look. Carol Vigil, Lorraine Chinana and others continue working in the
incised styles they developed in the 1990s. At the end of the ’90s, Verda
Toledo came forward with a fresh new design vocabulary. But perhaps the
most telling proof of Jemez’s return to pottery prominence lies with Joshua
Madalena, who in 2010 began creating homages to Jemez’s fifteenth-
century black-on-whites. By caring enough about his tradition to want to try
to re-create it, he’s providing hard proof that the tradition is back to life and
flourishing.

Here’s how Jemez has evolved. Redware like B.J. Fragua’s seed jar still
persists, but doesn’t dominate Jemez pottery the way it did before 2000.
Now when it appears, it often has added colors, like Teri Cajero’s jar at
lower right and Vangie Tafoya’s big jar with the bear sitting on it.
    After 2010, Glendora Fragua moved Jemez pottery forward by taking
painted redware in new, sophisticated directions, as on her jewel-like seed
jar at lower left. Shapes can get creative. Felicia Fragua’s perforated jar
and M.L.E. Teeyan’s butterfly jar are unusual, Marcus Wall’s bear-with-fish
isn’t like anything anybody else ever made, and Loren Wallowing Bull’s
eagle storyteller is every bit as wonderful as his name.
   Some potters, like Marcella Yepa and Patricia Daubs, work with cream
slips, and the color of Jemez creamware is almost as distinctive as the color
of the redware.
   Matte pottery persists at Jemez, as on Verda Toledo’s striking bowl in
the center, Felicia Fragua’s jar at left and Mary Small’s jar at upper right.
Maxine Toya’s watermelon-eating Koshare clown, a figure that traditionally
bedevils both performers and audience at Pueblo dances, foreshadowed
what became in the current century the most publicized Jemez pottery: the

large Koshare masks by Fannie Loretto and near life-sized figures by her
daughter Kathleen Wall.
   Probably the closest thing to a current mainstream style at Jemez lies
with Aaron Cajero and his daughter Teri. Their easily recognizable pieces
inspire other potters, like the ever-learning ever-improving Vangie Tafoya.
Her lidded bear jar is the most ambitious “Cajero” piece in the book.


KEWA (THE NEW/OLD NAME FOR SANTO DOMINGO)

It’s big, and it’s bigin the arts. And increasingly, it’s becoming big in
pottery. In 2010, Santo Domingo Pueblo dumped its Spanish-imposed name
and reverted to its original name of Kewa, which created mild concern
among fastidious academics. For years, they’d used the old name to
describe Santo Domingo’s most common geometric pottery design, but they
spelled it Kiua. The Pueblo chose a less fancy, easier to pronounce spelling.
   Kewa’s real estate stretches out over a hundred square miles on both
sides of the Rio Grande, and its twenty-five hundred people stay home,
mainly farming or creating arts and crafts. For years, the craft of choice has
been jewelry with the Kewa specialties: handmade heishi and turquoise
beads and inlay work with shell, turquoise, and jet.
   Kewa’s early Indian name is Guipi, “The Unknown,” and the Pueblo
remains largely unknowable to outsiders. Our first guidebook didn’t
recommend a visit and based that opinion on Kewa’s general conservatism
and lack of interest in tourism. Kewa has plenty of reasons to distrust
Spanish, Anglos and tourists. From Oñate’s soul-saving proclamations in
1598 to the present, Kewa has suffered one calamity after another.

One of those “Keresan” jars
                             9½" high, circa 1890

   The village of Guipi is relatively new. Floods destroyed it in 1606, 1700
and 1855, and each time it moved and rebuilt on higher ground. The 1680
Pueblo Revolt didn’t help it either, and many of its citizens fled westward to
establish the new Pueblo of Laguna during the reconquest.
   Nobody seems to know much about Kewa pottery prior to 1880. That
year, Bandelier praised their pottery as being of “very beautiful make,” but
James Stevenson collected few examples for the Smithsonian during his
1879 and 1880 excursions. From Stevenson’s time to the present, Kewa has
made black-and red-on-cream pottery in two styles.
   Kiua Polychrome (perhaps now, we should spell it Kewa) has black-on-
cream geometric patterns arranged in vertically segmented panels with the
red confined to the underbody. Santo Domingo Polychrome has naturalistic

flowers, leaves and birds, and red appears in the upper-body designs. Kiua
was the earlier style, but Santo Domingo Polychrome was well established
by the time Stevenson visited in the 1880s.
   Before 1900, both styles overlapped what they were doing next door at
Cochiti. Both Pueblos speak the Keresan language, and these days
observers tend to hedge their bets identifying earlier pieces as “Keresan,”
acknowledging that they could be from either Pueblo. The piece at left
shows the dilemma. It has a pure Kiua neck, but the rest of it belies Kewa’s
traditional insularity. Its polychrome birds could have been suggested by a
piece from Cochiti or, more likely, a piece from San Ildefonso or Tesuque.





   News of the commercial value of blackware reached Kewa by the
1930s, probably introduced by Monica Silva, who made the big red jar in
the back row. She was a married-in Santa Clara potter. For the most part,
Kewa blackware is easily recognizable because it’s almost always decorated
with Kewa flowers and leaves rather than San Ildefonso or Santa Clara
geometry and because with few exceptions, Kewa potters never quite got
the hang of blackware. Early examples tend to be clunky, streaky and not
very black. The next pages show black pieces by Monica and others from
both ends of the excellent-to-forget-it scale.
   Kewa kept making pottery through the 1940s, and nobody paid much
attention to it. But things were about to change for the better.
