Here, an array of pre-World War II Kewa ware. The small storage jar at top
left shows what utilitarian Keresan pottery from the nineteenth century and
before looked like. Its Kiua geometric design shows up on the two jars in
front of it, the pitcher to their right and the bowls in front.
   Four pieces in the front and the big one at upper right demonstrate the
floral/naturalistic Santo Domingo polychrome style. Kewa potters didn’t
draw a hard line between the two styles. The jar at lower right put red in a
Kiua design, and the footed pitcher and the elegant olla at front center have
Santo Domingo polychrome designs without the red. That jar in the center
has been attributed to Felipa Aguilar, whom we talk about on the next two
pages.

The tall jar on the right of the middle row and the olla at lower left have
a feature that collectors prize: the red band. Before 1930, potters from
Cochiti, Kewa, Santa Ana, San Udefonso and Zia left the bottoms of bowls
and jars unslipped and put a quarter- to one-inch wide band of polished red
slip at the top of the underbody. The red-on-red stripe was almost universal
before 1930 and almost never there after.
    Early-century Kewa was big on pitchers and big dough bowls, fourteen-
inches-and-more in diameter. Normally, they had a conventional bowl
shape, but the big bird bowl at left is a one-of-a-kind phenomenon. The
chile bowl at bottom left looks like the big ones looked. Footed pitchers like
the one in the front row were popular at Kewa, and the double-spouted
basket behind has an only-in-Kewa shape.
   When we found Monica Silva’s big red jar at top center, it had been
drilled to serve as a lamp base. We've showed it again on page 205,
restored as a lamp.


KEWA – BACK TO SEVERAL SOURCES

Major players enter the scene. After World War II, fewer and fewer potters
worked at Kewa. Production dried up and quality dipped. Things spiraled
ever downward as the Indian jewelry craze of the 1970s lured Kewa’s best
artists away from pottery.
   But down didn’t mean out. Some of those who kept going held to high
standards, and strong pottery families emerged. Santana Melchor (1889–
1978) learned from her mother, began making small pieces in the 1920s,
and by the 1930s had established herself as an important Kewa potter. By
1945, she was the most important Kewa potter. She worked continually
until her death, and her daughters and grandchildren continued the family
pottery tradition. Crucita Melchor was decorating pottery by 1950, and the
Melchors have been around ever since.
   Santana Melchor wasn’t alone during those years. Monica Silva, the
married-in Santa Clara potter, made beautiful large pieces in the Kewa
style, although she had problems with the Kewa lifestyle. She managed to
annoy the elders at Kewa, and her pottery probably contributed to that
annoyance. A 1928 book by Leo Crane, Desert Drums, devotes an entire

chapter headed “Infernal Affairs” to her treatment at the Pueblo and
features a photograph of Monica looking considerably battered.
   There were others, including the mysterious Santana Tenorio, who made
the beautiful unsigned red and gray Santa Clara-looking bowl in the center
of the opposite page in the 1960s. We knew it was made by a “Santana,”
and, years after John found it, we saw a signed piece in the same style.
   By the 1990s, Kewa was hitting stride. The pottery in the picture at the
right from the 1990s competes with the finest work from the high-end
pottery Pueblos. Helen Bird learned how to polish redware at San Ildefonso,
then worked in other styles. Mark Wayne Garcia made fastidiously polished
ware. Vidal Aguilar made major pieces like the jar below, and his brother
Robert followed right behind. As the 1990s ended, Ambrose Atencio made
big, beautiful Kiua polychromes like the old ones and Josie Martinez made
good blackware.
   These days, blackware by the Aguilar family gets more attention.
Rafaelita Aguilar, who made the big jar, learned from Monica Silva, who
made the black jar at lower right around 1930. Rafaelita’s blackware looks
good alongside good Santa Clara and San Ildefonso blackware.

The old days remain very much alive
                               Vidal Aguilar, 13¾" high, circa 1995

   “Aguilar pottery” didn’t always mean blackware. There’s a beautiful
large jar on the previous page that has been attributed to Felipa Aguilar, an
award winner at the 1924 and 1926 Indian Market. Around 1910, three
Aguilar sisters took the prompting of a merchant in Bernalillo, the nearest
town to the Pueblo, and began producing a variant Kiua polychrome that
covered the cream-colored slip almost entirely with black and red. The style
had largely disappeared by 1920, but it didn’t vanish forever. The tall jar in
the back row of the picture opposite is the work of the now internationally
famous Harlan Reano and Lisa Holt. Lisa is Cochiti, and we could have put

the piece on page 71 along with pieces by her relatives in the Ortiz family,
but Harlan, who paints her pieces, is Kewa, and here he’s done a
magnificent contemporary version of the Aguilar pottery from nearly a
hundred years earlier.
   This reverse-painted Aguilar style also resurfaced as part of the
repertory of another important Kewa pottery family. Turn the page for the
story of Robert Tenorio and the rest of his family, who through the 1990s
and into the 2000s dominated Kewa pottery.

twentieth century. Monica Silva, married in from Santa Clara, worked in
both styles, as on the big wedding vase in the back row and on the
blackware olla at lower right.
   Santana Melchor got more attention than Monica at mid-century. She
also made pieces in both the Kiua and the Santo Domingo style and
managed to find new ways to express them. The bird in the front row is
masterful, and the jar at left center has a design that you’d think came from
Cochiti and Virgil Ortiz rather than from a Kewa potter.
   Many pieces in the picture display a range of work by unheralded Kewa
potters. The slipper-shaped candleholder is a poor piece of blackware by
even the most charitable standards. Helen Bird is a notable exception. Her
little red jar from 1993, the black-on-white bowl at upper right from 2008
and the polychrome jar at lower left center from 2014 are all at the top of
the pottery ladder. The most unexpected piece in the picture is the Santa
Clara-looking polychrome bowl in the center. It’s by Santana Tenorio, a
potter who’s so forgotten today that it took us twenty years to identify her
piece. Obviously, she deserves to be remembered.

Crucita Melchor’s painted bowl is much like her mother Santana’s
work. Alvina Garcia made pieces that feel like the old ones, and Ambrose
Atencio, like Vidal and Robert Aguilar, made really big ones like the storage
jars from a century before. And Julian Coriz, who says he comes from a
“non-pottery family,” did something else entirely.
   From the 1990s into the current century, Kewa pottery standards have
escalated at a dizzying rate.


KEWA – TENORIO

Another family emerges. Andrea Ortiz, who made the little red bowl on the
previous page, was a potter in a family of jewelers. Sometimes she had her
jeweler daughter Juanita paint her pottery.
   She also let Juanita’s son Robert Tenorio (1950–) work with the clay,
but there were few thoughts in the family of letting him stay with it. As
expected, he went to the Institute of American Indian Arts to learn the
jeweler’s skills. However, he kept wandering into the pottery classroom to
get his hands into the clay.
   When he decided he wanted to be a full-time potter, his grandmother
and a great aunt, Lupe Tenorio, came to his support, and Lupe showed him
how to boil down the Rocky Mountain bee plant to make his paint.
   By the 1970s, Robert’s work was attracting attention. In 1980, John
Barry noted that Monica Silva was gone and Santana Melchor had died two
years earlier, and wrote in American Indian Pottery, “Robert Tenorio is the
only potter today making large traditional pots at the Pueblo.”
    In the 1980s, Robert coaxed his sisters into the pottery world. First
sister Hilda and her husband Arthur Coriz made pieces, and Robert
decorated them. That didn’t last long. Arthur and Hilda became full-time,
award-winning potters who might rank with Robert today if they’d had his
longevity.

Same name, different family: stardom in the 2010s
                        Thomas Tenorio, 9½" diameter, 2012

   Next, Paulita Pacheco entered the ranks and quickly built her skills up
to the family level. Then her son Andrew Pacheco began winning his own
awards with his dinosaur designs. Mary Edna was next. Robert painted for
her, and her fireplace corners drew attention. Meanwhile, Arthur and
Hilda’s daughter lone started doing fine work as well.
   By then, Robert’s leadership was unquestioned. Although he was
determined to work within the conservative strictures of his Pueblo, he
wasn’t content just to make “Santo Domingo pottery.” Instead he became a
pottery scholar, experimenting with prehistoric techniques and the design
conventions of other Pueblos. Generous with his time and with his
knowledge, he became a missionary for Kewa pottery.
   Around the turn of the twenty-first century, the Tenorio family picture
changed dramatically. Arthur Coriz died in 1998. Hilda followed in 2007,
and, shockingly, Paulita went the next year. Andrew’s pottery output
diminished, and suddenly a family powerhouse appeared to be reduced to
Robert, Arthur and Hilda’s daughter lone Coriz and not much else.

Then Paulita’s daughter Rose entered the scene, and working with her
husband Billy Veale, developed a dramatic floral presentation that put new
life in the family portfolio. Arthur and Hilda’s son-in-law, Warren Coriz
took lessons from Robert, and lone kept working.
   As did Robert. After 2010, he remained prolific and held his place as
the unquestioned leading Kewa potter. Robert’s dynasty may have lost a bit
of steam, but another Tenorio came forward in the late 2000s. The name
Tenorio at Kewa is like the name Smith elsewhere in America, and over the
years, we’ve met several Tenorios unrelated to Robert. There’s an excellent
piece on the previous page by Santana Tenorio, and we haven’t been able to
find any family connections for her.
   Today, the new star is Thomas Tenorio (1963–). In the 1990s, Thomas
was an in-and-out potter, doing good work but never recognized as anything
resembling a leading artist.
   Then, around 2010, Thomas set other things in his life aside and
determined to become the artist he always knew he could be. Thomas’s
post–2010 work verges on greatness. The piece at lower left gives a hint of
how powerful an artist he’s become.
   For the foreseeable future, Robert Tenorio will remain the king of Kewa
pottery. But at the rate Thomas’s reputation is building, the king might have
an unrelated heir.

By the 1990s, all the Tenorios were making large traditional pots just as
Aunt Lupe had done thirty years before. Robert’s olla at the top impressed
us so much as a true traditional piece that we dated it as 1920 in the first
edition of this book, but he actually made in 1982. It did a few years of
service under a downspout at his home, hence the look of age. Paulita
Pacheco’s dough bowl at upper center is big enough to qualify as large by
anyone’s standards.
    Robert’s 1980 double canteen dates from a period when he was just
beginning to become known. It’s signed “Robert Tenorio Santo Domingo in
America”—evidence that his confidence level in his own and Santo
Domingo’s celebrity was considerably less than it became later. He made
the circus-train bowl in the front for a railroad-themed exhibit at Santa Fe’s
Adobe Gallery. It shows Indians contemplating a monkey cage that fell off
the train and deciding “tail like a cow, face like a boy. Must be a cowboy.”
   The large shallow jar at center right by Arthur and Hilda displays a
Tenorio version of the reverse-painted Aguilar pottery style of the 1910s.
Robert is primarily responsible for reviving the heavy paint coverage of this
distinctive approach. Arthur and Hilda’s bowl second from left has an early

1990s Tenorio aberration: blurred edges on the black painting. Collectors
didn’t care for it and newer pieces don’t have it.
   Andrew Pacheco’s trademark dinosaurs climbed rapidly in popularity
and price. Ione’s bowl shows her command of the Tenorio family idiom.
Rose Pacheco’s piece is the style that she and her husband Billy Veale
developed in the 2010s and Warren Coriz’s fish shows he’s a fast learner.


LAGUNA

The Pueblo next door. Because Acoma’s white pottery has had so much
attention for so many years and because Sky City is such a spectacular
attraction for tourists, Neighboring Laguna spent years as a Rodney
Dangerfield among pottery-producing Pueblos.
   Laguna is the new kid on the block. In 1699, refugees from Cochiti, Zia
and Kewa, all Keresan-speaking Pueblos, fled General de Vargas’s
reconquest following the 1680 Revolt and headed for empty land near
Keresan-speaking Acoma.
   They didn’t exactly escape. The Spanish let them form a village, but
stood over them while they did it. The mission started going up
immediately and was finished by 1701. Today San Jose Mission in Old
Laguna is one of the most lavishly decorated churches at any of the
Pueblos.
   Laguna filled with emigrants from Jemez, Sandia, Zuni, Hopi and
neighboring Acoma. By the early eighteenth century, it was a cosmopolitan
town with a heavy Spanish tilt, and the influence remains. Today it has
seven thousand people, the Keresan language and one of the largest pieces
of Pueblo land, 2,750 square miles.

Josephine Foard’s “improved” pottery
                       Probably originally Acoma, 13" high circa 1905

   Laguna’s modern history has been shaped by two major events. In 1880,
the railroad came through, and it stopped at Old Laguna. In the 1950s,
uranium fever infected the reservation. If you drive north of I-40 from Old
Laguna, you can see long, lifeless brown mountains, the tailings from
abandoned mines. Tribal and federal officials puzzle over what to do about
them. Both the railroad and the mines provided major sources on income
for Laguna residents and diverted their attention from arts and crafts. For a
hundred years, Laguna had other things on its mind beyond pottery
production.

Even so, Laguna had a pottery tradition, but so confused with Acoma’s
that today, experts can’t really be sure who made what.
   The designs on Laguna ollas may have bolder geometric patterns than
their fussier Acoma counterparts, Laguna jars may be a bit heavier than
Acoma pieces, and Laguna potters are more likely to temper the white clay
with sand rather than with ground-up sherds. We’ve been told this
knowledge allows you to guess the identity of an older jar. You rub your
hand inside the unpolished part, and if it feels fine-textured, it should be
Acoma. If it feels sandpapery and if it’s heavy, it’s supposed to be Laguna.
We’re sorry to report that this test has misled us so often that we’ve lost all
faith in its accuracy.
   From the 1920s on, good Laguna pottery gradually disappeared,
replaced by quick tourist pieces, often like the ones they made over in
Isleta. In 1929, in The Pueblo Potter, Ruth Bunzel quoted the following
Laguna attitude: “We don’t make good pottery here any longer. Why don’t
you go to Acoma? When we want pottery, we buy it from Acoma.”
   That seems to have been the case quite a bit earlier than 1929. In 1899,
an Anglo lady from Delaware named Josephine Foard moved to Laguna
and took it as her mission to show Pueblo Indians how to make practical
pottery. By that, she meant pottery that her friends back East could use as
flower vases without having to worry about water discoloring or weakening
it.
   She settled in Laguna, gathered good Pueblo pieces, more from Acoma
than from Laguna, coated the insides with a commercial ceramic glaze, and
refired them.

They were now practical, but the Indians hated them. Once the pots
were glazed, they lost their natural porosity and no longer cooled water
from exterior evaporation. The magnificent jar at left, almost certainly
originally from Acoma, is a true piece of pottery history and a wonderful
example of Josephine’s finest work.

LAGUNA – REBIRTH

Thank you, Evelyn. Much as Mary Small came forward at Jemez, Evelyn
Cheromiah and her family started the move back to good pottery at Laguna
in the 1970s. In Acoma and Laguna Pottery, Rick Dillingham quoted her as
saying that after “looking at my mother’s pottery-making tools, I got the
urge of going back to making pottery.”
   This urge seems to be strong in pottery families. Jemez potter Flo Yepa,
who was born in Laguna, resisted making pottery for years. She worked in
the prison system and, familiar as she was with the underside of life, told us
bluntly that she didn’t want to become “just another potter supporting an
alcoholic husband.” But when Flo married into Jemez, she told us she
“heard her grandmother calling” and went to work full-time as a potter.

During the 1980s, others got the urge. Laguna pottery got better and
better and more traditional. Suddenly, there was not only the Cheromiah
family, but new potters like Melissa Antonio doing traditional work. There
was Gladys Paquin researching traditional ollas and creating her modern
versions of them. There was Myron Sarracino painting Tularosa swirls as
well as they could be painted. There was Miriam Davis doing totally
traditional jars. There was even Max Early leaving the kiln behind and
returning to pit-fired pottery, fire clouds and all.
   By 2000, there were more. Calvin Analla was making beautiful
traditional jars, and one in the picture opposite caught our attention.
Experimenting with traditional firing, he created a shaded coloring like we
only expect to see on Hopi ware. Alan Early continued in his father’s
footseps. Marquis Lente, who made the spectacular traditional olla in the
upper left middle, should have been one of the great ones. Still in his
twenties, he was on the path to stardom when, encouraged by his new
success, he moved to Albuquerque in 2008. It was a terrible neighborhood,
and in one of those ugly urban incidents that keeps us shaking our head
over what goes on in the world, someone shot him in the street. What would
have been a spectacular career ended senselessly.

Michael Kanteena: antiquity brought up to date
Mimbres bowl 2001, kachina figurine 1998, frog figurine 2001, candlesticks 2002, fish figurine 2010.
                               The kachina is 6" high.

   One of our favorite potters, Michael Kanteena was hitting stride. One
observer dismissed his work as “just doing fake prehistorics,” but we felt
our faith was rewarded when we saw that a few years after the turn of the
millennium, he received official recognition: an entire case devoted to his
creations at the Museum of New Mexico. The array at left features some of
those “fake prehistorics”: a Mimbres bowl, Anasazi frog and fish figurines
and a kachina figure, all instantly recognizable not as wannabe prehistorics,
but as genuine Michael Kanteenas. It also includes a pair of candlesticks,
part of a set he made similar to ones that disappeared from the mission at
Old Laguna.
   There was exploration away from Laguna traditions. In the early 1990s,
we’d seen some dreadful precast ceramics painted black with commercial
paint in matte-and-polish and signed by a Laguna. But we’d never seen a

piece like the 1995 jar by Sally Garcia, a pot that would make any Santa
Clara potter proud.
   Andrew Padilla’s pure white pieces combine his Santa Clara and
Laguna heritage. Terence Cooka’s micaceous jar reminds us of Hubert
Candelario’s work at San Felipe. And Andrew Rodriguez’s animal
sculptures have the look of mainstream contemporary art. Laguna is alive
and well.
   Except, sadly, for Marquis Lente.

Evelyn Cheromiah and her daughters work within the old tradition—white-
slipped coiled pottery, traditionally painted. M.W. Cheromiah Victorino’s
1985 effort has a striking design, but it’s not too-far removed from the
mainstream Lucy Lewis/Marie Chino-inspired Acoma pottery. Her 1994
effort looks much more like Laguna.
   Gladys Paquin’s jars are deliberately traditional. Before she made
them, she looked at pictures of old jars in books, then re-created their
designs on new ones, which she made and fired traditionally. The 1880 jar
that inspired the one at top right appears in Larry Frank and Francis
Harlow’s Historic Pottery of the Pueblo Indians, 1600–1880. Myron
Sarracino has made a career out of pieces decorated with variations of the
ancient Tularosa swirl design. Max Early’s canteen is in the old
Laguna/Acoma tradition, and Miriam Ortiz Davis, Marquis Lente and Max
Early’s son Alan honored that tradition.
   So does Calvin Analla, but with experimentation, as on the jar at right
center, traditionally fired and shaded in the firing. You can see the shading
in the subtle difference between the orange on the neck and the tan at the
midbody.
   Andrew Padilla, Gladys Paquin’s son, found his own expression, making
heavier white pottery that owes much to the Santa Clara side of his family
tree. The pure white melon jar with a kiva-step lid is a signature piece, a
design he’s made for twenty years.
   The orange jar, the blackware jar and the bear at the bottom of the page
go far afield from Laguna. Terence Cooka got firing help for his micaceous
jar from Glenn Gomez in Pojoaque. Sally Garcia didn’t learn how to make
blackware like this from older Laguna potters. And Andrew Rodriguez’s
creature draws more inspiration from mainstream art pottery than from the
tradition of any Pueblo.


MARICOPA

If they weren’t totally different, you couldn’t tell them apart. For centuries,
the Maricopa and the Akimel O’odham have been lumped together in the
eyes of the outsider. They have different languages (the Maricopa speak
Yuman, while the Akimel, like the Hopi, speak Piman, a Uto-Aztecan
language), different traditions and a different craft emphasis (the Maricopa

make pottery while the Akimel make baskets), but none of that seems to
matter to anyone who isn’t Maricopa or Akimel.
   Unlike other linguistic groups, neither has its own reservation. Instead,
they’re split up between the Salt River Reservation just east of Phoenix
(mostly Akimel) and the Gila River Reservation to the south, where most
Maricopa live.
    Actually, the historic basis for the confusion predates the coming of the
Anglos. Somewhere around 1700, the Peeposh, the easternmost of the
Yumans, migrated from western Arizona to the Phoenix basin and came to
live with the Akimel. The Spanish renamed them the Maricopa, and today
they’re reintroducing the Peeposh name in the same way the Akimel
dumped their Spanish name of Pima back in the 1990s.
   Between the 1740s and the 1780s, the Peeposh and the previously more
peaceful Akimel formed their own version of NATO, promising to defend
each other from all attacks. At the time they had more problems with the
western Yumans and the Apaches than they had with the Spanish. The
Pima-Maricopa Federation became a force strong enough that not only the
Spanish, but the Mexican and American governments had to deal with it as
a major political entity. The Mexican War of 1846–1848 brought Arizona
under the American flag, and an alliance with the Pima-Maricopa
Federation was one of the deciding factors. Until the Civil War, the
Federation’s army was the strongest military force in Arizona.

Back then, they called this a “scalp jar”
                           7¼" diameter, circa 1880.

    In 1857, a band of Mojave attacked a Maricopa village on the Gila
River near what is now Phoenix, and it was a terrible idea. The Pima-
Maricopa forces slaughtered them, thereby ending Indian vs. Indian war in
the desert. As a reminder of Maricopa ferocity, the books told us that jars
shaped like the one at left were considered “scalp jars.”
   Then the settlers arrived. Originally, the Maricopa and Akimel farmed
rich river-basin lands along the Salt and Gila Rivers. They sold their crop
surpluses to the early settlers and for the next century, taught their children
to get along with the settlers, a task that became increasingly difficult once
they were confined to reservations, and politicians and developers siphoned
off their water supply.
   By 1900, their populations were depleted by epidemics brought in by
the settlers they once helped, and the once proud Akimel and Maricopa
were hungry and dependent. The last general of the Federation army died in
1908, and the Akimel and Maricopa were so forgotten that the government
that once depended on them didn’t allow them to vote for another forty
years.

Maricopa pottery has looked about the same from the mid-nineteenth
century. In Dirt for Making Things, Janet Stoeppelmann and Mary Fernald
told of a thousand-piece Maricopa pottery collection gathered between 1885
and 1912 and acquired by two Phoenix museums, the Heard and the Pueblo
Grande, in 1938. In 1971, Mary Fernald tried to locate the collection and
could only account for 272 pieces—262 between the two Phoenix museums
and 10 on loan to the Museum of New Mexico.
   Those other 700-plus pots were probably dumped into the market years
ago. Some of them could even be in the picture, but who knows?

The picture shows the three kinds of Maricopa pottery that have existed for
over a century: black-on-red, black-on-cream and black-on-cream-and-red
polychromes. Potters rarely leave the black paint off.
   Our compulsion to date everything could get us into trouble here.
There’s so much published material on other types of Southwestern pottery
that any mistakes we make in dating should be offset by the weight of other
evidence, but we’ve found so little literature on Maricopa that our mistakes
might get more attention than they deserve.
   With prehistoric pieces, scholars place type examples in tree-ring-dated
ruins and agree on fairly accurate date ranges. After 1700, pottery loses its
connection to excavated sites, and dating depends on early accounts and
fitt-in-the-blanks assumptions. Leslie Spier, in the authoritative 1933
Yuman Tribes of the Gila River, said the Maricopa copied all early designs
from Hohokam sherds. There’s too much variety here to make that blanket
claim.
   So for the record, every date we’ve put on every piece on these two
pages is a guess, based on several factors: wear, fashions of the period, the
presence of fire clouds (they seldom appear after 1900), and the fact that

pre-1937 Maricopa pottery has a different look and feel from the revival
pieces on the next pages. You can see the differences in pre- and post-1937
work by the same potters, like Ida Redbird and Lena Mesquerre. (Fernald
and Stoeppelmann spell her name “Meskeer,” a spelling we’ve seen on
descriptor cards in Arizona museums. We took the fancy Europeanized
spelling from a 1923 book that wrote a long, admiring description of her.)


MARICOPA – REVIVAL

Here comes Elizabeth Hart. In 1937, the United States Indian Service
Home Extension Agent, Pima Jurisdiction, Sacaton, Arizona, wrote letters
to three major Southwestern museums—the Heard and the Pueblo Grande
in Phoenix and the Museum of New Mexico in Santa Fe.
    Elizabeth Hart had noticed that Maricopa potters were only getting a
nickel for well-made pots and decided to do something about it. She felt
that if Maricopa potters could improve the quality of their work, they’d be
able to get higher prices, and she thought the museums might help. She had
precedent. Mary Colton of the Museum of Northern Arizona had pointed
out market realities to Hopi potters in the late 1920s. Kenneth Chapman of
the Museum of New Mexico had done the same for San Ildefonso potters
ten years earlier.
   By 1937, Maricopa pottery needed improvement. The art had been
drying up for twenty-five years as the number of potters diminished and the
pendulum swung away from carefully made, carefully painted pieces and
toward unimpressive, dashed-off tourist pieces.

An early great, still going strong in the revival
                      Lem Mesquerre, 9½" wide, circa 1940

   There had already been recognized Maricopa potters. In 1923, J.F.
Breazeale wrote about one of them: “Almost anyone who has seen her work
can go into a room half full of Indian art and pick out the work of Lena
Mesquerre.” He described her as “the best pottery maker of her tribe,”
equated her with Nampeyo, and credited her with “the grace and dignity of
a highborn.”
   Lena wasn’t alone. In the 1933 Yuman Tribes of the Gila River, Leslie
Spier devoted seven pages to Maricopa pottery, and said the pictures of
pottery were “drawn by Mrs. Redbird.” Spier not only neglected to give her
a copy of the book, he also neglected to mention that Ida Redbird was, by
then, regarded as the preeminent Maricopa potter. Her preeminence had a

lot to do with her personality. She was outgoing and comfortable with the
Anglo world, while Lena Mesquerre, according to Breazeale, pretended not
to understand English.
   Lena and Ida were still around when Elizabeth Hart sent the letters, as
was Ida’s cousin Mary Juan. Mary was less comfortable with the public, but
she was later generally acknowledged to be the best potter of the period. A
few months later, Elizabeth and Odd Halseth of the Pueblo Grande Museum
had organized the Maricopa Pottery Association with the charismatic Ida as
president.
    In Dirt for Making Things, the authors quoted Ida rattling off the names
of the Cooperative members: beside herself, Lena and Mary, she added
Pearl Miller, Sally McKinley, Maggie Colt, Agnes and Josephine Bread,
Cora and Mabel Sunn, Alma Lawrence, Lula Young, Mary Loring, Ruth
Anton, Lou Johnson, Grace Perchero and Susie Sundust.
   Halseth arranged for the Cooperative to have showings at Pueblo
Grande. They were supposed to dress in native costume, do demonstrations
and sell pottery. Ida said they could have done without the costumes, but
they did get to set prices and keep the money.
   By 1938, Maricopa pottery was better than ever, largely thanks to a ten-
point quality standard Elizabeth Hart borrowed from what Mary Colton told
the Hopis. The good days ended quickly. Elizabeth Hart died in 1941, and
in 1942, World War II turned everyone’s attention elsewhere. None of the
potters had cars, Phoenix was a long way over dirt roads, gas rationing was
in force, and there was no retail outlet on either reservation.
    Elizabeth Hart’s legacy lived on, however. Her ten-point standard
influenced potters for years after. There were fewer potters after the war,
but Maricopa pottery held to her standards.

page 105 and the wedding vase in this picture. Ida’s weddingvase, like
Mary Juan’s pitcher, has had years of handling and its black design has lost
some of its strength. (The Mary Juan attribution came from Wenima
Washington, Ida and Mary’s cousin.)
    After World War II, Maricopa pottery stayed alive into the 1970s, thanks
in great measure to Association potters. In addition to Ida, Lena, and Mary,
the picture shows significant work by Alma Lawrence, Lula Young (Mary
Fernald quoted Ida Redbird as saying “the two best potters are Lula Young
and Mary Juan”) and Mabel Sunn. Mabel and her daughters started

another Maricopa pottery upswing in the 1970s. Mabel also got special
attention by responding when a Phoenix dealer asked her to make Mojave-
style effigies like the one in the top row. Advisers told her she should stay
with traditional work, but Mabel defined tradition more correctly. After all,
the Maricopa actually were Mojave, in language and heritage.
   New potters joined the ranks after the war, and Vesta Bread Grace
Monahan, Mabel’s daughters Barbara Johnson and Gertrude Stevens and
others did work that lived up to Elizabeth Hart’s Association standards.


MARICOPA – REVIVAL AGAIN

Here comes Mary Fernald. Then Phyllis Cema. Then Dorothea Sun. In
1938, Elizabeth Hart lived with the Maricopa and took matters into her own
hands. In 1970, Mary Fernald was writing a master’s thesis, and she came
to Ida Redbird with a hat rather than matters in hand, just hoping for a litde
acceptance and instruction.
   Mabel, Ida and Barbara gave her her thesis, which lay buried at the
University of Arizona until Mary and Janet Stoeppelmann made a book out
of it in 1995. But Mary gave Mabel, Ida and Barbara a great deal as well:
pictures and information about earlier Maricopa pottery and encouragement
to continue and to stretch the art. Whether it happened because Mary
Fernald appeared in their lives or coincidentally, Maricopa production
turned upward in the early 1970s, to the point that Stoeppelmann’s Dirt for
Making Things could talk about “the 1970 revival.”
    Pieces from this second revival have the sharpness and polish of the
1940 pieces, but they’re easy to identify because almost all have signatures.

A century later, the tradition still hangs in.
                              Dorothea Sun, 5¼" high, 2003

    After its early 1970s flurry, Maricopa pottery went into another long
downward slide. By the early 1990s, Ida Redbird and Mabel Sunn were
gone. Mabel’s daughter Barbara Johnson, Ida’s daughter Malinda Redbird
and Susie Sundust’s granddaughter Theroline Bread were still around, but
only a handful of potters, almost all of them elderly, still kept working.
   Then, in 1994, another of Vesta Bread’s daughters, Phyllis Cerna,
started teaching at the Salt River Reservation. She passed along the
knowledge she’d learned from her mother and her mother-in-law, Mabel
Sunn, and new potters began to learn the art. In 1995, we saw examples of
student work in a showcase at the Hoo-Hoogam-Ki Museum at Salt River,

and some of the pieces approached the quality of the best of the 1940
revival.
   Theroline Bread produced an important body of work between 1980 and
2000. There were also Barbara Johnson’s daughter, Vickie Johnson
Howard, and Vesta Bread’s daughter, the second Loretta Bread to make
Maricopa pottery (the first was active in the 1930s).
  Now we have Theroline’s daughter Dorothea Sun, whose traditional
pieces match up favorably when you put them alongside pieces from the
Idas, Lenas, Marys and Mabels of earlier years. Dorothea’s son, Kermit
Bread Jr., and her nephew David Soke were working after 2000. New faces
included Jaylee Miles and Matillas Howard, whose work was so good as a
teenager that the Arizona Republic devoted half a page to him in 2002.
   There were also some non-Maricopas—Akimel O’odham potters
Warren Oliver and Clayton Wahpeta and the late Tobias Manuel. They
explored, and explore, the full vocabulary of their neighborhood pottery,
from the Hohokam to recent Maricopa.
   Because they’re O’odham rather than Maricopa (those Pimas who
always got confused with the Maricopa), we put their work farther on in the
book, on page 133, but since Wally Oliver especially has made so many
pieces that fall under the Maricopa umbrella, we could just as well have
shown his work here.
   By 2010, Maricopa pottery was alive and well, but not exactly robust.
Big changes were happening. The giant Huhugam Heritage Center and the
Sheraton Wild Horse Pass Hotel and Casino were up and running on the
Gila River Reservation and the McKillips Road Casino was an established
fixture on the Salt River Reservation.
   As the Phoenix-area casinos play an ever-increasing role in the life
around the reservations, Maricopa artists have more opportunities to earn a
living, and it creates a cultural dilemma. Whether ever-improving living
standards will ultimately provide more leisure time for arts or simply
provide more distractions away from art remains to be seen. We’ll keep
watching.

The latter-generation work offers hope for the future, but doesn’t guarantee
smooth progress for the art. Most of these are small tourist pieces, but what
else is new? Maricopa pottery has mostly been small tourist pieces ever
since 1880.
   Three major pieces in the picture hold their own against the best work
from any period. Malinda Redbird’s tall jar offers a silent demonstration of
the fact that after Ida died, Mary Juan took over as her teacher. Mary’s
influence is so strong in this jar that some observers think she might have
had a hand in it.
    Theroline Bread’s red-on-buff effigy holds its own against the pieces by
Barbara Johnson and Mabel Sunn that established the standards for these
Mojave and Hohokam revival pieces.

And Dorothea Sun’s large polychrome jar is simply magnificent. It
actually goes beyond the tradition. The color-on-color treatment of the
cream-colored neck was new to us, and that says something. We’ve owned
several hundred pieces of Maricopa pottery and have examined countless
more from every era, but this is the first and only time we’ve seen that
subtle color change in polished cream—far different from the usual positive
painting you see on the snake on her effigy jar in the front row or the handle
of the wedding vase on the opposite page.
   With her teaching at the Hoo-Hoogam-Ki Museum, Phyllis Cerna kept
Maricopa pottery alive during the 1990s, and her daughter and
granddaughter continued working. The jar in the back row by Matillas
Howard jar got its color from an experimental firing. Most of his work is
more traditional.


MATA ORTIZ

From out of nowhere. When the inhabitants of Paquimé vanished, the
Apaches took over northern Chihuahua. American troops rounded them up
and deposited them in reservations. The land became cattle country, and
foreigners developed lumber and agriculture until Pancho Villa kicked them
out.
   Bandelier had explored Paquimé in the 1890s and Di Peso examined the
ruins in the 1950s, but the post-Villa natives, Hispanics and Indians alike,
had little interest in ancient history.
   Mata Ortiz was an agricultural town just over the hill from the Paquimé
ruins twelve miles away, seventy miles south of New Mexico’s bootheel.
One citizen was a mestizo named Juan Quezada, who, like the other young
men in the Pueblo, learned to box, picked fruit and worked for the railroad.
   Unlike the others, he loved to draw and taught himself how to make
paints from the plants and minerals in the area, grinding them on stones left
over from the old days. He found Casas Grandes pottery sherds, and it
seemed plausible that if the ancients made beautiful things, he should be
able to as well.

The earliest days: Casas Grandes mimicry
                        Probably Juan Quezada, 6¾" high, circa 1975

   He learned about the clay through trial and error and learned how to
make the bottoms of his pots by forcing clay into one of his mother’s
dishes, rediscovering the puki, the mold used by prehistoric and modern
potters alike.
   His pots always cracked, so he looked at the edges of the old sherds and
rediscovered temper. He knew that clay hardened in firing, but how? And
with what fuel? He tried dried cow chips, the Rio Grande Pueblo standby.
He reinvented the technique of Southwestern pottery manufacture just by
looking at sherds.
   By 1970, he made good pots that the local traders sold as prehistoric.
When a friend told him about famous potters in the United States who

signed their work, he painted a signature on his, which the traders ground
off. So he etched his name instead, and the etched signature remains a Mata
Ortiz characteristic.
    In fairy-tale fashion, a Princeton-educated anthropologist named
Spencer MacCallum found a couple of Juan’s pots in a Deming junk shop in
1976. He found Juan in Mata Ortiz. For the next seven years, MacCallum
showed and promoted Juan’s work with evangelical zeal. In the meantime,
Juan taught his relatives and neighbors how to make pots and ultimately
taught most of Mata Ortiz.
   By 1990, Juan was a recognized celebrity, teaching summer seminars at
the Idyllwild School near Palm Springs, an honor accorded at various times
to Maria Martinez, Lucy Lewis and other notables. That year, a Japanese
investment company contracted to buy everything Juan made for worldwide
distribution. The deal fell apart in 1991, but the implications were clear.
Juan and the rest of Mata Ortiz now belonged to the world.

They also belonged to the world of Southwestern pottery, which the
Pueblo potters of the north found unappetizing. Juan’s fame didn’t change
the fact that, in the 1990s, the bulk of pottery from the area was mass-
produced, selling for $7.50 to $12 at places like the El Paso Saddleblanket
Company and Jackalope (slogan: “Folk Art by the Truckload”).
     It took a few years, but the prejudice broke down. Mata Ortiz pottery
shed its derivative Casas Grandes character and became an art unto itself.

MATA ORTIZ – BASIC (AND NOT SO BASIC) BLACK

Remembering Ramos Black and San Ildefonso. Turn to page 47, and
you’ll see an effigy jar and a little bowl like the ones Juan Quezada found in
his early wanderings. Ramos Black from Paquimé was the only consistent,
pure black, well-finished blackware in the whole prehistoric Southwest. It
was plentiful, and Juan knew it well.
    In 1978, Spencer MacCallum reported that Mata Ortiz potters had
already figured out how to fire pottery so that it came out black, like Ramos
Black, or like turn-of-the-century blackware from Santa Clara.

As Spencer introduced Juan to the world, the Quezadas were able to
travel. In 1980, Juan actually spent an hour with the ninety-two-year-old
Maria Martinez at San Ildefonso. That same year, Juan’s sister Lydia tried
to touch up the surface of a polished, fired blackware jar and saw an effect
that connected it with the black-on-black ware she’d seen at San Ildefonso.
Experimentation followed, and black-on-black became a staple at Mata
Ortiz.
   Mata Ortiz black-on-black differs greatly from its northern counterpart.
San Ildefonso and Santa Clara ware is thick, while Mata Ortiz ware and the
prehistoric Casas Grandes black is thin and fired at a higher temperature.
Mata Ortiz ware is just about the thinnest of all Southwestern wares, and its
rounded bottom makes it immediately recognizable. The round bottom was
universal in the Casas Grandes ware that inspired Juan, and Mata Ortiz
potters have retained it since the earliest days. If you want to put your Mata
Ortiz jar on the table top, set it in a padded ring or run the risk of having it
teeter around the table.





                            Blackware continues, in all its forms

Fito Teno, 3" diameter, 2007

   As the 1990s progressed, Mata Ortiz potters put new variations into
their blackware. First, they noticed the growing popularity of the grayed
“gunmetal” color developed by Maria and her son Popovi Da at San
Ildefonso and invented their own variant, working graphite into the surface
of the clay. The jar by Efrain Lucero in the front row at right shows the
Mata Ortiz version.
   Mata Ortiz potters found other unexpected things to do with blackware.
The picture below shows Fito Teno’s exquisite version of a prehistoric
corrugated piece.
   Their most dramatic innovation began in the mid-1990s. They did
something the potters up north almost never did: paint polychrome designs
on their blackware. Lela Gutierrez and others had experimented with
painted blackware at Santa Clara around 1930, but it disappeared almost as
quickly as it arrived. At Mata Ortiz, it became a full-flowered art form.
   Long before these experimentations happened, Pueblo potters began to
take notice that something important was going on down in Mata Ortiz.
Lucy Lewis met Juan Quezada at Idyllwild, and as the story goes, she
watched him work with the clay and said to her daughters in Keresan, the
Acoma language, that Juan must actually be an Acoma.
   One of the legends surrounding the church at Sky City says that when
the Indians completed the bell towers, the padres were out of money. With a
resourcefulness typical of the times, they took a group of Acoma children to
Mexico and traded them for a nice new bell.
   Lucy felt the most plausible explanation for Juan’s talent was that he
was descended from those lost children who bought the bell.
   As the twentieth century ended, potters in the north moved away from
Maria Martinez-style blackware in favor of newer treatments, and Mata
Ortiz followed. There’s less being made now than there was before 2000,
but blackware hasn’t disappeared from Mata Ortiz. As is the case up north,
there are still potters at the top of the food chain who owe their reputations
to blackware, especially the polychrome versions.

In the 1990s, polychromes on black made their appearance, an almost
unprecedented departure in Southwestern pottery. The little jar at left is by
Jesus Navarete who, along with family members Eli and Cesar, was among
the earliest Mata Ortiz potters to make polychrome blackware. The jars at
the top by Efron Nuñez and Antonio Sandoval represent the state of the art
a decade into the twenty-first century.
   By the 1990s, Juan Quezada’s brother Reynaldo, who made the big
textured jar at upper right, had established himself as the reigning master

of blackware and family members followed. The sculptured jar at middle
left is by Juan’s younger brother Jesus.
    In the following years, the standards got higher. The olla at upper left
by Cesar Sandoval pretty much explains the degree to which Mata Ortiz has
mastered the medium. Efrain Lucero and Hector Ortiz are just two of the
many artists who have been producing fine work since the 1990s.
    Rito Talavera, Lydia’s Quezada’s husband, developed a sculptural style
of his own, which younger-generation potters like Ivona, Rosa and Martha
Quezada followed. Rosa’s double canteen will look strange only to those
who aren’t familiar with its Casas Grandes antecedents. They made them in
the 1300s, and you can see one on page 47.
    In the 1990s, another major name emerged. Nicolas Ortiz started
making large blackware animal figures, and within months, his work was
commanding prices approaching Juan Quezada’s. The owl at right suggests
why.


MATA ORTIZ – CREATIVE EXPLOSION

High art. In the 1990s, Mata Ortiz pottery moved away from low-end mass
production and towards its ultimate goal of becoming a high-end art form.
For a while, some potters left the local designs behind and copied elements
from Acoma and San Ildefonso—Lucy Lewis Mimbres lizards and Maria
Martinez knifewings.
   By 2000, the copying was pretty much done with, and Mata Ortiz had
its own distinctive design vocabulary. It evolved as Juan Quezada moved
beyond imitating Casas Grandes Ramos Polychrome and developed a
personal style. As potters watched what Juan was doing and watched what
the Pueblo potters were doing up north, the art coalesced, with the results
you see on the opposite page.
   Through constant improvement Mata Ortiz pottery took away Acoma’s
position as the thinnest, most precisely painted Southwestern pottery, and it
achieved the position with a whole new, instantly identifiable look.
   When we visited Mata Ortiz in 2003, we saw striking contrasts. There
were five hundred potters in the town, all of whom recognized that the
world knew and wanted their work. Well-placed dealers were pushing the

prices for Juan Quezada’s finer pieces into the $10,000-and-up category,
and other potters like Nicolas Ortiz weren’t far behind.
   Yet there was no feeling of affluence. The homes had electricity, nice
kitchens, and elaborate new doors, but the streets were still dirt, there were
no street lights, and the homes looked on the outside much like they’d
looked thirty years before. There was one primitive general store, no
hospital and no services. We’d come into Mexico across an interminable
empty desert on roads spattered with cavernous, tire-eating chuckholes.
Once we made it to the city of Nuevo Casas Grandes, a few miles northeast
of the Paquimé ruins and the commerce center for a hundred-mile radius of
ranching country, we started the hard part of the trip.





                       It’s not always that serious. There’s time for fun at Mata Ortiz, too.
                   Bear figurines, Debi Flanigan, 2004. Canoe is 12" long

   Back then, we drove past the turnoff to the ruins and on to Colonia
Juarez, turned at the Mormon temple where Mitt Romney spent some of his
youth, and struggled for twelve miles more on an unmarked dirt road. Our
only navigational aid was counting cattle guards, hoping that we hadn’t
taken a wrong turn. A year later, there was a new highway built by a French

engineering company, described as the finest in all Chihuahua. It should
have signaled the beginning of a meteoric rise in Mata Ortiz’s fortunes, but
civil unrest in northern Mexico that escalated shortly after the new highway
opened cut into Mata Ortiz tourism and made it harder for traders to bring
new pieces to the north.
   Meanwhile, after thirty years of watching Mata Ortiz from a distance,
Spencer and Emi MacCallum moved to Nuevo Casas Grandes and a few
more concerned Norteamericanos set out to help any way they could. A
group of collectors and traders formed the Mata Ortiz Foundation, and they
collected enough money to build a library and finance other needed civic
projects. The group included Walter Parks, who in 1993 had self-published
The Miracle of Mata Ortiz, the book that first brought Juan Quezada and his
town’s pottery to wide recognition.
  A major publisher brought out a sleek, beautifully photographed edition
of Walter’s book in 2011. It has an epilog that brings the miracle up to date.
If you go to Mata Ortiz today, you’ll find that it still looks about the same as
it did when Spencer first visited. But don’t let appearances fool you.
Everything has changed.
   Mata Ortiz now has a kindergarten and a high school with high
attendance. Norteamericanos are building second homes or permanent
residences. Citizens can zip across the new highway to the stores, hospitals
and specialized schools in Nuevo Casas Grandes in less than half an hour.
   Behind the crumbling walls that line the streets, the Miracle happened.

The common thread between the fifteen pieces above is simple quality.
Fineness of finish, fineness of painting, fineness of shape. They’re all so
thin, so light in weight that you’re surprised when you pick them up. Their
thicknesses are uniform. The designs vary widely—abstract or figurative,
traditional or innovative, painted or applied sculpture, repetitive or random
—yet all are instantly recognizable as within the Mata Ortiz tradition.
   This marks a significant evolutionary step. During the eighties and into
the nineties, potters borrowed patterns that were clearly signature designs
for famous Pueblo potters such as Maria Martinez’s knifewing pattern. That
all ended in the 1990s, and you haven’t seen much of it on Mata Ortiz
pottery for a decade.
   Today, Mata Ortiz designs are unique to the Pueblo. If you look at
Evelyn Oliva’s white-on-red vase, Jorge Quintana’s polychrome olla,
Damian Quezada’s and Leonel Lopez S.’s large white polychrome ollas,
Vidal Corona’s little parrot jar or even Larige Corona’s whimsical fish,
uniqueness of origin comes through loud and clear. These couldn’t be from
anywhere but Mata Ortiz.

Mata Ortiz continues to explore new directions and expand the
traditional design repertory, even to the point of using purely Mexican
themes like Angel Trillo’s Day of the Dead jar. All but four pieces in this
picture were made between 2003 and 2011. Yes, Martha Quezada’s carvings
are like Rito Talavera did twenty years before, and yes, Angela Corona did
apply lizards like the ones from Acoma and Zuni on the seed jar at front
center, but the end results on both pieces are pure twenty-first century Mata
Ortiz.
   One more thing: Although Mata Ortiz is developing a powerful new art,
Marta Gonzales R.’s smiling pig reminds us that they have fun as well.


MOJAVE

Not all Southwestern pottery seems alive and well. This one is barely
quivering. In the early twentieth century, the western Yuman-speaking
peoples—the Mojave, the Cocopah and the Quechan—cranked out pottery
for tourists, and the Mojave sold it at the railroad station in Needles.
   Their eastern relatives, the Maricopa, split from (or were chased out by)
the western Yumans in the seventeenth century and allied themselves with
the Akimel O’odham.
   But the western Yumans stayed along the Colorado River. There they
remained, at least in their pottery, the heirs of the Hohokam, who may have
passed over the Yuma Crossing of the Colorado on their way to and from
California in prehistoric times. The resemblance to Hohokam red-on-buff is
strong in Mojave, Cocopah and Quechan pieces alike.
   By 1900, the Quechan and Cocopah had pretty well abandoned pottery,
but the Mojave, with their railroad station connection, kept at it, at least in a
small way, through the twentieth century.

There were others, downriver.
                             Quechan, 5½” high, circa 1870

    In 1970, two famous Mojave potters still worked where the Hohokam
had traded a thousand years before—Annie Fields, on the Mojave
Reservation in Needles, and Elmer Gates on a mixed-tribal reservation to
the south in Parker. The tradition seemed to have disappeared by 1990, but
Betty Barrackman, who had worked with Annie Fields, remained active to
her death in 2007. When we talked to Betty, she lamented that no young
people were taking up the craft, but we saw a couple of tentative
experiments made around 2000 by young potters. We suppose there’s still
hope.
   Despite the heading, we’re not sure we should label this pottery Mojave.
(Or Mohave. California has the Mojave desert, but just across the border,
Arizona has Mohave County. In 1970, the Tribal Council setded on the

California spelling.) We might be smarter to call these pieces Yuman, but
there are two reasons we didn’t.
    First, the word “Yuman” causes confusion. Until recently, writers used
“Yuman” to mean “Quechan.” Since the Quechan actually live in Yuma, it’s
hard to object, but you have to figure out whether the writer is talking about
the Quechan in Yuma or the Yuman-speaking peoples as a whole.
   The temptation to credit the Mojave with all of it and forget the others is
further encouraged by the fact that Cocopah and Quechan potters remained
anonymous to the outside world while Annie Fields and Elmer Gates
brought publicity to the Mojave.
   Today, this habit of mislabeling is almost universal. Just bear in mind
that if it’s pre-1960, red-on-buff and looks mildly Hohokam, it could be
Mojave, but there’s always a chance that one of the other Yumans made it.





  How do you tell Quechan from Mojave from Cocopah? A 1960 Arizona
Highways article gave us dubious help. It told us that Cocopah pottery was
“perhaps the crudest made by these river Yuman tribes,” while Quechan and
Mojave pottery was “rather crudely decorated, but it was better done than
Cocopah wares.”
   That analysis didn’t speak for Elmer Gates, whose work was as
meticulously finished and painted as the finest work of the late nineteenth

century, refined to the point where Betty Barrackman grumbled that he
wasn’t anywhere near traditional enough.

As with Maricopa, there’s not much published material on Mojave, but Jill
Furst’s Mojave Pottery, Mojave People helps with the history, and we spent
considerable time talking to Betty Barrackman about later developments.
   We don’t have a whole lot of assurance about some of our dates here,
but we’re pretty certain about the attributions. The Annie Fields pieces

came to us with good provenances, the Elmer Gates pieces were obvious,
and we bought the Betty Barrackman pieces from Betty.
   When we come to the 1920-and-before pieces, the dates become
guesswork. One thing we’ve pretty well decided is that the dark brown color
of the two pitchers at right center and the remarkable four-spouted effigy
jar in front of them is early, and we hesitate to put any of those pieces in the
twentieth century. The cleaner colors of the wedding vase in front and the
checkerboard pitcher and cup to the right suggest later dates to us.
   The four-spouted effigy is a shape unique to the Mojave. They made
them with and without heads and sold them to the tourists at the Needles
railroad station. We’ve even had one from the 1980s, head and all, by
Elmer Gates.
   Elmer Gates, Annie Fields and Betty Barrackman were three of the last
Mojave potters and the only well-known ones. Elmer had his individual,
well-finished style, while Betty emulated Annie Fields.
   When Betty died in 2007, Mojave pottery appeared finished, but Tony
Soares, a master of Cahuilla and Mojave pottery styles, has been teaching
classes. We don’t know whether Cherie Hines is continuing, but we’ll keep
looking for signs of life in an almost moribund art.


NAMBÉ

It’s more than oven-safe. It’s now highly respected Pueblo pottery. Not
many books have paid much attention to pieces from Nambé (say NOM-
bay). Today, if you know the name Nambé, it’s probably as a brand of
metalware produced in New Mexico not far from the Pueblo.
    Historic Nambé pottery is either micaceous, blackware or polychrome
like San Ildefonso’s and Tesuque’s. All types of it are rare enough so that no
book shows a lot of examples and undistinguised enough so that no authors
felt they had to chase down the examples to show.
   Nambé has been settled since the thirteenth century, and as an ongoing
reminder of the fact, Nambé farmers often turn up sherds of prehistoric
pottery when they work the fields. When the Spanish came, the Nambé
people lived in eight large villages, but the population dwindled over the
years to its present five hundred and fifty.

A guidebook from the mid-1980s advised us that, if we wished to visit,
we’d probably enjoy fishing at the Nambé Falls Recreation Area, but that
the Pueblo has “little to offer in arts and crafts,” and that its pottery is of
“poor quality.”





                             Robert Vigil demonstrates his skill.
                       The bottom of the 5" jar on the opposite page

    Actually, Nambé’s pottery renewal was already under way when the
guidebook was written. Pottery classes had happened back in the 1970s.
Virginia Gutierrez, from an important Santa Clara pottery family, was active
in the 1980s, and Lonnie Vigil was beginning his work.
   Micaceous ware from Taos and the other northern Pueblos had spent
most of the twentieth century as Southwestern pottery’s stepchild until
Lonnie Vigil came along. More than anyone else, he changed the pottery
establishment’s attitude toward Nambé and toward high-fired micaceous
ware.
    Pieces are seldom decorated. The micaceous surface is interesting
enough in itself that additional painted designs seem unnecessary, and this
lack of decoration may have kept it from getting the attention it deserves.

Major juried Indian art exhibitions like the annual Santa Fe Indian
Market had an almost stifling influence in the market. In 1994, Bruce
Bernstein wrote that these exhibits categorized pottery as “decorated” or
“utilitarian” with the assumption that the decorated pottery was the good
stuff.
   At the 1992 Santa Fe Indian Market, the jury selected a large Nambé
micaceous jar by Lonnie Vigil as the best pot in the show, which vaulted
him into the ranks of the elite. But the jury couldn’t bring itself to give him
the overall Best-In-Show prize because his pot wasn’t “art.” The reaction to
the decision was enough to make everyone involved reexamine their
attitudes towards micaceous pottery.
     It took three more years, but in 1995, Santa Fe put on a big micaceous
pottery exhibit, and it starred Lonnie Vigil. The event made the owners of
fancy galleries pay real attention to Lonnie, micaceous ware and Nambé.





    In the years since, Lonnie has remained an overshadowing presence, but
his output has dwindled, while his modest nephew, Robert Vigil is gaining
ever-growing notice. Robert made believers out of us in 1995 with the little
jar at right center on the opposite page. He makes the thinnest, lightest,
most exquisitely finished micaceous ware we’ve ever seen.
   By 2012, Robert had added a new brown color to his repertory, and you
could find his work at high-end galleries like Andrea Fisher in Santa Fe or
the Case Trading Post in the Wheelwright Museum, where we bought the
jar at top left. Beyond its grace and proportion, the photograph shows its
almost impossible thinness.
   Nambé’s once-clunky utilitarian ware is now indisputably art.

Whenever we see deep copper-red micaceous ware, we think it comes from
Nambé. Francis Harlow’s 1977 Modern Pueblo Pottery, 1880–1960 says
Nambé made micaceous pottery until the late 1940s, then production ended.
The oval dish seems old enough to warrant the 1930 date.
   Robert Vigil’s carved jar at middle right has that copper color. He
managed several remarkable things on this piece. First, he delivered high
polish on the raised portions, always difficult because the flecks of mica
pick out during polishing and leave little pits that look like flaws.
   Then, at a time when micaceous pottery was almost always heavy, he
made this exceptionally thin. In fact, it was the thinnest deep-carved pot

we’d ever seen. And, just to show he wasn’t lazy, he carved a Mimbres
knife-blade pattern and another avanyu on the bottom. That bottom
impressed us enough that we put it on the opposite page. The jars at top left
and front center came almost twenty years later and demonstrate his
mastery of the medium.
   The pieces by Pearl Talachy, Virginia Gutierrez and Gloria Trujillo all
look like they could have come from Santa Clara or San Ildefonso. There’s
much intermarriage among the northern Tewa Pueblos. Virginia Gutierrez
is a sister-in-law of Minnie Vigil, a well-known Santa Clara potter, and of
Thelma Talachy and Lois Gutierrez, equally well known as Pojoaque
potters. In 2013, Martha Romero was new to us, and she’s still learning.
   The two early Lonnie Vigil pieces are nice enough, but hardly
summarize his influence. Major pieces by Lonnie might be eighteen inches
in diameter, undecorated except for intentional fire clouds, and beyond this
museum’s budget.


NAVAJO

If it’s brown, rough and shiny, it’s probably Navajo. And probably came
from Cow Springs. When the Navajo met the Puebloans at Gobernador
Canyon around 1690, they made pottery, and the plainware of that time, so
far as we know, established the rounded and pointed bottom shapes that
distinguished Navajo plainware into the twentieth century. For a typical
early example, look at the 1920s jar in the middle of the picture opposite.
   The Navajo had come down from Canada perhaps 250 years before
Gobernador, nomadic Athapascans who made life uncomfortable for the
residents. “Anasazi,” after all, meant “enemy ancestors,” which pretty well
explains the Navajo attitude on the subject. (Like the O’odham, the Ohkay
and the Kewa, the Navajo are dumping their old Spanish-inflicted name. If
you want to address them correctly, call them Diné.)
   Like other nomadic hunter-gatherers, pottery wasn’t important in their
culture. Despite the Gobernador interlude, it remained a slow-developing
minor craft until the middle of the twentieth century. The Navajo
concentrated on plainware, and by 1950, their pottery was an undecorated
utility ware made by a few families in the Shonto/Cow Springs area.

Resin-coated and playful, but monumental
                                  Aleta Bitsi, 21" high (!), 1992

     It had two distinguishing characteristics: a lumpy fillet-rim decoration
around the rim of jars, a design convention that held through the nineteenth
and twentieth centuries, and a shiny piñon pitch coating for waterproofing,
put on after firing. It’s easy to distinguish Navajo resin coating from the
high polish of a Pueblo piece. It looks and feels like a thick, slightly sticky

varnish and fills every indentation on the pot. Surface polishing doesn’t get
down into the crevices. It’s not clear when the melted pitch first appeared,
but it remains on all traditional and on much contemporary Navajo
brownware.
    After 1950, outsiders started noticing Cow Springs brownware. Chuck
and Jan Rosenak’s The People Speak told how Bill Beaver was working up
at Shonto and he and the trading post’s owner’s wife started encouraging
potters. Back then, everything that wasn’t ceremonial was either utilitarian
fillet-rim jars or pottery imitations of pieces normally made of metal or
glass: frying pans, coffee pots and the like. The pitcher in the center of the
picture on the opposite page was made by Mary Henderson, who, we were
told, was the last Navajo potter to make true, high-fired, fire-safe utilitarian
resin-coated pottery.
   Beaver had to tell Louise Goodman to “make something different”
before her pottery began to sell to the outside world. By 2000, her
“something differents—coiled jars, pig banks and giant bears—brought
high prices and found their way to folk art museums far more prestigious
than this one.

At Navajo, pottery still takes a back seat to rugs and jewelry, but the
reservation has three hundred thousand people spread out over a plot of
land bigger than many states. In a population base like this, even a
secondary art finds practitioners.
     It may be easy to recognize what’s on this page as Navajo, but the art
isn’t standing still. Two forces tug at Navajo potters. The folk art market
encourages its off-center, humorous aspects, while the upper-end
Southwestern pottery market pushes it toward the mainstream galleries.
   The next pages show what’s happening in both directions.

The jar second from left in the bottom row, the even cruder one at bottom
right and the old one in the center are classic Navajo. The shape and fillet
rim with the ceremonial break (a missing lug in the circlet) are typical, as
are the resin coating and the fire clouds. Mary Henderson’s pitcher shares
its utilitarian hard surface with the jar behind it.
   Everything in the picture bears a Cow Springs stamp. Betty Manygoats
joined her relatives in Cow Springs in 1973. Wedding vases overrun with
appliqued homed toads became a family signature as Elizabeth
demonstrated with her over-the-top effort on the right. Aleta Bitsi took the
toads to new heights with her giant on the opposite page.
   Louise Goodman turned stacked coil pots like the handled jar at top left
into a personal trademark. There was one on the cover of Hartman and
Musial’s definitive Navajo Pottery. Her daughter Stella, who made the little
one in the front row, is Betty Manygoats’s clan sister.
    Silas and Bertha Claw made three-spouted wedding vases. They were
Cow Springs too, neighbors of Rose Williams, matriarch of another Cow
Springs group.
    Alice Cling, Rose’s daughter, brought pitch-coated brownware to a new
level (left in the lower middle row). She took the piñon-coated surface and
turned it into graceful polished jars that rank in the top echelon of
Southwestern pottery prestige. Susie Crank, another of Rose’s daughters,
works in Alice’s idiom, as does Arnold Spencer (bottom, third from left), an
in-law. After 2000, Samuel Manymules, who made the jar next to the old
one in the middle, raised the bar even higher.

NAVAJO – FOLK ART

To Cow Springs, add Sweetwater and Fruitland. It was ever thus in the
world of art, we suppose, but nobody outside the Southwest paid much
attention to art from the backwaters of the Navajo Reservation until a
couple of lawyers named Rosenak focused on it. In 1987, Russell Hartman
and Jan Musial mentioned a few artists in their book, Navajo Pottery, but
the book’s main thrust was elsewhere. The Wheelwright had a Navajo folk
art show with a book-length catalog in 1987, but the craft remained
relatively low profile.

Then Chuck and Jan Rosenak came along, fresh from their impressively
titled 1990 book, Museum of American Folk Art Encyclopedia of Twentieth-
Century American Folk Art and Artists, and they set to work publicizing an
enthusiasm they’d acquired in their general folk art research.

These giant bears made Louise Goodman famous
          21½" high (!!!), 1995

They showcased Navajo folk art in a traveling exhibition that appeared
in museums in Missouri, New Mexico and Arizona between 1987 and 1990.
But their 1995 book, The People Speak, made it official that Navajo folk art
had arrived.
   The category included weavers, painters and carvers as well as potters,
but pottery played a big part, and the potters of Cow Springs were as
important as any. Potters from obscure places like Sweetwater and
Fruitland, just west of Farmington, play important roles as well. Bill
Beaver, who’d worked with the Cow Springs potters at Shonto in the 1980s,
had settled in a trading post near Flagstaff, where we met him and Louise
Goodman’s giant bear.
   The basic Navajo resin-coated brownware had evolved over the years in
the hands of artists like Alice Cling and Lorraine Williams, who have left
the folk art world behind, but Cow Springs potters like Louise Goodman
and Betty Manygoats kept the folk tradition alive into the twenty-first
century. However, Cow Springs had to share billing with an even older
tradition: mud toys. These little painted, unfired figurines make the crudest
Cow Springs brownware seem downright sophisticated.
   Mamie Deschillie (1920–2010) made mud toys, but she also made, and
was better known for, cutouts and paintings on cardboard, sometimes
dressed in bits of fabric. A self-taught Navajo counterpart of Grandma
Moses, Mamie had such an imposing air that she affected us much like
Lena Mesquerre had impressed J.F. Breazeale in 1923. Like Lena, Mamie
had “the grace and dignity of a highborn.”
   Her work first appeared in influential books in the 1990s, and by the
end of the decade, she’d achieved worldwide recognition. She knew mud
toys as a child. According to the Rosenaks, mud toys had been written
about as early as 1880, but the tradition of making them had apparently
been forgotten and had died out by 1940.
    In one sense, it’s mildly amazing that there are any mud toys left. Since
they’re nothing more than dried mud, they’re so fragile that they can fall
apart for what can seem like no reason at all. People who sell them refuse to
ship them (they won’t survive the transit), and we’ve had a couple just
crumble under their own weight while they were sitting undisturbed on a
shelf.
    Elsie Benally started making mud toys in the early 1980s, and her yarn-
wrapped sheep, goats and buffaloes seem to define the art. She reportedly

spoke no English, and even the Rosenaks, for all their ferocious pursuit,
were never able to find her for an in-person interview.
     If folk art has to come from unspoiled, out-of-the-way places, those
mud toys qualify without question, and much of the brownware isn’t far
behind.

This is the pottery side of Navajo folk art as defined by the Rosenaks in

piggy bank outdoes Louise’s for pure whimsy. Silas and Bertha Claw’s

note on three-spouted wedding vases. We wondered why two and three-
spouted pieces exist in prehistoric ware until the lightbulb went on over our
heads, and we realized you could put a thong through the spouts of a two-
spouted one and carry it over your shoulder, hands free. And if you made a
three-spouted one, you could drink out of it without putting your nose in the
thong.)
   The jars by Lorraine Williams and Irene White in the middle and bottom
rows hover on the outer edges of folk art. Any Navajo pitch-coated
brownware qualifies, we suppose, but these examples are too contemporary
to fit the genre comfortably. There’s one by Lorraine on the next spread
that, as we see it, leaves folk art completely behind.
   That can’t be said about the mud toys. They radiate folk art. We’re sure
of the attributions on Mamie Deschillie’s yarn-tailed pink-saddled elephant
and on Elsie Benally’s somber looking buffalo. However the appaloosa
horse looks like it might have been made by the same person who made the
elephant, and the three sheep show a definite kinship to the buffalo. The
giraffe and the pickup truck are by others. Together, attributed or
anonymous, they tell the whole story.
    Finally, Larry Ben’s resin-coated pinto in the bottom row splits the
difference between mud toys and traditional brownware right down the
middle.


NAVAJO – TOWARD THE MAINSTREAM

The outside world intrudes. When you observe Navajo pottery from a
distance, it’s comforting to think of it as a pure art, and pockets of
consistent production like Cow Springs confirm that pleasant concept.
   But it’s never been a pure art, which is a mixed blessing. Commercial
pressure constantly tears at its integrity, but competition keeps pushing the
standards higher. The picture on the opposite page testifies to both sides of
the issue.
   The incised seed jar at right center of the middle row was made at the
Mesa Verde Pottery Company of Cortez, Colorado, precast and decorated
on an assembly line in a pattern developed by Ute Mountain potters. Why is
it even in this book? Well, it was signed by a Navajo and sold as art.

That’s not too long a reach. Lorraine Williams, born in Sweetwater, wife
of Cow Springs matriarch Rose Williams’s son George, once worked at
Mesa Verde Pottery. She made pots like this one for a whole winter.
  Now she makes pots like the big one in the center of the next page. She
gets written up in the fancy books and each year brings the Navajo resin-
coated style to higher and higher levels.
   Like it or not, machine-made Ute design pottery was about the only
Navajo pottery you could find easily throughout the 1990s, and a book that
tries to define Navajo pottery can’t leave it out. In the 1990s, Wallace Nez
went so far with the idea that pieces like the seed jar at the right of the front
row now sell for high prices in the fancy stores.
   The picture on the next page might be called “influences from all over.”
There’s a pre-cast jar painted to look like San Ildefonso blackware and a
blackware piece in the front row that looks a lot like good San Ildefonso
and Santa Clara pottery.
    There’s incised redware so elaborate that it immediately conjures up
Santa Clara’s priciest potters. There’s moderately successful pottery in
imititation of Hopi ware, and there’s a piece by Ida Sahmie, who learned
pottery-making from Priscilla Namingha, Nampeyo’s great-granddaughter.
There are imposing sculptured pieces that meet anyone’s definition of
serious art, one by Arlan Dempsey in resin-coated brownware, and several
pieces of fine-finished resin-coated brownware.
   The picture below suggests how high up the pottery-as-art ladder
Navajo pottery has come. Nathan Begaye was a leading artist through the
1990s and, until his death in 2010, was always represented in galleries that
specialized in the finest cutting-edge art. His work could be Hopi-
influenced or, just as often, so individual and experimental that it defied
categorizing.
   He was one of the five potters included in the book Free Spirit: The
New Native American Potter, published in the Netherlands by the Stedlijk
Museum in 2006. The others were Virgil Ortiz and Diego Romero of
Cochiti, Susan Folwell of Santa Clara and another Navajo, Christine
McHorse. She used to make resin-coated brownware but now makes dead-
white vessels that make you think of Henry Moore sculpture, and she would
have been featured alongside Nathan on this page if we’d ever found one
we could afford.

   Free Spirit chose those five internationally known potters to represent
the peak of the art in the twenty-first century, and few would argue with the
selection. However, that selection might suggest a little rethinking. For
years, the world has looked to Hopi, Acoma, Santa Clara and San Ildefonso
for the finest pottery. The fact that two of the five artists shown in Free
Spirit were Navajo and two others were from Cochiti is something of a
wakeup call.
