David John’s and Nora Yazzie’s matte masks, Mary Mitchell Trejo’s and
Nora Yazzie’s tall figures and Arlan Dempsey’s resin-coated sculpture show
how far Navajo pottery has moved into the world of mainstream
contemporary art. Dempsey, by the way, is Laguna/Navajo.
Experimentation is no stranger to Laguna these days, but we couldn’t bring
ourselves to put a resin-coated brownware piece anywhere but with the
Navajo half of his heritage.
   Lorraine Williams’s beautifully detailed tall jar serves as strong
evidence that resin-coated brownware is way past its primitive folk art
beginnings. Samuel Manymules, Michelle Williams, and Melissa Johnson

and Jerome Begay have taken Alice Cling’s immaculate brownware another
step further into the contemporary mainstream.
   Casha Blue Sky’s Santa Clara-inspired redware is superb. Fabian
Norberto’s blackware jar in the front row is almost as good. Wallace Nez
has taken the Ute Mountain idea to a higher level with his fastidious incised
pieces.
   Ida Sahmie put a full Navajo pictorial on her jar—hogan, sheep,
windmill, rug weaver and trading post. As sister-in-law to Rachel, Jean and
Bonnie Sahmie, she learned the Nampeyo family lessons well. Ida’s work
straddles both cultures, and she reached the celebrity plateau years ago.
  On the lower end, Gerry and Saressa Whitehorse made pots that look
Hopi, but without the finesse. CBA’S blackware jar may be greenware, but
if it is, it fools the eye. And, of course, E. Etsitty’s effort is factory-made all
the way.


OHKAY OWINGE (THE NEW/OLD NAME FOR SAN
JUAN)

Today everything is Ohkay, but there were some rocky years along the
way. Coronado knew that Puebloans lived up the Rio Grande at Ohkay, but
he spared them the pleasure of his company. Ohkay saw its first Spanish in
1593, and according to a contemporary account, the women were so
frightened that they wept at the sight. Future events proved the
appropriateness of their reaction.
   Governor Oñate came to call in 1598, and he not only declared all its
residents members of the Catholic church, he liked the village so much that
he kicked everybody out, declared it the capital of his new fiefdom, and
renamed it San Juan de los Caballeros—St. John of the Horsemen. We’ve
seen prepared-in-Santa-Fe literature that translates it as “St. John of the
Gentlemen,” but there seems to have been little gentlemanly behavior
towards the natives on Oñate’s part.
   Ohkay lasted only a month as Oñate’s capital. He moved to an
abandoned Pueblo just across the Rio Grande and built the first mission in
New Mexico. Eleven years later, the capital moved to Santa Fe, but Ohkay

had been the first Pueblo to feel the full weight of Oñate’s heel. Resentment
towards the Spanish built early and strong.





                     A classic 1890s Ohkay serving bowl
                                    It’s 13" in diameter, and it was made byamaster.

    In 1675, the Spanish decided to quash heathen worship for good and
tried forty-seven religious leaders from several Pueblos for murder and
witchcraft.
    In their wisdom, they hung four of them and flogged the others. Popé of
Ohkay Owinge escaped the noose, suffered a flogging and spent the next
five years planning a reprisal. Today he’s generally credited with having
been the architect and leader of the brilliantly synchronized guerrilla
uprising of 1680 that burned the missions and drove the armed, mounted
Spanish military machine all the way down to El Paso.
   Camelot only lasted twelve years, however, and almost immediately
after the reconquest, General de Vargas made sure that Ohkay Owinge had
the opportunity to build a brand-new mission.
   From that time on, Ohkay has had a low profile, even though its current
population of fifteen hundred makes it one of the larger northern Pueblos.
An early player in the casino-building spree of the 1990s, Ohkay’s people
have been more interested in agriculture and jobs in town than in the arts.

As a result, Ohkay Owinge pottery has a low profile, even though it has
a distinctive tradition (actually several traditions), demands great skill and
is highly recognizable.
   Nineteenth-century Ohkay pottery differed from that made by its Santa
Clara neighbors to the South. It was thinner and it had a harder surface
created by a higher firing temperature, and it had a distinctive color break
between the high-polish upper body and the unslipped lower body as on the
underside of the bowl below.





   Ohkay pottery has a relative lack of market appeal compared to work
from Santa Clara and San Ildefonso. For better or worse, Santa Fe drives
the market for Southwestern art. Through the twentieth century and into the
current one, starting perhaps even before Edgar Hewitt began working with
Maria Martinez, the curators, critics and dealers who comprise Santa Fe’s
art establishment have encouraged, influenced, directed, commissioned and
promoted the work of Santa Clara and San Ildefonso potters while they
largely ignored the artists from Ohkay.
  We can smile at the distinction. Mary Ellen and Laurence Blair’s 1986
Margaret Tafoya shows a black jar with an Ohkay-style color break that’s
the same size and shape as the big one in the picture on the opposite page.
According to the book, Margaret credited it to her legendary Santa Clara
mother, Seven Families matriarch Sara Fina, and put an 1890 date on it. If
the one in the picture received the same blessing, it would immediately be
worth ten times what we paid for it.
   Once again, marketing trumps intrinsic value.

Before 1900, thin, high-fired, hard-surfaced Ohkay Owinge pottery was
some of the most practical pottery made anywhere in the Southwest. Giant
nineteenth-century Ohkay storage jars, two feet or more in diameter, were
the lightest and strongest big jars anywhere. Today, collectors pay major
dollars for those beautifully made ollas.
   Ohkay pottery before 1900 was either red or black, showed micaceous
flecks in the slip and was normally undecorated. However, fire clouds on
the redware are so prominent that they seem to have been intentional.
   There was some overlap with Santa Clara, especially with blackware, as
the Sara Fina Tafoya suggestion for the big black jar indicates. If Sara Fina
actually made it, however, she made it exactly the way a skilled Ohkay
potter would have made it—thin, light and impeccably finished. It has a

distinct color break between the high polish of the slipped upper body and
the less shiny unslipped lower portion. That feature did show up
occasionally on early Santa Clara blackware, but it was almost universal
on Ohkay pieces. In the picture above, the color break is most obvious on
the sugar and creamer at front left, but it’s present on all the 1910-and-
earlier pieces, red or black.
    After 1900, according to some sources, Ohkay Owinge pottery went into
eclipse, only to be revived around 1930 by potters with a new set of
standards. We find it difficult to accept such a big time gap, and we’ve used
some intermediate dates. The Mexican-inspired pitcher to the left came with
a 1923 date and, like the little basket, has no color break or fire clouds. The
fire-clouded moccasin has white decoration which seems to relate to a later
period.
   As a final transition to the 1930 revival, the jar at upper right with
white decoration on a matte band above a polished underbody signaled
what was to come.


OHKAY OWINGE – BUILDING A STYLE

An incisive approach. In the nineteenth century, Ohkay Owinge made and
traded a large amount of pottery. But Jonathan Batkin’s Pottery of the
Pueblos of New Mexico, 1700–1940 points out that there were no potters at
Ohkay in 1910 according to the census.
   This doesn’t mean, of course, that those potters vanished like their
prehistoric ancestors. Census records of the Pueblos have always been
unreliable because Pueblo Indians haven’t always shared the Census
Bureau’s compulsion to record every possible fact. However, it does
suggest that there probably weren’t a lot of highly visible potters working at
Ohkay Owinge in the first quarter of the twentieth century, and that one’s
chance of turning up Ohkay pottery from that period is correspondingly
slim.
   Beginning about 1930, a whole new style emerged, led by seven potters
working under the urging of Regina Cata, a married-in Hispanic, who in
turn was urged either by the ubiquitous Kenneth Chapman or, more likely,
by Chester Faris, the superintendent of the Santa Fe Indian School (and the
man who told Maria Martinez to sign her name “Marie”). The new group

included Crucita Trujillo, Gregocita Cruz, Crucita Talachy, Reyecita
Trujillo, Luteria Atencio, Tomasita Montoya and one other whose name no
one seems to remember. The picture on the next page features three of
them, Crucita Trujillo, Reyecita Trujillo and the prolific Tomasita Montoya.
   Cata and the others were told that they should make pieces that honored
their ancestral style. The helpful Anglo advisors pointed to an eccentric
fourteenth-century style called Potsuwi’i Incised that showed up in the hills
behind the Pueblo. The curators of this museum tend to believe that people
made pottery like their neighbors made and when they moved, continued to
make pottery like they’d always made. For us, Potsuwi’i Incised doesn’t
compute as Ohkay Ancestral Puebloan pottery. It doesn’t look like anything
Ancestral Puebloans ever made, but it looks a whole lot like the pottery
made by people from the Mississippian culture over in Texas. Our guess is
that, in the way that a few Hopi went to southern Arizona in the fourteenth
century, some Texans parked at Ohkay and left their pots behind.
    Potsuwi’i pottery, like much Mississippian pottery, used fine parallel
incising as decoration. It also had an extra wrinkle that we thought was a
twentieth-century conceit when first saw it on modern pieces. The Potsuwi’i
potters rubbed glittery micaceous clay into the incisions.

Basic 1930s revival
                     7½" high, circa 1935, with all the features

   The advisors’ suggestion wasn’t just a push for pottery purity. The well-
meaning Anglos believed that the potters would fatten their incomes if they
made pieces that the market would accept as properly traditional.
    In the 1930s, Regina Cata and the other seven group members
developed their “ancestral” style: polished redware with a matte tan incised
band in the Potsuwi’i manner, with the glitter added in the incisions. These
new pieces were heavier than the old Ohkay Owinge pieces and were
always free of fire clouds. The jar below has it all: the heft, the cloud-free
polish, the matte band, the Potsuwi’i parallel incisions and the glitter.
   As the style developed, the Potsuwi’i model was far too confining for
Ohkay artists. The tan band became a mural space, to be carved and painted
with natural slips in a rich variety of designs. The incised linear designs
quickly became replaced by whatever designs the potters felt like making,

and the mica largely disappeared, supplanted by white outlines and accents
spruced up with areas of matte red. We even found a jar where the potter
painted gray over white areas, and left enough of the white showing through
to give you the impression that she’d painted them silver. It’s to the left on
the next page.
   Ohkay’s ancestral revival was short-lived, and the instantly recognizable
style that came out of it seems to be fading away. The newer pieces on the
next pages point in other directions.

From the 1930s to the current century what you see in the picture has been
the essence of Ohkay Owinge pottery.
    In Pueblo Pottery of the New Mexico Indians, Betty Toulouse described
how Cata and her followers studied Potsuwi’i sherds. One can almost hear
the helpful suggestions of Faris, Chapman and their friends. In their
relentless search for the authentic, they never missed an opportunity to
encourage a Pueblo potter to switch over to historic or prehistoric
decorative motifs, thereby making the art more purely “Indian,” less
“debased” by European influences. The fact that this purity was obtained at
the suggestion of a non-Indian never seemed to bother them.
   Dominguita Sisneros’ bowl in the front row is closest to the model.
Rosita de Herrera’s incised piece in the middle came much later, and by
then the rules had relaxed. It has the Potsuwi’i hatching and some mica but
the white puts it far past the original model. When revival pieces have
micaceous slip, it’s almost like gold paint, way beyond the random flecks
that show up in the old pieces.
    In any event, it didn’t take long before Regina Cata and her gang
started using any designs they pleased on their pots, authentic pre-
European or not. The Tomasita Montoya pot at top left, her bowl at left
front and Rosita de Herrera’s jar at middle right differ from the original
model in that they have deep carving rather than shallow incision. Tomasita
was entitled to fool around a bit. After all, she was the most prolific of
Regina Cata’s original seven followers.
   Sometimes art simply refuses to sit still for authenticity. Art will do that
even when the authenticity is truly authentic.


OHKAY OWINGE – BEYOND THE STYLE

A different kind of evolution. Regina Cata’s legacy endured for a long time.
Through the twentieth century, potters at Ohkay Owinge continued within
the style she defined.
   But today, most citizens of Ohkay Owinge have their minds on things
other than Pueblo pottery. Farming and sheepherding still exist, but so does
commuting to jobs in Española, Los Alamos and Taos, and so do all the
distractions that exist in what is now a casino-rich Pueblo. Regina Cata’s
style is old news.

Twenty years ago, we wrote about driving into the Pueblo and finding
the impressive Oke Okweege Arts and Crafts Cooperative, and said you
probably wouldn’t find much contemporary pottery there. On our 2013
visit, we couldn’t even find any evidence of the Cooperative. We suppose it
could eventually reemerge as part of the casino complex next to the
highway.





                                  Twenty-first century magnificence
                               Clarence Cruz, 2009, 17¾" high

The fact that there’s little immediate evidence of top-level pottery at the
Pueblo doesn’t mean it’s not being done. It does signal that there’s not a lot
of it to be found. Pottery isn’t anywhere near as important to Ohkay
Owinge’s well-being as it is, say, to San Ildefonso, Cochiti or Santa Clara.
   At those Pueblos, you can still park your car, walk a couple of minutes
and find good pottery for sale. That doesn’t work at Ohkay. Instead you
have to go to Santa Fe or Albuquerque, find the better retail neighborhoods,
and if you look carefully, you might find beautiful work like the pieces in
the picture. We had to go to the Poeh Museum in Pojoaque to find our first
post-2000 pieces.
    In the 1990s, cream, red and micaceous slips and blackware reappeared.
Potters occasionally experimented with non-traditional things like
commercial paints, as on Dominguita Naranjo’s micaceous bowl in the
picture to the right.
   During those years, potters took the work by Regina Cata and her
contemporaries and moved it to a point where the older pieces look
downright primitive by comparison, but the big advances over Regina
Cata’s style were over by 2000.
   Few new potters have emerged, but they include one transcendent one.
Clarence Cruz received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2011 Indian
Market, and the giant micaceous jar at left explains why. To understand the
importance and quality of his pottery, you only need to know that no Pueblo
supports contemporary Indian arts more than Pojoaque, and that the
Pueblo’s Governor uses bowls and plates by Clarence Cruz for ceremonial
dinners. Cruz teaches at the University of New Mexico and at Poeh, and
Doree Garcia, who made the micaceous corn jar on the left side of the
picture, is one of his students.
   Today, Ohkay potters mainly do micaceous ware. Older artists like
Myrtle Cata and the Tapias continue to do beautiful work, but Alvin Curran
died in 2000, and we’ve seen little from Lawrence Dili and Mary Maestas
who showed so much promise when wrote about them in 1996. The
innovative Diego and Martina Aguino belonged to an earlier pottery
generation, and Gilbert Olivas looks elsewhere for inspiration.
  A few years ago, a dinner conversation in Santa Fe with the people at
the next table turned to the casinos and their effect on Pueblo life. They told
us that what they used to refer to as “spooky Tesuque” had become a
thriving, vital community thanks to casino money. However, prosperity

doesn’t always produce immediate magic. It hasn’t yet produced a pottery
renaissance at Tesuque like the ones at Pojoaque and San Felipe.
   At Ohkay, we’re still waiting for the magic. Perhaps Clarence Cruz is
the beginning.

The Mary Maestas jar, the Lawrence Dili wedding vase and the Diego and
Martina Aguino pieces are direct inheritors of Regina Cata’s legacy, but
more in line with Golden Age demands for technical mastery and design
skill.
   Myrtle Cata shares Regina Cata’s name, but her shaped plainware jars
in some way echo earlier times at Ohkay Owinge. They’re thin, graceful

and free of painted decoration, a result of the ever-increasing sophistication
demanded from the best potters at every Pueblo.
   Dominguita Naranjo’s bowl in the center departs from the Cata
tradition, but she has unarguable credentials. She’s Tomasita Montoya’s
granddaughter and mother of the inventive Jennifer S. Tse-Pe, whose work
prodded San Ildefonso’s Gonzales family in new directions.
   The late Alvin Curran’s little bear underscores the cross-cultural nature
of Southwestern pottery. His wife Dolores, who works in her native Santa
Clara style, is every bit as famous as a potter, and Gilbert Olivas makes no
secret of his Santa Clara connection. Tom and Sue Tapia’s incised
blackware has been widely known since the 1970s and seems to owe as
much to Santa Clara and San Ildefonso as it does to anything from Ohkay.
   Clarence Cruz, today’s leading Ohkay potter, does blackware and
micaceous pieces that explore several pottery avenues. His student, Doree
Garcia, made the impressive red-on-micaceous corn jar after only a single
year of study.
   And Lawrence Dili was as versatile and imaginative as any potter in the
Southwest. We’ve never seen another frog quite like this one. We can only
hope that he, like so many artists, hasn’t disappeared.


O’ODHAM

Three hundred years ago, the Spanish garbled their names. It’s time to
correct the mistake. Until the 1980s, all the books referred to the people
who occupy the big reservations around Phoenix and the bigger ones west
of Tucson as the Pima and the Papago, a mispronunciation of the name the
Pima called them.
   Now, let’s put those names in the wastebasket. They’re both O’odham
—the northern branch, the Akimel O’odham or River People, the southern
group the Tohono O’odham or Desert People. (You really have to have
cotton in your ears to hear Tohono as Papago.)
   They speak the same language, and today both groups are better known
for basketry than pottery, but the O’odham have been making pottery for a
long time. A 1698 manuscript tells of Gila River Indians carrying water in
jars, probably much like the ancient one on the opposite page.

Four pieces by a great Tohono potter who sold her work at San Xavier and remains an unsolved
                                            mystery.
                           All are circa 1870–1890. The pitcher is 13" high.

   Of course, there had been pottery in the area for a thousand years—this
was Hohokam land, and current thinking puts the O’odham as their most
likely descendants.
    Until the middle of the nineteenth century, Gila River pottery meant
mostly storage jars, big and a bit ungainly to modern eyes. You can get an
idea of their scale from the picture at right. They were red on buff,
undecorated red, or later on, black on red.

After 1880, when the railroad came, O’odham potters began making
Maricopa-style tourist ware. Recent thinking says Maricopa black-on-red is
really nothing more than O’odham pottery copied and improved upon. After
all, the Akimel and the Maricopa were close allies, and idea exchange must
have happened all along.
  We stumbled on one Tohono potter who made tourist ware before 1880,
and it doesn’t look like any O’odham or Maricopa pottery made before or
since. We know the date because we’ve seen a piece by this potter with a
penciled note on the bottom saying it was bought in 1874 at San Xavier del
Bac, the Tucson mission on the O’odham Reservation. Based on the four
pieces to the left and the five others we’ve seen, we guess that she was
married-in and learned the craft elsewhere, but she sure learned it. Her
name may be lost, but her work was a clear signature.
   That doesn’t mean we picked up on it right away. Our first piece was
the cup, and we called it Maricopa. Our second was the swirl jar, and in our
The Desert Southwest, we put its date as 1920. Until we learned about the
1874 jar, found the other two pieces and saw the others buried in museums,
we were clueless.
   The picture to the right includes standard Tohono pottery of the day, and
the Maricopa really did improve on it. Tohono tourist pieces often show
polishing striations while the average Maricopa piece has a more refined
surface. A small group of Akimel who lived near the Maricopa made
refined polished ware, but those pieces are scarce.

In the twentieth century, O’odham pottery evolved and split into
regional styles. The O’odham were more widespread than any pottery group
except the Navajo, and like the Navajo, pottery wasn’t their prime art. The
next pages show what happened.

The array sums up what we think about early O’odham pottery, beginning
at the beginning. The big buff jar in the back might be as early as the
1600s, and it comes closer to being a direct descendant of late Classic-
period Hohokam pottery than anything else we’ve ever seen.
    In the nineteenth century, the O’odham were still making the big storage
jars, by then mostly red, but they also made figurines that seem more Casas
Grandes than Hohokam. We’d originally called the little hooded effigy at

front left Maricopa, but since it seems really early, the odds are better that
it’s O’odham. Later examples like the giant lady have also been identified
as Maricopa in other books, but after staring at them, we’re pretty sure
they’re all O’odham.
   The one thing we won’t try to do is try to decide which of these, either
the big ones or the small tourist pieces, are Tohono or Akimel. The odds are
that most are Tohono—a bigger population and more craft emphasis on
pottery.
   The hooded effigy with the big necklace was dated at 1880 by an expert
who looked at the beadwork and the trade cloth and made the call. Like
several other pieces in the picture, the tall lady has a satin finish in one of
the shades of the almost indescribable off-red that shows up on many early
O’odham tourist pieces and almost nowhere else.
   To us, these pieces say that the O’odham made fine pottery really early.
Maricopa pottery gets most of the attention now, but in the years when they
learned their craft, the O’odham were just as skilled. Few early Maricopa
pieces can compete for quality with the cup, the dove and the footed bowl.


O’ODHAM – REGIONS AND FAMILIES

Divergence, as always. The Akimel and the Tohono weren’t always bonded
at the hip. They both spoke Piman, but they had different second languages.
   The Tohono, who had years of exposure to and comfortable coexistence
with the missions, spoke Spanish. The Akimel met the gold rush migrants
who came through the Salt and Gila Rivers, and learned English, which
gave them a much greater presence with the territory’s new occupants.
   As a result, the Akimel got big riverfront reservations while the Tohono
got a tiny little plot of land at San Xavier mission in Tucson, then eight
years later, a little reservation out west, and almost forty years later, in
1912, another little one up north near the Akimel reservation. Finally, in
1917, they got real land, the Sells Reservation, one of the largest pieces of
Indian real estate in America. It didn’t have any rivers, but it did have rain,
and the Tohono turned to cattle raising. They also continued making pots.
    In the 1962 Papago Indian Pottery, Bernard Fontana concluded that it
was “abundantly clear that by the late 1800s and the early 1900s, Papagos,
Pimas and Kohatks were making black on red.”

One short-lived style: folk art
                         Laura Kerman, 6" diameter, circa 1970.

   The Kohatk were Akimel, eighteenth-century Akimel-to-Tohono
migrants who played a big role in the development of O’odham pottery and
Maricopa pottery as well. They figured out how to polish, and quite
possibly the high polish on Maricopa ware came to them through the
Kohatk.
   O’odham pottery can’t be bundled into a tidy homogenous style. It’s
more like what comes out of the Pueblos between Taos and Albuquerque.
Those Pueblos are just medium to small towns, each with its own artistic
identity. Even though they’re only a few miles apart, anyone who’s looked
at a few typical examples has no difficulty telling a Taos pot from a Cochiti
pot from a Santa Clara pot. The local and family traditions that dictate what
each pot looks like have held for centuries.

Something similar seems to have happened with the O’odham, and the
differences are far wider than just Tohono, Akimel and Kohatk.
  On the next page, you’ll see a bowl and a standing figurine with funny
faces. They’re called ee-ee toys, and they were the product of a single
family. According to Papago Indian Pottery, published more than fifty
years ago, the Montaña family had been making them for “four or five
generations.” The big bowl has a hard attribution to Frances Montaña and a
1932 date, and we can easily attribute the tall lady on the previous page to
an earlier-generation Montaña.
   The bird effigy jar at the right of the front row was made at Shoposk in
the northern Sells Reservation. It has an obvious striated un-Kohatk polish
that signals immediately that it’s Tohono rather than Maricopa or Akimel.
It’s a piece of family pottery. Lena Albert worked with her sister Sally
Havier making pieces with exactly the same finish.
   There were other families. The Manuel family has worked in a variety
of styles for years, and after 2000, Billy and his sister Annie, who died too
young in 2009, made highly individual pieces, mainly in a matte finish, that
show more connection with the Hohokam than they do with modern work.
   At Akimel, the late Tobias Manuel also did homages to the Hohokam,
while others like Pearl Norris, Susie Miguel, Warren Oliver and Clayton
Wahpeta worked mostly in the Maricopa/Kohatk style.
  On the western part of the Sells Reservation, there was white kaolin
clay near a town named Hickiwan, and dead-white pottery started to show
up in the area around 1950. Early pieces like Cross Antone’s jar gave
advance warning of what’s on the next two pages. Whiteware has been the
dominant O’odham pottery ever since the 1980s.

Poupenay bought it in 1970, so it’s most likely pre-World War II.
   The three pieces by Billy and Annie Manuel show family range. From
Billy, we have a matte red bird that brings to mind the Hohokam bird on
page 33 and a polished whiteware piece that looks like it was made by
someone from the Angea family, the stars of the next two pages. Annie gave
us a matte red-on-buff effigy wedding vase that doesn’t look like any
wedding vase we’ve ever seen anywhere else.
   Tobias Manuel’s two pieces, the dish and the bowl behind Lena Albert’s
bird bowl, came closer to the old Hohokam pottery than any modern potter
ever managed, while Warren Oliver’s effort in the same vein, the bowl at far
right, more clearly conforms to contemporary painting and finishing
standards.
   Pearl Norris’s little shoe and Susie Miguel’s canteen have a mirror
polish that any Kohatk would admire.
   The one piece that defeats us in our attempt to pigeonhole everything is
the jar at top left. After considerable pondering we put a 1920 date on it,
which could be way off. We’re sure about this much: It’s not Maricopa and

it’s not Kohatk. Its swirl design shows up in one form or another all along
on Tohono pieces. And it’s a true polychrome, which wasn’t supposed to
have happened before World War II.
   However, post-World War II polychromes, like the older pieces on the
next pages, don’t relate to this one at all. We spent a lot of time on this one,
but our investigations reached a dead end. For the moment, we’ll leave the
task of finding out more about it up to you.


O’ODHAM – WHITEWARE AND ANGEA

Tohono gets a new look. The style that now dominates O’odham pottery
developed out west in Hickiwan, not far from Stoa Pitk, a place whose
name means “white clay.” When you see pure white on a Southwestern pot,
it’s because the potter had a kaolin-based clay like what the Hickiwan
potters found a few miles north.
   When Hickiwan white pots started appearing around 1950, they weren’t
all that impressive. The grayish jar in the middle of the front row and the
white jar at the right of the front row in the picture on the opposite page
were early efforts. By the 1960s and through the 1970s, pieces like the
geometric black-on-white olla below and the one with the feathery swirls at
the left of the back row were sending a message that something new was
happening in Hickiwan. That’s when the white polychromes started to
appear, like the bowl with the crenellated rim in the back row.
   By end of the twentieth century, one Hickiwan family had become far
and away the best-known O’odham potters. The Angea family turned
pottery-making into a craft industry, to the point where, if you’d set out to
buy a Tohono pot at almost any time since the 1990s, you’d almost certainly
have ended up with an Angea piece, and if you’d done it much before 2005,
it almost certainly would have been a friendship jar.

Whiteware from the 1960s
                         9½" in diameter, maker unknown

   Like musicians who vault to the top of the charts with one big hit, the
Angeas made it big with an original design that tourists couldn’t keep from
buying. The friendship jar (there’s one at right center in the middle row)
features a circle of dancers, usually four as on this example, but eight or
more on bigger pieces. The dancers face the inside of the jar and have their
arms around each others’ shoulders. You see their faces painted on the
inside of the jar. To complete the effect, the jar has cutouts under the arms
of the dancers. The result is a crowd-pleaser, the type of art that makes
purists shudder and souvenir-hunters applaud.
   The success of the friendship jar has probably kept the Angeas from
getting all the recognition they deserve. Curators, upper-end gallery owners
and collectors tend to diminish the too popular and too easily available as
not worth serious consideration.

That’s too bad, because there’s far more to Angea pottery than
friendship jars. Family pottery workshops have a long-standing tradition,
and they follow a classic pattern. Originally, one family member creates an
experiment that appeals to buyers, and as demand increases, relatives pitch
in to help with production.
   Almost without exception, important Southwestern pottery artists—
Nampeyo of Hopi, Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso, Lucy Lewis of
Acoma, Juan Quezada of Mata Ortiz and many others—had, or have,
family members who worked alongside them, collaborated with them and
continue to work in the family’s style.
   The Angea style predates the friendship jar by many years and builds on
the work of artists from thirty and forty years before. The swirls on the
polychrome jar at the right of the middle row echo the mysterious old jar on
the previous page. The “man-in-the-maze” design on the quail’s chest is a
basket design so traditional that it serves as the tribal logo.
   Dismissing Angea work as mass-produced or as tourist curios isn’t fair.
The next page gives a truer picture of what the Angeas have brought to
contemporary O’odham pottery and why they, more than anyone else, kept
the art alive.

The jar at the left and the howl at the right of the top row and the jar on the

a mature pottery force. Despite the dramatically different designs, the
consistent level of skill and taste tells you that those three pieces weren’t
random experiments.
   During those years, the Angea family emerged, and any of those three
might have been by an Angea. However, our own research has a huge gap
between our earliest attributed family piece and apiece that starts to
resemble the evolved style. The 1950s jar in the front row has been
attributed to Joe Angea, Sr., and all it tells us is that back then, Hickiwan
and the Angea family had a long way to go.
   However, the jar at the right of the middle row, which we believe to be
from the 1970s, is signed Angea, and it shows where the family was
heading. The rest of the pieces, friendship jar and all, show the family style.
   The Angeas probably do themselves a disservice by signing most pieces
simply “Angea.” That practice gives the impression of factory production
rather than of careful work by individual artists. We had to do some digging

to find the names of Gladys, Joe, Jr. and Rupert, the best-known family
member.
   Those names should be upfront. Rupert’s lizard bowl in front and
Gladys’s quail figurine in the middle row serve as strong reminders that
these are important artists, not faceless workers in a pottery factory.


PICURIS

A lot of places make micaceous pottery, and a few of them make a lot of it.
But at Picuris, ifs the whole story. For more than a century, if you asked
who makes this glittery, micaceous ware, the quick answer was always
Taos, a bigger, much better-known Pueblo. But the better answer is Picuris,
the longtime masters of the art.
    Picuris (say PICK-ur-eese) is really off the beaten path, a one-mile side
trip off the high road from Santa Fe to Taos. The high road itself is a route
mostly taken by tourists who want to explore rather than drive the much
quicker main highway.
   When Oñate Christianized Picuris in 1598, his lieutenants described it
as a warlike community with three thousand inhabitants. Picuris warriors
were among the fiercest rebels in 1680, and they rebelled again four years
after the 1692 Reconquest, ultimately fleeing to join a band of Apaches in
southern Colorado. After ten years of homelessness, disease and intertribal
warfare, they returned to Picuris, their population down to five hundred.
Not much has happened since at Picuris.
   Today, fewer than a hundred people live there, but that doesn’t mean the
pottery has died out, or that Picuris isn’t an important Pueblo any more.
When you visit, Picuris might seem sleepy and off the beaten path, but the
Pueblo had enough energy to restore the old mission church with adobe
bricks and to develop, own and operate the stylish Santa Fe Hotel in Santa
Fe.

Basic Picuris: the family-dinner bean pot
                            Anthony Durand, 8" diameter, 1990

    Identifying Picuris pottery isn’t always easy. They make similar pottery
at Taos and much more of it. At both Pueblos, the emphasis on micaceous
ware is utility rather than art. This hard-surfaced ware with its glittery
flecks is safe for cooking, as the well cooked-in older pieces in the picture
to the right testify.

Artists at most other Pueblos, even Taos, paint decorations on their
pottery, even on micaceous pieces, but not here. We’ve never seen a Picuris
piece with painted decoration.
   When we did this book the first time, we got a graphic, unforgettable
lesson in what makes Picuris pottery stand alone. When Brenda bought the
bowl at bottom left on the opposite page from Cora Durand, she told us the
reason that Picuris pottery was superior to all others (including, of course,
similar pottery from Taos) was that Picuris potters fired their work hotter
than anyone else. That made the pottery more serviceable and oven-safe.
She made certain that we knew that you could test firing temperature by
ringing a pot—the higher the tone, the better the firing. She was out of good
pots that day and hesitated to sell us that less-than-perfect little example,
but she proved her point about the superiority of Picuris firing by pulling
out all the throwaways she had around the house and tapping them. Even if
they had big cracks, or in one case, a huge hole in the bottom, they rang like
chimes.
   Despite Cora’s bravura performance, the only differences we’ve been
able to see between a Picuris piece and a Taos piece is a subtle difference in
the color of the clay. Generally, but not universally, Picuris mica slip has a
slightly greenish cast while Taos pottery tends to be a tan or yellow gold,
and the same tan-to-yellows show up on recent Jicarilla Apache micaceous
pieces. When you see a coppery-red piece, it’s more apt to be from Ohkay
or Nambé.

Wherever it’s from, micaceous clay can make pieces strong and safe
enough for cooking, and for much of it, that’s its main purpose.
   At Picuris, if Cora’s sermon was accurate, they make the best cooking
pottery of all.
     It’s said that you can’t really appreciate Southwestern pottery or proper
Southwestern cooking until you’ve eaten beans cooked in a Picuris pot.

From the 1960s into the 2000s, Cora Durand and her grandson Anthony
were the most recognized Picuris potters, a preeminence that lasted until
Anthony’s untimely death in 2009. Anthony’s work brought him enough
celebrity to warrant a Wikipedia biography.

Cora’s jar at the left of the front row is the one Brenda brought back
after we saw Cora’s demonstration at the Pueblo, and Anthony’s three
pieces in the picture above and the one on the opposite page all have the
kind of hard surface and immaculate finish that Cora’s throwaway pot
would have had if it had survived the firing.
   Making Picuris pottery was an uphill struggle for Anthony. Potters had
been collecting Picuris clay for over four hundred years from a source four-
and-a-half miles east of the village. During the 1960s, a mining company
put up fences around the source, and by the 1990s, the clay was buried
under tons of mining rubble. The Picuris people had lost all access.
   Anthony experimented with clays from other sources, new burnishing
techniques and a gray sandstone temper. Fortunately, Picuris potters still
have access to the slip material, so his pottery could keep the Picuris look.
   Anthony’s tile is worth special mention because of its design. For
centuries, the padres were delighted that the Indians made pieces using the
Cross of Lorraine, not always aware that back in the Pueblo it represented
a dragonfly.
   With Anthony Durand gone, we’d feared that Picuris pottery would
quietly disappear, but there are four pieces made after 2010 in the picture.
Irene Simbolo and her daughter are still working, as Irene has been since
the 1980s. Then, in our 2013 explorations, we discovered Wayne Yazzie,
who made the jar with the turquoise bead and the jar-with-handle at the far
right. Picuris pottery is alive.


POJOAQUE

The totally reborn modern Pueblo. In the late nineteenth century, poverty
and smallpox caught up with Pojoaque, and it went the way of Pecos.
   By 1915, it was abandoned, its adobe buildings dissolving in the annual
rains. Then, in the 1930s, the government restored the land, and eventually
forty descendants of the original families resettled the Pueblo. Some came
from places like Chicago and Los Angeles, some from neighboring
Pueblos. Now more than twelve hundred people live in Pojoaque. Its
pronunciation is tricky—say “Pawhockey” fast and you’ll come close.
   This reincarnated community has managed, more than any other Pueblo,
to beat the outside world at its own game. Pojoaque was the first Pueblo to

build a casino, creating more income for what had already become the
highest per-capita income Pueblo.
   Pojoaque’s governor is an artist and the Pueblo offers art classes in
many genres to people from any Pueblo. Its cultural center includes a
museum that offers a walk-through historic timeline that tells its story with
figurines by Santa Clara’s Roxanne Swentzell arrayed against backdrops
painted by Zia’s Marcellus Medina. The craft store at the museum is a
polished retail outlet. Next door, Roxanne Swentzell’s tower gallery
reminds you of ancestral ruins and features her work.





                  Now great pottery is everywhere in Pojoaque.
                       Lois Gutierrez and Derek de la Cruz, 8¾" high, 2008

  Down the road, the Pueblo opened the luxurious Buffalo Thunder
Resort and Casino, including a Hilton Hotel whose vast lobby areas display

the single most breathtaking exhibit of contemporary Pueblo pottery you’ll
see anywhere.





    You’ll see a bit of Pojaque pottery in that exhibit, with more to come.
Until the 1990s, you could count the number of Pojoaque potters on the
fingers of one hand without using your thumb. They were apt to be Santa
Clara potters like Lucy Year Flower, who married Joseph Lonewolf of
Santa Clara, signed her pots Pojoaque/Santa Clara, and made them in Santa
Clara with Santa Clara clay in the Santa Clara style.
   Cordi Gomez is the closest thing to an established homegrown Pojoaque
potter, but she’s not quite the matriarch of a Pojoaque family dynasty. Her
son Glenn considers himself a Taos potter, and her son James makes Santa
Clara-style work and signed the piece in the picture J. Gomez Taos.
   Joe and Thelma Talachy live in Pojoaque, as do Lois Gutierrez and her
husband Derek de la Cruz. Thelma and Lois are granddaughters of an
important matriarch, Petra Gutierrez of Santa Clara, and sisters of Santa
Clara’s Minnie Vigil.
   The bulk of Joe and Thelma’s work looks like Minnie’s, although
Thelma did make a few pieces in the eighteenth-century Pojoaque
polychrome style. Those were homages like Evelyn Vigil’s and Joshua
Madalena’s prehistoric recreations at Jemez and didn’t look much like
Thelma’s core work.
   Lois and Derek, however, are something else. In the 2000s, they’ve
identified themselves as Pojoaque, which attaches a genuine top-echelon
pottery name to the Pueblo. Now that Roxanne Swentzell, the world-

famous Santa Clara potter/sculptor has her gallery there, you’ll see more
fine contemporary pottery at Pojoaque than you will at any other Pueblo.
   Joe and Thelma’s daughter Melissa Talachy Romero is another story. In
addition to making breakthrough pottery like the dragonflies-and-airplanes
piece on the next page, she’s important on another level as well, She’s
married to the great Cochiti painter Mateo Romero and is sister-in-law to
his equally prominent potter brother, Diego.
   Pojoaque is no longer just the Pueblo of hotels and shopping centers.
It’s now a powerhouse in the arts as well.

Melissa Talachy Romero’s dragonflies and airplanes came to us just
before a major 2008 show at the Poeh Museum at Pojoaque that gave the
floor to her pottery and the walls to her husband’s paintings. The show was
so impressive that an important dealer went up to Melissa afterwards and
told her, “You know, you’re famous.” When Melissa gave a startled
response, the dealer told her, “After this show, you are.”
   Fame doesn’t happen quite that quickly. Motherhood and other things in
her life kept Melissa from being a prolific potter, and Melissa’s truly
deserved widespread recognition is yet to come, at least at this writing.
   The other top-row jars are by Lois Gutierrez, who works with her
husband, Derek de la Cruz. We avoid words like “best” when we talk about
potters, but if there’s a better pottery painter anywhere than Lois, we
haven’t noticed him or her. For decades, Lois and Derek have made
beautifully designed and painted pieces, and if you need more proof, look at
the olla on the opposite page.
    Lois’s sister (and Melissa’s mother) Thelma and her husband Joe made
decorated polychromes from the 1970s on like the two seed jars in the
picture, reminiscent of Thelma’s sister Minnie Vigil’s work at Santa Clara.
   We met Cordi Gomez a few years ago at the Santa Fe Powwow, and she
graciously took us to her home, where we found the five pieces in the
picture. The micaceous jar is proof that pots can talk. She made it in 1984,
sold it at the San Juan Crafts Center, and forgot all about it. In 1994, she
saw it again at a yard sale and, as she put it, it called out, “Mommy, it’s
me.” She bought it back and kept it until she found it a better home. Which,
we suppose, was us.


SANDIA

From 1540 on, it was a rough go. Now things are better. Sandia sits on the
edge of Albuquerque’s urban sprawl, on the lower slopes of 10,768-foot-
high Sandia Crest. If you stumble into Sandia past the casino and hotel
complex, it’s probably because you’re on your way to enjoy one of
Albuquerque’s prime tourist attractions, the tram ride to the mountain top.

Sandia (the accent is on the second syllable: San-DEE-ya) has been there
since about 1300, barely recognized, often stepped-on. Both its traditional
and Spanish-imposed names indicate the lack of respect and attention it has
always been accorded. In the original Tiwa, Sandia’s name is Nafiat—“A
Dusty Place.” When the Spanish renamed it, they didn’t bother giving it a
saint to honor it, they named it “Watermelon” because that’s what they
thought the local squash were.
   The Pueblo now has 138 square miles of landscape that extends from
the Rio Grande well up the mountain slope. It was one of the twelve Tiguex
Pueblos that Coronado visited in 1540, most of which were on today’s
Sandia land. Historians aren’t sure whether Sandia itself was one of the
ones Coronado burned down, or whether by escaping the torch, it might
have had one of its last strokes of good luck before the unpleasantness of
the next four-and-a-half centuries.
    In 1598, the Pueblo fell under Governor Oñate’s heavy thumb, and the
subsequent Spanish treatment of the Pueblo was sufficient to make it an
enthusiastic participant in the 1600 Pueblo Revolt. Poor Sandia couldn’t
even enjoy the success of the revolt. In 1681, Governor Otermin made an
abortive attempt at reconquest, accomplishing very little beyond burning
down Sandia and forcing the residents to move all the way to Hopi.
   They built the village of Payupki on the Second Mesa and stayed there
until the priests rounded them up in 1742 and brought them back to Sandia
to rebuild the mission. Ever since, Sandia has been overwhelmed by
Albuquerque, New Mexico’s only urban complex.
   Today, Sandia has only six hundred people, but those six hundred
people manage two thousand employees in a big resort/hotel/casino and one

of the most impressive craft stores anywhere.
  Now Sandia has wealth but almost no artistic heritage. In Pottery of the
Pueblos of New Mexico, 1700–1940, Jonathan Batkin reported on two
nineteenth-century observers. One of them wrote about Sandia blackware
while the other wrote about black-on-white.
    In American Indian Pottery, John Barry told us that one woman was
producing pottery at Sandia in 1931, and that he had seen one bowl of
recent origin in 1978 (most likely by Helen Garcia). Neither book showed
any pictures.





                                 Small Pueblo, small piece
                           John Montoya, 1½" high, circa 2000

   When we went searching for Sandia pottery for the first edition, we
started at Bien Mur, that fabulous Sandia craft store, and found a treasure
trove of fine work from other Pueblos. We asked about Sandia pottery, and
the clerk told us, “Well, Gina the bookkeeper used to make pottery, but
since she got the job here, she doesn’t have time to make it any more.” A
year later, we found a ten-year-old pot by Gina the bookkeeper at a store in
Tucson.
   There were and are others, and we found a few pieces, but we didn’t
find any consistent Sandia heritage or style. The pottery we did find was
mostly derivative from other Pueblos, mainly Jemez and Cochiti and even
Zia on one piece. We did, however, find one potter whose work rose above
the ordinary and imitative.

John Montoya started out doing everything he wasn’t supposed to do,
making pieces on a wheel and decorating with designs from other Pueblos.
By the mid-1990s, though, he was doing superb work like the big bowl in
the picture opposite and showing in the finest galleries. We’d hoped he’d
lead a Sandia resurgence in the way Hubert Candelario and Daryl
Candelaria did at San Felipe.
     It wasn’t to be. John died in 2005, and with his death, Sandia pottery
submerged again. We’ll keep looking, hoping that some of the Pojoaque
phenomenon rubs off on Sandia.

The big bowl at the top says about all there is to say about John Montoya’s
skill and importance. One look tells you why his work vaulted him to the top

of the prestige ladder. The bowl underscores how much the Pueblo lost
when he died, still only in his forties.
  On the other hand, his jar at the right, probably made when he was just
beginning shows how far he came. It was done on a wheel, and its
decorative elements include a Zuni heartline deer, a San Ildefonso avanyu,
an Acoma butterfly, a Hopi bird and a Santa Clara cloud and rain design.
   Gregory Schaaf’s encylopedic Southern Pueblo Pottery mentions
Dorothy Montoya and gives considerable space to John Montoya but
doesn’t suggest any family connection. Dorothy’s jar might be a little off-
center and kiln-fired, but it’s nicely designed, with elements borrowed from
Zia and clay and slip that suggest Jemez. The 1980 date we gave it is based
on pottery fashions rather than hard knowledge, so it might have been made
considerably later.
   The bowl in the center is by Gina the bookkeeper, who came from a
talented Jemez pottery family, and the bowl could pass for Jemez if it didn’t
say Sandia on the bottom. From the look of her bowls in the front row, it’s a
good bet that Helen Garcia was a Jemez potter as well. There was so little
pottery at Sandia back then that when the Pueblo Cultural Center in
Albuquerque put together windows showing the art of all the Pueblos, a
little jar by Helen was all they could find to represent early Sandia pottery.
    Trinnie Lujan’s storyteller is nice enough but hardly representative of
Sandia. Except for the signature, it’s a Cochiti or Jemez storyteller.


SAN FELIPE

Here, there’s a pottery heritage to recover. But the potters are doing
something else. Today, that heritage is pretty well hidden, but so is San
Felipe itself. Not that it’s far off the beaten path—reservation lands cover
three hundred square miles along a fifteen-mile stretch of the Rio Grande,
and I-25, the highway from Albuquerque to Santa Fe rims right past the
Pueblo’s Casino Hollywood. But the Pueblo itself is so little publicized that
you’d think San Felipe is as small as Sandia.
   Much of this lack of publicity is intentional. The Pueblo has one of the
most conservative tribal governments, offers little encouragement to visitors
beyond the casino, and devotes most of its attention to agriculture.

If you’ve looked at the histories of the other Rio Grande Pueblos, San
Felipe’s won’t come as a surprise. It was probably settled by Ancestral
Puebloans before 1400; it was Christianized in 1598; it was punished by the
Spanish cavalry for objecting a few years later. It participated eagerly in the
1680 Revolt, had its rebels flushed out of their mountain hideout by General
de Vargas in 1692 and put to work building new missions in 1702. Over the
years, the citizens of San Felipe were given plenty of reasons to decide they
wanted little to do with Spanish or Anglo settlers.





                          Old and older San Felipe brownware
         canteen, circa 1900, 6" high, bowl, Candelaria Montana, circa 1960, 7½" diameter

   San Felipe’s early pottery gets little attention. As with Sandia, both
Batkin’s Pottery of the Pueblos of New Mexico, 1740–1940 and Barry’s
American Indian Pottery dismiss it without a picture. Neither mentions
what, based on the couple of dozen examples we’ve seen, seems to be a
genuinely distinctive pottery heritage: San Felipe brownware.

The two pieces in the picture below were done more than half a century
apart, and that time span indicates that brown pots from San Felipe were
more than a minor aberration. If you enjoy speculating about things like
this, you might compare Candelaria Montana’s bowl with the eighteenth-
century Gobernador Canyon bowl on page 48. We haven’t seen any recent
old-style brownware from San Felipe, but the tiny brown dish on the
opposite page leans against a jar that has the same fine brown clay as
Candelaria Montana’s bowl.
   Current San Felipe pottery has nothing to do with brownware, and it
explores possibilities from everywhere. The new creative outburst really
began with two transcendent potters, who, in the 1990s, found styles that
pushed them into the inner circle of Southwestern potters. Hubert
Candelario’s orange micaceous pieces are packed with theatrical appeal
while Daryl Candelaria vaulted to the top of the ladder based on late-1990s
experiments like his “mosaic” pot on the opposite page. Note the spellings
—Daryl’s name ends in an “a,” while Hubert’s ends in “o.” We assumed
they were brothers until we looked carefully at the bottoms of their pots.
   The Candelario/a explosion was only the beginning. Since 2000, we’ve
seen powerful work featuring unexpected slip colors by others including
Joseph Latoma, Gerren Candelaria and Ricardo and Victoria Ortiz.
   There are two thousand people in San Felipe, and we’re learning that
the population includes more excellent contemporary potters than we ever
expected to find when we began our quest. One of the pieces in the picture
opposite was made in the 1960s, one about 1980, two in the late 1990s, and
all the rest in 2010 or after.

While the creativity at Pueblos like Ohkay Owinge and Acoma seems to
be losing steam, it gives us new hope to see creative outbursts like we’re
now observing at Pojoaque and San Felipe.
   At San Felipe, as the picture demonstrates, it’s happening right now.

The two jars at upper left center help explain Daryl Candelaria’s current
reputation. When we saw our first “mosaic” jar at the 1998 Indian Market,
we asked Daryl how he managed to fire just one portion of the pot like San
Ildefonso blackware. He smiled enigmatically and made it clear he wasn’t
about to tell us.

Hubert Candelaria’s orange micaceous pieces inspired a few imitators
when he first started making them, but he quickly grabbed exclusive
possession of the genre. He started with plain shapes, then turned to swirl
jars, then developed his black-decorated jars like the one on the left, which
we can’t stop thinking of as orange brains. In the late 1990s, and after
2000, he introduced unexpectedly delicate perforated hollow orange globes,
and they got so pricey we never managed to get one.
    After 2010, Joseph Latoma and his family joined Daryl and Hubert at
the top of the San Felipe pottery ladder. He makes big dead-white pieces
and explains that because San Felipe has no clear pottery tradition, he
searches for designs from other sources.
   During the same years, Gerren Candelaria and Ricardo and Victoria
Ortiz came forward, and Ray Duck followed. San Felipe pottery is no
longer dormant, although it never went into total hibernation. During the
slow years, Bernard Chavez, Joseph Latoma’s uncle, made beautifully
painted pieces. The one in the front at right center is unsigned, but in 2014,
he confirmed his authorship.
   And we found a tiny reminder of where San Felipe pottery came from.
The little dish in the bottom row, dated 1964, goes all the way back to the
beginning.


SAN ILDEFONSO

A hundred years ago, pottery was the number one industry here. Not
much has changed since. San Ildefonso’s history is pretty much like the
history of the other Rio Grande Pueblos. Pretty much, but not entirely.

San Ildefonso’s ancestors settled what is now one of Santa Fe’s
premiere tourist attractions, Bandelier National Monument, adjacent to the
lower left-hand corner of the reservation. Somewhere around 1300, they
moved to a village a mile west of the current Pueblo, where the Spanish
found them in 1593. For the next eighty-seven years, they enjoyed the
pleasures of mission-building and confiscatory taxation. Then, in 1680, they
joined the rebellion and helped torch Santa Fe. They made their first
divergence from the typical pattern that year—unlike their colleagues, they
didn’t burn their mission.
   When General de Vargas restored Spanish rule in 1692, San Ildefonso
maintained a truce for two years, then rebelled and moved to a stronghold
on Black Mesa, a table rock just north of the Pueblo. They made their
second departure from typical history in 1694. When the Spanish came after
them with troops and a cannon, the Indians won the fight. The Spanish
retreated, and ultimately San Ildefonso came off the mesa and wrote a truce
on its own terms.
     It lasted another two years, until San Ildefonso’s patience finally broke.
This time, they did burn the mission, sixteen years after everyone else had
burned theirs. It was the last straw for de Vargas, too. He sent a sufficiently
larger army to the Black Mesa and pacified San Ildefonso at gunpoint.
   Then, for three hundred years, San Ildefonso got better and better at
making pottery. Powhoge Polychrome, from Powhoge-oweenge (Where the
Water Cuts Down Through), San Ildefonso’s Tewa name, became the
standard pottery from San Ildefonso, Nambé and Tesuque during the

eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, but they made it a little better at San
Ildefonso.
    In the second half of the nineteenth century, they added some red to the
decoration on the upper body, and Powhoge polychrome became San
Ildefonso Polychrome. About 1905, they began using a grainy slip from
Cochiti, and now it was Tunyo Polychrome.
   Our old friend and mentor, the late Dick Howard, lost patience with
these hair-splitting classifications and insisted it was all San Ildefonso,
whether it was polychrome or black-on-red. If, unlike Dick, you like those
fussy distinctions, you can call the double pitcher in the picture at right and
the bird below Powhoge, the pitcher on the next page and the jar at lower
right San Ildefonso, and the rest of the polychromes in the picture Tunyo.





                           They had fun in the early days, too.
                      The bottom says New Mexico, 1882, 6¾" long.

   San Ildefonso made pottery for the curio trade as early as 1880, as the
bird below and Marianita Roybal’s double pitcher in the middle of the next
page confirm.
   Before 1920, San Ildefonso pottery remained either polychrome or, after
1900 or so, black-on-red. Between 1900 and 1920, black-on-red became

almost as important as polychrome at San Ildefonso, then pretty much
submerged after 1920, drowned under the wave of new fashion. In those
years, potters at the Pueblo pretty much ignored the blackware they were
making next door at Santa Clara.
   From the late nineteenth century on, there were potters at San Ildefonso
whose work is still considered magnificent and still commands a premium
price, but there were others who were more casual about their art. The
polychromes in the picture at right show a range of skill and care.
    After 1920, everything changed. The old colors didn’t totally disappear,
but in 1919 Maria Martinez and her husband Julian learned how to decorate
blackware.
   Once that happened, San Ildefonso pottery was no longer important
merely among the Santa Fe Pueblos. It was a tiny community, barely worth
a dot on the map, but a few years later, the whole world was talking about
it.

The double pitcher in the lower middle (attributed to Marianita Roybal
based on the quirky handle treatment) is what the hair-splitters call
Powhoge polychrome. The pitcher at the left and the jar at lower right are
San Ildefonso Polychrome, while the other polychromes are the later Tunyo
Polychrome.
   The designs can be the same on San Ildefonso and Tunyo pieces, but the
surfaces are different. The older San Ildefonso pieces have a hard, smooth,
stone-polished surface, while the later Tunyo pieces are rag-polished and
have a slightly gritty surface. San Ildefonso black-on-red generally had ta
smooth stone-polished surface, even during the years the polychromes
didn’t.
    Tonita Roybal, whose blackware appears on the next pages, was the
queen of black-on-red, and the attribution on the smaller jar is a “who
else.” We’re a bit less confident of the attribution on the big jar at upper
right. Normally Tonita’s painting was more precise.
   We found the Maria and Julian Martinez shallow bowl in the middle of
a huge general antique show. The dealer was pretty sure it was “Indian.”
Every collector stumbles on a treasure like this once or twice in a lifetime,

and this was our fifteen minutes of fame. Identifying it wasn’t rocket
science. It’s right down the middle of what Maria and Julian did in the
decade before Maria became the most famous potter in the world.
   One thing that points to Julians painting is the sure-handed outlining
around the designs, to be fitted in later. On Julian’s polychromes, you can
often see a density difference between the outlining and the fill-in painting.


SAN ILDEFONSO – MARIA MARTINEZ

The Seven Families #4: Martinez. In 1908, Maria Montoya Martinez
(1887–1980) and her husband Julian (1885–1942) were building a
reputation for their Tunyo Polychromes. Maria could make big, graceful
pots fast, and Julian painted their red-and-black-on-cream designs with a
sure hand.
   Then, history gets fuzzy. According to Susan Peterson’s The Living
Tradition of Maria Martinez, Edgar Lee Hewett, the director of the Museum
of New Mexico, needed a good, fast San Ildefonso potter. His party had
been excavating around the Pueblo and had turned up some black sherds.
Fascinated with the new discovery and driven by the same impulses that led
Thomas Keam to ask Hopi potters to recreate Sikyatki ware nearly thirty
years before, Hewitt asked Maria if she could make whole pots that looked
like what those black pieces might have been.
   Other accounts disagree emphatically. Equally credentialed authorities
insist that Hewett asked Maria to reproduce black-on-cream ware, and that
the pottery that made Maria famous was an unrelated discovery by Maria
and Julian. In any event, in the winter of 1919–1920, they made the first
modern black-on-black pieces.
   They didn’t invent black-on-black, however. An obscure Mogollon type
made eight hundred years before, which Maria and Julian had probably
never seen, put matte black on polished black inside brownware bowls. The
one on the right shows what black-on-black looked like in antiquity.

Maria wasn’t the first.
                  Reserve Plain, Starkweather variety, 6” diameter, circa 1100

   The Museum of New Mexico has two of Maria and Julian’s first large
black ollas. They have overall matte backgrounds decorated with polished
avanyus, a traditional water serpent design. The matte backgrounds with
polished images disappeared after that first firing. Ever after, almost every
piece of matte-and-polish has a polished background with matte decoration.
The avanyu, however, never left, probably because Maria and Julian
favored the design.
   The avanyu had a lot to do with Edgar Hewett and his eager assistant,
Kenneth Chapman. Bruce Bernstein told how Hewett and Chapman favored
“authentic” designs and suggested that Maria and Julian use motifs from
their excavations. Julian’s first avanyu, copied on a redware piece ten years
before Maria developed black-on-black, came from a petroglyph that
Chapman showed him.
   Only two of the pieces in the picture to the right have an avanyu, but
turn the page and you’ll see those feathered serpents wrapped around pot
after pot, page after page, Pueblo after Pueblo.
   Maria and Julian’s black-on-black became a commercial success, and
she taught other family members how to make it. The family included her

eldest sister, Juanita Vigil, who died in 1930, older sister Maximiliana, who
signed “Anna” and was considered the best painter, and younger sisters
Desideria and Clara. All but Clara, who polished for Maria and occasionally
signed pieces for her, became respected potters in their own right.
   One of the essentials of “Maria Pottery” was a silvery-black mirror
polish that made it a little bit different from all other blackware. In the
1940s, Maria developed a true gunmetal gray, unique until the 1990s when
Mata Ortiz potters figured out a way to do it.
   By 1925, Chapman had her signing her pots. She signed them “Marie”
because, as the story goes, someone told her that Anglo buyers wouldn’t
like pots made by foreigners. As her work became better known, she was
afraid her success would attract jealousy within the Pueblo, so she got
Julian’s permission to show anyone in San Ildefonso how to make the
blackware.
   The secret got out. We’ve found jars made around 1930 by two
important Santa Clara potters. Pascuelita Gutierrez and Lela Gutierrez, that
are unashamed knockoffs of Maria pottery, complete with avanyu. Lela’s jar
is on page 164.
   By 1930, Maria was world-famous. And San Ildefonso was famous as
the place where Maria Martinez came from.

This is the ware that captured the world’s attention and lifted the prices of
Pueblo pottery from the under-a-dollar range into the rarefied atmosphere
of hundreds and eventually thousands and tens of thousands of dollars
each.
   Maria’s sister Desideria Sanchez and in-law Tonita Roybal achieved
such stature that first names were enough. Say “Maria” and everybody
knows who you mean. To anybody who knows a little about the pottery,
same holds true for Tonita and Desideria, and later on, for Popovi and
Santana as well, and, to a lesser degree, sister Anna.
   “Juanita” is an important signature, too, but three people used it:
Maria’s sister Juanita Vigil, her cousin by marriage Juanita Wo-Peen and
another fine San Ildefonso blackware potter of the 1930s and 1940s,
Juanita Peña. Handwriting analysis can be difficult, since they apparently
all learned penmanship in the same school.
   One problem in reviewing pre-World War II San Ildefonso pottery is that
important potters drift out of memory simply because they all were satellite
to Maria and her collaborators. She worked with Julian until 1943
(pronounce his name HOOLEON, the Spanish way), then with her daughter-

in-law Santana Roybal until 1956, and with her son Popovi Da until his
death in 1971. The unsigned Popovi piece above was attributed by its
original owner, who bought it directly from him. In the 1970s, the Maria
Poveka signature appeared. At Popovi’s urging, Maria added her Tewa
name on undecorated pieces.
   By the 1970s, Popovi’s son Tony Da (he pronounced his name “Day”
while Popovi said “Dah”) was already internationally famous. He’s
covered on the next pages.


SAN ILDEFONSO – AFTER MARIA

Matte-and-polish evolves, and polychromes rejoin the party. After 1930,
Maria was an institution, invited to expositions, museums and universities,
producing pottery that became the standard high-priced commodity of the
Indian art market.
   As the years passed, the torch passed as well. The post-Maria era really
began in the 1950s as she collaborated with her son Popovi. She produced
less and less, and potters other than her direct descendants were gaining
fame.
   But her shadow was huge. From 1920 and through the rest of the
century, “Maria Pottery” was at the center of San Ildefonso’s economic
welfare. No matter how much restless young potters experimented, Maria
Pottery—matte decoration using traditional designs on a highly polished
unsculptured vessel—continued, but it wasn’t all black-on-black. The
surface could be red or cream, and the decoration could be almost any color.
   The picture to the right includes pieces that look like Maria made them,
pieces in styles her relatives developed, and pieces that shake completely
free of the tyranny of Maria’s institutionalized black-on-black.

Tony Da: in a class by himself
                                    3" high, circa 1965

   Maria’s most immediate successors were Popovi’s brother Adam and
his wife Santana, and they and others helped keep black-on-black alive
during the twentieth century.
   Maria’s niece Carmelita Dunlap reached a high level of recognition,
both for excellent work and because she was the last surviving potter who
actually worked with Maria. Her black-on-blacks could pass for Maria’s,
and her daughter Martha Appleleaf and Martha’s son Erik Fender continued
in the tradition. Carmelita also made dramatic polychromes, as the one at
top left of the picture demonstrates and, as the bigger one next to it
emphasizes, so did Martha Appleleaf. Carmelita’s daughter Linda continued
with polychromes.
   Black-on-black hung in. Tonita’s daughter, senior citizen Margaret
Gutierrez, and a young Elvis Torres collaborated on a pure “Maria” piece.
Maria’s great-great-grandson Marvin Martinez and his wife Frances
continued to make family-quality black-on-black from the 1990s on.

Through the rest of the century, Carmelita, Adam and Santana, and Blue
Corn, who was entirely off the Martinez family tree, all displayed Maria-
like mastery of black-on-black. But none of them were one-note potters.
Adam and Santana experimented with black and sienna and Blue Corn
introduced startling color combinations and subtle effects.
    Carmelita’s brother Albert Vigil and his wife Josephine developed a
new white-on-red style. Their son Doug and his wife Charlotte made pieces
like mom and dad, as did cousins Kathy and Geraldine Gutierrez.
   By 2000, most of Maria’s descendants had broken free of her black-on-
black. Barbara Gonzales, Adam and Santana’s daughter, made the unusual
jar at front left that stares at the sky from a micaceous stopper. Her pieces
stretch San Ildefonso’s blackware boundaries.
   Maria’s son Popovi Da created a more important new style with black-
and-sienna, the result of a double firing. Adam and Santana experimented
with it, as did Santana’s daughter Anita and half the other potters at San
Ildefonso and Santa Clara. But as changing fashions rewrote history, one
potter emerged as San Ildefonso’s greatest after Maria.
   Popovi’s son Tony Da (1940–2008) had a too-brief career, ended by a
paralyzing accident in 1982. In the years since, his legend grew to the point
where anything he made commands an astronomical price. In 2011, the
Museum of New Mexico had a blockbuster retrospective. If After Maria
were a question, Tony Da is now the answer.

“Maria Pottery ” may have branched out over the years, but in the forty-
five years after Santana started painting for Maria in 1950, nothing much
happened with black-on-black. Margaret Gutierrez and Elvis Torres made
the jar at middle right and Martha Appleleaf and Marvin and Frances
Martinez made the two at far left. All of them were made in 1995 and all
could have been made in 1935.
   Blue Corn’s cigarette lighter adhered strictly to the program. The
lighter brings a smile today, but back in the 1960s, every coffee table had a
Ronson table lighter, and one in San Ildefonso blackware would have been
a gracious, exceptionally stylish touch.
   As other potters besides Albert and Josephine and Doug and Charlotte
explored white-on-red, it quickly reached the kind of ritual predictability
that, after a few years, becomes a “tradition,” then quietly submerged.
   Popovi Da’s black-and-sienna offered more possibilities. The examples
in the picture are mild specimens, but Tony Da and potters from other
Pueblos and even ones from San Ildefonso took the genre much further.

Meanwhile, Tony Da, Blue Com, Carmelita Dunlap and Carmelita’s
daughters Martha Appleleaf and Linda Dunlap brought new life to
polychromes. With each new generation, change accelerated.
  A few pages farther on, you’ll see post-2010 work by Carmelita’s great-
granddaughter and Adam and Santana’s great-grandson, and it’s nothing
like anything you see here.


SAN ILDEFONSO – ROSE GONZALES

The Seven Families #5: Gonzales. If Maria Martinez became the most
celebrated of all the Pueblo potters, her cousin’s wife Rose Gonzales
(1900–1989) has to be the least publicized of the seven matriarchs. A
yellowed clipping we found in the bottom of a bowl indicated the extent of
her anonymity. It showed her picture and said only Pottery making is
popular among the women. It is taught by Rose, from the San Ildefonso
pueblo near Santa Fe.
   Rose, her son Tse-Pe (1940–2000) and to a lesser extent, her sister-in-
law Juanita Wo-Peen, had a heavy influence on San Ildefonso pottery. Their
innovations became standard in the San Ildefonso repertory. Where Maria
got her reputation by making painted pots, Rose got hers by making carved
ones.
   Carved pots, however, weren’t all she did. Generally, carved blackware
and redware are more a Santa Clara than a San Ildefonso thing, and Rose
didn’t have a problem with poaching a little Santa Clara turf. She not only
made carved pieces like the Santa Clara ones, she also tried her hand at
Santa Clara polychrome redware like you see on page 161. There’s one in
the picture on the right, as well as a couple of her pieces in a borrowed
Maria black-on-black style.

Maybe Rose wasn’t the first, either
                            Rosalie Aguilar, 8¼" diameter, circa 1935

   Rose probably felt a little freer to fool around with styles than she might
have if she’d been brought up in San Ildefonso. She was married in, a Cata
from Ohkay Owinge. The carved ware she and Juanita Wo-Peen are
credited with originating was a genuine departure, subtly different from
what they were doing at Santa Clara. A Santa Clara potter carves deep relief
and creates a smooth matte indentation, but Rose-style carving is shallower,
the surface edges rounded rather than sharp-cut. Her son Tse-Pe added
another wrinkle when he began texturing the indentations and occasionally
polishing the high points.
   Rose may not actually have originated the shallow, soft-edged carving.
Back in 1951, Helen Wormington wrote in The Story of Pueblo Pottery that
“another popular innovation, also accepted by some of the other villages,
was begun by Rosalie Aguilar who produced a ware which had designs
carved in low relief ...” Whether or not Rose actually did it first, she made a
career out of it, while Rosalie produced relatively few pieces.
   Tse-Pe followed his mother’s direction, but wandered far afield. From
the 1960s on, Tse-Pe and his first wife Dora experimented with odd shapes,
double firings, inlays and unusual slips.
   Dora is a Gachupin, an important name in Zia pottery, but after she
married in 1961, she learned San Ildefonso methods, became a major San

Ildefonso potter by the 1970s and continued making pottery after their
divorce. Today, pots by Tse-Pe, who died in 2000, are prized, but his later
pieces don’t usually command prices as high as the collaborative work he
did with Dora during their marriage.
    After they divorced, Tse-Pe married Jennifer Sisneros, from an equally
talented Ohkay Owinge pottery family, and she too became an important
San Ildefonso potter. During their marriage, Jennifer signed her work
Jennifer S. Tse-Pe to distinguish it from that of Tse-Pe and Dora’s potter
daughter Jennifer Tse-Pe, who died in 1998.
   During his marriage to Jennifer Sisneros, Tse-Pe continued his
experimentation with odd slip colors, and at the end of his life, was
experimenting with a metallic bronze color. Jennifer also experimented with
slip colors, and there’s one of her green ones on the opposite page.
   Tse-Pe had three potter daughters, but only Candace Martinez remained
active. Her husband, Ray Martinez, is Maria’s great-grandson. Ray is a
potter himself, who owned a San Ildefonso gallery and became a student of
San Ildefonso pottery history.
    There’s life elsewhere in the family. Juanita Wo-Peen’s daughter,
Adelphia Martinez, Rose’s niece, worked in Tse-Pe’s style. And after 2000,
Rose’s grandnephew Russell Sanchez vaulted to the top of the Pueblo
pottery ladder. See the next pages.
