Rose. The jar at the top is by her sister-in-law Juanita Wo-Peen, and it
could easily pass for Rose’s work if it weren’t for the signature. The little
black jar at front right gives a close look Rose-style carving and the
redware bowl with avanyu at lower left pretty much tells you all you need to
know about Rose’s style.
   Or at least, the style she’s known for. Three of Rose’s five pieces in the
picture demonstrate how willing she was to work in other styles. The lidded
redware box is pure Santa Clara. The rectangular box at lower right is pure
Maria, and the lidded cylinder at front has a bit of Santa Clara on top of a
bit of Maria.
    Rose’s son Tse-Pe’s work, much of it done with his wife Dora during
their marriage, expanded and defined the style. His pieces had all the
carving variations: carving before firing (the seed jar at right), carving
after firing where the low part comes out raw (the egg at left), and carving
in the middle of a double firing where the low part comes out tan (the
black-and-sienna bowl at left).

The sharp color delineation on Tse-Pe and Dora’s black-and-sienna
bowl at the left shows how well they could control a double firing. They
explored the full range of pottery experimentation. Their bowl at upper
center has an inlaid stone. In the 1980s and 1990s, inlaid coral or turquoise
became standard show biz among blackware potters, but back in the 1970s,
it was progressive stuff.
    Tse-Pe’s bear is a showpiece. Instead of an arrowhead or feather
burden, it packs a turquoise surfboard. After Tse-Pe married Jennifer, she
continued stretching the genre. Like Tse-Pe, she worked with odd colored
slips as on the green jar in the front row and gave us a Tony Da-style black-
and-sienna piece with a silver stopper.


SAN ILDEFONSO – OTHER NAMES, OTHER IDEAS

Quiet explorations. San Ildefonso may have gained world renown for its
pottery, but it’s still just a tiny town—fewer than five hundred people in
2010. Perhaps forty artists provide the wares that keep San Ildefonso’s
legacy alive.
   This places a heavy burden on any San Ildefonso resident who makes
pottery. There’s no room for young potters who crank out tourist pieces
while they learn the craft. San Ildefonso’s century-long reputation as the
premier producer of quality pottery among the Pueblos was hard-won, and
it won’t be surrendered without a fight.
   These circumstances seem to leave little room for experiment. Any San
Ildefonso potter who leaves tradition behind risks heavy criticism. Susan
Peterson told how Maria hid her first blackware pieces because she felt they
weren’t true San Ildefonso pottery, and as a result wouldn’t be accepted.
Family pressures make it even harder to stray from the path. Almost
everyone has a Martinez or a Gonzales or a Roybal on the family tree,
either by blood or by marriage. Over the years, careful experimentation
continued, but the shadows of Maria and Rose hang over the entire Pueblo.

Russell Sanchez: the new Tony Da
                              6½" diameter, 2012

   There were other families. Helen Gutierrez, her sister Angelita Sanchez
and their brother Gilbert Atencio made a powerful threesome, and their
work graced finest galleries during the 1980s and the 1990s. Fate isn’t
always kind, however. Angelita and Helen both died in 1993 and Gilbert
followed in 1995. During their lifetimes, Gilbert was San Ildefonso art
royalty and his sisters had almost the same prestige.
    Earlier, we mentioned Rosalie Aguilar. Rosalie died in 1947, and her
husband Joe turned to making polychromes that dealers often confuse with
early Marias. (Compare the round tile on the opposite page with the Maria
on page 147.) The Aguilars keep working, and today, there’s an Aguilar
store at the Pueblo. In 2013, Joe’s great-grandson Bryce made the bowl in
the front row of the next page that sits below Joe’s 1947 polychrome.

Juan Tafoya and his sister Elizabeth Lovato, two underpublicized
potters, explored the full post-Maria world as redefined by Popovi and Tony
Da. A friend recently bought a Juan Tafoya jar for $500 that looked just like
a Tony Da one that sold for $20,000 at a 2008 auction.
   John Gonzales followed his potter father Lorenzo, but not until after
he’d acquired degrees from Stanford and MIT and been the youngest-ever
president of the National Council of American Indians. Still, most of the
action comes from the established families. In Maria’s family, Adam and
Santana’s grandchildren Kathy Sanchez and Barbara Gonzales both kept a
foot in the Maria world, but took side trips. Carmelita’s son Carlos Sunrise
Dunlap, who died tragically at 23, experimented with Maria pottery in
sienna brown instead of black, and grandson Eric Fender and great-
granddaughter Justine Fender went farther afield, as did Peter Pino with
sculpture and Rose-type carving.
    In Rose’s family, Jennifer Tse-Pe and Juanita Wo-Peen’s daughter
Adelphia Martinez continued Tse-Pe’s shallow carving style, and, like Tse-
Pe and Blue Corn, experimented with odd-colored slips.
   Although tradition seems to be winning the battle with experimentation,
two potters, Cavan Gonzales and Russell Sanchez, currently push the
envelope. Cavan is Barbara Gonzales’s son and specializes in large,
important polychromes and elegant black-on-blacks, beautiful and super-
refined, but only a short creative step from Joe Aguilar’s and Angelita
Sanchez’s traditional pieces.
  On the other hand, Russell Sanchez, grand-nephew of Rose Gonzales
and disciple of Dora Tse-Pe, seems to be channeling all facets of Tony Da—
beauty, imagination and intimidating prices. If you Google him, get ready
for a visual feast.

San Ildefonso isn’t hopelessly locked in place. Even members of the
Martinez family experiment. Kathy Sanchez and Peter Pino are great-
grandchildren and Cavan Gonzales and Johnny Cruz are great-great-
grandsons. Now Cavan Gonzales and Kathy Sanchez are major figures, as
is Carmelita Dunlap’s grandson Eric Fender. In the next generations,
Maria’s hand is almost absent. Check out nephew Eric Fender’s jar, his
daughter Justine Fender’s dish and Johnny Cruz’s totally unexpected
micaceous bear.
    Elizabeth Lovato and her brother Juan Tafoya did some of San
Ildefonso’s finest work: imaginative content, impeccable technique.
Elizabeth’s seed jar at right center was one of John’s first pieces and it
remains one of his favorites. Juan’s red bear is a shape he made repeatedly,
as did Tony Da, and it’s hard to say who made it first.
   Peter Pino’s kiva sculpture, Marie Kaehela’s incised jar and John
Gonzales’s Tony-Da inspired jar are at the outer edge of San Ildefonso
pottery, while Angelita Sanchez and her sister Helen Gutierrez gained
prominence by keeping comfortably in the middle.

Rose Gonzales’s family stayed within the family style until Russell
Sanchez exploded on the scene. Rose’s niece Adelphia Martinez made a Tse-
Pe-style wedding vase.
   Joe Aguilar’s dish from 1947 and his great-grandson Bryce’s
unassuming little bowl from 2013 make a final comment on legacy vs.
innovation. Joe’s design looked like an old Maria and Julian piece while
Bryce’s design is all his own, but underneath the design, the pottery
remained the same: matte red exterior and matte interior, just like Maria
and Julian did it a hundred years ago.


SANTA ANA

Rare pottery from the Pueblo of mystery. Old Santa Ana is closed to the
public more than 350 days every year.
   The barrier on New Mexico Highway 44 helps make Santa Ana seem
like the most remote and inaccessible of all the Rio Grande Pueblos.
Actually, the public isn’t missing much activity. The old Pueblo, a bit north
and west of the current center of activity along Highway 44, has been
reserved mainly for ceremonial use for more than a hundred years.
   Santa Ana and Zia are kindred Keresan neighbors with a comfortable
back-fence relationship. When Antonio de Espejo claimed them for the
Spanish crown in 1583, he lumped them together as the “Province of the
Punames.” They suffered together for the next hundred years. In 1688,
Spanish troops from El Paso inflicted the only significant punishment that
occurred between the 1680 Revolt and the 1692 Reconquest. Both Pueblos
were destroyed and their populations scattered. The Santa Anas hid in the
Jemez mountains, and when they returned after the reconquest, looked
around for better land. In the eighteenth century, they bought five tracts
along the Rio Grande from the Spanish, farmland rich enough to allow them
to leave the old Pueblo behind and establish Santa Ana II.

One of the hard-to-find old ones
                                  7" diameter; circa 1875

   Ever since, the balance of trade has largely remained one of Zia pottery
for Santa Ana crops, and made-in-Santa-Ana pottery has been
correspondingly scarce. Today, Santa Ana prides itself on its organic
farming business, but it’s become far more than a sleepy farming
community. It also runs the upscale Prairie Star restaurant on the outskirts
of nearby Bernalillo and the 27-hole Valle Grande golf course by the Jemez
Dam, all administered by fewer than five hundred people in the “new” two-
hundred-year old Pueblo by the Rio Grande.

Historically, both Zia and Santa Ana potters made the same ware,
Puname Polychrome, but when the Santa Anas moved east to the river, they
subsituted fine river sand for the black basalt temper the hillside-dwelling
Zias used and still use.
   This difference in temper serves as the easiest identifier between Zia
and Santa Ana pottery. If you find a nick or a scratch in the slip, look at it
through a magnifying glass. If you see black flecks of temper in the clay,
you’re looking at a Zia piece. The Santa Ana piece won’t show black.
   The white slip serves as another, less certain identifier. Santa Ana
whites often have a lumpy cottage-cheese texture, almost waxy, while Zia’s
white slip goes on more evenly.
   Because pottery was relatively unimportant at Santa Ana, it came close
to dying out. There was a little flurry of pottery-making around 1940, but
after World War II, two people kept it alive: Eudora Montoya and an
interested Anglo, Nancy Winslow of Albuquerque. Eudora learned pottery
from her mother, but didn’t become serious about it until 1946, when she
was in her forties. Back then, some of the older potters were still working,
but by the early 1970s, she was the only Santa Ana potter.
    In 1973, Montoya and Winslow organized a group of eighteen student
potters. Then, starting in 1994, a third pottery revival began when Elveria
Montoya, one of Eudora’s students, began teaching. Elveria retired in 1999,
but classes continued under her daughter-in-law, Lucille Montoya. All
through those years, pottery has trickled out of Santa Ana, all well made, all
worth admiring, but there’s never enough so that you’ll find it without an
effort.
    In the course of collecting and buying, we’ve only added two Santa Ana
pieces that were made after 2000, both in the front row. Donna Pino studied

with Elveria Montoya and Jean Robbins was featured in a 2005 book that
we hope gave Santa Ana pottery another jump-start: Harlow, Anderson and
Lanmon’s The Pottery of Santa Ana Pueblo.

SANTA CLARA

Now it produces the fanciest pottery of all the Pueblos. But it took a while
getting there. Santa Clara’s early history was much like San Ildefonso’s.
The Ancestral Puebloans built on Santa Clara land in the early 1300s, and if
you arrange a tour, you can visit the mesa-top ruins at Puyé today, right in
the middle of the reservation. Some time around 1500, the Puyé dwellers
joined their neighbors to the east on the banks of the Rio Grande.
   They encountered Coronado’s group in 1540, they had a mission by
1629, and, according to the fashion of the times, they burned it in 1680.
After the 1692 Reconquest, they joined the San Ildefonso people on Black
Mesa and held off the Spanish until 1696. When Black Mesa fell, many

Santa Clarans fled west to Hopi and Zuni, but by 1702, most of them were
back at work building a new and better mission.
   Today, Santa Clara lives in easy cooperation with the heavily Hispanic
population surrounding Española, and the Pueblo’s residents farm, work in
Los Alamos and make pottery.
   They really make pottery. Perhaps two hundred Santa Clara potters are
turning out stylish blackware and redware, including some of the highest-
priced pottery ever made.





                        History as it never was on an early Santa Clara jar
                circa 1900,11¾" diameter, almost certainly decorated by a non-Indian

     It wasn’t always thus, however. When James Stevenson and Frank
Cushing made the first Indian pottery-collecting expeditions for the
Smithsonian in 1879, they gathered black, red and micaceous bowls from
Santa Clara, all undecorated. There’s mention of a polychrome as well, but
none seems to have survived.

Early writers agree that most of the ceremonial polychrome pottery
Santa Clara used at the beginning of the twentieth century came from San
Ildefonso. Even the impressed bear paw, the most traditional design element
on Santa Clara pottery (you see it on two bowls and a basket in the picture),
wasn’t common until after 1900. One source dates the earliest documented
piece with a bear paw at 1903, but others say the device goes back to the
mid-nineteenth century.
   What did happen early was traders and tourists. In 1880, the Denver &
Rio Grande Railroad’s legendary “Chili Line” connected Española to Santa
Fe. Suddenly Santa Clara’s undecorated blackware became small in size
and varied in shape: cream pitchers, vases, cups, candlesticks, dishes, bird
and animal figurines, even a toy train. Bruce Bernstein suggested that,
rather than being just for tourists, Santa Clara condiment jars and sugar and
creamers became tableware staples in Hispanic and Anglo households
during the later years of the nineteenth century.
   The olla at top left on the opposite page has an iconic Santa Clara shape
that defines the best of nineteenth-century Santa Clara blackware, although
it wasn’t a Santa Clara invention. The shape evolved over the centuries in
the Pueblos and in prehistory. The fifteenth-century olla in the middle of
page 39 suggests an early origin for the shape.
   Back when that big jar was made and until the 1930s, Santa Clara
blackware could hold water. Modern Santa Clara and San Ildefonso
blackware is fired at a low temperature and is distressingly water-soluble, as
we learned when our roof leaked during a winter storm. The cream pitcher
on the next page is early enough so that if you actually left cream in it, it

probably worked fine. Santa Clara made these for years. Turn the page, and
you’ll see a later redware set.
   Betty LeFree, in her 1975 Santa Clara Pottery Today, called the years
between 1880 and 1920 Santa Clara’s “Period of Handles,” referring to the
proliferation of tableware. You can see a lot of those handles on the next
page.
   The Period of Greatness came later.

There are several pieces here from the “Period of Handles.” The eldest is
the little teapot, with the unslipped bottom half that persisted in Ohkay
Owinge pottery but seems to have disappeared from Santa Clara by 1900.
The wonderful big, beat-up bowl with the bear paws is an almost pure
statement of the essence of1900 Santa Clara blackware.
   The narrow-necked water jar and the large olla behind it have an
indentation where the neck flares out to meet the body, a design element
characteristic of early Santa Clara work. Santa Clara potters still use the
indentation on traditional jars. The early pieces in the picture were made
when Santa Clara pottery was reasonably water-safe, so calling it a “water
jar” isn’t a mistake.
   Plain blackware with and without impressed designs has persisted to the
present. The pieces in the lower part of the picture date into the 1960s and
represent various stages of evolution. Little moccasins appeared before
1900. Animalitos, whimsical, small animal figures, showed up around
1910. By the 1990s, Santa Clara potters had made so many of them, we’re
convinced they breed.
   The melon jar shape, like the small piece in the center, has been a Santa
Clara favorite. One expert suggested they might go back to the nineteenth
century at Santa Clara, and they go back a long time before that. If you
bounce back to page 35, you can see a Hohokam one from 1150.
     It didn’t take long for the jar to evolve. By 1940, Severn Gutierrez, a
contemporary of Maria’s and a major player, had gone beyond the vertical
lines and was making swirl jars. In the rest of the century artists like Nancy
Youngblood Lugo took the swirl jar to high art.


SANTA CLARA – REDWARE

Black, we leave black. Red, we put colors on. In 1879, when Stevenson and
Cushing wrote about Santa Clara redware, they pointed out that a Santa
Clara potter would fire all her pots to a red color and set aside the ones she
intended to remain that way. The others, she’d smother in cow chips and
refire, turning them into blackware.
   The redware Stevenson and Cushing saw was utilitarian and
undecorated but not necessarily primitive. Mary Ellen and Laurence Blair’s
Margaret Tafoya shows a polished redware jar from 1865 that looks

finished enough to pass for a modern polished piece. After 1880, redware,
never all that common to begin with, moved into the background, but it
resurfaced strongly around 1930 when potters began experimenting with
white paint, which they tried tentatively on both redware and, after the
firing, on blackware.
   Other colors followed, and in 1932, they even tried a commercial
orange paint on the blackware, but it scratched right off. Early in the 1930s,
potters added a buff and what Betty LeFree called a “weak red.” A bit later,
they’d discovered a blue gray. The buff and weak red appear on Ohkay
Owinge pottery as well, but the blue gray was almost exclusive to Santa
Clara.





                         An early one, in an early shape
                           8¼" diameter, circa 1935

   White almost always outlined the other colors. “Always” by itself
wouldn’t be much of an exaggeration, as the picture demonstrates, but once
we feel we’ve learned an absolute truth, the exception comes along to

embarrass us. We stumbled on a little mid-twentieth century piece that
followed all the rules except that the potter outlined the weak red design
with the blue gray and ignored the white completely. One dealer lamented
that the trouble was that those potters didn’t read the books and do what
they were supposed to do.
   At first, the designs were geometric, but pictorials followed soon after,
and even Bambi got a white halo.
   The two potters mainly credited with developing the style have
important pieces in the picture at the right. Flora Naranjo did the bowl with
avanyu at top left, and Belen Tapia made the squared-off jar in front of it.
    Flora Naranjo (1915—?) gets a lot of credit for developing the style,
and her daughter Glenda stayed with it long past its period of popularity. If
Flora was a pioneer, however, Belen Tapia (1914—1999) gets even more
recognition. She found her colored clays from private locations around the
Pajarito Plateau above the Pueblo, and more than anyone else, she’s
remembered as the potter most responsible for the conventions of Santa
Clara polychrome redware.
    All the above goes without mentioning a third important early redware
potter, Lela Gutierrez. Her work was so important and so individual that she
was recognized along with Maria, Nampeyo and the others as one of the
Seven Family matriarchs. She and her family rate their own pages in this
book, a few pages ahead.
   These two-, three- and four-colors-on-red pieces hit their popularity
peak between 1940 and 1960, but they hung on for years after. The turtle in
the front row dates from 1994, and it displays some newer developments,
like a matte yellow surface and the blue color that Belen Tapia first used in
the 1960s. The squared-off jar in the middle of the front row is by Flora
Naranjo’s daughter Glenda, and she made it as late as 2001.
   Although most Santa Clara redware from the last three-quarters of the
last century is polychrome, undecorated redware is still around, and
currently, a red piece from Santa Clara is apt to be sculptural rather than
painted. The Baca family has made a niche for itself with melon jars
(Angela Baca has been suggested for the unsigned black one on the
previous page), and Alvin Baca’s impeccable redware one on the right side
of the picture from 1992 confirmed his family’s mastery of the genre.

Santa Clara’s polychrome redware work ranges from serious work by
serious potters, like Flora Naranjo’s avanyu dish in the top row, to
unashamed tourist pieces like the canoe. The creamer might not hold
cream, the bird ashtray on the right of the bottom row says “Merry Xmas”
on the rim, and the holes in the salt-and-peppers may be too small and
rough to let much out. Even the unsigned tourist ones could be ambitious,
like the giant bird bowl that dominates the right center of the picture.
   Flora Naranjo’s avanyu and Reycita Chavarria’s deer show how Santa
Clara potters adapted the white-outlined style to pictorial subjects. The
basket with the single-twist handle is called an “engagement basket.’’ These
hefty, four or five-inch diameter pieces, more often black, became part of

the Santa Clara standard repertory, so well established that they’re now
close to the wedding vase on the tradition ladder.
   Belen Tapia remained a leading polychrome potter for more than thirty
years and gathered enough awards to answer any questions about her
importance. Her pure colors gave her pieces a cheerful look that her
daughter Anita Suazo has mastered and potters like Anna Archuleta
emulated. Meanwhile, Flora Naranjo’s daughter Glenda has kept the spark
alive, and her2001 jar has all the pretty colors and all the tradition.
    Alvin Baca is one of the leading lights in the Baca family, and his melon
jars are textbook examples of melon-jar perfection. These days, melon jars
are carved rather than impressed. You can tell the difference by feeling the
inside. If it’s impressed, you’ll feel the melon shape, but if it’s carved, the
inside will be smooth.


SANTA CLARA – SARA FINA TAFOYA

The Seven Families #6: Tafoya. By 1900, Sara Fina Tafoya (1863–1949)
was most likely the leading potter at Santa Clara, master of large and small
utilitarian forms, mainly in black, but also in red and micaceous clay. By
“large,” we mean really big. Some of her storage ollas approached thirty
inches in their largest dimension—almost three times bigger than the largest
piece in the picture at right.
   She was also an open, friendly woman, and this combination of skill
and temperament made her an early favorite of the new breed of curio-
seekers in Santa Fe. In turn, exposure to the outside world stimulated her to
experiment with new forms, unashamedly designed to appeal to the buying
public’s taste.
   During the 1920s, her children were young adults, just the right ages to
be swept into the rapidly developing market for better-quality Indian pottery
created by the growing interest in Maria Martinez and San Ildefonso. In
1926, Fred Harvey Detours, luxurious limousine tours run from the La
Fonda Hotel in Santa Fe, began regular visits to Santa Clara with ninety-
minute layovers for lunch and pottery shopping.
   As the 1920s unfolded, Sara Fina and her children sold their work in
Taos, in Santa Fe and at the Pueblo and won awards at the Santa Fe Indian
Fair, the predecessor of Indian Market.

By the end of World War II, the Tafoyas had a family car and sold their
pottery all over the Southwest. But Margaret’s and the Tafoya family’s fame
didn’t really begin to grow until the 1960s, when it launched like a rocket.
By the end of the twentieth century, Sara Fina’s children, grandchildren,
great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren had become the most
prestigious, highest-priced group in all of Southwestern pottery.





                                   Lonewolves, actual size
         daughter Rosemary 1995, Joseph 1986, son Gregory 1994, daughter Susan 1993

   Since the beginning, the Tafoyas have made all types of Santa Clara
ware. Sara Fina stretched the definition of size, quality and form. Her pots
were the biggest, roundest, best-finished and best-polished. According to
Mary Ellen and Laurence Blair’s Margaret Tafoya, she developed the first
carved Santa Clara blackware in 1922. Later, her son Manuel (1895–1922)
did deeper carving, and by 1930, the two were doing carved ware that
resembles modern Santa Clara pottery.
   Margaret continued raising the standards and worked in all her mother’s
forms, including polychrome redware (although Belen Tapia’s daughter
questioned the experts’ attribution on the large jar in the picture—she
thought her mother made it, not Margaret). Margaret and Christina’s carved
work changed the general perception of Santa Clara pottery. If the
archetypical twentieth-century San Ildefonso piece was a Maria black-on-
black, Santa Clara’s counterpart was a Margaret Tafoya deep-carved piece.
    In the 1960s, Margaret’s brother Camilio and his son and daughter,
Joseph Lonewolf and Grace Medicine Flower, developed a style of
meticulously carved miniature pottery. Joseph and Grace continued the

style, and it caught on so well that Grace and especially Joseph became
superstars, and their pieces became the first super-high-priced Pueblo
pottery. Joseph’s children, Gregory Lonewolf, Rosemary Apple Blossom
and Susan Snowflake Romero, continued the style, and it remained pricey
for the rest of the century.
   As the twentieth century wound down, the family began to move away
from carved blackware. By 2010, basic Margaret-style pieces seemed too
retro for most potters’ tastes, and Tafoya family potters explored other
avenues. Whatever they did, however, their influence remained strong.
   The family’s imprint on Santa Clara pottery is so deep that the Tafoyas
may well remain at the front of the pack far into the twenty-first century as
well.

to find the broken and repaired one that’s sitting in front of the big one in
the back row, and the only reason we have that big one is that we got
incredibly lucky at an auction, and by reaching well past our buying rules,
were able to bring it home for a small fraction of its normal retail price.

beginning before World War I and flourishing afterward. The carved
blackware starts with pieces by Camilio and his wife Agapita and continues
with an engagement basket by Margaret’s sister Christina, then goes on
through the generations. Mary Cain and Mida are Christina’s daughters,

Medicine Flower. The little incised eggs at bottom right and on the opposite

opposite are by his son and grandchildren.


SANTA CLARA – LELA GUTIERREZ

The Seven Families #7: Gutierrez. With most Santa Clara potters,
decorated redware achieved a predictable, ritualized presentation. This
happened as well with Lela Gutierrez (1874—1966) but her predictability
took a different path.
   She was among the first to experiment with the medium, predating most
of her colleagues by five years or so, and she was the most adventurous in
terms of color and design. Perhaps more precisely, her husband Van was the
adventurer, since he did the painting, but the style they began in the 1920s
continued after his death in 1942, and pieces in their style remained
influential and in demand into the 1990s.
  A reader might pick up this book and wonder why, in a twenty-first
century incarnation, it devotes so much space to a nearly forgotten potter
like Lela Gutierrez. After all, the Seven Families matriarchs were anointed
back in 1974, and it stands to reason that perhaps not all of them were truly
immortal. Granted, Lela’s dynasty lost its energy, but, some of us remember
her well. Chuck Rozansky, an influential expert and collector, felt such a
deep bond with Lela and Van’s work that, after 2010, his spiritual offering
to the art was to have a tattoo artist anoint his body with Van’s designs, all
taken from pieces he owned.

Lela Gutierrez, early on
                        Lela imitating Maria, 4½" diameter, circa 1925

   Before Lela hit stride with her polychromes, she was looking for a way
to make a living. She never would have made the Maria copy at right
(knock-off might be more accurate) after she and Van found their style.
    In Santa Clara Pottery Today, Betty LeFree placed the start of Lela and
Van’s polychrome efforts at 1930. We believe the red vase at left center
with the Frank Lloyd Wright-looking design dates from around then or even
earlier and is one of the earliest pieces bearing their trademark style.
    After Van died, Lela continued working with their son Luther, and under
her direction, the style remained pure. The large jar second from right with
the avanyu is dead center on Lela and Van’s style. Once Lela slowed down
and after her death, Luther worked with his sister Margaret until his death in
1987. With Margaret, the style became more fanciful and fussy, and you can
see the difference in the small 1970 jar at left center.
   By 1980, the storyteller craze had hit, and Margaret and Luther turned
to making small, eccentric polychromes, like the crawling mudhead and the
owl. Ten years later, Margaret was on her own. She continued traveling all

over the Southwest from the Grand Canyon to Denver, to get her slips and
she and her niece Stephanie continued making the little figurines and
animalitos ever more eccentric. To our eyes, the turtle in the center is
almost incomprehensible.
   By 2000, Luther’s son Paul and his wife Dorothy were better known
than Lela and Van or aunt Margaret, and for something else entirely. Since
the 1980s, they'd been making little unpainted blackware and redware
animalitos and mudheads in quantities that defy belief and began receiving
attention at Indian Market as early as 1981. In the 1990s, the world paid
more attention to them and they made a few larger pieces, most memorably,
a blackware Noah’s Ark populated by a couple of dozen pairs of creatures
and, at Al Anthony’s request for a train-centered show, a good-sized copy
of an early 1900s Santa Clara blackware toy train. They made the red eagle
spreading his wings in the foreground in 2001. It’s the newest piece in the
picture, and Dorothy and Paul are nearing their eighties.
   There are blackware pieces by Dorothy and Paul’s son Gary and a
black-on-black piece by Paul’s sister Pauline, but today, the star of Lela and
Van’s family only glows faintly. Now collectors look to other families—
Tafoyas, Naranjos and beyond—for important Santa Clara pieces.

The redware jar with the stepped vertical panel at middle left is a source
piece, a very early Van and Lela and our earliest signed Santa Clara piece.
Two indicators of its age are that it doesn’t have the decorated hand around
the upper body that became their trademark, and it has an incised “Lela”
signature instead of their customary painted “Lela/Van.” Some experts
might question our 1930-or-before date as too early, but we’ve seen a
polychrome jar that ostensibly has a provenance from 1928.
   Lela and Van made the two pieces to its left a few years later, and the
wedding vase at right and the large dish a few years after that.
   The jar at the right of the dish demonstrates that the Lela/Van design
integrity wasn’t all Van. Lela made it with Luther after Van’s death, but it
hewed so closely to Van’s style that if it were the only Lela Gutierrez piece
you ever saw, you’d know what her work looked like. It’s pretty clear that as
long as Lela was alive, her work kept its integrity.
   Margaret and Luther continued making jars, but made more and more
small figurines, each more grotesque than the last. The figures are about all
Margaret has made since the 1990s, and Luther’s granddaughter Stephanie
kept making them.

Meanwhile, Dorothy and Paul started making little blackware figurines
around 1980, and they haven’t evolved one bit. You can pick up one that’s
thirty-five years older than the one next to it, and unless it’s worn, you won’t
know which is which. Their son Gary also works in monochrome blackware
and redware, specializing in sculptured human figurines.


SANTA CLARA – SISTERS, COUSINS, AUNTS AND IN-LAWS

The Tafoyas may have started slowly, but my how they grew. Margaret and
Camilio Tafoya and Christina Naranjo all married and had families, who
had families, who had families.
   The Tafoya genealogy in Fourteen Families in Pueblo Pottery shows a
hundred and one Tafoyas descended from Sara Fina. Seventy-one of them
rate the red dots that identify them as working potters. Then, Rosemary
Apple Blossom Lonewolf married Paul Speckled Rock, which puts her into
the Gutierrez genealogy, with its sixty-four entries and thirty-one red dots.
And Stella Tafoya married Loretto Chavarria, which connects with the
Chavarria family and their forty-nine members and nineteen more red dots.
Then add all the red dots for potters who came into the field in the two
decades since the book came out, and you have a couple of hundred Santa
Clara potters, all producing upper-level work. Tafoyas, Naranjos,
Chavarrias and Gutierrezes who don’t fit into the official genealogies push
the number even higher.

Shawn Tafoya: “at Santa Clara, non-traditional is the tradition”
                              6¼" diameter, 1997

   Much of the Tafoya and Tafoya-associated work is deep carved,
polished blackware. A proper Tafoya pot has an inky black polish and deep
relief. The carved-out matte portion has very few tooling marks, and on the
best pieces, none at all. Even though the carving is deep, the pot itself will
be thinner and lighter than you might expect, and certainly thinner and
lighter than it would have been if it had come from a Pueblo with less
exacting standards. The same holds for carved redware, like the pieces from
earlier-generation Mida Tafoya and the younger Tina Diaz.
   Some of these sisters, cousins, aunts, in-laws and namesakes have
creative distinctive niches in painting rather than carving. You can pick out
Earline Youngbird Tafoya’s redware across the room because of her stylized
traditional forms. You can recognize Shawn Tafoya’s work because he

paints whatever he feels like and doesn’t bother with traditional forms at all.
The quote under his pseudo-Mimbres Tiny’s Gym bowl below came the
first time we met him.
    Teresita Naranjo, who made the big red bowl on the right side of the
picture, is near the top of the Tafoya family tree. She was so established as
an important artist that she had major exhibitions in 1974, 1976, 1979, 1985
and in 1998, the year before she died. Teresita worked so completely and
competently in the Tafoya style from the 1930s into the 1990s that she
achieved celebrity that approached that of her cousin Margaret.
   The wonderful buffalo on the opposite page is the result of a long-
standing collaboration between Jane Baca, sister of the celebrated painter
Pablita Velarde, and her daughter, Starr Tafoya. It’s signed as all their
collaborations were, Jane and Starr. However, since it’s a departure from
their normal blackware and since Jane passed away in 2011 and we bought
it new in 2012, we suspect it’s primarily if not entirely Starr’s work.
    Others, like Linda Cain, Autumn Borts and Tammy Borts Garcia built
their reputations with carved pieces that followed the rules, then branched
out. By the 2000s, Tammy and her husband owned Blue Rain Gallery, one
of Santa Fe’s most prestigious contemporary native art galleries, and her
glass and bronze sculptures got as much attention as her pottery, if not
more.
    Still others—Toni Roller (Ryan Roller’s grandmother), Virginia
Ebelacker and Nancy and Nathan Youngblood—created such an intense
demand for their trademark pieces that collectors far richer than the
proprietors of this museum stand in line for the privilege of buying them.
Like Tammy Borts Garcia, Nathan Youngblood turned to glasswork and
created one more place for deep-pocket collectors to spend serious money.

If the painted water serpent became a likely identifier for San Ildefonso
pottery, the carved serpent has assumed the same role on Santa Clara
pottery. The picture includes nine of them, each as individual as the artist
who carved it.
    Teresita Naranjo gave us a totally traditional scary monster. Mida
Tafoya’s avanyu looks sinister, and Stella Chavarria’s looks a bit sleepy.
Tina Diaz’s redware serpent bounces around her jar, animated and jaunty.
Laura Tafoya gave us one with a big triangular turquoise eye. The
Eckleberrys did one that wraps sinuously around his jar, carved so deep
that we’re almost afraid to handle the jar for fear of picking off part of its
nose. Tammy Sorts Garcia’s avanyu gets almost lost in foam and waves.
And Earline Youngbird Tafoya painted her avanyu in graceful pale swirls.
   The carved piece by Tammy Garcia’s sister Autumn Borts shows the
creativity that pushed both sisters to the top of the Santa Clara prestige
ladder. Jane and Starr’s brownware buffalo has a stolid dignity. Laura
Tafoya’s jar in the center of the front row has a touch of sienna around the
neck that moves us toward the subject of the next two pages. Gwen Tafoya’s

incised small vase next to it with the turquoise bird’s eye has the shallow
incised carving that became the norm at Santa Clara after 1990.
   Shawn Tafoya, on the other hand, marches to a different drummer. His
pieces are fired in coal, which leaves modern tradition behind. From
prehistoric times, potters have used a variety of fuels. Some current artists
have reverted to wood firing and prehistoric Jeddito and Sikyatki ware from
Hopi was often coal-fired.


SANTA CLARA – SGRAFFITO AND SIENNA

Once you can make a good pot, why not make it even better? Some time in
the 1960s, a whole new style of decoration came into Southwestern pottery.
Before then, the best work was big, and if a major piece had anything
intricate, the intricacy would be confined to the accuracy and detail of the
painting.
   The Gonzales family at San Ildefonso and the Tafoyas at Santa Clara
made an art form out of carving, but the carving was large in scale: avanyus
and geometric forms that may have been striking but never were fussy.
   But then Popovi Da began experimenting over at San Ildefonso in the
late 1950s, accompanied by his son Tony and by Rose Gonzales’s son Tse-
Pe and his wife Dora. Right behind them, Camilio Tafoya and his son and
daughter, Joseph Lonewolf and Grace Medicine Flower, started an entire
parade of followers from Santa Clara. The movement started out tentatively,
and the little pipe in the center of the bottom row typifies its modest
beginnings. But during the 1970s and the early 1980s, the watchword
became “the more the better,” and among this subgroup of ambitions young
potters, everything had to have inlaid coral and turquoise, double-firing to
create color changes and, above all, fineline sgraffito designs.

The Folwells: major players
  Polly Rose, 2005, 8" diameter; Kaa, 2014, 4½" diameter; Jody, 1995, 9¼" diameter; Susan, 1995,
                                7⅛" diameter

   Out of all this, potters like Jody Folwell, Ron Suazo and Corn Moquino
lifted the standards of this second generation to impressive heights.
Through the 1990s and beyond, as the picture demonstrates, the incised
patterns have a deft precision that strains the eye of anyone with less than
perfect close vision. Even the naturalistic drawing is good. Look at Dusty
Naranjo’s horses or Paul Naranjo’s raccoon. Miniatures gave potters the
chance to outdo each other. Camilio, Joseph and Grace set the standard
early (see page 163), and few ever outdid them, but tiny meticulous pieces
have seemed almost commonplace since the 1990s.
   Experimentation with sienna firing raised interest in colors between
black and red, and Paul Naranjo, Stephan Baca, Bernice Suazo Naranjo,
Karen Naranjo, Forrest Naranjo, Dusty Naranjo, Jody Naranjo and others
perfected an intermediate firing that produces a beautiful chocolate brown.
   Of that group, Jody Naranjo deserves special mention. She rose quietly
through the ranks to reach full superstar status by 2010, to the point where
important magazines devote long articles to her. She’s a celebrity today, but
it took years for her to reach the recognition level that her aunt and cousins
had already attained. Now her family sits at the top of the ladder in this
corner of the pottery-as-art world.

Jody’s family includes the world-famous Folwells, children,
grandchildren and great-grandchild of her grandmother, Rose Naranjo. Her
aunt Jody Folwell and cousins Susan and Polly Rose have been
acknowledged top-level potters since the 1990s, and in the 2010s, Polly
Rose’s daughter, Kaa Folwell, joined the elite circle.
   Dolly Naranjo, Jody Naranjo’s mother, is Jody Folwells sister. Now the
magazines are also writing about Dolly and her son Elijah, adding even
more luster to a small family group. On the next two pages, we’ll introduce
more of the family: Jody Naranjo’s aunt Nora Naranjo-Morse and her
cousin Roxanne Swentzell, both international superstars. If there’s a single
dominant tight-knit family in the world of Southwestern pottery, this is it.

In this world, small is beautiful. The big pieces by Forrest Naranjo,
Samantha Tafoya and Johnathan Naranjo are hardly the norm. What you
see in the front couple of rows is more like what you’d expect.
   One gets the feeling that people named Naranjo are good at this sort of
work. The picture features Jody, Jonathan, Dusty, Karen, Forrest, Paul
Dolly and Elijah, and those Folwells on the opposite page are really
Naranjos by a different name.
   However, Suazo is a big name too. Ron has been a leading exponent for
years. Bernice (who has Naranjo in her name as well) is one of the best,
and the married-in Candelaria does beautiful work too.
   Corn Moquino is a senior citizen in this group, and a definer of the
style. His daughter Jennifer is rising up the stardom ladder rapidly, and in
the 2010s has been collaborating with the illustrious Russell Sanchez of San
Ildefonso. Eric Tafoya, despite the name, is from the other side of the
Gutierrez family, a great-grandson of Van Gutierrez’s sister Severa Tafoya.
Gwen Tafoya, Severa’s granddaughter, is one limb higher on the family tree.
You’d expect Julie Gutierrez, who by 2013 had become one of the most

active and creative practitioners of the genre, to fall somewhere in those
lines, but she’s from a different Santa Clara family.
   The one red piece is by Norman Red Star, who isn’t Santa Clara at all,
he’s Sioux. However, he merits inclusion here because he learned from his
Sioux uncle, Red Starr, who lived at Santa Clara and became recognized for
decades as a genuinely important Santa Clara potter.


SANTA CLARA – SURPRISES

If you think you know what to expect from Santa Clara, guess again. For
a dozen pages, we’ve tried to describe the major styles and trends that
influence Santa Clara potters, even to the point of describing “Tafoya
pottery” and implying that if you simply look for a black pot with a deep-
carved avanyu, that’s all you need to know.
    In 1993, the Bloms and the Hayeses were checking out the exhibits at a
fall fair at Kewa (we called it Santo Domingo then), and we stopped to talk
to Shawn Tafoya and saw his array of off-center pottery. When Al asked if
it was traditionally made, he gave us the quote we referred to a couple of
pages back. His full statement: “Of course it’s traditional. At Santa Clara,
being non-traditional is the tradition.”
   We’re not sure that Margaret Tafoya would have given the same answer,
but the pottery in the picture corraborates his statement. The work ranges
from a bit unusual to off the charts and the earliest piece goes back to 1980.
Non-traditional experimentation has gone on for a long time at Santa Clara.

Two Superstars on one piece
               Roxanne Swentzell, polished by Diego Romero, 7⅛" high, 2000

     It makes sense, if you think about it. Other major pottery-producing
Pueblos have continuing traditions of design that go back to the eighteenth
century and before. Santa Clara, on the other hand, enjoys two liberating
factors—an explosion of restless young potters and an earlier tradition of
simple, utilitarian shapes, almost entirely undecorated. The boundaries are
still being drawn, and they’re in constant motion.
   One boundary switch took one of our favorite Santa Clara potters off
these two pages. When we first did them, we included a piece by Minnie
Vigil’s sister, Lois Gutierrez. It’s been suggested that she’s the most skilled
and most imaginative pottery painter of all, and it’s hard to make a strong

argument otherwise. However, Lois and her pottery partner husband, Derek
de la Cruz, have settled in Pojoaque, and she now claims Pojoaque as her
Pueblo rather than Santa Clara. You’ll have to turn to pages 140 and 141 to
see what she’s done lately. (Footnote: Lois wasn’t the first of Minnie’s
family to defect. Sister-in-law Virginia Gutierrez has always claimed Nambé
and Thelma Talachy married into Pojoaque. Only Goldenrod stayed in
Santa Clara.)
   Experimentation has gone in all directions. Some surprises are quiet,
like Paul Speckled Rock’s little black and blue ball. Some are emphatic,
like Corn Moquino’s goggle-eyed fish.
   The potters who’ve stepped the furthest forward are at the top of the
prestige ladder. It’s hard to say who the number one Southwestern potter is
these days, but Roxanne Swentzell’s figurative pieces have brought her
worldwide acclaim and her own multi-story tower gallery at Pojoaque. The
National Museum of the American Indian in Washington commissioned
Roxanne’s aunt, Nora Naranjo-Morse, for the sculpture at the museum’s
entrance.
   Joseph Lonewolf’s daughter, Rosemary Apple Blossom Lonewolf,
quickly mastered the family’s elegant miniatures, but she wasn’t content to
stop there. We met her at the Heard Museum in Phoenix. At the time, she
was taking university ceramic classes in order to learn glaze technology for
a commission on a civic building in Chandler, Arizona. The blue glazed tile
in the picture is light-years away from Santa Clara pottery, but the potter is
right at the center of Santa Clara’s art.
   The other tile in the picture, a Native American Wonder Woman, is by
Jason Garcia. He’s another of Severa Tafoya’s grandchildren, and his piece
makes us wonder if her brother Van Gutierrez were alive today, whether this
might be what he’d be doing.
   Every piece here testifies to an indisputable truth. You can learn to
recognize Santa Clara pottery, but you can’t ever assume that you know
what the next piece will look like.

    Finally, the most impressive piece on these two pages, at least to us, is
Roxanne Swentzell’s mask on the opposite page. It’s down the middle of
what made her famous, and for us, it’s two great ones on one piece. Back in
2000, she and Diego Romero were a couple, Roxanne made it, Diego
polished it, and they both signed it.


SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA

Down there, they make pots the old way. Compared to other native groups
in the Southwest, California Indians had a couple of extra centuries to live
undisturbed lives.The grace period ended in 1770 when the Spanish started
to build the California mission chain. Southern Californians had made
pottery much like the jar in the inset for a thousand years, but once the
Europeans made contact, everything changed. Pottery submerged as an art
form while basketry flourished.
   Basketry has always been California’s prime Indian art, and what little
California pottery exists has almost entirely come from the south part of the
state below the Tehachapi mountains, a lump that splits the state a few miles
north of Los Angeles, fertile valleys to the north and desert to the south.
   Desert Indians lived on both sides of the Colorado River, but they had
opposing attitudes. To the east, in Arizona, Yumans and Mojaves resisted
the Spanish through much of the nineteenth century while the Southern
California groups to the west, the Kumeyaay, Chemehuevi, Cahuilla and
others, were forced into the missions. Many adopted European dress, spoke
Spanish, remained Catholic and worked on Spanish farms and ranches. The
Cahuilla became so comfortable with Spanish life that they fought on the
losing side of the 1847 Mexican war.

A California desert water bottle
                      probably Cahuilla, 11½" high, circa 1920 or earlier

   By 1870, Southern California’s Indians had reservation land, and with
their ability to coexist with Europeans, began to blend into Anglo society.
To a small extent, the Anglos had to coexist as well. Thanks to reservation
boundaries and population growth, the Cahuilla now own a large chunk of
Palm Springs.

In the mission years, pottery almost vanished west of the Colorado. The
Yumans and Mojaves kept making it, but California’s Mission Indians were
increasingly pushed towards the buckets, pans and crockery of European
life.
  We saw a Kumeyaay pottery exhibition at the University of California a
few years back, and what we remember most was how few examples came
from much past the turn of the twentieth century, how large the time gaps
were between examples, and how few potters were known or represented.
   At the time, Kumeyaay was a new word to us. It replaced the old
mission name Diegueño, which included the Kamia, Ipai and Tipai,
California/Mexico border tribes. In 1977, Gena Van Kamp wrote a slim,
now-rare book called Kumeyaay Pottery. The fact that such a book exists at
all is remarkable simply because the Kumeyaay and other Southern
California Indian groups have been more concerned with survival than with
art.
   For more than a century, state of California and U.S. govenment actions,
no matter how well intentioned, managed to keep the Indians poor. Things
got better only when self-advocacy and self-government took over, helped
along by casino money. A by-product of the movement was increased
interest in tribal traditions and tribal art.

Official policy dealt the Indians lemons, but on these pages, you’re
looking at one small way they made lemonade.

With a couple of exceptions, this array represents southern California
Indian pottery at the turn of the millennium, and it mainly has the flavor
that desert pottery has had since Hohokam days. The odd red-on-black
three-spouted jar in the bottom row and its companion footed wedding vase

in front of it come from earlier times, before pottery making virtually
disappeared in the second quarter of the twentieth century.
   Aside from those two pieces and one 1980 example by the Cupeño
potter Willie Pink, it all dates from the 1990s and later, including Pink’s
2002 traveling companion figurine.
   Some of the newest pieces continue to look backwards. Martina Flores’s
fire-clouded redware jar at the left of the bottom row has fire-clouded
coloration that a Sinagua potter would have admired 600 years ago. The
plainware pieces in the middle and front rows evoke utilitarian pottery
made all across the Southwest for millennia.
     It’s not all antiquity replayed, however. A couple of pieces demonstrate
that in California, contemporary pottery-making does take note of what’s
happening elsewhere. Dealers have looked at Eva Salazar’s seated figurines
and happily sold them as Mojave with correspondingly inflated prices.
   Theresa Wildflower, a Chemehuevi, looks even farther afield. She makes
some of the most meticulous miniature pottery anywhere, and she makes it
with Pueblo designs. You can debate whether her tiny olla with climbing
green frogs is really a Cochiti piece or really a Zuni piece, but you’ll have a
hard time convincing anyone that it’s actually just another piece of
Southern California pottery.


TAOS

If you say “micaceous” the usual response is “Taos.” It’s the northernmost
Pueblo and perhaps the most visible and most-visited. Taos (it’s slurred into
one syllable, sounding like “Touse”) speaks the Towa language like Picuris,
Sandia and Isleta, but the four Pueblos couldn’t be less alike, and each has a
different economic base. Isleta people work at jobs in Albuquerque, Sandia
is tiny and casino-rich, Picuris is remote and sleepy and makes its money
from a hotel in Santa Fe, but the economic base for Taos and its twelve
hundred residents is the Pueblo itself.
   Today when you visit the town of Taos, you find all kinds of tourist
attractions: the Kit Carson Museum, two early artists’ homes now museums
and a historic Spanish hacienda. Then, you get to the Pueblo. Its five-story
apartment complex makes it the most architecturally spectacular of all the
Pueblos. It became an Anglo artist’s cliché, to the point that, no matter how

many you’ve already seen, the next Southwest painting you encounter will
probably be of Taos Pueblo. Its almost-in-the-city-limits location makes it
the most tourist-oriented and tourist accessible of all the Pueblos. At first
visit, it seems almost like a theme park, and when you leave, you feel a bit
guilty if you haven’t bought a souvenir.
   Today’s amicable coexistence with tourism and Anglos and Hispanics in
general is surprising in light of history. In 1628, the priests wrote smugly
that twenty-five hundred Taos Indians were now good Christians. Eleven
years later, the people of Taos were so disgusted with their lot that they fled
en masse to Kansas, where they’d still be if the Spanish hadn’t tracked them
down and herded them back to the old Pueblo two years later.





                           Old Taos, oven safe and well used
                             4½" high, circa 1915

In 1680, Taos helped lead the revolt, and Popé of San Juan lived there
while he planned it. During the reconquest, the people of Taos fled again,
and it took Governor de Vargas four full years to subjugate them.
   Taos didn’t get along with Mexicans or Americans either. In 1837, the
Mexican governor decided to arrest the Taos alcalde (roughly equivalent to
a mayor), thereby triggering a new revolt. Rebels captured and killed the
governor and set up a Taos Hispanic, José Angel Gonzales, in his place.
Mexican troops threw him out a month later and the Mexican government
ultimately executed him.
    In 1846, the American flag went up, and, repeating the pattern, Taos
warriors rebelled and did in Governor Bent the next year. When American
troops arrived, seven hundred Indians barricaded themselves in the mission,
and the American commander took care of the situation by blowing the
walls and many of the occupants apart with a cannon. Then, in case the
lesson hadn’t been learned, a military tribunal hung seven of the survivors
for treason. A troubled history is nothing unusual among the Pueblos, but
Taos seems to have had the least tolerance for oppression.
   Taos and Picuris make similar pottery. Originally it was made almost
entirely for utility, not art. What little decoration that appeared was almost
always confined to little sculptural touches like the handles and rim on the
hundred-year-old jar to the left. All but one of the utilitarian pieces in the
picture opposite have those little touches, and they span a century of work.
   As with Picuris, Taos micaceous clay with its glittery flecks produced
ware that was strong and safe enough for cooking, and for much of it, that

was its main purpose. The little pot on this page and the darkened pieces in
the picture opposite have all spent a share of their lives in ovens.
   However, it’s also true that Taos has been a tourist destination for a
century, so it’s no surprise that even among older pieces, you find tourist-
pleasers like the horno and the horse (or maybe a dog) on the next page.

This array of pots and pitchers covers a century, shows little stylistic
evolution, and was made for utility. The earliest of the darkened pieces was
made around 1900, the most recent in 1970, and all have been well used,
with much of the darkening coming from time spent in an oven. One look at

the three bean pots in the back tells you all you need to know about why
they were made and how they were used.
   The shiny pieces are newer, the oldest from 1940 and the newest from
2000. To us, the only real difference beween the older pieces and most
newer ones is that the new ones seem more carefully made, with most of the
improvement coming in the last years of the twentieth century. The mid-
century bowl in the left foreground and the souvenir horno have a casual
workmanship similar to the earlier pieces.
   Later on, Yellow Flower’s jar with the leaf sculpture has a finish that the
earlier pieces lack, and Angie Yazzie’s bean pot and her later tall vase add
another level of precision. By 2000, when Angie made the elegant vase, the
standards at Taos had risen to an Indian Market-worthy level.
  A couple of the earlier pieces fascinate us. The large water jar at the
right with four extra spouts around the neck must have had a use that its
maker and the people at Taos understood, but we haven’t been able to guess
what it is.
     If that piece confuses us a bit, the four-spout canteen in the center
mystifies us. Why and for what? And how do you use it? We’re afraid we’ll
never know.


TAOS – EXPLORATIONS

Looking backward, you know what to expect. Looking forward, all bets
are off. In 1980, John Barry wrote “Lack of participation by [Taos and
Picuris] potters at the 1979 and 1980 Indian Market suggests that their
tradition is declining. One explanation for this decline is lack of customer
interest. . . . If an effort were undertaken to produce and market quality
pottery at Taos and Picuris, in all probability collectors would welcome
these pieces to their collections.”
     It happened to some degree at Picuris, but pottery there remained as
always: undecorated mica with a greenish cast. Taos moved forward in the
1990s and beyond. Now we see variety, and we see artists making their
personal statements.
    Traditional micaceous ware began to achieve new identities. Juanita
Dubray put her trademark corn sculpture applique on the tan micaceous jar

at lower right center, a touch that’s so much in her personal style that it
identifies her as the artist from across the room.
   Angie Yazzie makes beautiful pieces you could call purely traditional,
but if you look at the shapes of the two on the opposite page and the two on
the previous page, it’s pretty clear that their thinness and grace sets them
apart from the older pieces.





                                       Tradition can be fun
                             Jason Mondragon, 3½" high, 2012

   For decades, potters had made little animalitos at Taos as part of their
tradition, but they never made any as lighthearted as the ones Jason
Mondragon has made since the 1990s. Until Jason, Taos animals looked
like the one on the previous page.
   Glenn Gomez, Mead Concha and Antonia Lujan all made Taos
micaceous pieces, but they fired them as blackware and made them in
shapes that few other potters ever made, in Taos or anywhere else.
   Pam Hauer makes elegant small pieces, and if the seed jar opposite isn’t
small enough for you, look at the tiny things on page 203. There’s one of

hers in that group as well. However, we’d be doing her a disservice if we
left the impression that those little pieces are all she does. She does
traditional micaceous pieces like the kiva jar behind the small one in the
picture and experiments in many other directions. Of all the Taos potters
who worked in the 1990s and after, Pam impresses us as the most
innovative.
   There are other departures, too. Henrietta Gomez made a bear
storyteller that, unless you knew she made it, you’d almost certainly
identify as Cochiti. However, she also made the micaceous one in the
picture, a singing mother that could only be from Taos, and she gave it
animation and gesture that rivals the work by Cochiti’s masters of the genre.
   Bernadette Track gave us yet another departure: a pottery model of the
church at Taos—the new one, not the one American cannons shot holes
through in 1847. We wondered who the “ Jevi” was who signed it, but years
later, Bernadette told us it was hers.
    After 2000, the picture changed. Bernadette Track contributed two other
pieces to the picture that really expand Taos pottery’s borders. The giant
micaceous jar decorated with kachina figures and the feather-bedecked
mask completely escape any confines that tradition might have placed on
her. Bernadette represented a second Taos generation for us. Her mother is
Juanita Dubray’s sister. Then, in 2013, John found a piece from one more
generation.
   Dawning Pollen Shorty is Bernadette’s daughter. She made the dazzling
standing figure at the right. To us, its combination of grace, sculptural
quality and flowing decoration bring Taos micaceous pottery up one more
level. We couldn’t help smiling at the fact that one of the tallest pieces in
the book was made by an artist named Shorty, but that reaction seems far
too disrespectful for what we think is a major piece of art.
   What all this means is that Taos potters took John Barr/s words to heart,
but with results no one anticipated. Today, Taos does anything and
everything, but if you look closely at the picture, the most impressive pieces
remain clearly Taos.

from Taos, but it doesn’t seem as much a departure as Glenn Gomez’s
lidded jar with the matte top, polished bottom and sienna highlight on the

   We had similar prooblems with Mead Concha’s shallow dish, and John’s
somewhat desperate call of “relish dish” was the best we could do. Carol
had no confusion about it. She took one look and said, “It’s a duck.”
   And the church speaks for itself. After all these years of collecting it
remains the only complete architectural landmark in the John & Al
Museum.


TESUQUE

If it was going to happen, it probably happened at Tesuque first. One
reason for the phenomenon is that Tesuque (say Te-SOO-ky) is barely
outside Santa Fe’s city limits, a proximity that never seemed to be of much
benefit to Tesuque.
   Tesuque’s classic mission compound was established about 1700. The
date isn’t surprising. The old Ancestral Puebloan village was about three
miles away, and that’s where Coronado’s army found it 1540. It was still
there in 1680 when Tesuque struck the first blows of the revolt. They were
the first to kill a public official and the first to do in a priest.
   Apparently the Spanish had a long memory. By the time the citizens of
Tesuque finished struggling against the reconquest, their original village
was destroyed, and they had little choice but to build a new Pueblo with a
nice new mission.
   During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, little Tesuque was one
of the three main makers of fine painted pottery. They made Powhoge
Polychrome, a style mainly associated with San Ildefonso, that had black
decoration on gray or white and red confined to the rim and the underbody.
Tesuque’s work equaled San Ildefonso’s for quality and was a little dressier
than Nambé’s. But fine pottery didn’t last.

CTCM: a Candelario bowl and the back of the smiling rain god on the opposite page
                    4½" diameter and 6½" high, both circa 1905

    First in line as always, Tesuque potters were in deep collaboration with
the Santa Fe traders by 1880. Not that the traders were much interested in
continuing a fine pottery tradition. In Jonathan Batkin’s Pottery of the
Pueblos of New Mexico, 1700–1940, there’s a circa-1880 photo of trader
Jake Gold with an array of Tesuque pottery, and it’s clear that the
righteously decorated Powhoge Polychrome ollas were almost entirely in
the past. Instead, Tesuque potters were turning out little figures much like
the monos being made at Cochiti. Gold’s eye was on commerce rather than
on art, but in his pursuit of the dollar, he created a market.

John Candelario opened his Original Curio Store on West San Francisco
Street in Santa Fe in 1890, and he had every bit as much energy as Gold in
promoting the art. Around 1905, he instructed Tesuque potters to mark
every piece they made for him by writing CTCM on it, for “Candelario the
Curio Man.” Unfortunately, his potters couldn’t read or write, so they had
no problem making their C’s, T’s and M’s conform to whatever designs
they had in mind. The pieces below suggest why Candelario’s trademark
was short-lived.
   By 1920, traditional pottery was history at Tesuque, and production had
switched over to mass manufacture of rain gods, strange little creatures that
look like space aliens holding buckets on their laps. When the first ones
appeared around 1895, they were micaceous and undecorated, but by 1900,
they were white-slipped and either undecorated or quickly colored with
inks. Merchants sold them as sacred items, but there was nothing sacred
about them. The Gunther Candy Company of Chicago gave them away as
promotional items, and Gold and John Candelario sold them by the barrel
for six dollars and fifty cents per hundred.
   One by one, pottery traditions evaporated. It was quicker, easier and
more predictable to paint a rain god after firing than before, and they
decorated fired pieces with ink as early as the 1880s. Then they found out it
was easier not to fire it at all, but just to let it dry in the sun or heat it on the
kitchen stove. And, of course, it was also easier to buy your paint at the
store than it was to make it yourself.
   By 1930, the rain god’s popularity was waning, but Tesuque potters
were happy to switch over to little bowls that were even easier to make.

Poster paints came on the market in the late 1920s, and, as always, Tesuque
potters were the first to use them.
   The next two pages show what happened.

Before 1900, Tesuque potters made well-finished wares in the Powhoge
polychrome style and occasionally in black-on-red. The main difference
between Tesuque and fine San Ildefonso ware in those styles was that at
Tesuque, the designs were freer, often floating in space like the cartouche on
the bird’s stomach in the picture above.

The older pieces in the picture, especially that squawking bird, would
look perfectly at home in that 1880 photo of Jake Gold standing over his
merchandise.
    After 1900, some potters still made pieces the old way, like the double
jar, the moccasins and the wedding vase, but increasingly, rain gods and
high production became the order of the day. The rain gods in the picture
show a progression. The micaceous one at front center is a really early
rain-god-with-bucket. Earlier Tesuque “idols” were micaceous and seated
or standing in various positions.
   Sometime before 1900, as production stepped up, the micaceous ones
disappeared. The next generation were cream-slipped and undecorated, like
the one in the top hat at left center and the one with the goofy smile and no
bucket at the right. We can date that one to 1905 with some precision, since
it has John Candelario’s CTCM down its back.
   Next came ink decoration. You can see it along the bottom of the little
jar with the arrows in the center. The ink-decorated see-no-evil, hear-no-
evil, speak-no-evil set speaks volumes about how seriously everyone
regarded the “sacred” nature of the rain god. Back in 1912 when these
were made, the usual postcard portrayal showed the “three wise monkeys”
lined up in this pose.


TESUQUE – POSTER PAINT

And now, we turn the whole idea of pottery-making upside-down. For a
couple of thousand years, perhaps a million people made pottery in the
Southwest. They went to the trouble of making it because it gave them
permanent, water-resistant tools and vessels.
     It didn’t take long for them to notice that if they made their pottery
better and more permanent, neighboring peoples would trade for it. By a
thousand years ago, pottery had become a valued commodity. It was the
beginning of an art market, but the only art that had value was well made
and useful.
  A bit before 1900, that started to change. The Santa Fe traders began
encouraging their Tesuque potters to take more and more shortcuts in order
to increase output. Potters didn’t have to fire their rain gods, and they could

decorate with ink and save themselves the trouble of digging up the old clay
pottery paints. Standards kept dipping lower and lower.





                               There was a high end here, too
                       Juan and Lorencita Pino, circa 1940, 6” high

   The pottery establishment was quick to take notice. Edgar Lee Hewitt of
the Museum of New Mexico and Kenneth Chapman of the Laboratory of
Anthropology felt they should differentiate between “good art” (classic
Pueblo ollas) and “bad art” (rain gods), and others agreed.
   Then came the Great Depression. Beginning about 1930, Tesuque
potters turned to poster paint decoration and made thousands of pieces that,
by the establishment definition, were even worse art. Now the paint would
smudge and come off if your hands were slightly sweaty and, if you left the
pot in water for a while, the colors wouldn’t just melt away, the whole pot

would dissolve. It was the least useful pottery in all the history of the
Southwest.
   However, it was a specific answer to a specific problem. Money was so
scarce during the 1930s that hungry artists had to find a way of making a
living. Clay was free, poster paints were cheap at Woolworth’s in Santa Fe,
and if you didn’t care about quality, you could make something sort of
pretty you could sell for a nickel and get something to eat.
   Now, that potters weren’t limited to all those dreary pottery earth colors,
the low-end curio stores were delighted. The Depression affected everyone.
Just like the potters, the dealers had to find new ways to make a living.
Now, they could buy the cheapest Indian pottery they’d ever bought and fill
their shelves with pieces in fantasy colors, brighter, cheerier and more
festive than anything anyone had ever seen.
  How cheap were they? In his 2002 When Rain Gods Reigned, Duane
Anderson reported that the Heard Museum in Phoenix sold a poster paint
rain god for forty-five cents. When you consider that rain gods are much
harder to make than little jars and that the piece probably acquired a couple
of trader’s markups and a retail markup on its journey to Phoenix, you can
imagine how much the potter got for her work.
    Surprisingly, given the pressures and the culture of the day, some potters
made careful and even thoughtful poster-paint pieces. The artists put a lot of
thought into the candlestick at left, varnished it to protect it, and were proud
of it enough to sign it. It’s the only pre-1980 signed poster-paint piece
we’ve ever seen.
   By the end of World War II, poster paint had become a tradition of a
sort at Tesuque, and a few artists made poster-paint pieces, or poster-paint-
style pieces, decorated with the acrylics that came along in the 1960s. A
couple of those appear on the opposite page.
  We don’t ask you to approve of poster-paint pottery. All the other books
seem to feel they either have to ignore it or to apologize for it, and our great
early mentor, Dick Howard, called them “uglychromes.”
   However, if you’re willing to set prejudice aside, you can join us in
celebrating an irrelevant art. Have fun looking at the most unashamedly
useless pottery the Southwest has ever seen.
    In Glorious Technicolor.

In 2012, John startled us all when he brought home the one thing in the
picture we thought we’d never see: a ten-inch poster-paint olla. It got us to
wondering about what prompted the artist to make a pure tourist curio
that’s too big for a tourist to take home conveniently.
   The items that pretend to be practical got our attention. You could
actually use the salt and pepper, and we suppose a candleholder makes
sense, but a cream pitcher? The most bizarre piece in the whole picture is
the cup and saucer. We’re glad no one ever tried to use it, but we’re a bit
sorry we’ve never had the experience of filling it with hot tea and watching
it melt down.
    There’s a range in quality here. The cup and saucer are quite well made,
and the seated duck in the front row is even better. Whoever made the

wedding vase at the right cared enough about it to varnish it, as the Pinos
did with their elegant rainbird candleholder on the opposite page.Most of
the pre-1980 pieces, however, are quick-and-dirty, like the little bowls with
their flaking paint.
    After the 1970s, when the world outside the Pueblos was discovering
Indian art, nobody wanted quick-and-dirty anymore. Now, poster paint
wasn’t poster paint anymore, it was durable paint, and the pieces were
properly fired.
   You can see the later generation in Ignacia Duran’s rain god at upper
right and in Reyes Herrera’s little jar in the lower right-hand comer. And
you really can see it in Terry Tapia’s little turkey from 1993. She remained
an important Tesuque potter into the 2000s.
    You’ll see more of Terry and her son Thomas on the next pages.


TESUQUE – ALL OVER THE LOT

Where did that tradition go? As the 1960s transformed itself from just
another decade into a sociological phenomenon, America decided it was in
love with Things Indian. By the 1970s, it took more than a quick little
poster-paint souvenir to satisfy the average Santa Fe tourist.
   Unfortunately for Tesuque, it had been too long since its potters had
faced a discerning market, and almost no one there was ready to meet the
challenge. Not that there hadn’t been good potters there. Around 1940,
Catherine Vigil did a few beautiful polished polychromes, now almost
unobtainable, that hovered halfway between redware and blackware and
challenged the finest work from Santa Clara. A few others continued the old
styles or experimented with carved work.
   But in 1975, Tesuque was in the same boat as Jemez, with one major
difference: Jemez had a population of two thousand and Tesuque’s was
barely a tenth of that. There simply weren’t enough working potters to
rebuild a tradition.

For forty years, tradition lingered
   unsigned, 6" diameter, circa 1980; Maria Duran and Priscilla Lilly Flower, 3¾" diameter, circa
                          1940; unsigned, 5" diameter, circa 1960

   The few that were working faced a fork in the road. Should they
continue making poster-paint pieces but make them better, or should they
relearn a craft they’d forgotten?
   Some went back to traditional micaceous ware, and we’ve seen simple
pieces by Priscilla Vigil, probably from the mid-1950s.
   There were also quiverings of life in the old polychrome tradition. The
1940 piece in front below by Maria Duran and Priscilla Lilly Flower seems
a direct descendant of the pre-rain-god pieces from the nineteenth century.
(We guess that Priscilla Lilly Flower is Priscilla Vigil, who was born in
1919, started exhibiting at Indian Market in 1933, and exhibited as late as
1992 at the Smithsonian Festival of American Folk Life.)
   The strange anonymous piece to its right from the 1960s shows skills
and philosophies from a different time, and the excellent unsigned piece

from around 1980 really has the earlier feel.
    There’s not much of that earlier feel on the opposite page. Yes, there’s a
polychrome duck painted with permanent paints that sort of evokes poster
paint, and there’s a rain god, an acknowledgement of times past, but now
properly fired and painted. There are three pieces by a unique mid-century
artist. Manuel Vigil made a name for himself with figures, storytellers and
nativity sets that looked sufficiently primitive for the sophisticated buying
public to embrace them as folk art. Manuel made the figures and his wife
Vincenta made the clothing and painted them with waterproof stain.
   Everything else on the page goes somewhere else. When we wrote this
book in 1995, we said, “One artist has to stand as the embodiment of
contemporary Tesuque pottery, the inimitable Ka’Ween, Claudia Vigil Fry.”
We added that “she borrows from everywhere, making excellent pots that
stand somewhere between homage and affectionate parody.” Sadly, her
career went downhill after we wrote that. She fell victim to the demons that
haunt the private lives of artists everywhere. We heard that a while ago, she
lived with another talented artist who soon after died from alcoholism. We
haven’t forgotten her, and we put four of her pieces in the picture.
   Others have taken over. Bea Duran Tioux, who made the four
micaceous pieces at the left of the picture, had a shop near the corner of the
old Pueblo plaza in the early 2000s and served as a major information
source for Duane Anderson’s When Rain Gods Reigned. Terry (Teresa)
Tapia continued with poster-paintish animal figurines through the 1990s
and into the present, now colored with righteous pigments.
   Today, Tesuque has a flourishing casino and a population of almost a
thousand. But still no pottery tradition.
