When we visited the Pueblo in 1998, we tipped our hat to the past and
bought the little rain god in the front row from Rene Herrera. Yes, potters
still make them occasionally, but when you look at the picture, it’s pretty
clear that that’s not where Tesuque is heading.
   Bea Duran Tioux’sfour micaceous pieces can hold their own against the
fine work being done at Nambé, Ohkay Owinge, Taos and Picuris. The big
jar, especially, has the kind of diginty that truly fine Pueblo pottery
commands regardless of Pueblo or period.
   Manuel Vigil’s work can’t be classified or criticized. If we moved these a
few pages and pretended they were Navajo mud toys from Sweetwater,
they’d fit in quite nicely.
   Ka’Ween’s four pieces show various levels of skill. At her peak, she took
the design for the cream-colored olla in the center straight off a 1750-
vintage Ako Polychrome jar from Acoma as shown on Plate XX of Frank and
Harlow’s Historic Pottery of the Pueblo Indians, 1600–1880. Yet no one
who knew her work at the time would have thought this was by anyone but
her. Other pieces by her were clearly Zuni or clearly Hopi. The wedding
vase in the picture is clearly something, but we’re not sure what and the

little guy with the feathers (they came with the pot) seems more Tesuque
than anything else. The big olla at the top was an early effort, and the
sloppy orange paint on the rim suggests that she had problems back then as
well.
    Terry Tapia accepts poster paint colors as a tradition, and her son
Thomas is moving forward, perhaps ready to emerge as the next important
Tesuque potter. His prayer meal bowl is the first one we’ve seen that has a
meal inside.


ZIA

Bad land plus bad luck equals good pottery. In 1540, Coronado’s men
reported that the village of Zia (say ZEE-yah) was sparkling and
whitewashed and that many of its thousand or more homes were decorated
in bright colors.
     It didn’t take the new administration long to correct that impression of
well-tended gaiety. In 1598, Oñate estimated its population to include
twenty-five hundred soon-to-be-Christians, all in urgent need of a large
mission. Zia’s oppression was early and thorough.
    Zia’s participation in the 1680 Revolt was typical, but the reprisals and
outcome weren’t. In 1688, Domingo Cruzate came up from El Paso in an
unsuccessful effort to recapture New Mexico for the Spanish, but, before he
retreated, he managed to break Zia’s spirit. Cruzate launched a major attack
on Santa Ana and Zia, and three thousand Puebloans chose to make a stand
at Zia. A few days later, six hundred of them were dead, seventy more were
on their way to El Paso as slaves, the remainder of the force fled to the
mountains, and the village itself was torched and destroyed.
   When de Vargas returned in 1693, Zia capitulated quietly, and Zia
warriors helped him in several battles against other Pueblos—a
collaboration that, according to some historians, continues to haunt Zia’s
relationship with its neighbors.

In the 1920s, they played with colors
                        lavender paint on a 6¾" diameter jar, circa 1925

   Today, the mission built after the reconquest still stands, and even if it
isn’t whitewashed and trimmed in bright colors, Zia remains one of the
most attractive Pueblos to approach. But despite the postcard setting, Zia’s
history has been hard for more than three hundred years.

Where next-door Santa Ana had negotiated with the Spanish for land
along the Rio Grande in the eighteenth century, Zia made do with what it
had: lots of acreage and little water. What had been a Pueblo of more than
three thousand people is now a water-poor community of fewer than a
thousand, most of whose residents work away from the Pueblo.
   What Zia has had, however, is pottery. For at least two hundred years,
the balance of trade was food from Santa Ana, Jemez and San Felipe for
pottery from Zia, and pottery remained Zia’s number one homegrown cash
crop.
     If you search, you can find big pottery from almost all the Pueblos, but
if you wanted to find an average-sized pot from each, Zia’s would almost
certainly be the largest. Because of our budgets and limited space, we’ve
confined ourselves pretty much to pieces under a foot in diameter, like the
ones on the next page. But during the years those pieces were made, Zia
potters were regularly producing some of the largest storage jars and dough
bowls made anywhere, sometimes more than two feet in diameter.
   Before World War II, there weren’t a lot of Zia pots that acknowledged
the existence of the curio market, the quirky ashtray in the front row aside.
Everything in the picture is sturdy enough to accommodate any practical
use the buyer had in mind.
    Zia’s language is Keresan, and its pottery shares design characteristics
with other important Keresan pottery, especially Acoma and Laguna ware.
They all have their favorite geometric patterns, stylized birds, rainbows and
flowers, but Acoma pots and Zia pots don’t feel the same.
   Where Acoma and Laguna’s bird is a parrot, Zia’s is a roadrunner, often
startled, sometimes taking off with jets roaring and sometimes skidding to a
stop with the afterburners going full blast. Acoma’s parrot-and-rainbow is
Zia’s roadrunner-and-rainbow. Acoma’s black and orange on stark white is
Zia’s dark brown and brownish red on creamy white, and Acoma’s hard,
paper-thin, white-clay ollas are Zia’s sturdy, granular, basalt-tempered red
clay jars.
   Zia pottery is unique unto itself, and you can spot almost all of it from
twenty feet away.

We do know that traditionally, Zia potters used the same designs over and
over for years. Harlow and Lanmon’s The Pottery of Zia Pueblo devotes a
whole chapter to pieces with a single design, and it’s so classic we started
the book with one on page vii, right after the Table of Contents.
   Two pieces, the canteen from 1940 and the large white olla above it
from fifty years earlier, give us a good look at Zia’s roadrunner, who
appears another eighteen times on the next four pages. That old olla, the
orange one below it, the one at top left and the one on the opposite page
show four different interpretation of the rainbow design that Zia shares with
Acoma. Several pieces have versions of a favorite Zia geometric, what the
books call the capped feather design: the four pieces at lower left and the
one at upper right. Yet with all this tradition and all this repetition, Zia’s

potters have found a remarkable design latitude. As proof, no single piece
on these two pages looks much like any of the others.
   One jar in particular, the one at the far left with the white cloverleaf,
struck us as being really different. We did, however, see a beat-up olla made
in the 1920s attributed to Ascenciona Galvan on page 268 of The Pottery of
Zia Pueblo that has some similarities, and it’s the only thing we’ve ever
seen that’s remotely like it.
   We do know that jar almost certainly came from the 1920 to 1930
period. During those years, some Zia potters abandoned the cream-colored
slip they’d used for a hundred years and switched first to tan and then
briefly to orange, as on the four jars across the middle of the picture. If you
find a Zia jar with an orange background, you can be reasonably certain
that it came from the 1920s.


ZIA – EVOLUTION

At Zia, change took its own sweet time. In most Pueblos, pottery history
shows a slump in the first quarter of the twentieth century, with revival
beginning in the 1920s, gaining momentum until the 1960s, then exploding
in many directions.
    Zia’s pottery history is much more stable. It followed the same pattern
of development, but its peaks and valleys are more like slight lifts and dips.
Odd Halseth made Edgar Hewitt/Kenneth Chapman-type inspirational visits
over several months in 1923, and according to his own account, got more
insults than attention. He visited the nearest trading post and tried to
encourage the trader to promote better, more “traditional” pottery and
evidently accomplished very little, either with the trader or with the Pueblo.
   As the cowboy hat below testifies, Zia potters did eventually discover
the curio market, but never in a big way. Nonetheless, pieces like the silly
ashtray on the previous page were sufficient to frighten Halseth and his
colleagues. However, Zia has always been conservative and has never been
particularly welcoming to outsiders. Its potters had less contact with
mainstream commerce than artists from Pueblos closer to Santa Fe and
Albuquerque.
   Despite Zia’s traditional insularity, a few Zia potters achieved celebrity
relatively early. Although potters almost never signed their work before

1950, Jonathan Batkin, in Pottery of the Pueblos of New Mexico, 1700–
1940, tells of a documented storage jar from 1922 signed by Isabel
Torrebio. (Modern family members usually spell it Toribio, as did Isabel
some years later.) She was a leading potter through the early years of the
twentieth century and remained active into the 1930s.





                             After 1950, Zia began to notice the tourists
                           4½" diameter, circa 1970

   Today, Trinidad Medina is remembered as Zia’s greatest early-century
potter, famous for giant storage jars and dough bowls. She toured the
country between 1930 and 1946, appearing at the Century of Progress
Exhibition in Chicago in 1933 and at the Golden Gate International
Exposition in San Francisco in 1939. When she demonstrated at the big
fairs, she wasn’t about to struggle with giant pieces. She was totally clear
about what her audience expected. In our first edition, we showed a minor
little piece she made for Chicago, but the one on the next page, which we
think she probably made for San Francisco, really tells the story. Of all
things, she made a flowerpot. Not just something that’s shaped like a
flowerpot, but a real one, with the standard flowerpot rim and a hole in the
bottom.

As Trinidad Medina slowed down, others came forward. Most observers
would name Seferina Bell as Zia’s leading potter in the 1950s and 1960s,
and the canteen and olla on the next page support the argument. For the rest
of the century, the mantle passed to Trinidad’s granddaughter-in-law, Sofia
Medina, and Sofia’s family remains preeminent. These pages feature her
and her late daughter Lois, and the next pages show more children and
grandchildren.
   Other names have attracted attention over the years. Pieces by Helen
Gachupin found their way into the collections of the Peabody Museum at
Harvard and the Boston Museum of Fine Arts. Diana Lucero won ten first
awards at Indian Market, was invited to the White House in 1974 and has a
pot in the Smithsonian.
   At Zia, however, rising to prominence is no guarantee of wealth and
fame. None of the number ones over the years—Isabel Toribio, Trinidad
Medina, Seferina Bell or Sofia Medina—ever had the marketing push that
came automatically to the leading potters from San Ildefonso, Santa Clara,
Hopi and Acoma and now extends to potters from Cochiti and recently
active Pueblos like Pojoaque and San Felipe.
   The same names occur over and over on Zia pottery—Pino, Gachupin,
Medina, Toribio. This shouldn’t come as a surprise. The Pueblos with a
strong pottery tradition have that tradition because a few strong families
kept it that way.
   And, at least at Zia, they kept evolution so gradual that, at times, it was
barely perceptible.

By the 1980s, orange slip was gone from Zia’s mainstream, Zia whites were
often pure white, Zia dark browns were almost black or pure black, and Zia
reds were deep and rich.
   But the traditional Zia designs remained largely unchanged, a bit of
geometry, a flower here and there, a red underbody and birds everywhere—
standing, trotting, taking off, landing and skidding to a halt. If the
roadrunner was common on Zia pottery prior to the 1980s, it was
omnipresent afterwards.
   Most of these pots look as though they could have been made by the
same potter. This is art from a genre discipline, not a collection of personal
expressions by a group of far-reaching artists.
   Some artists stretched more than others. Seferina Bell’s sister, Kathy
Pino, managed exceptionally creative and varied designs. She has two
completely different pots on this page and a third, still more different piece
from years later on the next pages.
   Small surprises in the picture include a reclining deer that we think is
by mid-century potter Harvianna Toribio, an odd-shaped bowl by Sofia

Medina’s auntBrijida Toribio, a silly flowerpot by the great Trinidad
Medina, and Lois Medina’s bear. Although we’d never seen anything
remotely like it, we knew at a glance it was Zia. There’s something about the
heft, surface, degree of finish and decorative style of a Zia pot that gives it
away every time. Don’t ask us to explain it. Just hold a few pieces and
you’ll understand.


ZIA – EXPERIMENTATION AND CONTINUATION

Even at Zia, change creeps in. And when change does come, it’s apt to
come within the families that lead the way.
    Sofia Pino married Trinidad Medina’s grandson, Raphael, who studied
art at the Santa Fe Indian School. Back in the 1950s, Sofia encouraged him
to paint. He started with acrylics on paper and got pretty good at it. Ten
years later, grandmother Trinidad got Sofia interested in pottery. Sofia,
according to her account in Fourteen Families, found it emotionally
rewarding. Trinidad, perhaps made a bit less sentimental by age, pointed out
that she could depend on it financially. The lessons took, and by the 1970s,
Sofia Medina was as good as anyone in the Pueblo.
   Also in the 1970s, the inevitable happened. Raphael tried painting on a
few pots. He started with natural pigments, but he’d spent twenty years
painting with acrylics, so he shifted over.
   He wasn’t the first to use acrylics on pottery. Jemez potters had used
acrylics for years, almost entirely on low-end pieces knocked out for
tourists. But as far as we can tell, he was the first established, talented
painter to use acrylics on pottery, and his efforts brought legitimacy to a
practice that made purists shudder. His brother José, also a talented painter,
occasionally did work on pottery much like Raphael’s. According to
Harlow and Lanmon’s The Pottery of Zia Pueblo, their portrayal of
elements of Zia ceremonial life brought criticism from Pueblo elders’ who
felt they were inappropriate to show outside the Pueblo.

At Zia, acrylics started with the Medinas
                         Elizabeth and Marcellus Medina, 3½" high, 1993

   Meanwhile, Sofia rose to the pottery forefront at Zia and kept her
position as queen of Zia pottery until her death in 2010 at 78. In the 1980s,
Raphael’s s son Marcellus carried on in his father’s style. Marcellus married
Elizabeth Toya of Jemez, but Sofia took her under her wing, and before
long Elizabeth and her sister-in-law Lois Medina were making pottery that
looked almost exactly like Sofia’s. Lois died in 2006 at 47, but the look of
Medina pottery continues through the generations. In the first edition, we
showed a slightly bigger and slightly more ambitious 1993 jar-with-turtle
lid by Elizabeth that’s almost identical to the one on the opposite page,
made in 2001 by her daughter Kimberley.
    In addition to making pottery like Sofia, Elizabeth and Marcellus
teamed together as Sofia and Raphael had. In 2006, they were selected to
create the permanent trophy for the New Mexico Bowl football game, a 20"
jar with the image of a running back. Official sanction like that underscores
their current prominence.

If you want a visual feast, stop by the Poeh Museum at Pojoaque and
check out the timeline: a multi-thousand year Pueblo history diorama told
with Roxanne Swentzell sculptures against a backdrop painted by
Marcellus.
   Meanwhile, Ralph Aragon, a San Felipe man who married Raphael’s
cousin Joan and settled in Zia, went in his own personal direction. He does
all the correct Zia things, uses the right clay and temper, stone polishes and
paints with natural pigments. It just doesn’t come out looking like anyone
else’s pottery. Where Marcellus and Raphael Medina painted realistic
figures on traditional white pottery, Ralph Aragon paints traditional
elements in non-traditional arrangements and colors. Where Marcellus’s
and Raphael’s figures look like “Indian Art,” Ralph’s figures look like
“modern art.”
   Beyond acrylics, contemporary Zia pottery experimentation is a short
stretch. The rest of the Medinas, Pinos, Gachupins and Toribios still do
pretty much the same thing. It’s a little crisper, a little different perhaps, but
it’s still pure Zia pottery, as beautifully made and as easy to recognize as
ever.
   You can look at the big pieces on the opposite page and see major
departures from the past, but before you draw any conclusions, take a close
look at most of the pieces across the bottom. There they are: roadrunners,
stepped feathers, foliage and flowers, just like all the pieces on the previous
pages.
   But things keep moving forward. Two side-by-side pieces in the bottom
row tell an eloquent story. They were made by the same potter: a
completely traditional jar from 2010 and a canteen from 2014 that gives a
whole new look to Zia.

acrylics, while the large one on this page uses traditional Zia clay

   Ralph Aragon’s two pieces describe his work: individual, unmistakable
and uncomfortable to purists who can’t accept a Zia pot in anything other
than Zia colors.
   The rest of the pieces show how closely other Zia potters have held to
the established idiom. Although a turkey, an eagle and a couple of
hummingbirds stopped by to check out the plant life, roadrunners still beep
along the roads with smile-provoking cartoony animation. Eusebia Shije’s
struts, Kimberley Medina’s hops, Reyes Pino’s waddles, Louise Negale’s
stops in bewilderment and Kathy Pino’s brakes to a screeching halt.
   Eusebia Shije and Reyes Pino made pieces in untraditional shapes.
Kimberley Medina put a turtle on the lid of her jar, just as her mother did
years before, and Kathy Pino, as she usually did, played with Zia design
elements to create a bird that wanders a bit from the middle of the road. The

key words for all of this are “a bit.” Zia pottery remains Zia pottery, now
and for the foreseeable future.
   But it won’t look exactly the same, Seferina Bell’s daughter, Ruby
Panana, gave us another roadrunner on a jar that looks exactly like what
Zia pottery has looked like for more than a century, then, a bit later, made a
canteen with a hummingbird and raised orange leaves that doesn’t look like
any Zia pot we’ve seen before. Change happens.


ZUNI

It all began here. On the day in 1539 that an annoyed Zuni warrior
despatched Estebán the Moor and sent Fray de Niza scurrying back to
Mexico City with tales of the gold of Cibola, the fate of the Southwest was
sealed. Coronado came, saw and conquered Zuni in less than an hour, and
foreigners have ruled pottery country ever since.
   Zuni tried its own Pueblo revolt in 1632, doing in two resident priests
and fleeing to the hills to avoid retaliation, but a new set of priests coaxed
them back down until the revolt of 1680, when they went back into the hills
along with the rest of the Pueblos. Zuni capitulated quickly during the
reconquest. It had problems even worse than the Spanish. In 1670, Apache
raiders had destroyed the village of Hawikuh, burned the mission and killed
most of the inhabitants. In 1692, the protection of armed Spanish troops
seemed preferable to slaughter by Apaches.
   Today, Highway 53 cuts through a Pueblo that shows no evidence of
age or permanence. But there’s far more to Zuni than you see at first. Walk
around in back of the Turquoise Village Trading Post and wind through a
small track of alleys, and you’ll find yourself face-to-face with Old Zuni.
And if you walk through the little door at the side of the seventeenth-
century mission, you’ll see the most amazing juxtaposition of old and new,
Indian and Spanish, Kachina and Catholic in the whole Southwest. Alex
Seotewa’s Shalako Procession murals surround the walls, right above the
Stations of the Cross in a church restored through a joint effort of church
and tribe.

Stevenson brought this to the Smithsonian; the number tells you how much he collected.
                         5¾" diameter, collected in 1884





   Since early historic times, mainstream Zuni pottery has looked like
Acoma or Laguna at first glance. Researchers now believe that both Zuni
and Acoma made the seventeenth-century Hawikuh polychrome we show
on page 45.
   When you look closely, you see differences. Much Zuni clay is pink
where Acoma’s is white, and the thinnest white Zuni olla can show pink

through a scratch. Zuni black paint is apt to be brown, and since 1880 or so,
Zuni jars have dark brown or black underbodies rather than red. It may
seem like a minor divergence, but the dark bases of the hundreds of jars and
bowls in this book are all red until you get to Zuni.
   When the railroad came in 1879, ethnologists descended on Zuni. James
Stevenson and his wife Matilda Coxe began collecting pottery at a ferocious
rate for the Bureau of Ethnology, later the Smithsonian. Their collections
filled the Bureau’s basements and their findings filled reports that gave the
basis for most later scholarship on historic pottery. At left, you see the back
of the small bowl in the front row. We checked the number, and learned that
the Smithsonian gave it away in 1930.
   1930 is a critical date for Zuni pottery. From then until the 1990s, the
best Zuni artists concentrated on jewelry, and pottery made in that 60-year
gap was nowhere near as good as the earlier work. Fine pre-1930 pieces are
now scarce, highly priced and highly publicized, but even in the great years,
Zuni potters made baskets, jars and odd little ceremonial pieces at every
level of quality. On the opposite page, you’ll see a scattering of older Zuni
pieces of the type that books about historic pottery usually ignore.
   Zuni potters like sculpture and appliqué and water symbols and hunting
symbols. Frogs, tadpoles, owls, heartline deer and dragonflies show up
from time to time on pottery from other Pueblos, but they’re Zuni designs.
The tourist olla at the right of the lower middle row takes care of everyone
by giving us three traditional Zuni design clichés on a single pot: appliquéd
frogs, heartline deer in what’s called the “deer in house” shape and a row of
ducks swimming around its middle.

There are pieces in the picture above that approach the finesse, high polish
and hard finish of the best historic Zuni ware. The best is probably the olla
at top left—apiece that, if it didn’t have an old pitch repair on the other
side, we never would have been able to afford.
   The others vary in quality, ranging from nearly as good (top center and
the one below it) to unashamed, quickly made tourist ware (the small olla at
lower right and the later-than-the-rest frog ashtray in the front).
    Several pieces are worth special attention. The prayer meal basket at
far left is a shape the Zuni made and still make for ceremonies. If it weren’t
for the almost singular attitude Zuni has about ceremonial pieces, it would
be wrong for us to own it. At Zuni, once a piece has been used in a
ceremony, it loses its magic, and it’s perfectly acceptable for the owner to
sell it to whomever he or she pleases.
   The scoop at left front surprised us because of its design: birds sitting
on what appears to be a rug. The two red pieces are from a brief circa 1900
revival of a fourteenth-century white on red style. As near as we can tell,
they first appeared around 1895, disappeared again around 1915 and
haven’t been seen since.

The bowl at front center is notable for two reasons. First, it’s one of only
a handful of pieces we know of that put white and red with polychrome on
the same pot. (The beat-up jar up two rows diagonally suggests the
polychrome style of the day.) Also, the shape of this two-on-one bowl
interests us. Back then, traders encouraged potters to make shapes they
sold as flower pots. Not a good idea, considering what water does to
unglazed pottery.


ZUNI – DECLINE, THEN A COMEBACK AT ZUNI HIGH

All it takes is a couple of good teachers and thirty years of intensive effort.
By the 1950s, Zuni pottery was in a slump. It wasn’t quite as near death as
Mojave pottery was in the 1950s, but the vital signs were fading. You can
see how much of a slump by looking at the pieces in the lower left corner of
the picture opposite. Almost every artist at the Pueblo was in the jewelry
business, and those who weren’t were making things like the figures at
bottom left. They made a lot of these, and they marketed them as “Zuni
Looneys.”
   There had been a few fine potters at Zuni between 1920 and 1950—
Tsayutitsa, the great potter whom Anglo collectors knew as “Mrs. Milam’s
mother” because they couldn’t pronounce her name, and Catalina Zunie, the
great teacher. But they were gone, and only Nellie Bica kept the tradition
alive.
   Then an amazing lady—Daisy Hooee, Nampeyo’s granddaughter, one
of the great Hopi potters, graduate of L’école des Beaux Arts in Paris—
married a Zuni man. She moved to Zuni, taught at Zuni High School, and
became a conscientious and competent Zuni potter and teacher. She never
left Hopi and the Nampeyo discipline design behind, however. She put
white Zuni frogs on a yellow Hopi jar to create the remarkable piece at right
and managed to show everybody how much at home she was in both
idioms.

A teacher with a foot in two Pueblos
                  Daisy Hooee Nampeyo, 1976, 6⅛" diameter excluding frogs

    Later, another accomplished married-in potter, Jennie Laate from
Acoma, took over the pottery classes at Zuni High. She knew the old
designs and taught them to her students.
     It took a while for the results to show. In 1980, John Barry’s American
Indian Pottery told us this: “Through the years, various individuals and
institutions have tried to encourage the Zunis to revive pottery making.
These attempts have not been successful for the reason that there must be
Pueblo support and individuals with an interest in making pottery.... At the
1979 Indian Market, only one potter, Jenny Laate, displayed Zuni pottery.”
   But Jennie Laate’s students kept at it, and others encouraged family
members to turn back to pottery from jewelry. In 1983, Margaret Hardin
and the Heard Museum worked with Zuni to put together a show that
rekindled interest in the art. In 1985, Josephine Nahohai received a
fellowship from the School of American Research to teach Zuni women

traditional pottery. Quanita Kalestewa got tired of breathing the dust from
grinding shells, and when the price of silver went up, quit jewelrymaking
for pottery. In 1986, James Ostler wrote in Zuni Pottery about what
happened when the Zuni Tribal Arts & Crafts Enterprise sent six potters to
the Smithsonian. “I had thought that the results of seeing historic pottery by
the Zuni potters would be diffused and slow in taking effect: in fact, they
were almost immediate. No less than a month after the museum visit, I was
seeing pots of different shapes and designs.”
    In the 1990s, Zuni High continued. Daisy Hooee and Jennie Laate were
gone, but Noreen Simplicio and Gabriel Paloma continued the teaching.
There were strong Zuni pottery families: the Nahohais, the Kalestewas and
the Peynetsas foremost among them. And there were pieces coming out of
Zuni that no one had made for more than half a century. There were
beautifully finished rainbird and deer-in-house ollas, the kind whose
nineteenth-century versions can bring five figures at today’s auctions. There
were prayer meal baskets and turquoise-covered fetish jars.
   Perhaps more important, there were fanciful new extensions of the art
that made everyone take notice. Today’s Zuni potters aren’t merely re-
creating the old, they’re building a new, strange and wonderful pottery
tradition, and the next four pages give you a taste of it. Carlos Laate
symbolizes the continuum. He didn’t learn from Jennie, he learned by
watching his step-grandmother Daisy, and his owl at the right is up to the
minute.

ZUNI – FUN WITH THE PEYNETSAS

Jennie Laate's legacy: a great pottery family. The picture on the right
shows an array of important work by four family members: Anderson
Peynetsa, his sisters Priscilla and Agnes and his wife, Avelia. A fifth
member, nephew Scott, made the prayer meal bowl on the opposite page
and a sixth, brother-in-law Darrell Westika, made the honking bird on page
202. The important thing about this array is that it all started with Jennie
Laate and Zuni High, not from learning through the family.
   When you stop to think about it, this is unusual. In Zuni Pottery, Jennie
Laate commented that she didn’t know why so few of her students kept up
with the craft. The answer, of course, is that it’s easier not to. It’s a sad fact
that in all the arts, everywhere in the world, a high percentage of talented
young people drop out and do other things with their lives, and most of the
students in Jennie Laate’s classes at Zuni High were no exception.
   Anderson Peynetsa was the exception. He started making pottery in the
eighth grade under Jennie’s wing, kept at it and never stopped, building a
body of work that by the mid-1990s had put him at the forefront of Zuni
pottery. His long suit, early on, was sculpture and appliqué. On his site, he
says that he and his wife Avelia “enjoy making large pots, and also make
ducks, canteens, owls and lizard pots.”

It began with Jennie Laate’s lessons
                                 Priscilla Peynetsa, 6½" diameter, 1990

    (Footnote: Owls like the ones on the previous pages are a Zuni
necessity. Speaking in the 1990s, Zuni potter Milford Nahohai offered an
elegant inter-tribal needle when he explained that “the reason everybody at
Zuni has an owl in the window is to scare away the Navajos.” To the
Navajo, the owl is a symbol of death, and that belief isn’t lost on the Zuni,
who, during those long mid-century jewelry-only years had perhaps a bit
more contact with the Navajo than they’d have preferred.)
    In the beginning, Priscilla Peynetsa’s career path was more typical. She
took the pottery classes in high school but wasn’t particularly interested.
After an accident, she went back to night school and took the classes in
earnest. That began a ten-year career that placed her right next to Anderson
in importance. In an ironic twist, a career that began with an accident was
altered by one. In early 1995, Priscilla lost an arm in a car crash, and

although she still could decorate pottery, she’ll probably never be able to
shape a pot again.
   Agnes came next. At first she worked with Anderson and has worked
with Berdel Soseeah since Anderson married Avelia, whose name often
appears mistakenly as “Aurelia.” There are a lot of pots signed “A. A.
Peynesa.” The older ones are Anderson and Agnes, the later ones are by
Anderson and Avelia. Avelia, by the way does have a family pottery
heritage. She’s a direct descendant of the great teacher of the 1920s,
Catalina Zunie. Then in 2012, we found the newest member, nephew Scott.
   At Zuni High, potters learn about greenware, commercial paints and the
kiln, and many stay in that world. The Peynetsas dig their own clay and
make their own paints, but like most Acoma and Zuni potters, they use the
electric kiln.
    In 1995, Noreen Simplicio defended the kiln in Milford Nahohai’s and
Elisa Phelps’s Dialogues with Zuni Potters: “Over at Indian Market, when
you try to enter your work, they’ll downgrade it because it’s fired in a kiln. I
think it’s good that they have that for people who are totally traditional, but
they should have room for people that, like myself, are both traditional and
contemporary.” The rules have changed since then. Now kiln-firing and
multiple firings are okay if they’re stated at submittal.
    Traditional and contemporary describes the Peynetsas perfectly. All
Peynetsa work is excellent: excellently decorated, excellently sculpted,
often with a quiet sense of humor, never with an inflated sense of
importance. Where else can you see museum-quality pieces alongside a
refrigerator magnet, all done with the same loving care?

Anderson Peynetsa loves sculpture, and you can appreciate it in the way his
lizards and frogs clamber about his pieces. Agnes shares his affinity, as the
birds at the left and right of the bottom row attest. (After much deliberation,
John decided the one at the left is a loon—a genuine Zuni loon, worthy of
full respect, unlike the Zuni Looney figurines on the previous page.)
   However, if you’re looking for loony, check out Anderson and Avelia’s
giant bird in the back. And then turn a few more pages to our collection of
Implausible Beasts on page 202. You’ll see an effigy by Priscilla’s husband
Darrell Westika that defies description. Al is convinced that if you pinch its
beak hard enough, it’ll honk out of the horn on the top of its head. We were
told it was inspired by a book on pre-Columbian art, and looking at the
pieces on the next pages, we think that book must have circulated through
the Zuni art community.
   Others in the picture have a more controlled looniness. Consider
Priscilla Peynetsa’s cloud-blower pipe and turtle with the distracted stare
and a traditional rosette on its shell, the ferocious avanyu handle on
nephew Scott’s prayer meal basket and Agnes’s odd bird bowl with a
tadpole and lizard cargo—all far off the center of the traditional path.

Sometimes, the looniness is absent altogether, as on Anderson’s
carefully re-created rainbird jar at the right and on his two heartline deer
jars, one with a modernized deer-in-house and rosette design. There’s
almost no modernization on Priscilla’s painstakingly correct deer-in-house
jar on the opposite page. Or, for that matter, on her just-as-correct
refrigerator magnet.


ZUNI – AND EVER MORE FUN

Now, Zuni pottery is on a roll. If you look carefully at the preceding pages,
you see an art that was pretty well frozen in place for more than a century. It
flourished through the latter days of the nineteenth century until 1930, then
went into a decline for the next fifty years. If you look at one of those hard-
to-find better pieces from 1980, the connections with pieces made a
hundred years before are obvious.
   Then, sometime around 1990, give or take a few years, the explosion
came. Its aftereffects were so powerful that, if you look at the pieces on the
opposite page, it’s almost impossible to see any connection with the pieces
five pages earlier.
     It wasn’t just the Peynetsas who detonated the blast. Had we singled
them out, we could have compiled an array from the Nahohai family as
impressive as the one we’ve shown on the previous two pages from the
Peynetsas. Mother Josephine made pottery the old way, like the small
traditional rainbird jar on page 193, and kept the skills alive in the family.
Son Randy led the parade, daughter-in-law Rowena Him followed close
behind, brother Milford worked with mother and wrote and lectured about
the art, and by the early 1990s Randy and Rowena had already become
recognized as leading Zuni potters.
   Staying on top is no easy task, and others followed right behind. By
1990, Noreen Simplicio had taken over the classes at Zuni High, and it
wasn’t much later that her almost implausibly detailed appliqués got frill
attention. Her work quickly separated her from the pack, and by the early
2000s, she was clearly an important potter. In 2010, we saw her featured
alongside Caroline Carpio of Isleta in one of the most prestigious shops on
Canyon Road during Indian Market month.

By the late 1990s, we started seeing work in the fine galleries by
Deldrick and Lorenda Cellicon. They made large pieces that came out of
the same general creative movement that drove the Peynetsas and the
Nahohais. The Cellicons work with natural pigments, but, like Noreen
Simplicio and most other Zuni artists in the movement, they qualify as
artists who are “both traditional and contemporary.”
  Tammy Bellson found a special niche with small, highly polished
redware combined with appliquéd creatures like the ones that crawl all over
pieces by Noreen Simplicio, the Cellicons and the Peynetsas.
   Angelina Medina, who has Zia and Acoma in her ancestry as well, took
the appliqué idea to its outer limits. We’ll never stop smiling at the droll
bathtub-surprise bowl at bottom center.
   Marcus Homer took another direction with his canteen at right center, as
evocative of Eric Lewis’s work at Acoma as it is of anything that ever came
out of Zuni. Others, like Travis Penketewa and Tony Lorenzo pushed the
boundaries.
    Together, they’ve created a newly defined dominant Zuni pottery style.
But at Zuni, there’s room for more than one style.





                            And then, another direction
                       “Spring Equinox,” Alan Lasiloo, 7½" long, 2012

The bowl in the picture at the right is by Alan Lasiloo. Beginning about
2005, he started making pieces like no one else makes anywhere. He begins
with a white clay that other potters only use for slip and forms it into
graceful, highly polished no-two-alike sculptural shapes. Then, before he
fires them, he paints them with lard. During firing, the lard creates softly
varying color changes that give his pieces a surface look that’s unlike
anything we’ve ever seen in all of Southwestern pottery.
   These white pieces (there’s one at the beginning of the book on the
Table of Contents page) aren’t Alan’s only surprises. He does boldly
painted pieces like the bird jar at lower left, and doesn’t stop there. We ran
across the heavy pink micaceous jar at top left on the opposite page at an
auction. It may only have been an early experiment, but with Alan Lasiloo,
you never know what’s coming next.
   These days, we suppose you could say the same for Zuni as a whole.

This picture shows how far afield Zuni pottery has strayed from the
traditional model. If you turn back to the picture on page 191, you can see
what, for more than a hundred years, the world thought Zuni pottery looks
like.
    Students of traditional pottery who haven’t paid attention to the present
could look at this picture and not have a clue that these were all Zuni, or for
that matter, even Southwestern.
     It’s not that the connections are lost. If you look around the picture, you
can see a redesigned rosette, a couple of deer in their houses and a couple
of prayer meal bowls, one with dragonflies and another with tadpoles and
(forgive us, tradition) a blue heartline dog. But on most of the pieces, the
differences are much more apparent than the connections, recognizable as
Zuni mainly because we know that the artist is Zuni and that’s what that
artist does.
   Like many artists, Marcus Homer made more traditional pieces for
years, but the canteen in the picture shows how far he’s moved past the old
conventions. Angelina Medina, with her mixed Pueblo heritage, has mostly

made Acoma pottery, but when we met her at Indian Market in 1998, she
assured us that her strange and wonderful bowl was a Zuni piece.
   Noreen Simplicio, Randy Nahohai, Tammy Bellson and the Cellicons all
have easily recognizable personal styles.
   We suppose the same could be said of Alan Lasiloo, at least to the point
where, if it’s big, simple and doesn’t look like anything anyone ever made
anywhere eke, it’s probably his. Whether his constant envelope-pushing will
lead to yet another tradition remains to be seen.


THE OTHERS

In this many pages, we should have been able to cover it all. We didn’t. In
traveling through the alphabet from Acoma to Zuni, we stopped in twenty-
six different places where Indians make pottery. Each place has, or had, its
own style, its own traditions and its own recognizable pottery. So do others.
   Most Cherokee live across the New Mexico border in Oklahoma and
draw on two pottery traditions: their Carolina ancestors’ Woodlands
brownware., as on Jane Osti’s elaborate platter, and on Oklahoma
prehistory. Roberta Wallace wrote “Spiro Mounds” on the bottom of her
fish jar, an acknowledgement of that thousand-year-old east-Oklahoma site
as her design inspiration.
   West and a bit north of Taos, the Jicarilla Apache make micaceous ware
much like their Taos neighbors make, and they make it just about as well.
Tammie Allen, Sheldon Nunez-Velarde, Emanuel Vigil and others keep the
art alive.
  Down by El Paso, the 182 prisoners of war who left the scene of the
Pueblo Revolt and founded Ysleta del Sur in 1681 didn’t make much
pottery. But when Indian art came back in style in the 1970s, there was a
brief revival down south. It was all uninspiring cast pottery, and when we
went there in the 1990s, we thought Ysleta del Sur pottery was history.

And to round out the selection, an Anglo
                        Michael Peter Hawley, 18¼" diameter, 1987

   Not so. In 2013, we found pieces by Colt Dunbar and learned that he
studied with Clarence Cruz at Ohkay Owinge. (He signs his pieces with a
high-flown J. Colt Dunbar, but when you ask around, everybody calls him
Jerry Dunbar.) His website tells us “All pottery pieces are handmade,
formed and painted using only traditionally made clay and natural mineral
pigments. No commercially made clay or paints are used. No molds or
pottery wheel used. All pieces are traditionally fired outside.” We’ve now
seen several pieces, and he’s a talent to watch.
   The Yaqui, whose main population is across the border in northern
Mexico, overlap into southwestern Arizona. At least one potter made
exceptionally fine eggshell-thin blackware. It was hardly a tradition. The
cup in the middle row just looks like basic Mexican tourist pottery.
   There are top-level potters from other parts of the country who fit under
the Southwestern pottery umbrella by association. Pahponee is
Kickapoo/Potawatomie, which places her in the Great Lakes region, but her
work has been in the fine Southwestern galleries for a couple of decades.
The person who sold us the piece in the picture bought it from her at a

prestigious IACA show in Mesa, Arizona. Pahponee called it “Pink Rose.”
Jacquie Stevens, a Winnebago, and Glen Nipshank, a Bigstone Cree, both
studied at the Institute of American Indian Art in Santa Fe, both have lived
there for years, and during those years, both have been winning awards at
Indian Market.
   There are individual potters who don’t fit in anywhere. Dalawepi (Ergil
Vallo) made easily recognizable fine carved blackware decorated with non-
traditional colors, and we’ve seen his work sold as Santa Clara. Vallo
himself was Acoma/Hopi, and his disassociated pottery places him here
with The Others.
  We felt the book wouldn’t be complete if we didn’t acknowledge one
Anglo. Michael Peter Hawley (1948–2012) was an unforgettable
Southwestern character: landowner, amateur archeologist and entrepreneur
who built a roadside-attraction museum replete with giant dinosaurs on I-40
and drove a white convertible with steer horns on the hood. Mike ran afoul
of the authorities every so often, but between pecadillos, he was a brilliant
potter whose work appeared in major exhibitions in the finest galleries. He
crafted huge, painstakingly authentic re-creations of sixteenth-century Hopi
Sikyatki polychromes so correctly that Hopi potters came to him for lessons
in traditional firing. If you see a major Hopi/Sikyatki-looking piece that’s
far too good to be true, and it’s signed “Chakoptewa,” that’s Mike.

Some of the artists on these pages warrant special attention. Jane Osti, who
made the wonderful incised brownware platter that dominates the top half
of the picture, was named a Cherokee National Treasure in 2005, and she’s
the only one of those who’s still alive. Her fellow Cherokee, Roberta
Wallace, uses local Oklahoma clays and has been recognized as a major
artist for decades.
   Pahponee, the Kickapoo/Potawatomi, has an even greater nationwide
reputation. The U.S. Department of Interior’s Indian Craft Shop in
Washington DC tells us that “today, Pahponee is one of the top Native
American potters, with awards from juried shows.” The same could be said
for Bigstone Cree Glen Nipshank and Winnebago Jacquie Stevens, who was
kind enough to include a translation sheet for the names on her animal-
tracks olla: huntl=bear, ho=fish, tca=deer and so forth.
     If Jicarilla Apache ware keeps improving, we’ll have to apologize for
not giving it its own pages in this book. Tammie Allen’s cousin Felipe
worked to revive the art among the Jicarillas, and Sheldon Nunez-Velarde
really impressed us with the exuberant horse on his blackware jar.

Yaqui pottery seems to have disappeared with even less trace than
Mojave ware, and, until Jerry Dunbar came along, we thought the same
fate had befallen Ysleta del Sur.
   And there will always be mysteries, like Pecos Rose and her giant,
Medina-like greenware jar. Navajo? Pueblo? Non-Indian? Who knows? We
still have a lot to learn.

COLLECTIONS

KITSCH, PRE





Little collections make perfect sense, too. This book happened because
four collectors got together and tried to buy one of everything. As we
searched, each of us found separate side interests that led to little
collections.
  We recommend little collections, six or nine pieces or so. It can get out
of hand. Early on, Carol tried to buy every little pottery moccasin in the
world, and through the book, you’ll see some of the hundred or so she
found.

Carol’s weakness

   One collection we all agreed on is tourist kitsch, the more outrageous
the better. They started making it early, and if you look for early pieces like
the pre-World War II ones on this page you’ll find surprises everywhere,
like a two-handled Maricopa jar with an Indian chief that might have been
copied off a Wild West Show poster or a penny, but with no resemblance to
any Indian that lived within five hundred miles of Maricopa. Or an old Hopi
pot that has every cliché “Indian” design motif, almost none of which ever
appear on traditional Hopi pottery, and a two-headed Acoma pitcher that we
decided was a Turducken. At right center, there’s a strange Zuni five-pot
thing that we’re convinced got made because traders told them to make
weird things so that tourists would accept them as authentic.
   They also made shapes they knew tourists would understand, like the
Mojave teapot or the Maricopa bedside carafe and cup. Sometimes they
were serious pottery, like the cup and saucer by Juanita and Wo-Peen
Gonzales of San Ildefonso or the horno/ashtray complete with cigarette
burn by Seven Families matriarch Lela Gutierrez.
   However, if this is your collection, you won’t find all that much to get
serious about.

A collection like the one one opposite, only newer. We know that collectors
with delicate artistic sensibilities turn their noses up at pieces like these. It’s
also not hard to imagine a collector a hundred years ago looking at the
Maricopa Indian chief or the Hopi war drum with equal distaste.
   The Zia horno and the Kewa canoe are mild examples made by serious
potters, but the Acoma Mickey Mouse and the Jemez wedding vase with the
imprisoned bridal couple get a lot closer to the taste level we’re really
looking for. Where it really gets flagrant is with things like the blue shoe
from Acoma, the big green Navajo jar with the pictures of Monument
Valley and the litde blue wedding vase with the end-of-the-trail Indian. The
two refrigerator magnets—the shoe from Acoma and the wedding vase
from Isleta—drop even further down the kitsch ladder. The Navajo piled
basket thing is in a whole other category. The best explanation Carol could
come up with was to call it a “paper clip holder.”
   At the bottom rung, we have the turquoise-covered wedding vase that
an observer thought looked like something found on the back shelf in the
chicken coop and the most unspeakable of all, the night light to the left of it
that brings to mind a line from a souvenir postcard: “These Indians are
Taiwans. It says so right on their pottery.”
     If we had to pick a favorite, we’d vote for this beautiful Santa Clara
bowl that Fidel and Tonita Naranjo made in 1992. It has NEW • MEXICO
deeply and fastidiously carved around its perimeter. Al’s sons are currently
fighting over who gets it in his will

New Mexico

IMPLAUSIBLE BEASTS





This collection took a few years to build. Pretty much everybody makes
animal figurines, and most of them look pretty much like the animals they
represent.
   But not all of them, and not all the time. Here, the beasts take a new
tangent, and there’s nothing new about the effort. The snake on the
thousand-year-old Hohokam censer has the head of a horned toad. Zuni’s
nineteenth-century bird at left has four legs and no wings, while Cochiti’s

bird has ears and no legs. These bizarre beasts persist to the present. Cochiti
offers a sweet-looking horse/dinosaur and a horned what-is-it. Maricopa
gave us a strange humanoid. Santa Clara contributed a technicolor sort of
bear/gopher. From Acoma, we have the ferocious avanyu water serpent,
removed from his place on a jar, tamed and put to work carrying mom, pop,
the kids and a dog named Beer Can. From Lisa Holt and Harlan Reano, we
have a beast that would terrify a Komodo dragon.
   And from Zuni, we found perhaps the most implausible of all. Darrell
Westika’s bird, snarling from his toothed beak while howling to the moon
from the other side of his head.
   Not all of these creatures are figurines. They appear painted on pots as
well. We’re still trying to figure out the aerodynamics of the bird on the
nineteenth-century pitcher to the right.





                     A bird biplane, from Zuni about 1880

MINUTIA

This collection doesn’t take a lot of space. Some potters in the Southwest
have made a career out of creating tiny things, some so tiny they’re almost
beyond belief.
    In this picture, we have replicas of a prehistoric pitcher and three
historic ollas along with a contemporary one, a contemporary wedding
vase, a standing bear, two pigs and a cup that the bear just might be able to
pick up. Then, just so you’d appreciate how small they all are, we put a
penny in the middle.
   There are pieces here by Pam Lujan Hauer of Taos, Agnes Peynetsa and
Tammy Bellson of Zuni, Geri Naranjo of Santa Clara, and two potters
whose reputations are solely based on these tiny efforts. Thomas Natseway
of Laguna made the replicas, and for twenty years, no one has done them
better. His wife, Charmae Shields Natseway does equally important work,
but it’s a lot bigger.
   For us, the winning potter is Judy Shields of Acoma, another of Dolores
Sanchez’s granddaughters, who made the four-passenger storyteller. In the
first edition, we called her three-eighths inch long pig the ultimate in
miniaturization. Then Judy introduced us to Mrs. Pig—only a quarter of an
inch long, yet decorated in black and red, able to bat her flirtatious eyes and
tease us with her long eyelashes.

ZUNI CANDLESTICKS

This collection was too easy. It’s not that these are particularly common.
It’s just that a collection like this should be laboriously gathered, and
someone else did most of the work. We got seven of these from a single
auction lot and added a couple we already had.
   Harlow and Lanmon’s exhaustive The Pottery of Zuni Pueblo suggests
they made these at Zuni around 1920. We think they probably exist because
a trader like Tobe Turpen in Gallup or Andrew Vanderwagen down the road
told artists that these were easy to sell.
   They were usually square, almost always had a handle on the column,
and the handle was often shaped like an animal. Here we three dogs and
what might be a mountain lion on the tall one in the middle. We also have
three frogs. One came headless and is now back to health. Decapitation was
a common ailment among the frogs that the Zunis often applied to the sides
of their jars, and the one on the candlestick second from right suffered from
it.
   We’re pretty sure that several artists made these during those years, but
the pair at rear right center look that they were made by the same person,
probably on the same day, and the same is probably true of the frog pair.

TABLE LAMPS

This collection, we can’t recommend. After World War II, people got
interested in making lamps out of found objects, and Southwestern jars
seemed like excellent candidates. We’ve found a few that were soullessly
drilled right through the artist’s signature.
     It didn’t take long for dealers to notice and to suggest that artists make
lamp bases as well as jars. During the 1950s, quite a few potters made
pieces with designed-in cord openings and holes in the top to accommodate
the hardware. All of the pieces in the picture above date from those years,
all were made to be table lamps, and some were by important artists: Lena
Charlie of Hopi, Agapita and Camilio Tafoya of Santa Clara, Monica Silva
of Kewa and Maria’s sister Desideria from San Ildefonso. There’s one by
Sadie Adams of Hopi on page 75. Lately, Thomas Tenorio of Kewa has
made some again.
     It’s probably not a good idea to start a lamp collection. They take a lot
of space, and after you have a couple, where do you put the others? We got
these because back in the 1980s, Carol Hayes learned how to restore
antique lighting.

Some of these might not have started out as lamps

   She saw that dealers considered these hard to sell if they weren’t
completed as lamps and even harder to sell if they had cheesy hardware,
fraying cords and no shades. It was a golden opportunity, and she fixed
these up.

SINGING FROGS

This collection just happened. We realized that we suddenly had a lot of
mostly Maricopa and Cochiti frogs, and they all sat there with their mouths
open. Then we found a big Tohono O’odham frog in the same style that
Mabel Sunn and her daughters made at Maricopa, and it occurred to us that
he’d make an excellent choirmaster for the chorus.
   However, when we put the group together, we realized he was less than
pleased with the result. Nevertheless, this is his group, and he’ll have to
deal with its lack of discipline. One of his singers is eating and another is
humming with his mouth shut. That particular one might be distracted
because he really has a different job. Antiques dealer Carol Hayes looked at
the one second from left in the back and realized he actually should be
serving as a Victorian ladies’ companion. Pack his back with cotton, cover
it with a bit of velvet, and he’s a true relic of the past: a pincushion.
   Meanwhile, years after we started collecting, we found a special
Maricopa one from the 1920s. The wealthy landowner to the right is the
most interesting frog we’ve seen so far. He has his own pond, complete
with waves and fish.

This one came with a pond

ISLETA BIRDS





This collection, we could never duplicate. It could be the most special
collection in this book, and it seemed like just the right way to end this last
little section.
     It’s not that these little birds are all that rare. Between 1900 or so and
1920, they made hundreds of these at Isleta, many as nearly useless coin
banks, and almost all flew to the Albuquerque railroad station. From there,
they nested in tourist suitcases and rode the trains all across America—

pocket-sized souvenirs for the kids or feel-good tokens for the kids back
home who didn’t get to go.
   So we can’t claim that gathering these birds was any special feat of
collecting. What’s special is the little bowl in the middle of the picture. It
was made at Isleta around 1910, right in the middle of the time when they
were making the birds, and the inhabitants of this aviary couldn’t have a
more appropriate companion.
   Years ago, someone stuck that bowl out on a porch, and real birds
discovered it. When we saw it at a show, the dealer had the good sense to
have one of these Isleta birds sitting in it, and there was no point in further
discussion. Both had to come home with us.





                        The nest, as created by the birds of Isleta

     It completed our Isleta bird collection and gave us the opportunity to
end the book with a final wonder: a genuine Isleta bird’s nest.

MUSEUMS AND BIBLIOGRAPHY


Museum Collections
The collections of Southwestern pottery in many of America’s museums
aren’t all on open display. So when we say any given museum has a pottery
collection worth checking out, it doesn’t mean you’ll be able to see it just
by walking in and looking. But if you’re seriously interested, ask about an
appointment for a collection tour. Also, when museums assemble pottery
exhibits, they may travel. Watch the museums and universities in your area.
The museums in this list all have significant Southwestern pottery
collections.

AFTERTHOUGHT





                              Al’s first. Acoma, Evelyn Garcia, 3" high, 1989





                        John’s first. Hopi, Lunas Navasie,  3" high, 1991

Looking back, several things occurred to us. In 1996, at the end of the first
edition, we wrote that we were rather stunned by what had happened.

When we started, we didn’t really believe that our benighted quest to
cover the subject from A to Z—from Anasazi and Acoma to Zia and Zuni—
could come close to the mark. Or that people who had devoted their lives to
the study of the subject could have taken two amateurs seriously enough to
help with the project.
   But perhaps our green enthusiasm was our strong point. A lot of those
serious students of the field helped us far more than we ever hoped they
would, and many set things aside for us and sold them to us for less than
they should have.
  We came to realize that, in an upside-down way, we had excellent
credentials for writing the book in 1996. We were authentic beginners, and
as such, we had a pretty good idea of what beginners needed to know. That
might help explain the astonishing going-on-twenty-year longevity of this
book.
   Maybe it really began with where we made our first purchases.
    In 1989, on their first-ever visit to the Southwest, Al and Carol went to
Sky City, the ancient Acoma mesa, and bought a souvenir: the greenware
puppy on the left.
   Two years later, on their third Southwest vacation, Al and Carol talked
John and Brenda into joining them. We all went to another ancient
settlement, Walpi on Hopi’s First Mesa, and John bought his first souvenir.
   Had we bought our first pieces from a helpful dealer in a nice store
somewhere, we might not have felt the connection with antiquity so acutely.
  We learned in school that the history of our nation begins with the
Pilgrims barely four hundred years ago, but those trips taught us otherwise.
Each of us drove a thousand miles across the country and bought an
example of a two-thousand-year-old art from an artist in a thousand-year-
old village.
   That art became so important to us that we devoted a large portion of
our lives to it over the next two decades.
   What happened to us, and why we fell into this so easily, underscores
one of the main propositions of the book: that this pottery is not only one of
the world’s important art forms, it’s also one of the most accessible—so
accessible that in just four years, our spare-time hobby turned into a
collection that described more than fifteen hundred years of development.
  Now it’s 2015. That collection grew threefold, and many of the new
pieces we added were ones we only wished we could find when we wrote

the original edition. This new version of the book tells the same story, but
with fewer gaps and half-again as many pieces.
   What we said in 1996 is every bit as true today. Southwestern pottery is
a national treasure, but it’s not locked up in a vault. It’s there for anyone to
touch, hold and collect.

                                                AL, CAROL & JOHN
                                                     January 2015
